comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee structure because of its potential impact on regional universities, smaller institutions, and specialized graduate programs.

International students contribute significantly to the academic and financial sustainability of many American universities. These institutions often operate with limited budgets and depend on their ability to attract students from diverse international backgrounds.

Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations could create substantial financial and administrative challenges. Universities may respond by restricting access to practical training or reconsidering international student enrollment.

The proposal could particularly disadvantage smaller universities that lack the financial resources available to larger institutions.

I respectfully request that DHS conduct a comprehensive assessment of the effects on regional universities, graduate enrollment, institutional budgets, and local economies.

A fee structure that places extraordinary financial pressure on educational institutions risks weakening the accessibility and international competitiveness of American higher education.

I urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the fees due to their negative impact on regional universities and requests withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee requirements because they risk undermining America's long-term national interests, technological leadership, and global competitiveness. The United States has maintained its leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductor technology, biotechnology, and advanced engineering partly through its ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent from around the world. According to the National Science Foundation's Science and Engineering Indicators 2026, international students holding temporary visas earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctoral degrees in 2024, including 61% in computer and information sciences and 54% in engineering. These figures demonstrate the importance of international talent to America's scientific and technological ecosystem. Imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT could discourage highly qualified graduates from contributing their expertise to American universities, research institutions, and businesses. Instead, these individuals may pursue opportunities in competing economies, allowing other nations to benefit from talent educated and trained in the United States. At a time when technological innovation is closely connected to economic strength and national security, creating unnecessary barriers to retaining skilled talent could weaken America's strategic advantages. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, imposing exceptionally high fees on legitimate participants does not directly address misconduct. Targeted enforcement, stronger verification, and risk-based oversight would address program integrity without creating the same barriers to lawful participation. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and pursue alternatives that safeguard both immigration integrity and America's long-term national interests.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the OPT fee requirements because they undermine U.S. technological leadership.

comments.title: MM15 Comment Submitted by Inchul Cho
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Inchul Choinchul.cho@masm.eduNew York, New York 10029
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee hikes as unreasonable, harmful to workers, and damaging to U.S. higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a physician practicing in Texas, and I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

Working in healthcare has taught me that the quality of patient care depends on far more than physicians alone. Hospitals and clinics rely on laboratory scientists, medical researchers, biomedical engineers, health data analysts, and many other trained professionals. Their work is often less visible to patients, but it is essential to keeping healthcare systems functioning safely and efficiently.

Many of these professionals receive their education at American universities, including international students pursuing degrees in biomedical sciences, public health, biotechnology, and related fields.

OPT provides an important opportunity for these graduates to apply their academic knowledge in real healthcare and research environments. A student who has spent years studying laboratory techniques or medical data analysis still needs supervised professional experience to understand how that knowledge translates into actual clinical workflows, quality control procedures, and patient safety requirements.

I am particularly concerned about how the proposed fees could affect smaller hospitals, medical laboratories, and research institutions in Texas.

Not every healthcare organization has the resources of a major academic medical center. Smaller institutions already face challenges recruiting specialized personnel, particularly in communities where the available workforce is limited.

Although the proposed fees would be imposed on educational institutions, the consequences could extend well beyond university campuses. If schools become unable or unwilling to support OPT applications because of these costs, healthcare employers may lose access to qualified graduates who have already received their education in the United States.

This does not necessarily mean those positions would be filled by American workers. Some specialized positions may remain vacant, increasing workloads for existing employees or delaying important laboratory and research activities.

I also question whether such substantial fees are an effective way to prevent immigration fraud.

A $70,000 payment does not demonstrate that a graduate is properly trained, that an employer is legitimate, or that an individual is complying with immigration requirements. These matters should be evaluated through appropriate verification and oversight.

I support protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, those objectives should be pursued through measures that directly address documented violations rather than financial barriers that may affect legitimate educational and professional training.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and consider targeted compliance measures instead.

Healthcare depends on a reliable pipeline of qualified professionals. Policies affecting that pipeline should be evaluated carefully, including their potential consequences for medical research, workforce availability, and the communities that depend on these services.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses concerns that the proposed OPT fees will harm healthcare and research institutions.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. As an international graduate currently working in the United States, I find this proposal deeply concerning. Like many international students, I have invested significant time, money, and effort into pursuing an education and building a professional future here. OPT provides an important opportunity to apply what we have learned, gain meaningful work experience, and contribute to the U.S. economy.
The proposed fees would introduce tremendous uncertainty for students who have followed immigration rules, secured legitimate employment, and planned their futures around existing policies. It is especially unfair to those who are already studying or working in the United States and have made major life decisions based on the current system.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and consider fairer alternatives. The United States should continue to attract and retain international talent, rather than make it increasingly difficult for qualified graduates to contribute to the country where they have chosen to study and work.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Troy Anderson
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,As an American citizen and a biomedical scientist, this policy would be disastrous to not only domestic research, but also to American-born researchers. Our research programs are the best in the world, allowing us to attract the most talented scientists from across the globe. Foreign scientists enter the pipeline and most commonly stay to start their own labs, which in turn train American citizens in science from undergraduate to postdoctoral training. Among these scientists, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make American science great across fields, from energy to medicine. This proposed increase in OPT fees for both initial and renewed F-1s will not only make American science less competitive with other countries, but also prevent our future American scientists from being trained by the best and brightest across the globe. We stand to fall behind other countries, whose collaboration and ability to poach other countries’ scholars allows them to do impactful work. Proposed Increased fees will only mean that more funding for research will be put towards administrative fees than funding life-saving research, wasting taxpayer dollars and slowing medical breakthroughs. Further, non-citizens hired through the F-1 process contribute significantly to a tax pool that they cannot draw from, alleviating the tax burden on American citizens to fund infrastructure, education, and strengthen our country. By increasing the fees for foreign scholars to work in our country, we stand to lose. We lose trained American scientists, a boost to the economy, and first access to the best technology in the world all while some of the best scientists in the world stay in their home countries rather than moving to the United States. For the sake of the health of the American people and the exceptional science in this country, please rescind this rule. Troy Andersontcanderson97@gmail.comNew York, New York 10029
comments.reason: The commenter argues the policy would be disastrous to research and makes American science less competitive.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I serve as a Director of a STEM university Career Center.  Our university has historically had, over the past couple of decades, some of the highest numbers of international students as a percentage of the overall student population.  I want to make a couple of points as it pertains to this proposed rule.

1) I've worked with hundreds of employers who are seeking talented engineers and scientists of all stripes.  I can count on one hand the number of employers who prefer to hire international/f-1 talent.  Almost all recognize the red tape that already exists to limit opportunities for F-1 students in this country, so they ask to connect with domestic students first.  Companies have by and large only interviewed/hired our F-1 student talent when they have failed to find the talent they need in our domestic student pool.  This is a supply-side problem (ie not enough domestic talent to meet employer needs), and not one that is going to be fixed by just closing the door to international talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Toledo
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed OPT fees described in Section V.A and urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

OPT allows students to apply their academic knowledge through practical experience directly related to their field of study. Fees of this magnitude could make that opportunity financially inaccessible to otherwise eligible students. Access to legitimate practical training should not depend on whether a student, university, or employer can provide tens of thousands of dollars.

Although schools would be responsible for submitting payment, this does not eliminate the financial burden. Schools may lack the resources to cover these amounts, and employer funding cannot be assumed. If costs are passed to students, those without substantial personal or family wealth could lose access. If schools cannot fund the fees, students could be excluded despite meeting the academic and immigration requirements.

I support preventing fraud and protecting workers. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular amounts are necessary and why targeted audits, verification, and enforcement against documented violations would not adequately address its concerns.

Regarding Section V.C, I also urge DHS to protect currently enrolled students from any new fee requirements. A 60-day transition would provide little opportunity to adjust educational plans and financial commitments made years earlier.

Please withdraw these proposed fees and pursue proportionate measures that address misconduct while preserving access to legitimate practical training. Any alternative should include a transparent justification for its costs and a meaningful assessment of its effects on students, educational institutions, and employers.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees because they create prohibitive financial barriers for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I'm writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. As an American professional working in corporate finance, I believe this proposal is a big mistake that will severely damage our offices, our companies, and our national economy.

The justification for this rule is that it protects American jobs and fights fraud, but the math does not add up. Charging a $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and another $30,000 for a STEM extension is a functional shutdown of the program. Universities cannot absorb a $100,000 cost per student, and neither can the vast majority of businesses.

In my day-to-day work life, I see how critical international graduates are to keeping our teams running smoothly. They do not take away our jobs. Instead, they help fill talent gaps that allow our companies to scale, which actually creates more management and operational roles for American workers like me. According to data from the National Association of Foreign Student Advisers, international students contributed over $40 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 370,000 jobs in a single academic year. Stripping our workplaces of this talent pool will shrink corporate growth and lead to less opportunity for domestic workers.

Furthermore, a survey of over 800 higher education institutions showed that 92 percent of college leaders believe international students would simply choose to study in other countries if OPT were gutted. If we drive these bright minds away, we lose the tuition revenue that keeps our local universities funded, and we lose the next generation of innovators to competitors in Europe and Canada.

DHS suggests that schools can just pass these astronomical fees onto employers. In reality, a $70,000 price tag just to get a graduate through the door will cause small and mid-sized companies to stop hiring international talent altogether. Only the massive tech giants will be able to afford it, further consolidating wealth and hurting regular mid-market businesses.

We can protect American jobs and fight fraud through smarter enforcement, not by pricing talented graduates out of our economy. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule entirely.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they act as a functional shutdown of the program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Poorya Khajouie
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These excessive fees would create significant barriers for international graduates, employers, and American universities.

1. The $70,000 Fee Makes Employment Financially Unrealistic

How can a recent graduate realistically find an employer willing to absorb an additional $70,000 just to hire them? Although universities would formally pay the fee, they may pass the cost to students or employers. This financial burden would discourage hiring, especially among small businesses, startups, and research institutions.

2. The Fees Punish Legitimate Students Rather Than Targeting Fraud

Preventing immigration fraud is important, but imposing enormous fees on all international students unfairly penalizes those who follow the rules. DHS should focus on targeted investigations and stronger compliance measures instead.

3. The Rule Would Harm American Businesses and Discourage International Talent

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research, and economic growth. Making OPT financially inaccessible would discourage talented students from studying and working in the United States, potentially pushing skilled graduates toward other countries.

4. The Fees Disproportionately Harm Recent Graduates

Many international students already face financial challenges after paying substantial tuition and living expenses. A $70,000 fee for potentially just 12 months of work authorization is unreasonable and would make professional opportunities dependent on financial resources rather than qualifications and skills.

5. DHS Should Reconsider the Economic Impact

The proposal does not adequately demonstrate that students, universities, or employers can realistically afford these fees. DHS should carefully evaluate the consequences for employment opportunities, university enrollment, and American economic competitiveness.

Conclusion and Request

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and consider more reasonable, evidence-based alternatives to prevent fraud while preserving legitimate OPT opportunities.

International graduates who have invested in American education should have a fair opportunity to contribute their knowledge and skills to the U.S. economy without facing unreasonable financial barriers.

Thank you for considering my comments and the concerns of students, graduates, universities, and employers affected by this proposal.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

First, regarding evidence (Sec. IV.A), DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

Second, to claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

Third (Sec. IV.C), DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. This does not support the principles of academic honesty and fair competition but rather whoever can afford the price tag will be able to apply. Additionally, DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

Fourth, the money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

Fifth, benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

Sixth, DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

Seventh regarding reliance and perverse incentives, DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

Eighth, regarding small entities and states. In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

Lastly, regarding process and baseline. DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

I am writing to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to increase fees for the OPT and STEM OPT programs. This regulation is an essential step toward restoring the proper boundaries between international education and the domestic labor market.
United States universities provide world-class education, and it is entirely appropriate for foreign students to come here to learn and benefit from our academic systems. I urge DHS to finalize this rule immediately to protect the job prospects of domestic graduates and ensure that international study remains temporary.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. I am a student current pursuing my Master in the United States. 

Supporters of the rule, and the preamble itself (Sections IV.B and VI), rely on two claims: that F-1 is a study visa and should carry no work rights, and that restricting OPT will return jobs to American workers. Both are mistaken.

1. Practical training is part of studying, not a departure from it.

Practical training has been part of the F-1 framework since 1947, and Congress has revised immigration law many times since without eliminating it. OPT must be directly related to the student’s major area of study (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)). In engineering, architecture, accounting, public health and many other fields, applied training is how an education is completed, and many professional licenses require supervised experience. The D.C. Circuit upheld OPT and the STEM extension as lawful conditions of F-1 status in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022), and the Supreme Court declined review in 2023.

The rule is also internally inconsistent. If work were truly incompatible with study, a fee would not cure the problem. A $70,000 charge does not make OPT more educational; it only makes it available to students whose schools or families can pay. That rewards wealth, not merit or educational purpose.

Our competitors understand this. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Germany all offer post-study work options as part of international education. Pricing out OPT sends the strongest students to those countries.

2. Restricting OPT will not bring manufacturing or other jobs back to Americans.

OPT is available only to students who have completed at least a full academic year at a U.S. college or university, and the job must relate to their degree. Participants are mostly graduates in STEM and business fields, and most come from India and China. They are not the workforce in factories, construction, agriculture or service industries. The rule’s own labor analysis (Section IV.B) focuses on computer occupations, not manufacturing. Workers from Mexico and other countries in those sectors are in entirely different visa categories, which this rule does not touch.

Manufacturing jobs left largely because of automation, global supply chains and trade, not because of international graduates. Rebuilding domestic manufacturing in semiconductors, batteries and advanced materials requires engineers and scientists, and U.S. universities train many of them on F-1 visas. Driving them out deepens the talent shortage that slows new factories.

When companies cannot hire talent here, they hire it abroad. Work moves to offices in Toronto, Bangalore or London, along with the American support jobs around it. Many major American companies were founded by immigrants who first came as students.

The rule also harms American students directly. DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to “all students” (Section IV.C), meaning higher tuition for Americans. Lost international enrollment also cuts revenue that supports programs, faculty and local jobs.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it, defending practical training as part of study.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tai Simpson
comments.commentText:
I would like to express heavy opposition to the proposed rule, ICEB-2026-0100, which would impose $70,000 in initial and $30,000 in subsequent fees for OPT, and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. 

The actual issue the proposed rule aims to address is fraud, however, there are many processes in place to deter it, such as site visits, employee verification, and reporting requirements, all of which happen at the employer level, not before employment. The proposed rule to charge schools for students seeking employment does nothing to address the root of the issue which is occurring at the workplace. Even still, the evidence presented in the proposal is based on scant evidence of the effectiveness of the fee ad relies on cherry-picked anecdotes that support the position rather than assessing the facts. 
The fee also creates a financial barrier that would perpetuate inequality and discriminate against universities who could not afford the fee. It is unlikely schools would even be willing to pay, meaning the responsibility would fall on students, which would deter them from seeking education in the US. Not only would we lose their dollars at business, in housing, or local economies, but we would also lose their knowledge, talent, and skills. 

The proposed rule has potential for long-term consequences for individuals, institutions, and the nation. OPT is important because there is only so much a person can learn in the classroom. It provides students with important skills of knowing how their knowledge can be applied in the real world. F1 visas help US institutions to attract students from other nations, and in my experience, international students have contributed large amounts of labor, time, and knowledge for the betterment of our social, political, and economic institutions. Without international collaboration, I am confident the US would not be where it is today. 
The United States was built upon the work of immigrants, and we would not be as “advanced” without their perspectives and knowledge. We also need to consider that this rule is rooted in discrimination, racism, and xenophobia, which are not valid reasons to impose this rule.
For these reasons, I urge the DHS to withdraw this rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB)
comments.submitterName: Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB)
comments.commentText:
The Honorable Markwayne Mullin
Secretary, U.S. Department of Homeland Security
Washington, DC 20528

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 
Comments of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) on Optional Practical Training Fees, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Secretary Mullin: 

The Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) respectfully urges the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw its proposed rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026). 

FASEB represents 21 scientific societies and more than 100,000 researchers in the biological and biomedical sciences. For more than a century, we have advanced biomedical research and education in the United States. American labs compete for the best scientists in the world. Many scientists who now lead those labs, train American students, and serve in our societies first came here as international students. OPT was often their bridge from a U.S. degree to a U.S. research career. It let the nation keep the return on its investment in their training. Today, our members train, mentor, and work alongside the next generation of international scientists. This rule would decide whether those scientists stay to advance American research. 

FASEB supports DHS's goal of preventing fraud in OPT. The proposed rule does not show that a fee would advance that goal. It would require schools to pay $70,000 to $100,000 or more for each international student who uses OPT, whether or not any fraud is involved. DHS estimates that schools would pay $12.4 billion a year. Under the proposed rule, that money would go to the general Treasury, not to fraud prevention or oversight. The rule reports no fraud rate, and it cites no OPT fraud case involving a research institution.

DHS states that it cannot confidently predict how much OPT participation would decline. However, the available evidence indicates it would fall sharply. If schools pay the fee, independent estimates project that OPT participation among bachelor's and master's graduates would fall by nearly two-thirds at $70,000 and by about four-fifths at $100,000. Doctoral graduates have even more at stake. Two-thirds of international doctoral graduates on F-1 visas are approved for OPT. Temporary visa holders make up 58% of postdoctoral researchers in U.S. science, engineering, and health. This rule would narrow the path that brings these highly skilled, U.S.-trained scientists into our research workforce. More broadly, researchers estimate that a sustained one-third decline in international STEM graduates entering the U.S. workforce could reduce annual U.S. economic output by $240 billion to $481 billion after a decade (Clemens, Neufeld, and Nice, 2026).
 
FASEB's recommendations: 
1.	Withdraw the proposed fees. DHS has not shown that fraud is common or that a fee would reduce it. The fees would go to the Treasury, not to oversight. DHS should pursue targeted oversight of the employers and schools it has already identified. 

2.	Exempt universities and nonprofit research organizations. Congress exempts these employers from the H-1B training fee and the H-1B cap. DHS's concern about avoiding the cap does not apply to them, and none of the OPT fraud cases DHS cites involves a research university or nonprofit research organization. To implement this exemption, schools should not be charged the OPT fee for students employed by universities or nonprofit research organizations. 

3.	Exempt the STEM OPT extension. It already requires E-Verify, a signed training plan (Form I-983), and DHS site visits. DHS's own STEM OPT site visits uncovered some of the fraud it cites. 

4.	Do not extend the $70,000 fee to each new degree level. The rule sets no maximum fee per student. This option would multiply fees for students who pursue advanced degrees. 


Please see the attached letter from FASEB President Michael N. Lehman, PhD, for our complete comments.

CC: Darla P. Henderson, PhD 
Executive Director & Chief Executive Officer 
Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology 




See attached file(s)
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule on OPT fees, arguing it harms U.S. research and scientific competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees for the following reasons:
 
1. These positions can be scientifically valuable without generating enough direct revenue to justify an additional $100,000 cost per person. A principal investigator with a limited grant budget may be unable to retain a talented researcher even if that researcher is essential to the project.

2. DHS says the proposal is intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, protect U.S. workers, and prevent employers from using OPT to circumvent other employment-based visa requirements. However,  the fee is triggered by an institution's OPT recommendation—not by a finding of fraud, underpayment, or displacement of an American worker. Consequently, a legitimate university hiring an exceptionally qualified graduate could face the same fee as an institution whose practices raise serious concerns. A more proportionate approach would target documented violations, improve compliance audits, enforce existing labor protections, and impose penalties where misconduct is established.

3. It treats educational and employment circumstances as interchangeable: OPT is associated with education; it allows students to gain practical experience related to their field of study. The proposed fee, however, is partly designed to prevent OPT from being used to bypass the H-1B system. That rationale risks treating legitimate educational training as an alternative route to ordinary employment-based immigration. Yet a graduate undertaking a research fellowship, for example, may be gaining experience directly connected to their degree rather than exploiting a visa category. The distinction matters because a policy designed around suspected misuse can discourage legitimate educational and scientific activity.


4. It creates a particularly harsh barrier for STEM graduates: For eligible STEM graduates, the proposed $30,000 subsequent fee would apply to the STEM OPT extension. Combined with the initial $70,000 fee, that produces the $100,000 total. The extension is especially important for graduates whose work involves long experiments, complex software, specialized laboratory methods, or other activities requiring sustained training. The financial barrier could make these graduates much less attractive to employers and universities. The harm would not necessarily be limited to international students: U.S. research groups and employers could lose access to trained personnel and the knowledge those individuals contribute.

5. It could shift the costs onto people who had no role in the alleged abuse: If a university spreads these expenses across its general budget, domestic students and other research programs could also bear some of the cost. If it passes them to individual students or employers, those parties bear the burden instead.

In other words, the proposal creates a large financial penalty without ensuring that the people who ultimately pay are responsible for any misconduct.


6. It could undermine U.S. competitiveness

International graduates trained in the United States are already familiar with U.S. institutions, research practices, and professional networks. OPT offers a way to retain some of that expertise after graduation. If universities and employers cannot afford to retain these graduates, some may pursue opportunities in other countries. That could weaken the return on U.S. educational investment and make it harder for American institutions to recruit international students in the first place. The magnitude of these effects remains uncertain, but they are legitimate concerns in evaluating the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they impose undue financial costs and burden legitimate researchers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

As an international graduate student pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal would create significant financial barriers, undermine the competitiveness of American universities, and discourage highly skilled international graduates from contributing to the U.S. economy.

First, the proposed fees are disproportionately high and would restrict access to practical training opportunities. Although the fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial costs. This could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for many qualified students, regardless of their academic achievements, professional skills, or potential contributions. Access to practical training should not depend primarily on an institution's financial resources.

Second, this proposal could weaken America's ability to attract and retain global talent. International students invest significant financial resources and years of effort in obtaining American degrees. Many pursue specialized training in fields such as healthcare, engineering, data science, and quantitative analysis. OPT provides an important bridge between academic education and practical professional experience. Creating additional barriers to this transition could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in countries with more accessible post-graduation employment pathways.

Third, the proposed fee structure does not appear sufficiently targeted toward its stated objectives of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, imposing the same substantial fee regardless of an individual student's compliance history, educational qualifications, or employment circumstances risks penalizing legitimate participants without directly addressing misconduct. More targeted enforcement, stronger employer verification, and improved reporting mechanisms may offer more proportionate alternatives.

Finally, the proposal could damage the long-term relationship between American higher education and the U.S. labor market. International students contribute to university communities, support local economies, and develop specialized skills through American educational institutions. Making practical training substantially less accessible could reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education and diminish the potential economic returns from educating these students.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and consider more proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that address compliance concerns without imposing excessive barriers on legitimate students and educational institutions.

The United States has long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. Preserving reasonable opportunities for international graduates to apply their education in practice is important not only for students, but also for American universities, employers, and the broader economy.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the high OPT fees, arguing they create financial barriers and undermine U.S. talent retention.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Strong Support for DHS Proposed OPT and STEM OPT Fees – Prioritizing American Graduates and Workers

I strongly support the DHS proposal to introduce significant fees for OPT and STEM OPT programs. I hope this proposal is implemented because American graduates and workers deserve a fair opportunity to find employment, build their careers, and achieve financial independence.

Right now, American college graduates are facing an extremely difficult job market. From startups to medium-sized companies and major technology corporations, layoffs and hiring reductions have created significant competition for limited job opportunities. At the same time, companies are investing heavily in AI infrastructure and automation, making it even harder for recent graduates with little or no professional experience to secure their first jobs.

One major concern is that some employers may prefer hiring international students on OPT because they believe these workers will accept lower compensation, longer working hours, or less favorable employment conditions in hopes of eventually obtaining H-1B sponsorship. While this may not apply to every employer or OPT worker, the government should take this concern seriously and ensure that American graduates are not placed at an unfair disadvantage.

The transition from F-1 student status to OPT, STEM OPT, and potentially H-1B creates an extended pathway for foreign graduates to participate in the American workforce. At a time when many qualified American graduates are struggling to find entry-level employment, the government should carefully examine how these programs affect domestic hiring opportunities.

Unemployment and underemployment among young American graduates have consequences far beyond the job market. When young people cannot find stable employment, they struggle to repay student loans, pay rent, purchase homes, start families, and become financially independent. Many are forced to continue living with their parents because they cannot afford to support themselves.

This is not just an employment issue. It affects consumer spending, housing demand, family formation, and the long-term economic stability of the country.

The United States has invested significantly in educating its own students. Those graduates should have meaningful opportunities to enter the workforce and gain the experience necessary to build successful careers.

I believe the proposed OPT and STEM OPT fees could help discourage employers from relying on these programs primarily for labor-cost advantages. I also encourage DHS to strengthen wage protections, enforce reasonable working conditions, and increase oversight to ensure that OPT employment does not undermine opportunities for qualified American workers.

International students can contribute valuable skills to the American economy. However, immigration and employment policies should also protect the interests of American citizens and the domestic workforce, especially during periods of widespread layoffs, technological disruption, and limited entry-level hiring.

America First should include putting American students, recent graduates, and workers first when it comes to economic opportunities. These young Americans need jobs to pay their bills, build families, purchase homes, and contribute to the nation’s economic growth.

For these reasons, I strongly support the DHS proposal and hope it will be finalized and implemented with appropriate safeguards and enforcement.

Thank you for considering my public comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly supports introducing significant fees for OPT and STEM OPT to prioritize American workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fees**

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations for F-1 international students. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

**1. Financial Burden on International Students**

OPT allows eligible international students to gain practical experience related to their academic programs. Students and their families invest substantial resources in tuition, housing, insurance, and other educational expenses. Although the proposed fees would be charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, institutions could pass on costs through higher tuition, reduced financial assistance, or fewer OPT opportunities. This could disproportionately affect students from modest-income families.

**2. Harm to Universities and the Economy**

International students contribute to American universities through tuition, research, and academic participation. The proposed fees could discourage institutions, especially smaller colleges, from recommending eligible students for OPT. Reduced enrollment and participation could affect university finances, research programs, employment, and local businesses. DHS should consider these consequences before adopting the proposal.

**3. Loss of Skilled Talent and Innovation**

The United States attracts international students through its educational excellence, research opportunities, and career development pathways. These graduates contribute to technology, healthcare, scientific research, and entrepreneurship. Excessive OPT fees could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, weakening America's ability to attract skilled workers and remain globally competitive.

**4. Impact on Employers and Workforce Development**

OPT helps eligible graduates apply their academic knowledge in professional settings. Employers benefit from their specialized skills and experience. If universities reduce OPT recommendations because of the proposed fees, employers could face recruitment challenges and lose access to qualified graduates. Protecting American workers is important, but this goal should be pursued without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational and workforce opportunities.

**5. Disproportionate Fees and Better Alternatives**

DHS has a responsibility to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, these objectives do not automatically justify fees of $70,000 and $30,000. DHS should explain how these amounts were determined and provide evidence that they are necessary and proportionate.

Less burdensome alternatives include stronger verification procedures, targeted compliance reviews, improved reporting systems, and appropriate penalties for proven violations. These measures could address legitimate concerns without creating excessive financial barriers for educational institutions and eligible students.

**6. Wider Economic and Family Consequences**

Many international students rely on family savings, scholarships, and loans to complete their education. The proposed fees could increase financial pressure on institutions, resulting in reduced student support and fewer practical training opportunities. International students also contribute to local economies through housing, transportation, food, and other spending. Reduced enrollment or OPT participation could harm universities, employers, and local communities.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the proposal's educational, financial, economic, and workforce consequences before proceeding.

**Conclusion and Request**

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, regulations should be evidence-based, proportionate, transparent, and fair to educational institutions and eligible international students.

At a minimum, DHS should reconsider the proposed fees, explain their justification, evaluate their likely consequences, and consider less burdensome alternatives.

The United States should continue promoting educational excellence, research, innovation, and responsible workforce development while protecting the integrity of its immigration system. Excessively high OPT fees could undermine these goals and encourage talented international graduates to contribute their skills to other countries instead.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and adopt a balanced approach that protects American workers without imposing unreasonable financial burdens on universities or restricting legitimate opportunities for eligible international students.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Valeria Vasquez
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee structure, which would require employers or institutions to pay $70,000 for the first year and $30,000 for each subsequent year.

I came to the United States as an international scholar and benefited from the OPT program to continue my scientific training. Through OPT, I completed my postdoctoral work and contributed directly to the U.S. scientific enterprise. I am now a U.S. citizen and lead my own research group, where I create jobs, support the local economy, train scientists, and contribute to discoveries that advance medicine and science.

Without OPT, I would have been forced to return to my home country, an authoritarian regime where my opportunities to contribute freely to science would have been severely limited. The United States would have lost my work, the jobs created by my laboratory, and the broader benefits of the research and training I have conducted here.

The proposed fees would make OPT inaccessible to many universities, laboratories, startups, and research institutions. They would discourage talented international students and researchers from coming to the United States, weaken scientific collaboration, and undermine the country’s ability to remain a global leader in research and innovation.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure and preserve affordable access to OPT for international students, postdoctoral researchers, and other scholars who contribute substantially to the U.S. economy, scientific community, and public good.

While DHS has a responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system and prevent fraud, that responsibility must not come at the expense of the international students and researchers who are vital to U.S. scientific innovation, research excellence, and global competitiveness. Rather than imposing excessive fees without a clear justification or demonstrated connection to program costs, DHS should strengthen targeted fraud detection, improve verification of employment and training arrangements, and hold employers, intermediaries, and institutions that violate program requirements accountable. Punitive fees are not a substitute for effective oversight and risk placing an unnecessary financial burden on legitimate students, researchers, and employers who strengthen the U.S. scientific enterprise.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule.

The NPRM justifies the fee as a way to “combat fraud,” yet the revenue is not directed to fraud detection, site visits, or SEVP compliance. A $70,000 charge bears no relationship to the administrative cost of a DSO entering a recommendation in SEVIS.

Anonymous

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dhananji  Karunarathna
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100 - Optional Practical Training Fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international student from Sri Lanka, currently in my fourth year of graduate study in the United States. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and the $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a graduate student, I cannot afford these amounts. Using an approximate exchange rate of 330 Sri Lankan rupees per U.S. dollar, the proposed initial fee of $70,000 would equal 23.1 million Sri Lankan rupees. An additional $30,000 fee would equal 9.9 million rupees. If both applied to my training, the combined cost would be $100,000, or approximately 33 million Sri Lankan rupees. For me, these amounts represent an insurmountable financial barrier, not simply an additional application expense.

I understand that the proposal would require schools to submit payment before recommending OPT. However, allowing schools to obtain funding from students, employers, or other sources does not ensure that such funding will be available. If my university could not cover the fee, I could not afford to pay it myself. I also cannot assume that a prospective employer would be willing or able to pay tens of thousands of dollars to support my practical training.

I have already devoted years of effort to my graduate education and professional development. OPT would allow me to apply the knowledge and skills gained through my degree in a practical setting directly related to my field. These proposed fees could prevent me from pursuing that opportunity because of my financial circumstances, regardless of my qualifications or the educational value of the training.

As a fourth-year graduate student, I am particularly concerned about the impact on students who are already well into their degree programs. We have invested substantial time and effort in our education. Introducing such a large financial barrier at this stage would create serious uncertainty as we prepare to complete our studies and plan our careers.

I support appropriate oversight to ensure that OPT serves its intended educational purpose. However, I respectfully urge DHS to pursue targeted measures rather than impose fees that make practical training financially inaccessible to students like me. Access to degree-related training should not depend on personal wealth or the ability to find a university or employer willing to pay such large amounts.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees. If DHS proceeds with a new fee structure, I ask that it consider substantially lower, clearly justified fees, meaningful financial-hardship protections, and protections for students already enrolled in U.S. degree programs.

Please consider the real financial impact on international students from Sri Lanka and other countries where these dollar amounts translate into enormous local-currency costs. For me, the proposed fees would make OPT financially inaccessible.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees due to insurmountable financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing from the perspective of an American small business and startup employer to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 extension fee. Simply put, this rule is a massive handout to Wall Street banks and tech monopolies at the direct expense of Main Street businesses and early-stage American startups.

When a small manufacturing firm, a local engineering shop, or a seed-stage startup hires a recent college graduate, $70,000 to $100,000 isn't "regulatory pocket change"—that is an entire annual salary. Whether this fee is billed to the university and passed down, or shifted onto the student and their prospective employer, the result is the same: small and mid-sized American businesses will be completely priced out of hiring top STEM graduates from our own local universities.

People who don't run businesses often assume that if you block an international graduate from working on OPT, that job automatically goes to a U.S. citizen the next day. In the real world, that is not how hiring works. We always look for qualified local candidates first because it is simpler and faster. When we hire an engineer, data analyst, or specialist on OPT, it is because we spent months trying to fill a critical technical role and found a graduate from an American university who had the exact skills we needed to launch a product or fulfill a contract.

And here is what economists and business owners actually see on the ground: every time we bring on a specialized engineer or product developer, that person enables us to grow and hire three or four more American citizens in sales, marketing, customer support, and operations. If you slap a $100,000 tax on that pipeline, small companies won't magically find missing specialists—we will simply lose contracts, cancel expansion plans, or be forced to hire offshore contractors overseas instead of employing people who live, rent, and pay taxes right here in our community.

Only the wealthiest trillion-dollar corporations can shrug off a $100,000 fee. If DHS wants American startups and small businesses to compete and create domestic jobs, please withdraw this rule immediately.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule.
As an international graduate student currently pursuing my education in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the significant financial, educational, and professional consequences this proposal would have for international students.
International students already make substantial financial commitments to pursue higher education in the United States. In addition to tuition, living expenses, health insurance, and immigration-related fees, many international students face restrictions on employment opportunities while completing their studies. The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier, potentially making practical training inaccessible to many students. Even if these fees are initially imposed on educational institutions, the financial burden could ultimately be passed on to students or discourage institutions from supporting OPT applications.
OPT is not simply an opportunity to work in the United States. It is an important extension of students' education, allowing them to apply their academic knowledge, develop professional competencies, and gain meaningful experience in their respective fields. As a graduate student preparing for a career that requires specialized professional training and practical experience, I understand how essential these opportunities are for connecting academic learning with professional practice. Restricting access to OPT through excessive fees would undermine an important component of the educational experience that attracts many international students to the United States.
I am particularly concerned that the proposed fees would disproportionately affect students from less financially privileged backgrounds. Students should not be denied opportunities for professional development simply because they or their educational institutions cannot afford such substantial costs. Access to practical training should be based on students' educational preparation, qualifications, and professional goals rather than their financial resources. This proposal risks creating a system in which only students with significant financial support can fully benefit from the educational and professional opportunities associated with studying in the United States.
I am also concerned about the implications for students pursuing careers in education, mental health, and other public service professions. These fields provide essential services to individuals and communities, yet they may not offer the financial resources necessary to absorb such substantial fees. As a result, the proposed rule could disproportionately limit opportunities for international graduates who wish to contribute their professional knowledge and skills to schools, healthcare settings, and underserved communities. It could also discourage students from pursuing careers in fields where their expertise and contributions are greatly needed.
Furthermore, international students contribute to American universities, research institutions, local communities, and the broader economy through their academic work, research, cultural perspectives, and professional engagement. Many of us choose to pursue higher education in the United States because of its academic excellence and opportunities for meaningful professional development. Imposing such substantial financial barriers could discourage talented students from diverse socioeconomic backgrounds from studying in the United States, potentially weakening the country's ability to attract international talent and maintain its position as a global leader in higher education.
I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the OPT program and preventing fraud or misuse. However, I believe these objectives should be addressed through targeted oversight, appropriate enforcement, and evidence-based measures rather than imposing excessive financial barriers on students and educational institutions. The proposed fees would place a substantial burden on students pursuing legitimate educational and professional opportunities, without necessarily addressing the underlying concerns regarding program integrity.
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule and consider alternative approaches that protect program integrity while preserving equitable access to practical training. International students who have invested significant time, effort, and financial resources in their education should have a fair opportunity to apply their knowledge, develop professionally, and contribute to the communities in which they study and work.
Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed rule's financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lauren Perry
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,Dear Secretary Mullin,I oppose the proposed rule. It is likely to be both contrary to the Administrative Procedures Act and to undermine moral and economic goals. First, imposing the fee likely exceeds DHS' statutory authority. It also fails to consider the reliance interests of F-1 students and employers who considered this a bridge program or relied on their ability to be able to gain valuable work experience before returning to their home countries. Moreover, the proposed rule appears to require the student's school --- not the student-worker or the employer --- to pay the proposed fee. It is the government's job to screen prospective students effectively for admission to the United States and this is an abdication of that responsibility. It places an extraordinary financial burden on schools, and a large burden on DHS itself and banking institutions because of proposed refunds. Moreover, the proposal is likely to undermine its own economic goals. The program is used to recruit and employ workers with skills American workers lack. Preventing them from working does not suddenly give American workers those skills. Companies may be forced to relocate or slash jobs if there are insufficient skilled workers and no means to recruit them. The program may also incentivize fraud by encouraging workers to perform under-the-table work or have schools alter the program descriptions to make them eligible for different forms of OPT. This will drive up enforcement costs without addressing the underlying problem. Finally, America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international doctoral student in bioengineering at a U.S. research university. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on OPT and STEM OPT recommendations. Doctoral students are in a different position from other OPT participants, and the proposal does not account for that.

1. The fee exceeds what a doctoral graduate would earn in a year.
Most international PhD students are on F-1 visas, and after graduating, most of us go directly into postdoctoral research positions. A first-year postdoc earns roughly $60,000 to $65,000, in line with NIH’s own postdoctoral stipend scale. A $70,000 fee for one recommendation is more than the salary of the position OPT is meant to make possible. No lab or department can reasonably absorb that, and federal research grants are unlikely to cover it. Schools will either decline to recommend doctoral graduates, or pass the cost to students, labs, or employers. I ask DHS to state who is expected to bear this cost for research trainees.

2. OPT is how doctoral graduates enter the U.S. research workforce.
OPT and the STEM extension give up to three years of work authorization, which is the bridge from graduation to a postdoc and then to a permanent position. This pipeline depends on international scientists trained in U.S. labs with public funding. Pricing these graduates out of OPT would send them to Canada, Europe, or Asia, and the U.S. would lose the return on its own investment in their training.

3. The fraud rationale does not fit doctoral students.
DHS cites fraud involving shell companies and suspect employers. Doctoral graduates work at universities, hospitals, and research institutes, under named mentors, with documented STEM OPT training plans. A flat fee on every student penalizes legitimate participants far more than it deters bad actors. Targeted tools such as employer verification, site visits, and SEVP audits address fraud without cutting off research trainees. At minimum, DHS should consider exempting doctoral students, or students employed by accredited institutions of higher education and nonprofit research institutions.

4. The fee amount has no stated relationship to administrative cost.
I ask DHS to explain how $70,000 and $30,000 relate to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation, and what statutory authority supports fees of this size.

5. Enrolled students relied on existing rules.
Doctoral students commit five to six years to a program, often after moving countries, on the understanding that OPT would be available afterward. DHS should clarify how grandfathering applies to students already enrolled when a final rule takes effect, and whether a student whose OPT was authorized before the effective date would owe $70,000 for a later STEM extension. I also urge DHS not to adopt the alternative that would charge the $70,000 fee again at each degree level. That would double-penalize students who earn a master’s and then a PhD, which is common in my field.

6. Many international graduate students are in dual-student households.
Many of us are married to other international students whose own timelines depend on OPT. Compounding costs and uncertainty make it much harder to plan a career, and to stay, in the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal or, at minimum, to exempt doctoral students and accredited research institutions and to give enrolled students a transition period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This public comment is submitted in formal opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the imposition of unprecedented fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. The proposed financial barriers—specifically $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent STEM extensions or pre-completion OPT—would effectively dismantle the OPT program, inflict severe unintended consequences on U.S. higher education, exacerbate domestic economic vulnerabilities, and weaken overall national competitiveness.

DHS should fully withdraw this proposed rule based on the following policy and economic considerations:

1. Arbitrary Disruption to Current Students and Lawful Visa Holders
The proposed fee structure abruptly alters the foundational rules under which current international students and existing OPT participants made their academic and financial investments. International students enter the United States lawfully, adhering strictly to federal regulations and contributing substantial tuition. Imposing prohibitive financial costs at the practical training stage retroactively devalues their education and undermines the reasonable expectations established upon enrollment.

2. Disregard for Lawful Contributions and Fiscal Impact
Participants in the OPT program operate entirely within the legal frameworks established by federal immigration law. During their post-graduation training, OPT employees pay federal, state, and local income taxes while drawing minimally from public benefits. Imposing punitive administrative fees overlooks the fiscal contributions made by these high-skilled, lawful taxpayers.

3. Financial Instability for U.S. Higher Education and Increased Costs for Domestic Students
The steep fee increases will make American universities cost-prohibitive for global talent, leading to a sharp decline in international student enrollment. Because international students frequently pay full tuition, institutions rely heavily on this revenue to maintain academic programs, research infrastructure, and institutional stability. A sudden drop in international enrollment will destabilize university budgets, potentially forcing campus downscaling, program closures, and tuition increases for domestic U.S. students to offset operational shortfalls.

4. Disruption of the High-Skilled Talent Pipeline for U.S. Businesses
The OPT program serves as a critical bridge connecting American industry with top talent educated within the U.S. higher education system. Restricting access to OPT through cost-prohibitive regulations will sever this pipeline, restricting access to specialized skills essential for research, development, and market competition.

5. Mismatch with Domestic Labor Market Needs in Critical STEM Disciplines
The overwhelming majority of OPT participants are concentrated in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields—sectors characterized by chronic domestic labor shortages. OPT graduates fill technical roles that exceed the current supply of domestic graduates. Restricting OPT participation will result in unfilled critical technical positions across sectors vital to economic growth, including information technology, advanced engineering, and healthcare.

6. Offshoring of U.S. High-Tech Jobs and Corporate Capital Flight
If domestic regulations hinder U.S. enterprises from retaining qualified foreign graduates, businesses will not simply absorb the labor deficit locally. Instead, multinational firms will be incentivized to relocate research centers, software operations, and engineering jobs abroad to jurisdictions with predictable, competitive talent acquisition framework (e.g., Canada, Europe, and Asia). This outcome results in a net loss of domestic employment and capital investment.

7. Erosion of Long-Term National Competitiveness and Innovation Leadership
For decades, the accessibility of practical training has made the United States the primary destination for world-class talent. Enacting prohibitive administrative fees sends a signal that damages the global reputation of the U.S. innovation ecosystem. Over time, reducing the inflow of global talent will diminish technological innovation, weaken economic capacity, and permanently erode American leadership in global markets.

Conclusion

The proposed OPT fee increases represent an economically counterproductive approach that burdens U.S. academic institutions, disadvantages domestic businesses, and threatens broader national interest. The Department of Homeland Security should withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the standard operation of the OPT program.
comments.reason: The commenter submits formal opposition to the rule, citing arbitrary disruption and severe consequences for higher education.
