comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01)

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am an international PhD student currently studying in the United States on an F-1 visa. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a PhD student in a STEM field, I have dedicated years of my life to scientific research and advanced training in the United States. International doctoral students contribute substantially to American universities through research, scientific publications, technological development, and the training of future scientists. Many of us work on projects supported by federal research funding, contributing directly to the advancement of American science and innovation.

First, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier for international PhD graduates. Doctoral students typically spend five to six years or longer completing their degrees while receiving modest stipends. A $70,000 initial fee, potentially followed by another $30,000 for STEM OPT, is far beyond what most students could reasonably afford. Although the proposal places the payment obligation on educational institutions, it explicitly allows universities to pass these costs on to students or employers. This would effectively make access to practical training dependent on financial resources rather than academic achievement, scientific expertise, or professional qualifications.

Second, the proposed fees would particularly harm academic research and the postdoctoral workforce. Many PhD graduates pursue postdoctoral positions at universities, medical schools, and research institutions. These positions are essential to scientific progress but generally offer salaries that cannot justify a $70,000 or $100,000 employment-related fee. Universities and academic laboratories also operate under limited research budgets. Requiring institutions to absorb these costs could prevent them from retaining talented researchers whom they have already spent years training.

Third, the proposal could undermine America’s ability to attract and retain highly skilled scientific talent. International students choose American universities because of their research excellence and opportunities for professional development. OPT provides an important bridge between academic training and professional research. Making this pathway financially inaccessible could encourage talented students to pursue doctoral education and scientific careers in other countries. The United States would risk losing researchers whose education, expertise, and discoveries could otherwise benefit American institutions, industries, and society.

Fourth, the proposed fee structure does not adequately distinguish legitimate academic training from the fraud and misuse it seeks to address. I recognize the importance of maintaining program integrity and protecting American workers. However, imposing exceptionally high fees on all OPT participants would also penalize students who have complied with immigration requirements and completed rigorous academic programs. More targeted oversight and enforcement measures would better address potential abuse without disproportionately burdening legitimate students and research institutions.

Finally, I am particularly concerned about the impact on students who are already pursuing their degrees in the United States. Many international PhD students made long-term educational and career decisions based on the existing OPT framework. Introducing such substantial financial barriers after students have invested years in their education would create significant uncertainty and could fundamentally alter their ability to complete their planned professional training.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. Any future changes to OPT should carefully consider the financial realities of graduate education, the essential role of international researchers, and the long-term consequences for American scientific competitiveness.

As an international PhD student, I hope to continue contributing to scientific discovery and innovation in the United States. I believe that access to practical training should be based on educational qualifications and compliance with program requirements, not the ability to pay an extraordinary financial fee.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

An International PhD Student in the United States

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Karen Ferguson
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Fighting fraud is legitimate, but this fee cannot reach the fraud DHS describes, rests on misread data and an untenable legal theory, and would impose billions in costs on American employers, universities, and workers.

The fee does not target fraud (III.D, IV.A, V.A). DHS documents fraud at shell employers and phantom worksites, yet the fee is paid by the school, “would not be tied to a specific employer,” and comes due before a first OPT recommendation, when no employer need exist. DHS calls DSOs “overwhelmed” and “not fully trained” (IV.B), then makes them the fraud filter. Schools may pass the cost to students, employers, or “all students” (IV.C); visa mills can price it in. The 10,000-student figure is roughly 3.5% of the 289,938 OPT and STEM OPT starts in 2024 (Table 2), rests on an ICE YouTube video (nn.55-56, 67), and conflicts with n.56 (10,000 employers). Where HSI has identified bad actors, investigation, SEVIS termination, and decertification can reach them directly. Taxing everyone else is not tailored.

The data are misread (IV.A-B). DHS says OPT growth “exponentially outpaced” its review capacity, but Table 2 shows 2024 OPT starts only 27% above 2017 (194,554 vs. 152,681), after a 2021 trough. DHS says STEM OPT “far surpassed” its 2016 projection by citing 165,524 participants, yet Table 2 shows 95,384 STEM OPT starts in 2024, near the 92,000 projected for 2026. The 165,524 figure appears to count overlapping 24-month cohorts (2023 and 2024 starts alone total 157,420), so comparing it to the annual H-1B cap is apples to oranges. The wage study quoted at n.111 matches Bound, Khanna & Morales (NBER 23153), which modeled 1994-2001 H-1B inflows, not OPT, and found immigration raised U.S. natives’ overall welfare. Table 1 lists the rule’s “Effects on wages” as “N/A.” 
nber

DHS shows costs, not benefits (VII.A). DHS’s primary estimate is $4.1 billion in annualized costs, $12.8 billion in annual transfers, and no monetized benefits (“Not Estimated”). Opportunity cost is proxied by unpaid fees, which DHS concedes may be too high or too low. The fee is flat: $70,000 whether OPT lasts three months or twelve, and $100,000 if split before and after graduation, which DHS expects to deter pre-completion training (VII.A.5.d), undercutting its “educational value” rationale. In year one, 841 of 1,389 small institutions would bear costs above 1% of revenue and 116 above 20% (Table 17), yet Table 1 lists effects on State governments as “N/A” despite 1,044 state-run universities (n.137).

DHS lacks authority for this charge (III.A, IV.C). INA §214(a)’s “time and conditions” language does not authorize a $12.4 billion-a-year levy. DHS concedes the statute gives ICE no authority to keep the money, which goes to the Treasury’s general fund. A charge untethered to agency cost (more than 130 times the $470-$520 OPT work-permit filing fee), pegged to the H-1B payment, and earmarked for no program is a tax, and taxing belongs to Congress. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Daniel Smith
comments.commentText:
The proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on Optional Practical Training is completely unworkable, legally vulnerable, and effectively acts as a backdoor ban on practical training. Labeling this astronomical fee structure as a measure to combat fraud or protect American workers completely misses the reality on the ground. The underlying logic of the rule collapses entirely when examining how the funds are actually handled. DHS openly admits that these collected fees will not be retained by ICE or SEVP for administrative oversight or enforcement; instead, they are dumped directly into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302. Slapping a $70,000 price tag on an initial OPT recommendation has zero rational connection to actual administrative costs and functions purely as a punitive deterrent and disguised tax. Furthermore, penalizing hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students, legitimate employers, and accredited universities because of isolated criminal incidents involving a handful of bad actors and shell companies is entirely disproportionate and violates basic administrative law principles against arbitrary and capricious rulemaking.

The broader economic and innovation impacts would be disastrous for the country's competitive standing. In recent years, approximately 200,000 students participated in post-completion or pre-completion OPT, while nearly 100,000 participated in STEM OPT extensions. These graduates fill critical talent shortages across engineering, software development, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced research. Choking off this pipeline does not magically create jobs for American workers; it simply forces global tech and research companies to shift talent acquisition, capital, and innovation overseas to countries like Canada, the UK, and Singapore that are actively courting this expertise. Moreover, the administration's reliance on arguments surrounding FICA tax exemptions ignores that these programs are foundational for bringing top-tier global talent into our ecosystem. Forcing employers and institutions to shoulder an insurmountable $70,000 upfront barrier completely destroys the entry-level hiring market for high-skilled graduates and handicaps American firms against international competitors.

The proposal is equally devastating for educational institutions, especially smaller schools, regional colleges, and non-profit universities. DHS's own Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis reveals that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-certified institutions are small entities, and over 60 percent of small institutions will face severe financial burdens ranging from 1 percent to over 20 percent of their annual revenue. For regional universities and colleges operating on tight margins, absorbing or passing on a $70,000 liability per student is an absolute impossibility. This rule will gut institutional budgets, force massive administrative overhead regarding compliance tracking, and destroy practical training options for students who rely on them to bridge the gap between classroom theory and professional experience.

Furthermore, graduate education—particularly Master's and PhD programs in STEM fields—will suffer catastrophic enrollment declines. International graduate students who fund their education and contribute significantly to university research labs and academic publications will simply look elsewhere if U.S. post-graduate training is placed behind an insurmountable paywall. Even designated school officials are set up to fail under this rigid framework. DSOs will be forced to act as tax collectors and financial auditors, confirming wire transfers, validating institutional funds, and verifying complex ledger entries before entering recommendations into SEVIS. The administrative chaos this introduces—coupled with rigid and unfair refund policies where fees are entirely non-refundable once an Employment Authorization Document is issued—creates an untenable operational nightmare. Docket Number ICEB-2026-0100 fundamentally misdiagnoses the challenges facing the U.S. labor market and immigration system. Rather than enhancing integrity or protecting workers, these punitive fees will drive top-tier global talent away from American shores, cripple institutional budgets, and erode U.S. technological preeminence. DHS must withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: Argues the fees act as a backdoor ban and punitive deterrent that harms innovation and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Richard Williams
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS’s proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation. Fraud involving sham employers and false records is a serious concern, but DHS has not shown that charges this large, imposed on legitimate students and schools, are necessary or effective. DHS should withdraw it and pursue targeted enforcement.

The fees are not tied to an applicant’s risk, employer, training period, or government processing costs. They apply across pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT, regardless of risk. DHS estimates $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers, compared with $15.7 million in annual OPT review and payment-processing costs. The money would go to the U.S. Treasury, not directly fund ICE or SEVP oversight, and would not be reserved for OPT enforcement. DHS has not explained why a fee so far removed from administrative costs is proportionate.

DHS’s economic analysis raises further concerns. It estimates primary 10-year costs of $35.1 billion at a 3% discount rate ($29.0 billion at 7%) and government fee transfers of $109.4 billion ($90.6 billion at 7%), while leaving monetized benefits unestimated. DHS does not quantify how much fraud the rule would prevent, how many jobs it would create for U.S. workers, or what wage gains would result. Without comparable estimates, the public cannot assess whether benefits justify the costs. DHS acknowledges it cannot fully measure the value of lost OPT opportunities. Using fees collected as a proxy for the value of opportunities that disappear risks circular reasoning. Its projections depend on unverified assumptions about how schools will respond.

The fraud cases cited do not establish that lawful OPT participants are responsible for wider labor-market problems. Cases involving sham companies, false documents, and fraudulent job offers justify investigating and penalizing those involved, not imposing a six-figure barrier on every participant. Increasing STEM OPT participation alone does not prove that OPT caused unemployment or wage depression; broader outcomes are also affected by economic cycles, layoffs, and employer demand. Using a lawful training period while pursuing another immigration status is not, by itself, proof of fraud. DHS should demonstrate a measurable connection between lawful OPT participation and the harms it alleges before restricting the program nationwide.

The fee would select for ability to pay, not legitimacy. DHS says schools may seek funding from students, employers, or other sources, but many cannot absorb a $70,000 charge per student. They may pass the cost on, stop recommending qualified students, or experience reduced enrollment. The burden is especially disproportionate for non-STEM graduates eligible for only 12 months of OPT. The proposal can also trigger $100,000 in fees when a student uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT, encouraging schools to discourage legitimate training simply to avoid the extra payment.

DHS estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small institutions would face transition-year fee impacts exceeding 1% of revenue, including 116 facing impacts above 20%. These burdens could harm enrollment, tuition revenue, research capacity, and employers’ access to qualified graduates. It does not adequately assess effects on innovation or U.S. competitiveness. A policy that disproportionately excludes students whose schools lack resources does not reliably identify fraudulent applicants; it risks driving talented people to study and work elsewhere.

The problems DHS describes call for targeted enforcement, not a blanket financial penalty. Its examples involve fake worksites, shell companies, false records, and networks facilitating fraudulent documentation. A flat fee verifies none of these facts. Better measures include risk-based employer site visits, verification of employer identities and payroll records, analysis of suspicious networks and addresses, fraud training for designated school officials, timely school recertification, and meaningful penalties for employers and intermediaries that facilitate fraud. GAO-19-297 identified opportunities to strengthen SEVP oversight and risk management. These measures target warning signs and permit evaluation. Administrative convenience is not enough to justify a fee that could effectively eliminate lawful opportunities.

DHS should withdraw this proposal. Before considering any new fee, it should explain how the amount was calculated, quantify expected fraud-prevention and labor-market benefits, assess effects on students, schools, employers, and U.S. innovation, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Protecting U.S. workers and immigration integrity are legitimate goals. A near-prohibitive fee imposed indiscriminately on legitimate participants, without demonstrated proportionality or dedicated enforcement funding, is not a justified way to achieve them.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees as disproportionate, unjustified by administrative costs, and harmful to legitimate participants.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Many of my colleagues are international students. They contribute greatly to our lab and research. With these increased fees, my international colleagues will find it increasingly difficult to find postgraduate work in the US. As scientists, we rely on collaboration to form and test new ideas. Excluding international students will be a disadvantage to the entire scientific community in the US.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Emma Derrick
comments.reason: Opposes the excessive OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule to protect the U.S. talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jessie Li
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule in its entirety and ask DHS to withdraw it. A full comment with citations is attached.
No statutory authority (Sections III.A, IV.C). INA 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of admission. It does not authorize a $70,000 charge on schools deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt. DHS concedes ICE cannot retain the funds and does not claim the amount reflects any cost of service. A charge that raises general revenue beyond the cost of service is a tax. National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States (1974). Congress enacts immigration fees expressly (8 U.S.C. 1356(m), 1372(e), 1184(c)(9), (12)). After Loper Bright (2024), DHS gets no deference, and a rule with $74.6–144.3 billion in ten-year transfers requires clear authorization. West Virginia v. EPA (2022).
The fee does not target fraud (Section IV.A). Every fraud example DHS cites involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. The fee is charged to schools, is not tied to any employer, and is due before initial OPT requires a job offer. DHS's latest probe flagged about 10,000 students, under 3% of the roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. The rule charges all of them.
The enforcement rationale defeats itself (Section IV.C). DHS says compliance resources have not scaled with the program and rejects site visits as too resource-intensive. The fee proceeds, a primary estimate of $12.8 billion a year, fund no enforcement.
The fee selects for wealth (Section IV.C). DHS allows schools to pass the fee to students. The practical selection criterion becomes ability to pay $70,000 to $130,000, which excludes qualified students and leaves well-funded bad actors untouched.
The labor rationale does not fit the amount (Section IV.B). The FICA exemption DHS cites is worth about $6,900 a year on a $90,000 salary. The fees for OPT plus STEM OPT total $100,000. DHS's own low scenario eliminates about 106,000 of 194,554 initial OPT placements. That is abolition of most non-STEM OPT by price, without acknowledgment or justification.
Irrational structure (Section V.A). Part-time pre-completion OPT triggers the full $70,000. Pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT total $130,000. Fees are non-refundable once an EAD issues, even if an offer is rescinded; earlier refunds are discretionary and unappealable.
Change in position unexplained. The 2016 STEM OPT rule rested on findings of benefit to institutions, the economy, and U.S. workers. DHS does not quantify the benefits it would forgo. FCC v. Fox (2009). The repeated statement that DHS "may shut down the program entirely" is not a reason for this rule.
Reliance interests (Section VI). About 280,000 students used OPT in 2024. Students chose STEM programs and borrowed tuition in reliance on OPT. DHS grandfathers only students with a DSO recommendation before the effective date and never considers grandfathering all currently enrolled students. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires that analysis.
Procedure. The rule is economically significant, yet DHS allowed 30 days instead of the 60 days EO 12866 and EO 13563 call for. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption in one sentence although 56% of affected schools are small entities.
Requested action: withdraw the rule. Otherwise: extend the comment period 60 days; limit any fee to administrative cost; target employers through I-983 plans, E-Verify, and site visits; grandfather all enrolled students; exempt pre-completion OPT; reject re-charging $70,000 per degree level; make refunds appealable.
comments.reason: Argues the rule lacks statutory authority, does not target fraud, and asks DHS to withdraw it entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and reconsider its approach to preventing fraud in the OPT program.

1. The proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier to employment.

International students already make substantial financial investments in their education in the United States, including tuition, housing, health insurance, and other living expenses. Many students rely on their personal savings and family support to complete their degrees. An additional fee of $70,000 would make OPT financially inaccessible to an overwhelming number of qualified graduates, regardless of their academic performance, professional skills, or compliance with immigration requirements.

The proposed fee is particularly concerning because OPT is intended to provide eligible international students with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. A fee of this magnitude would effectively prevent many students from accessing this opportunity, undermining the educational and professional value of their U.S. degrees.

2. The proposal would undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.

International students choose the United States because of its educational institutions, research opportunities, and professional development pathways. The opportunity to apply their education in a professional setting is an important consideration when deciding where to study.

If graduates face a $70,000 fee before they can pursue initial OPT, prospective students may increasingly choose universities in other countries that offer more accessible post-study employment pathways. This would weaken the United States’ ability to attract talented students, reduce the international competitiveness of American universities, and potentially diminish the long-term contributions of U.S.-educated graduates to the American economy.

3. The proposal would disproportionately harm small businesses and entry-level employers.

Many industries depend on early-career professionals who bring specialized knowledge, technical skills, and new perspectives. In fields such as architecture and design, graduates often begin their careers at small and mid-sized firms, where entry-level compensation is constrained by business size and project-based revenue.

A $70,000 OPT fee would create a substantial obstacle for graduates seeking entry-level employment and could discourage smaller employers from hiring otherwise qualified candidates. Even if the fee were formally imposed on students, employers would face a narrower talent pool, increased recruitment uncertainty, and greater difficulty filling positions. The resulting burden could be especially severe in industries where professional experience and technical training are essential to career development.

4. Fraud prevention should be proportionate, evidence-based, and targeted.

I recognize the government’s responsibility to maintain the integrity of the immigration system, prevent fraud, and ensure compliance with employment authorization requirements. However, the existence of these legitimate objectives does not establish that an exceptionally high fee is a necessary or effective solution.

A fee of $70,000 risks treating eligible students who comply with immigration rules as though they were responsible for the misconduct of others. The Department should demonstrate, with transparent evidence, why this specific amount is necessary, how it would reduce fraud, and whether less burdensome alternatives could achieve the same objectives.

Potential alternatives include enhanced verification of employment and employer information, targeted investigations of suspected fraud, improved oversight of noncompliant employers, and stronger coordination between educational institutions and the relevant government agencies. These measures would more directly address misconduct without imposing a prohibitive financial burden on the broader population of eligible students.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposal because the fees create an unreasonable financial barrier and hurt U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100
Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose finalizing the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee on the evidentiary rationale presently disclosed. Please consider the attached comment, "Fraud Evidence and the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees," including its claim ledger, incident-family index, sampling and denominator audit, program/time matrix, and specific disclosure requests. Research cutoff: October 29, 2026.

The record establishes serious fraud mechanisms. The Huang guilty plea describes a substantial false-employment-document business, and the connected Ji prosecution establishes a serious national-security case. Preventive action need not await convictions in every investigation or a nationally representative prevalence study. The unresolved question is how the evidence supports this fee's payer, trigger, amounts, and coverage.

The audit makes these findings:

The same May 2026 announcement is cited repeatedly. Footnote 56 describes 10,000 employers; the narrative describes more than 10,000 students associated with suspect employers. The original ICE video-page description supports the student unit. Correct the footnote, disclose the distinct employer and worksite counts, and identify any analysis affected by the error. This correction alone does not defeat the case for oversight.

The principal counts cannot be added into a national total of fraudulent students. The Huang plea's approximate components are 2,025 F-1 customers, 660 F-1 customers, and eight H-1B customers. The earlier criminal complaint’s Findream roster expressly includes Ji. The 2020 operation reports 15 arrests, not 15 convictions. Associations, documents, arrests, findings, and convictions require separate units and outcome definitions. Unlocated dispositions do not imply exoneration.

GAO-19-297 is a school-controls and fraud-risk audit, not a current national OPT prevalence study. Its selected interviews and covert tests expressly do not support population generalization. The NPRM acknowledges five implemented recommendations and two partially implemented recommendations. DHS should identify residual weaknesses and their relevance to current OPT categories, rather than assume historical conditions are unchanged.

Reducing participation, lowering the share of violations, and improving detection are different effects. A smaller program could reduce total fraud without preferentially excluding fraudulent actors. That supports one agency rationale but does not establish that ability to finance the fee identifies lawful participants or explains the two fee amounts. DHS permits cost shifting and does not tie payment to a particular employer. Its high-participation scenario assumes no contraction. Those features require a specific causal explanation.

I request that DHS:

Publish de-identified definitions, observation periods, selection methods, distinct counts, overlap information, and aggregate outcomes for the principal investigation, distinguishing indicators from substantiated findings.

Map the demonstrated mechanisms to initial OPT, STEM OPT, school-admission/attendance misconduct, and other programs; identify which weaknesses persist after reforms.

Explain separately the expected effects on participation, violation risk, school screening, and detection capacity, including cost shifting and misconduct arising after recommendation.

Connect the evidence and predictive assumptions to the school payer, recommendation trigger, $70,000/$30,000 amounts, and uniform coverage. State the actually operative screening baseline, including the preliminary postponement of the July 2026 duration-of-status rule.

Identify the material technical basis already public and provide an authenticated transcript and aggregate methods sufficient for meaningful comment, protecting sensitive investigations.

The attachment does not estimate national fraud prevalence or assert that every independent rationale fails. Some underlying materials were inaccessible through this audit's retrieval routes; that is not itself proof of agency nondisclosure. Withdraw the fees as presently supported, or resolve the material evidentiary and causal questions and revise the proposal before finalization.
comments.reason: Opposes finalizing the proposed OPT fees based on the evidentiary and quantitative rationale presently disclosed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS/ICE Docket ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01
OMB Control Number 1653-0038

I oppose finalizing the proposed OPT fees on the institutional-oversight rationale presented. Please consider the attached comment, "School Information and Control in Optional Practical Training," researched through October 29, 2026.

The attachment maps who possesses relevant information, when it becomes available, and who can act. It includes an actor-information-authority-time matrix, the end-to-end workflow, eight rule-grounded hypothetical cases, a risk-control matrix, incentive assumptions and counterexamples, and three narrow alternatives. It distinguishes verified requirements from inference and unresolved evidence.

The central problem is the connection between payment and a specific additional control. DHS acknowledges that initial OPT can be recommended before an employer is selected, while requiring the school to pay before recommendation. A school can verify academic eligibility and explain reporting duties at that point. It cannot authenticate the identity, premises, or supervision of an employer that has not yet been chosen. A STEM applicant with an employer-signed I-983 presents a materially different information setting. See 91 FR 64569-64570, 64574-64577.

Schools have genuine continuing duties. They review eligibility and required STEM plans, assess the relationship between work and study, maintain SEVIS, and receive reports and evaluations. But the 2016 STEM rule explains that DSOs are not expected to perform outside employer research or independently verify wage comparability. Existing duties and optional additional diligence must be distinguished from government investigation powers. See 81 FR 13095-13096 and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)-(12).

DHS has estimated extra review work: 0.5 additional DSO hours per application, including fee logging, plus 0.5 administrator hours for payment. The PRA discussion separately describes five minutes for payment confirmation. Please identify the new verification tasks, data access, exception handling, and ongoing monitoring represented by these estimates. The attachment does not assume that the five minutes must be subtracted from the half hour or that the resulting time is necessarily inadequate. See 91 FR 64584-64585, 64595, 64598.

The financial incentive also depends on who retains the cost. DHS expressly permits pass-through and outside funding. Before commitment, useful screening can prevent a school from wasting its own payment. After the specified authorization milestone, the payment is nonrefundable; an employer change does not itself trigger a new fee. A fixed sunk payment does not automatically increase the return to later monitoring, although reputation, existing duties, future participation, financing, or changed governance may do so. DHS should specify which mechanism it predicts under each funding arrangement.

I request that DHS:
1. Identify each additional school action by OPT category, risk, data source, lawful access, and timing, including no-employer and changed-employer cases.
2. Connect the half-hour review assumption and payment-confirmation collection to actual tasks and disclose or identify the fee-specific supporting analysis.
3. Explain retained incentives under school funding, reimbursement, employer funding, pooled costs, and financing, including after payment becomes nonrefundable.
4. Compare targeted employer-discrepancy review, STEM change-and-exception review, and independent review of potentially complicit schools, including workload, privacy, false flags, and correction procedures.
5. Distinguish reduced participation from improved compliance among remaining participants and from reallocated government enforcement effort.

DHS already considered broader procedural alternatives and separately invokes participation reduction and protection of U.S. workers. This comment does not deny those rationales or demand perfect information. It asks for a reasoned, verifiable connection between the proposed payment and the particular institutional behavior claimed. The attachment also reconciles its operational baseline with the September 14 postponement of the separate fixed-duration rule and identifies inaccessible supporting materials without asserting that the entire docket is silent.
comments.reason: Opposes finalizing the proposed OPT fees on the institutional-oversight rationale presented.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
Comment on Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I oppose finalizing the proposed fee rule on its present specification and quantitative explanation. Please consider the attached "Verification of the proposed OPT fee specification and population model," including its clause-linked reference model, synthetic scenarios, calculation reproductions, and complete executable source.

The attachment distinguishes proposed regulatory text, preamble explanations, national estimates, school-level estimates, and reported SEVP communications. Its principal findings are:

1. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3) makes the $30,000 fee depend on both prior OPT participation and payment of the $70,000 initial fee. That condition does not expire after one year. A legally feasible synthetic student with a pre-effective-date post-completion recommendation can first become liable for $70,000 on a Year 2 STEM recommendation, while the national proxy assigns later STEM $30,000. This is a conditional event-level difference, not an estimate of national error. Recommendation-date and authorization-start-date effects can offset and must be reconciled.

2. The national model classifies ordinary OPT and STEM authorizations by employment-start year. The legal obligation arises before a recommendation and depends on individual history. Later ordinary OPT can qualify for the subsequent fee, and two recommendations within Year 1 can be initial and subsequent. The school-level analysis uses a different historical classification and separately selected annual maxima. DHS should explain and reconcile these methods.

3. A paid initial attempt followed by denial or withdrawal without participation does not clearly satisfy the subsequent-fee condition. Refunded payment history, replacement recommendations, and EAD issuance versus receipt also need precise treatment. The reference model returns UNRESOLVED where the text does not select a rule. It does not charge for every SEVIS edit or employer change.

4. All 84 monetary summary cells in Tables 4 and 6-10 reproduce within display rounding. The attachment therefore rejects an arithmetic-error allegation. It separately shows that the high/low scenarios change both baseline populations and participation assumptions. The inferred lagged aggregate ratio does not itself establish a linked-person transition rate. The PRA body follows the primary population while footnote 143 names the high population; that appears to require a targeted correction.

5. DHS already acknowledges $100,000 for split pre-completion and post-completion OPT versus $70,000 for post-completion alone and predicts substitution. The attachment tests that assumption without calling the acknowledged distinction an undisclosed defect. Equal training duration alone does not establish irrational treatment.

Please publish an event-definition crosswalk; carry unpaid and paid cohorts through all analysis years; reconcile national and school methods; define payment history, participation, and replacement recommendations; identify the controlling refund milestone; and disclose full-precision calculations and aggregate counts sufficient to test these issues. Separate baseline choice from participation restrictions, clarify the 157,494 historical average versus the 88,374 low scenario, and reconcile the PRA footnote.

Aggregate or de-identified counts and a reproducible method are sufficient. No personal student records or perfect prediction are requested. If revised methodology or fee incidence materially changes the supporting basis, provide an opportunity for public comment before finalization. The attachment supplies specific requests and the agency's strongest responses, without claiming that a synthetic counterexample establishes nationwide materiality.

Research cutoff: October 29, 2026. This comment addresses the October 8 NPRM. The published rule-comment deadline is November 9, 2026; the separate December 7 information-collection deadline does not extend it.
comments.reason: Opposes finalizing the fee rule due to flaws in its specification and quantitative population model.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
Comment on Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I oppose adopting the proposed OPT fee provisions in their present form. Please consider the attached "Treasury Receipts and Refunds for Proposed OPT Fees," including its authority matrix, twelve transaction cases, process map and reproducible calculations. This comment assumes charging authority solely to examine whether collection, correction and refund rules operate coherently.

The most direct finding is a mismatch in refund cutoff events. The preamble describes receipt of an EAD, while proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) uses issuance, a grant of the document and a grant of an OPT extension. DHS should define one controlling event, identify its timestamp and explain what happens when approval or issuance occurs during refund processing. Physical delivery should not be assumed to control.

The post-EAD refund bar also needs an express distinction between a refund of a valid fee and correction of duplicate, excess or misassociated collections. DHS may reasonably intend the bar to apply only to a properly assessed charge. Please say so and identify an applicable correction procedure that does not require removal of an otherwise valid recommendation merely to correct money never owed or a record association.

Refund and reapplication outcomes remain insufficiently specified in the authenticated NPRM. The subsequent-fee provision requires both prior OPT participation and initial payment. A retained initial payment after denial or withdrawal does not by itself establish participation. Please publish outcomes for initial payment refunded, payment retained without participation, replacement of an erroneous recommendation for the same period, and actual prior participation. Explain reuse of retained payment and when an approved refund extinguishes payment credit.

This comment rejects the claim that miscellaneous receipts cannot be refunded. 31 USC 1322(b)(2), Treasury account 20X1807 and existing Treasury procedures provide a route for qualifying erroneous receipts. GAO's SEC decision, B-239769.2 (July 24, 1992), also recognizes that valid substantive exemption authority can make an earlier payment refundable. The narrower question is how DHS will classify and certify a granted no-EAD refund of a fee validly paid before recommendation. Please identify the substantive basis, appropriation, certifying agency, payee and accounting treatment by event.

Please also define when payment is legally effective, what evidence the DSO may rely on, and how a timely payment attached to the wrong record is corrected. Explain recommendation removal while a USCIS application remains pending, the consequences of later payment returns and the prevention of duplicate redress through a bank reversal and an agency refund. The attachment does not assume a particular payment platform or allege an actual system failure.

DHS already permits outside funding and acknowledges financial-system and refund costs. Ordinary processing work is included in Table 5. Please assess incremental correction, refund and reconciliation work separately and avoid counting the same work twice. The attachment's cash and financing figures are labeled scenarios, not measured error rates, national forecasts or claims to government-paid interest.

Finally, publish refund criteria, written-decision procedures, acknowledgment and decision targets, and a factual-error correction route. The proposal's administrative-appeal bar does not itself determine court jurisdiction. General timing and denial-reasons duties already exist under 5 USC 555; operational targets would make the procedure usable. Resolve material obligations in the final rule or an authoritative explanation and identify which later guidance merely implements those choices.

Research cutoff: October 29, 2026. Direct docket access was unavailable, so the attachment does not claim exhaustive coverage of supporting documents or existing comments. Its decisive textual findings rest on the official NPRM, and its fiscal analysis identifies existing authorities that defeat broader objections.
comments.reason: Opposes adopting the fee provisions due to uncoordinated treasury receipts, refunds, and calculation issues.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100
Optional Practical Training Fees, RIN 1653-AB01

Please consider the attached comment, "Transition Feasibility and Reliance Cohorts for Proposed OPT Fees," including its six analytical appendices. I oppose adopting the proposed fees with the transition arrangements presently described.

DHS expressly considered reliance interests. This comment asks whether its chosen transition adequately addresses distinguishable existing commitments and the legal calendars governing adjustment. It does not claim a right to OPT approval, immutable rules, or automatic grandfathering.

First, the proposed regulatory text uses the DSO recommendation date, while portions of the reliance discussion refer to applications or subsequent requests. DHS should harmonize these terms and expressly preserve an otherwise valid pre-effective-date recommendation through a timely application and adjudication. It should distinguish an unchanged replacement I-20 from an expired recommendation, substantive change, or new recommendation.

Second, the attachment provides an executed, reproducible calendar analysis. Under the operative baseline identified there, initial post-completion filing opens 90 days before completion and must follow a recommendation within 30 days. A usable recommendation therefore cannot precede completion by more than 120 days. The corresponding necessary outer bound for STEM is 150 days before initial OPT expiration. These mathematical bounds do not authorize early recommendations. They show why some enrolled students cannot obtain a usable pre-cutoff recommendation even with timely preparation. Other scenarios are only calendar-compatible and still require school, employer, filing, and eligibility prerequisites.

Third, protecting existing initial OPT does not necessarily protect a defined STEM continuation. A first recommendation after the cutoff can require the $70,000 initial payment even after substantial initial OPT participation. A timely pending-STEM work extension depends on a proper application; it cannot replace the recommendation and payment prerequisites.

Fourth, DHS should reconcile its legal baseline with the September 14, 2026 nationwide postponement of the fixed-admission rule. That was preliminary relief, not final invalidation. The attachment uses the prior baseline, supplemented by the 2025 cap-gap amendment, and identifies variables requiring updating if the litigation posture changes.

I request that DHS:
1. Clarify the controlling trigger and adopt an explicit recommendation savings and correction rule.
2. Assess enrolled, near-completion, recommended, pending, approved, active-OPT, and STEM-window cohorts separately, using aggregate counts and disclosed missing fields.
3. Test transition feasibility across plausible effective dates, distinguishing legal deadlines from uncertain processing intervals and continuous work authorization from permission to remain.
4. Compare finite alternatives: existing-recommendation savings, a specified existing-program cohort, one defined STEM continuation stage, and a longer implementation lead period. Specify cutoffs, proof, transfer and degree treatment, sunsets, anti-gaming safeguards, administrative costs, and integrity tradeoffs.
5. Distinguish delayed receipts from permanently forgone receipts and fiscal transfers from resource costs. Identify evidence supporting or defeating the need for a cohort accommodation.

The legal analysis addresses Fox, Regents, Encino Motorcars, Bowen, and the adverse 2025 FDA v. Wages and White Lion decision. Prospective operation and discretionary approval matter, but they do not alone answer every concrete reliance question. DHS may conclude that supported policy objectives outweigh serious reliance after a reasoned comparison.

The attachment states its October 29, 2026 research cutoff and access limits. It does not claim exhaustive docket review, national cohort estimates, or verified private commitments. Its contribution is a source-grounded cohort map, reproducible boundary tests, and operationally specified alternatives with explicit tradeoffs.
comments.reason: Opposes adopting the proposed fees with the transition arrangements and timeline calculations presently described.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Formal Objection and Request for Withdrawal of Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

To the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE):

This public comment is submitted to formally and register a profound and comprehensive objection to the Department of Homeland Security’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published on October 8, 2026, which proposes exorbitant fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent extensions.

Rather than serving its stated goals, this proposed rule will inflict severe, lasting damage on U.S. higher education, undermine America’s global technological leadership, and trigger widespread economic collateral damage. Because the rule is fundamentally unsupportable from both an economic and a legal standpoint, we urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 in its entirety.

The primary reasons requiring the immediate withdrawal of this proposal include:

1. Severe Destabilization of U.S. Higher Education and Regional Economies
Financial Strain on Non-Profit Institutions: DHS’s own analysis concedes that over 60% of small and regional non-profit educational institutions will face severe budgetary pressures, with impacts ranging from 1% to over 20% of annual revenue. For many institutions, international student enrollment and the associated programs are essential to operational stability. Imposing these prohibitive costs will force many colleges to cut academic programs and face acute financial distress.

Disruption of Regional Innovation Hubs: Academic institutions serve as the economic and intellectual anchors of their local communities. By sharply curtailing practical training opportunities and draining institutional resources, this rule will set off a negative economic ripple effect throughout college towns and regional technology sectors across the country.

2. Undermining U.S. Technological Competitiveness and Talent Retention
Accelerating a Critical "Brain Death" in STEM: The United States is engaged in an intense global race for supremacy in critical sectors such as artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and biotechnology. International graduates from U.S. universities are a vital component of this talent pipeline. By erecting a massive $70,000 financial barrier, DHS is actively driving top-tier scientific and engineering talent away from the United States.

Directly Benefiting Global Competitors: Highly skilled graduates who are priced out of the U.S. labor market will redirect their talents to our primary international competitors—including Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union—all of which actively welcome high-skilled professionals. This policy creates a self-inflicted brain drain that directly harms U.S. long-term economic growth and national security.

3. Undue Burden on Employers and Incentivizing Offshoring
Acute Labor Shortages: From research laboratories and academic medical centers to innovative tech startups and enterprises, employers depend on practical training to address specialized workforce needs. A six-figure financial barrier will severely restrict access to this essential talent pool.

Disincentivizing Domestic R&D: When employers are legally or financially foreclosed from hiring top-tier specialists within the United States, they will not automatically replace them with local workers for specialized technical roles. Instead, companies will be heavily incentivized to relocate their research, development, and high-tech operations overseas, moving valuable economic activity and tax revenue entirely outside of the U.S. economy.

4. Flawed Justifications and Internal Contradictions
Disproportionate Collective Punishment: DHS attempts to justify these sweeping fees by citing isolated instances of fraud and bad actors. However, penalizing thousands of accredited, law-abiding non-profit universities and hundreds of thousands of honest students with a prohibitive financial penalty is an disproportionate and arbitrary regulatory approach.

Contradictory Agency Statements: The rule explicitly acknowledges that these collected fees will be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and will not be retained by ICE or SEVP to fund enforcement or oversight operations. This internal contradiction undermines the agency’s central premise that the fees are required to sustain program integrity, rendering the rulemaking logically flawed and vulnerable under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Conclusion
This proposed rule miscalculates the immense value of international students and practical training to the United States. Rather than strengthening the immigration system, it inflicts profound, disproportionate harm on the U.S. economy, academic institutions, and technological competitiveness.

We strongly urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 immediately.
comments.reason: Registers comprehensive objection to the NPRM and urges DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to implement an unprecedented $70,000 fee for the initial 12-month Optional Practical Training (OPT) period and an additional $30,000 fee for the 24-month STEM OPT extension. If finalized, this aggregate $100,000 fee will inflict severe, long-lasting damage on American innovation, compromise our national security, and fundamentally undermine our nation's economic competitiveness.

The United States has long been the premier global destination for the world’s most talented STEM students. OPT and the STEM OPT extension are the primary bridge allowing these high-skilled, domestically trained graduates to enter the American workforce, transition into employment-based visas, and contribute directly to our economy. International students represent nearly half of all physics PhD graduates from U.S. universities, three-quarters of whom choose to remain in the U.S. to work after graduation. Furthermore, over 80% of these foreign-born physics PhDs rely on OPT to begin their careers in industry or academia.
By introducing an insurmountable financial barrier, this rule will deter the world's best minds from seeking education in the U.S. and force existing graduates to leave. 

American industries face significant workforce shortages in leading-edge, physics-relevant sectors, such as semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing. Independent economic analyses demonstrate that a one-third reduction in international STEM graduates would lower the high-skill STEM workers in the country, cutting economic productivity growth by an estimated 3% to 6%.
The Department’s justification that universities can simply absorb or selectively fund these fees ignores the rigid financial realities of public and non-profit higher education. Academic institutions cannot legally or ethically redirect research grants, tuition dollars, or taxpayer funds to cover individual post-graduation employment fees. The real-world consequence of this rule will be the immediate elimination of international student participation in vital post-graduate industrial training and postdoctoral research.

Instead of protecting American jobs, this regulation serves as a direct subsidy to foreign competitor nations. Forcing thousands of highly trained, U.S.-educated scientists out of our national ecosystem ensures that their innovations, patents, and entrepreneurial endeavors will benefit economies abroad rather than driving wealth and technological preeminence here at home.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Louis Lyu
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (ICEB-2026-0100). A $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT per student would effectively end Optional Practical Training as a workable program.

Although the fee would formally be paid by SEVP-certified schools, no school can absorb tens of thousands of dollars per student. Schools will either pass the cost on to students, who cannot pay it, or stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, the practical effect is the same: the pathway is closed.

OPT is how many international students gain the professional experience that U.S. employers need and that often leads to longer-term employment-based immigration. Eliminating it in practice would push talented graduates trained at U.S. universities to other countries, harming American employers, research labs, and the competitiveness of U.S. higher education.

The stated goal of deterring fraud does not justify a fee of this magnitude. Fraud should be addressed through enforcement against bad actors, not a blanket fee that punishes every legitimate student and school. I urge DHS/ICE to withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the rule as it would end OPT in practice, urging DHS/ICE to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yeyi Su
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed $100,000 fee for OPT. International students already contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through tuition, taxes, and innovation. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The American higher education system truly is one of the world's best places to gain access to advanced research exposure and graduate coursework. I consider myself fortunate to have been a part of it and to have worked closely with American faculty - alums of top-tier U.S. institutions like CMU whose teaching and research credentials are second to none - across advanced facets of Computer Architecture, Computer Networks, and Operating Systems. Without their tutelage, my ability to understand and build reliable systems in this new age of AI would not be what it is today.

I understand I do not speak for everyone, but I have no intention of overstaying my welcome in the United States. All I ask is that genuine students who follow every rule and simply wish to complete their education with real-world practical training in fields like Kernel Development and Distributed Systems get the opportunity to do so lawfully. During OPT, students work alongside American peers, contribute directly to U.S. engineering and infrastructure teams, and fulfill the hands-on training component of degrees they invested heavily to earn at American universities before returning home.

The field of computer science became what it is today because people from multiple backgrounds came together to build innovative solutions. Linus Torvalds from Finland and Richard Stallman from the United States both contributed to giving us GNU/Linux—a platform that powers billions of machines across the world right now, including the one I am typing this on and the government server rack where this comment will be stored. Many of us still care deeply about exchanging ideas and building reliable systems that benefit everyone, including American citizens. The OPT program is the vital bridge that allows students to see how classroom theory maps to production reality.

Therefore, it is my humble request that DHS withdraw or reconsider this proposed rule (ICEB-2026-0100). Even though the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent STEM OPT fee are nominally assessed on universities, DHS's own economic analysis acknowledges that schools will either pass these astronomical costs onto students or cease recommending students for OPT entirely. Turning a $470 application process into a $70,000 to $100,000 burden does not target fraud. It simply prices legitimate universities and honest students out of existence. Heavier scrutiny, site visits, and strict verification of genuine roles, employers, and degrees are completely welcome; those of us who have nothing to hide and have come here with pure, lawful non-immigrant intent are more than happy to comply with rigorous verification requirements.

Thank you for your time.
comments.reason: Argues the proposed rule and fees would harm international students and impede practical training opportunities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sri CM Consulting
comments.commentText:
RE: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 / RIN 1653-AB01
I am writing to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to establish a 70,000 dollar fee for initial Optional Practical Training recommendations and a 30,000 dollar fee for subsequent extensions. This regulatory update is a necessary step to protect American workers, ensure fair labor practices, and address the funding imbalances within our immigration and educational oversight systems.
First, the current framework creates an unintended subsidy that disadvantages domestic graduates. Because employers are exempt from paying FICA taxes for foreign graduates on OPT, hiring from this pool carries a built in financial incentive over hiring American citizens or permanent residents. Implementing this recommendation fee on institutions creates a much needed economic counterweight. It ensures that the utilization of foreign student work programs is driven by genuine, specialized talent needs rather than a desire to reduce labor costs at the expense of American workers.
Second, the administrative and investigative burden of managing the OPT program has grown exponentially. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program requires significant federal resources to monitor compliance, track employment data, and prevent fraud. The proposed fee structure appropriately shifts the fiscal responsibility of this oversight from the American taxpayer onto the institutions that actively benefit from marketing these work pathways to international students.
Finally, this rule encourages universities to reinvest in domestic talent. By attaching a significant cost to the administrative pipeline of foreign student placement, institutions will be incentivized to focus more heavily on the career placement, recruitment, and training of American students, particularly in critical STEM fields.
For these reasons, I urge the Department of Homeland Security to finalize and implement this rule as proposed to safeguard the domestic labor market and ensure a self-sustaining oversight model.
Sincerely,
Sri CM Consulting
comments.reason: Expresses strong support for the proposed OPT fees to protect American workers and balance oversight costs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01
Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I oppose adoption of the proposed OPT fees on the present explanation of their connection to documented oversight deficiencies. Please consider my attachment, "Oversight Remediation and Residual Risks in the Proposed OPT Fees," which provides recommendation histories, source pinpoints, status and confidence tables, agency defenses, and targeted alternatives. Research cutoff: October 29, 2026.

The record supports a narrower objection than a claim that DHS ignored all prior reforms. Footnote 81 correctly acknowledges five implemented and two partially implemented recommendations from GAO-19-297. The current GAO page confirms that distribution and adds July 2026 information about developing a training platform within an existing contract. The two unfinished recommendations concern mandatory DSO training, including fraud-specific training, and verification of completion. Payment does not itself deploy that platform, supply instruction, or verify completion. It may affect incentives or workload, but those are separate mechanisms.

The longer chronology shows both real corrective actions and continuing gaps. All six GAO-14-356 recommendations are now Closed Implemented following employer-data, monitoring, risk-assessment, and guidance changes. GAO-23-106114 nevertheless found missing required employer information in later 2016-2020 records. ICE reported operational follow-up in 2020 and, after the later report, 1,291 letters in February 2023, with 593 updates and 188 inquiries. Inquiries are not completed corrections, and these outputs do not establish a national fraud reduction. The earlier and later missingness figures are not comparable causal estimates.

The attachment also distinguishes the 2020 Ombudsman report's two mitigation strategies from formal recommendations, records later coordination and communication measures, and separates school, employer, official, and student workloads. Recommendation closure establishes action within its scope, not fraud-free operation. Open status does not establish inactivity. Recent fraud can defeat earlier controls, and training cannot by itself prevent deliberate collusion.

DHS expressly states that these receipts would go to Treasury and could not be retained or used by ICE. The relevant claimed benefits are therefore deterrence, greater school scrutiny, and workload reduction. Fewer student cases could help, but school recertification, official training, and employer-network investigations do not necessarily decline proportionally. DHS already discusses site visits and reporting alternatives; the request is a more specific comparison informed by its own remediation history.

Before deciding whether to adopt these fees, please:

1. Identify the present residual mechanism for each material oversight finding, its corrective-action history, and how payment is expected to address it.
2. Update the training rollout, mandatory coverage, completion verification, and remaining contract or staffing dependencies; explain how the November 2025 initiative relates to the July 2026 GAO update.
3. Provide recent aggregate operating evidence for controls materially relied upon, including employer-data follow-up, analytics use, and recertification queue aging, with defined periods and denominators.
4. Link the material 2025-2026 examples to applicable controls and underlying conduct dates, using de-identified summaries where needed.
5. Explain the workload pathway, including new payment and refund tasks, and compare completing training, systematic data follow-up and analytics, and targeted use of existing review authority.
6. Establish measures that distinguish reduced participation from improved compliance among remaining participants.

These requests seek a reasoned connection between evidence and the selected measure. They do not demand zero fraud, perfect information, or exhaustion of every alternative. The attachment identifies evidence that would narrow or resolve its objections and records material retrieval limits. Please withdraw or revise the proposal unless the final record supplies an adequate current explanation.
comments.reason: Explicitly opposes the adoption of the proposed OPT fees due to lack of adequate explanation and oversight.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). This comment is about startups and small employers. The NPRM expects employers to help pay the $70,000 and $30,000 fees, but it never counts these employers, sizes them, or asks whether they can pay.

1. DHS relies on employer money it never analyzed

The NPRM says schools "may pass the financial obligation" of the fee onto "F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." The RIA assumes that if OPT is worth more than the fee, "affected parties could collectively cost share to preserve OPT." The IRFA then says school impacts "may be overstated" because schools can obtain funding from "employers or organizations." So employer payments are used to shrink the small-entity findings. Yet the RIA gives employers one line: they "may face productivity losses." It has no count of OPT employers, no size data, and no estimate of what share of the fee they would bear. DHS cannot lower its burden estimate for small schools by assuming payments from small businesses it never studied.

2. Cost sharing works only for large, planned hiring

The initial fee must be paid before the DSO enters the recommendation, and initial OPT requires no job offer. Employers who can commit $70,000 per student months ahead of a start date are large firms with campus recruiting pipelines and steady budgets. A seed-stage startup or a 15-person engineering firm hires when it wins a contract or closes a funding round. By then the student's recommendation window has passed or the fee has already been paid by someone else. The cost-share mechanism DHS relies on is open to big incumbents and closed to most small firms.

3. For STEM OPT, the fee is a per-hire charge on the best-documented employers

For the STEM OPT extension, the employer is known before the fee is due. The student must submit Form I-983, with the employer's attestations, to the DSO "prior to the new DSO recommendation." STEM OPT employers must also use E-Verify (NPRM footnote 52). The $30,000 subsequent fee therefore lands on a specific, identified employer that has signed a training plan, enrolled in E-Verify, and is subject to site visits. A large firm can spread $30,000 across a big payroll. For a small company hiring one graduate, it is a large share of that role's first-year cost. The rule taxes the most transparent hiring channel hardest, and hits small firms hardest within it.

4. The fraud DHS cites is the kind a fee does not stop

DHS's evidence describes shell companies, "phantom employees," shared addresses, and residential worksites. Operations that sell job letters can add the fee to their price. Legitimate small employers cannot pass it to anyone. A flat charge drives out honest small firms and leaves well-funded schemes in place. DHS also concedes that STEM OPT employers "are not required to submit any business documents" and that attestations are not verified "unless and until there is a site visit." Asking for an EIN check or proof of business at the I-983 stage would target the shell-company problem directly. It would cost a real small employer little.

5. DHS already holds the data it says it lacks

The RIA says DHS lacks data "on the value placed on OPT by ... employers." But Form I-983 asks each STEM OPT employer for its EIN, its NAICS code, and its number of full-time U.S. employees. DHS could tabulate STEM OPT employers by size and industry from records it already collects. It did not. It also says employers "can minimize this impact by recruiting U.S. citizens." A small firm cannot easily do that for a specialized role when it competes with large firms for the same graduates. E.O. 12866 asks agencies to consider distributive impacts. A rule that changes which firms can hire STEM graduates calls for that analysis.

6. Entrepreneurship by graduates

[Optional, if the commenter can supply facts: describe a startup founded or staffed by OPT or STEM OPT workers, its size, and how the fee would have affected hiring.] The NPRM does not discuss graduates who start companies on OPT or the small firms that hire them first.

7. Request

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any fee, it should: (a) use I-983 and SEVIS employer data to count OPT and STEM OPT employers by size and industry; (b) estimate what share of the fee small employers would bear and treat that in the RFA and E.O. 12866 analysis; (c) stop counting employer contributions as relief for small schools until it has shown employers can pay; and (d) adopt employer-side verification, such as EIN and proof-of-business checks at the I-983 stage, in place of a flat fee.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed rule, arguing DHS failed to analyze the severe impacts on small employers.
