comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed fee increase for Optional Practical Training (OPT) processing. While framed as a measure to generate revenue and combat fraud, a proposed hike of this magnitude—raising filing fees from $470 to $70,000 for Post-Completion OPT and $30,000 for STEM OPT—is fundamentally prohibitive. Rather than reforming the system, this rule would effectively eliminate experiential learning opportunities for international students and cause irreparable harm to American higher education and the U.S. economy.

International students already navigate an extraordinarily competitive and challenging job search environment, often accepting unpaid internships or volunteer roles simply to gain valuable U.S. work experience within their limited authorization window. An exorbitant fee structure creates an insurmountable financial barrier:

-Impact on Higher Education Institutions: Educational institutions are not in a position to absorb tens of millions of dollars in processing costs to recommend eligible F-1 students for OPT benefits. Furthermore, because international enrollment directly funds critical academic programs and research, driving international students away will severely compromise university revenue streams and threaten the viability of many degree programs.

-Impact on Students and Employers: While the rule places the financial burden on schools, DHS acknowledges that many schools might not be able to afford this and would pass on the fee burden to students.  Expecting students to bear a $70,000 filing fee—an amount that frequently exceeds an entire year of tuition—is entirely unrealistic. Likewise, few employers, particularly small businesses and startups seeking top international talent, can afford such substantial fees to support entry-level practical training.

-Misalignment with Anti-Fraud Goals: The application process already includes rigorous safeguards: Designated School Officials (DSOs) thoroughly vet eligibility before issuance, and USCIS formally adjudicates every OPT application. Particularly with STEM OPT, each job must meet eligibility requirements before a DSO can even recommend the student, and each student/employer fills out a comprehensive training plan which includes frequent evaluations. Punishing law-abiding students who have maintained continuous status, satisfied all academic requirements, and adhered strictly to prior employment regulations (such as CPT) is not a targeted anti-fraud strategy; it is an outright prohibition of the F-1 practical training benefit.

The Department's projection of significant revenue generation rests on the false assumption that participation rates will remain constant. In reality, schools, employers, and students simply cannot pay these amounts.

According to data from NAFSA, international students contributed over $40 billion to the U.S. economy in recent years. Practical work experience is a primary driver for prospective students choosing to invest their tuition dollars in the United States. If this pathway is effectively closed, bright and talented global scholars will choose to bring their skills, innovation, and economic contributions to competing nations. Moreover, domestic students will lose the rich, diverse perspectives and cross-cultural collaboration that international peers bring to American classrooms and research labs.

This proposed fee hike would effectively dismantle the F-1 OPT program, severely diminish global trust in U.S. higher education, and hurt American competitiveness. I strongly urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and maintain reasonable, accessible fee structures for international student practical training.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed fee increase, stating it is prohibitive and harms the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by United Methodist Church Summit
comments.commentText:
**Re: Public Comment Opposing Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees**

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees for international students. As a psychologist, a graduate of theological seminary, and the Minister of Mental Health Ministry at a United Methodist church in New Jersey, I have witnessed firsthand the extraordinary contributions international seminarians make to our churches and communities.

Our congregation has been fortunate to welcome international theological students into our ministries. These individuals bring far more than academic knowledge or a desire to gain practical experience. They bring their faith, compassion, cultural perspectives, theological insights, and a deep commitment to serving others. They enrich our worship, challenge us to broaden our understanding of the world, and remind us that faith and service transcend national boundaries.

In my own ministry, I have had the privilege of working alongside an international seminary intern. Our work focuses on supporting the mental health and emotional well-being of people in our congregation and the wider community, including children, families, and individuals facing difficult life circumstances. The opportunity to collaborate with someone whose life experiences and cultural background differ from my own has enriched our ministry in ways that cannot be measured financially.

As a psychologist, I understand the importance of learning from people whose experiences and perspectives are different from our own. Such relationships foster empathy, challenge assumptions, and help us become more compassionate and effective in serving others. These are not incidental benefits of international educational exchange; they are essential to building healthy, inclusive communities.

The United Methodist Church is a global denomination. Our understanding of ministry is grounded in the belief that we are connected to one another across geographic, cultural, and national boundaries. International seminarians make that connection tangible. They remind us that the church is not simply a local institution but part of a much larger human family.

The proposed OPT fees, potentially reaching tens of thousands of dollars, would create an overwhelming financial barrier for international students and the congregations that might otherwise welcome them. Churches, particularly those with limited financial resources, simply cannot absorb such costs. The result would be the loss of valuable opportunities for practical ministerial training and the loss of gifted individuals whose contributions strengthen our communities.

There is also a fundamental contradiction in welcoming international students to study theology and prepare for lives of service in this country, only to place extraordinary financial obstacles in their path when they seek to put that education into practice.

Our communities need more opportunities for understanding, connection, and service across cultures, not fewer. At a time when division and isolation are significant challenges in our society, international students offer us opportunities to build bridges rather than barriers.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and preserve accessible opportunities for international graduates to gain meaningful professional and ministerial experience.

The loss of these opportunities would not simply be a loss for international students. It would be a profound loss for our churches, our communities, and the people we are called to serve.

Sincerely,

**Alison W. Johnson, PsyD, MDiv**  
Minister of Mental Health Ministry  
United Methodist Church of Summit  
Summit, New Jersey

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Hannah Ewing

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published at 91 Fed. Reg. 64566. comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section VI, particularly 91 FR 64578.
I oppose the inference that the reported approximately 20-percent annual OPT participation share demonstrates that reliance on OPT is generally weak. This objection recognizes DHS's authority to change policy and the proposal's existing transition provisions; it requests a better-supported assessment of affected cohorts.

First, annual OPT participation divided by the entire F-1 higher-education population is not a graduating cohort's eventual participation rate. The denominator includes students who have not reached graduation. Nor does the ratio identify how the availability of OPT influenced enrollment choices. DHS should publish cohort-based estimates and distinguish descriptive participation from evidence about the reasons for choosing U.S. education.

Second, OPT need not be the sole reason for studying in the United States to create a substantial reliance interest. Educational quality, degree choice, and opportunities for related practical training can jointly influence commitments. DHS v. Regents explains that temporary or discretionary benefits do not automatically eliminate reliance interests; the agency must assess their existence and significance and weigh them against competing concerns.[1] Regents does not require permanent continuation of OPT or a particular exemption. Here, DHS has discussed reliance, so the question is whether its evidence and accommodations adequately address the affected groups.

Third, relevant public experience varies sharply by field and career stage. AIP reports that 82 percent of surveyed non-U.S.-citizen physics and astronomy PhD recipients from academic years 2022–23 and 2023–24 who remained in the United States to work used OPT.[2] This is a conditional, field-specific survey result, not a participation estimate for all international students or a forecast of departures. It demonstrates the need for disaggregated analysis rather than reliance on one aggregate ratio.

The proposed 60-day delay and protection for recommendations predating the effective date are meaningful. They do not by themselves explain the treatment of already enrolled students who cannot yet seek recommendations. The transition text and transition-year analysis indicate that a later STEM recommendation can trigger the new $70,000 initial fee when no such initial fee has previously been paid (91 FR 64583, 64594; proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), 91 FR 64600). An existing approved OPT period is distinct from a future recommendation.

Please replace the unsupported inference with cohort-, degree-, and field-specific analysis. Compare protection through an already enrolled student's current degree and associated OPT/STEM sequence, a longer transition, and phased implementation, and explain why the selected approach reasonably balances reliance and enforcement objectives.

[1] DHS v. Regents, opinion pp. 23–26: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-587_5ifl.pdf

[2] AIP, Table 1 (Nov. 18, 2025): https://www.aip.org/statistics/international-physics-and-astronomy-graduate-students-and-phd-recipients-in-u-s
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule's rationale regarding OPT participation and requests a better assessment of affected cohorts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section IV.C, 91 FR 64575–64576; proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), 91 FR 64600.
I oppose finalizing the $70,000 initial charge and $30,000 subsequent charge without a more specific explanation of their statutory basis and calibration. The proposal's general immigration-management authorities and references to H-1B payments do not resolve why these particular OPT amounts are authorized and reasonably suited to their stated purposes.

First, comparison with H-1B payments does not establish equivalence. OPT and H-1B have different eligibility rules, durations, institutional roles, and legal frameworks. Likewise, the observation that students already incur substantial tuition does not establish willingness or ability to pay an additional charge for practical training. DHS should explain the expected effects of different fee levels on both substantiated abuse and legitimate participation.

Second, authority to regulate nonimmigrant admission and continued stay should be distinguished from authority to impose this particular financial obligation on schools. INA section 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), grants substantial authority over time and conditions.[1] Washtech upheld broad authority to regulate OPT, but did not decide the validity of this monetary obligation.[2] DHS should explain precisely how the statutes cited in Section III.A authorize this school-paid, deterrence-oriented collection and the criteria limiting its amount. 31 U.S.C. §3302 concerns the disposition of money received; routing funds to Treasury does not itself supply authority to collect them. This comment does not assume that every regulatory charge must equal administrative cost, or that Treasury deposit alone makes a charge unlawful.

Third, the rule's own implementation analysis illustrates a poorly explained consequence of the schedule. Section VII.A.5.d(3) recognizes that dividing the same total 12 months between pre-completion and post-completion OPT would trigger $100,000, compared with $70,000 for post-completion OPT alone, and predicts institutions will discourage pre-completion OPT. DHS should explain why this additional $30,000 reflects a relevant difference in risk or policy benefit rather than merely a difference in recommendation timing.

DHS's strongest response is that these are regulatory conditions intended to deter abuse, not ordinary service-cost charges. That makes the connection between authority, amount, deterrence, and collateral effects particularly important. A claim that some participation should be discouraged does not select $70,000 or $30,000 from the range of possible amounts.

Please withdraw the proposed amounts, or publish their specific statutory rationale and a reproducible comparison of lower amounts and designs related to risk or authorized training duration. Identify the associated enforcement benefits, lawful participation losses, and distribution of financial burdens before adopting a final schedule.

[1] 8 U.S.C. 1184(a): https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/8/1184

[2] Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022): https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2022/10/21-5028-1967339.pdf
comments.reason: The commenter opposes finalizing the charges without a more specific explanation of their statutory basis and calibration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section IV.B, 91 FR 64572–64574
I oppose the inference that the cited labor-market evidence adequately supports a uniform $70,000/$30,000 OPT charge. Protecting U.S. workers, including recent graduates exposed to competition, is a legitimate objective. The proposal still needs to connect that objective to this instrument across the populations covered.

First, the quoted 2.6–5.1 percent wage and 6.1–10.8 percent employment counterfactuals match Bound, Khanna, and Morales's 2017 study of H-1B immigration, calibrated using 1994–2001 data.[1] The same study reports gains to complementary workers and consumers and an increase in overall U.S.-native welfare. It is a general-equilibrium model of a historical H-1B setting, not an estimate of this OPT fee's effect. DHS should address its full findings and explain their relevance to contemporary OPT rather than rely only on its within-occupation distributional losses.

Second, an increase in foreign labor supply and elevated unemployment do not, by themselves, identify the effect of OPT on U.S. employment. Substitution can differ by age, field, experience, and location, while firms may adjust investment and scale. A uniform school charge also does not directly require higher wages or prevent a particular employer from replacing workers. DHS should compare the proposed instrument with feasible measures directed at the specific labor practices it seeks to change.

Third, evidence unfavorable to blanket defenses of OPT deserves explicit consideration. Demirci's 2020 study of a STEM-related visa-policy change finds lower employment for recently graduated native-born master's holders alongside higher earnings for experienced native-born master's holders in the same field.[2] That evidence supports concern for exposed workers. It also demonstrates that the effects are heterogeneous and cannot simply be treated as uniform harm from every category of OPT participation.

DHS can choose to prioritize particular groups even where aggregate gains exist. The objection is not that aggregate welfare mechanically defeats a distributional objective, but that the rule should explain which groups this charge helps, how much, at whose expense, and why a more targeted approach would be inadequate.

Please publish field-, degree-, career-stage-, and region-specific evidence and evaluate feasible wage, verification, anti-fraud, and non-displacement protections alongside the charge. Identify the benefits and costs to different U.S. workers, consumers, institutions, and employers. The available evidence does not establish that the proposed amounts are an appropriately matched response.

[1] Bound, Khanna, and Morales (April 20, 2017 version), abstract and introduction: https://nicolasmoralesg.github.io/papers/BoundKhannaMorales.pdf

[2] Demirci (2020), Canadian Journal of Economics 53(4), 1495–1522, DOI 10.1111/caje.12478: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/caje.12478
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the labor-market evidence used to justify the uniform OPT charge.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Taran Samarth
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate worker in political science at Yale University, where I study democracy and social movements and develop quantitative methods for analyzing political behavior. I write to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees imposed on SEVP-certified schools [8 CFR 214.13(i)], and the related bar on DSOs entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS until the school has paid [8 CFR 214.2(f)]. My field relies on international scholars. They bring the language skills, regional expertise, and access to data and fieldwork that make comparative research on democratization, protest, and authoritarianism possible. They also build many of the statistical and computational tools that U.S. government agencies, polling firms, and tech companies now use. OPT is often the only way these scholars can take postdoctoral positions, research jobs, or methods-focused industry roles after graduating. Universities have limited budgets, and they will not pay $70,000 per student for the social sciences. So this rule would effectively end OPT in fields like mine. My international colleagues would lose access to it. Our labs and coauthor networks would lose people who carry projects to publication. Departments like mine at Yale would struggle to recruit the strongest applicants, who would go to Canada, the U.K., or Europe instead.

The harm reaches well beyond academia. Research on elections, political violence, misinformation, and public opinion informs U.S. policy and national security. Losing the international talent pipeline would weaken that work and erode America’s standing as the world’s leading destination for scholarship. DHS’s own estimate of $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual fees shows how large this burden is. Fees that size would push universities to drop OPT altogether rather than “ensure genuine educational value.” I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they would effectively end OPT in fields like political science.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The fees are unrelated to the cost of service

The proposed fees bear no reasonable relationship to the cost of administering OPT. USCIS currently charges $470 to $520 to adjudicate an OPT employment authorization application. The proposed $70,000 initial fee is roughly 150 times that amount, and DHS itself estimates the rule would collect $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year.

Charges of this size, deposited into the general Treasury rather than used to fund the program, operate as a revenue-raising tax, not a user fee. INA 214(a) authorizes DHS to set the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. It does not authorize the agency to impose levies of this magnitude, a power the Constitution reserves to Congress. At minimum, DHS should disclose how the $70,000 and $30,000 figures were calculated and identify the specific statutory authority that permits fees untethered from the cost of the service provided. Absent that, the proposal should be withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are unrelated to the cost of service and requests the proposal be withdrawn.

comments.commentText:
DHS’s own economic analysis is internally inconsistent

The Regulatory Impact Analysis for 91 FR 64566 rests on assumptions that contradict the rule’s stated purpose. DHS says it wants “a smaller pool of participants,” yet its analysis assumes a 0% reduction among STEM graduates even in the scenario where non-STEM participation is maximally reduced, while conceding it “cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation.” If STEM participation truly does not change, the fee cannot deliver the fraud reduction or labor market benefits DHS claims for that population.

DHS also understates OPT’s importance by reporting that roughly 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024. That figure divides one year’s participants by all enrolled students, including those years from graduation. SEVIS data show that among F-1 graduates, 54% use OPT, including 64% of STEM graduates and 67% of PhD graduates. 
ifp

Peer-reviewed style evidence points to far larger effects than DHS models. Economist Michael Clemens (IZA Discussion Paper 18933, 2026) estimates that, depending on who bears the cost, OPT participation would fall by 23% to 99%, and that reduced OPT access would cut international enrollment by 3% to 31% at the bachelor’s level and 5% to 58% at the master’s level. DHS does not model the enrollment effect at all. 
ifp

DHS should re-run its analysis with empirically grounded elasticities for both STEM and non-STEM students and for enrollment, and republish it for comment before proceeding.
comments.reason: The commenter points out inconsistencies in DHS's economic analysis and challenges the justification for the fees.

aau

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The rule undermines U.S. scientific and economic leadership

OPT is the primary bridge that keeps U.S.-trained scientists and engineers in the United States. Eighty-two percent of international STEM graduates who stay to work in the U.S. obtain OPT before an H-1B (Clemens, Neufeld and Nice, National Academies commissioned paper, 2025). Because the H-1B lottery runs in March and employment begins in October, removing OPT creates a gap that pushes graduates to leave. 


These are graduates the country has a strong interest in keeping. Temporary visa holders earned 62% of U.S. computer and information sciences doctorates, 56% of engineering doctorates, and 53% of mathematics and statistics doctorates, and 73% of temporary visa holders who received U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2017 to 2019 were still in the United States about five years later (NSF NCSES, NSF 25-325). 


They also create American jobs and companies. A Georgetown CSET study of 550 recipients of leading STEM awards found 47% of those connected to the U.S. were foreign-born, and two-thirds of those traced first arrived as students. 
business-standard.


Competitor nations are actively recruiting this talent. A rule designed to shrink the U.S. pipeline hands them an advantage, and DHS’s analysis does not quantify any cost to innovation or growth. It should.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 graduate student in computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, expected to graduate in May 2027. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the rule.

The fee is not tied to the cost of adjudicating OPT. It is orders of magnitude above the current employment authorization filing fee, and DHS itself estimates billions of dollars per year across about 2,478 schools. A fee of this size does not recover processing costs; it prices students out of the program.

The rule also makes the fee a precondition to a recommendation: no payment, no SEVIS recommendation, no employment authorization. Most schools cannot absorb $70,000 per student, and most new graduates cannot pay it before their first paycheck. Schools will either stop recommending OPT, pass the cost to students, or ask employers to pay it. For startups and smaller employers, a $70,000 upfront charge for an unproven new graduate will simply end sponsorship consideration. That is a de facto elimination of OPT, not a fraud control.

The fraud rationale does not justify a blanket fee on all compliant students. DHS has not shown that charging every student deters fraud better than targeted measures, such as SEVIS audits, employer verification, and enforcement against bad actors. The proposal punishes the majority who follow the rules, including STEM graduates the United States says it needs.

The fee is also arbitrary in its uniformity. It is the same whether a student earns a high wage or a modest entry-level wage, whether the school is large or small, and whether the work is in a shortage field. The STEM OPT extension — the very pathway that lets employers evaluate a graduate over three years before an H-1B decision — is penalized with an additional $30,000, bringing the total to $100,000.

If DHS does not withdraw the rule, it should at minimum extend the comment period to 60 days, publish a real cost-based justification, and consider less restrictive alternatives that target fraud without ending practical training for compliant F-1 students.
comments.reason: The student opposes the proposed OPT fees, requesting that DHS withdraw the rule because it prices students out.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS/ICE Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I am an F-1 graduate student studying computer science at a U.S. public university, commenting in my individual capacity. I support preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fees because the analysis does not adequately establish that these charges would distinguish legitimate training from abuse or justify the burdens on current students.

1. Demonstrate the anti-fraud mechanism (Section IV.C).

Payment establishes access to money; it does not verify an employer, the educational value of a placement, or labor compliance. DHS permits schools to shift the charge to students, employers, or other students. If a school can pass on the entire cost, what evidence shows that the fee will improve its scrutiny? DHS should distinguish fewer participants from less fraud and explain why these amounts are more effective than lower, targeted measures. Because the proceeds are not retained by ICE for OPT oversight, increased fee collections should not be treated as increased enforcement capacity.

2. Protect existing educational commitments (Sections V.C and VI).

I have already invested time and resources in a U.S. degree. Applying computer science in supervised, degree-related practical training would complement that education. An additional charge imposed after enrollment could make that opportunity inaccessible. My concern is the loss of a meaningful educational option, not a guarantee of employment or permanent status.

DHS's proposed 60-day transition does not allow enrolled students to undo substantial educational commitments. Nor does the cited one-year share of F-1 students in higher education participating in OPT establish how graduating cohorts relied on practical training. OPT need not be the sole reason for enrollment to have materially influenced educational planning. DHS should justify imposing the fee on current students despite their different reliance interests from future applicants who can choose a program knowing the new costs.

3. Test affordability and costs to U.S. stakeholders (Sections VII.A.3.b and VII.A.5.b).

DHS should test scenarios with substantial participation losses among STEM students as well as other students. The possibility that OPT creates benefits greater than the fee does not establish that a student, university, and employer can jointly raise the money before a recommendation. Benefits can be delayed and shared broadly, while each party faces cash and coordination constraints. Please test those constraints and quantify, where feasible, foregone research, employer productivity, university enrollment, and costs passed to American students. Treating an unpaid fee as a proxy for lost social benefits needs empirical justification and sensitivity analysis.

4. Compare feasible alternatives and adopt a clear safeguard (Section IV.C).

DHS discusses alternatives such as site visits and training plans. Please compare their total costs and effectiveness with the proposed fees, including risk-based audits, employer verification, and sanctions for proven misconduct. Ease of collecting a fee is not sufficient evidence that it best protects workers or program integrity. Any alternative fee should have a transparent statutory basis and a proportionate, documented rationale.

Please withdraw this proposal. If DHS proceeds with a revised measure, exempt students already enrolled when the proposal was published from the new fees for otherwise eligible OPT and STEM OPT associated with their current degree. This safeguard would preserve existing eligibility and compliance requirements while allowing future students to plan under known conditions.

Please address these specific evidentiary questions and the grandfathering alternative in any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fees because the analysis fails to establish that charges distinguish fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees - Student Debt and Affordability
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fees because they would impose an unreasonable financial barrier to degree-related practical training, particularly for students who have already borrowed to finance their education. This comment addresses the student cost impacts discussed in Sections IV.C and VII.A.

Students who finance tuition and living expenses with education loans may reach graduation with substantial debt and little remaining access to credit. Rent, food, health insurance, transportation, and loan obligations continue during the transition from study to practical training. Requiring another large payment at this stage could force otherwise qualified students to take on unaffordable debt or abandon the opportunity to apply their education.

Although schools would make the payments to the government, the proposal expressly allows costs to be passed on to students. Naming the school as the payer therefore does not resolve student affordability. If a school cannot absorb the charge and a student cannot finance it, the practical consequence may be the loss of access to OPT.

The proposal compares the fees with the cost of one or two years of U.S. education. That comparison does not establish affordability. For a student who borrowed to pay those original costs, it describes another major financial burden. The ability to finance a degree does not demonstrate the ability to produce an additional $70,000 before beginning practical training.

For perspective, if the full $70,000 initial fee were passed to a student seeking 12 months of OPT, the charge would be equivalent to approximately $5,833 for each month of potential training, before any financing costs. This would be additional to existing educational debt and necessary living expenses. The payment would be required before the school recommends OPT, so DHS cannot simply assume that future training income will cover the upfront cost.

Neither a suitable position nor a particular level of earnings is guaranteed. Additional borrowing could therefore expose students and any family co-signers to substantial financial risk without ensuring that the student can repay the new debt. Losing access to training would not erase the original educational loans; it could instead leave graduates with continuing obligations and fewer opportunities to develop the professional skills for which they studied.

Access to legitimate educational practice should not depend on whether a student has wealthy relatives or can obtain another large loan. Academic ability, compliance with program requirements, and the educational value of the training are more appropriate considerations. Making practical learning financially inaccessible to otherwise eligible borrowers would undermine its educational purpose.

I urge DHS to withdraw these proposed fees. Before proposing any replacement, DHS should evaluate existing educational debt, necessary living expenses, access to credit, interest costs, realistic training earnings, and the effects of passing institutional charges to students. Any revised approach should use proportionate fees supported by a transparent justification and include meaningful financial-hardship protections.

Students who have already made a substantial investment in their education should have a financially realistic opportunity to pursue lawful, degree-related practical training. They should not have to jeopardize their ability to meet basic needs or incur another major debt merely to access that opportunity.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the fees due to unreasonable financial barriers and student debt impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section VII.A.5.b, 91 FR 64588–64589.**

I oppose the proposed rule's reliance on unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the social opportunity cost of lost participation. DHS acknowledges that actual benefits may exceed the fee but assumes affected parties could collectively finance participation when benefits are sufficiently large. That assumption needs support before it can anchor the regulatory analysis.

First, the proposal itself identifies practical obstacles to that financing. Initial OPT applicants need not already have an employer, and Section VII.A.5.d recognizes additional budgeting, funding, and transaction burdens. An unidentified future employer cannot necessarily commit funds before the school must pay. The ability to pool sufficient funds therefore cannot simply be presumed.

Second, a student's liquidity, a university's recoverable return, an employer's private benefit, and benefits to U.S. society are different quantities. Research spillovers and benefits to other workers or consumers may not be recoverable by the parties required to finance the fee. Even a project with social benefits above $70,000 can disappear when its participants cannot capture or finance those benefits. OMB Circular A-4 discusses externalities, transaction costs, and public goods, including basic scientific research; it does not assume that private bargaining always captures social value.[1]

Third, behavioral effects require explicit incidence assumptions. Clemens's 2026 working paper separately models effects when the economic burden falls on students, universities, or employers.[2] Its estimates are conditional projections, with substantial limitations; they are not observed effects of this proposed rule. They nevertheless illustrate why DHS should test financing and participation responses rather than infer social losses from a chosen fee alone.

DHS reasonably acknowledges that valuation is uncertain and that alternative workers may replace some OPT participants. Those considerations justify transparent ranges, rather than establishing that the fee is an appropriate ceiling or unbiased proxy. This objection does not establish whether the proposal's aggregate cost estimate is too high or too low, and fee transfers should not be double-counted as resource costs.

Please withdraw this unsupported assumption, or publish a revised analysis distinguishing private returns, financing constraints, coordination costs, and domestic spillovers. Include sensitivity and break-even analyses for replacement rates, participation, and unquantified effects, with an opportunity for supplemental comment before finalization.

[1] OMB, Circular A-4 (Sept. 17, 2003), pp. 2–4: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/CircularA-4.pdf

[2] Michael A. Clemens, IZA Discussion Paper 18933 (Sept. 2026), Sections 1–4 and 6: https://docs.iza.org/dp18933.pdf
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed rule's economic assumptions regarding unpaid OPT fees and financing burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section IV.C, 91 FR 64574–64576.

I oppose the proposition that the proposed uniform fee reliably distinguishes lawful, educationally valuable OPT participation from abuse. Fraud prevention is a legitimate objective. The missing step is evidence that this price-based mechanism improves compliance sufficiently to justify its exclusion of otherwise eligible participants.

First, Section IV.A describes serious cases, but the evidence has different statuses. Convictions, ongoing investigations, and students associated with highly suspect employers are not interchangeable. These materials establish reasons for investigation; without a sampling frame, denominators, case dispositions, and overlap checks, they do not establish a program-wide fraud rate or the relative effectiveness of a $70,000 charge. Please disclose the evidence needed to evaluate those inferences.

Second, fewer participants do not necessarily mean a lower fraud rate among those remaining. A well-financed violator may pay while a verified, lawful participant at a financially constrained institution cannot. This is a possible mechanism, not a claim that adverse selection will necessarily occur. Moreover, DHS expressly permits schools to pass the charge to students, other students, or employers. Nominal payment by a school therefore does not establish that the school bears the economic stake on which the proposed screening mechanism relies.

Third, GAO-19-297 identifies specific controls, including fraud-risk assessment, network analysis, school recertification, and fraud-specific DSO training.[1] Subsequent implementation updates show that several recommendations have been implemented. DHS should identify the residual risks after those measures and compare targeted improvements with the uniform charge. The proposal does discuss and reject expanded visits and other procedures; my objection is to the adequacy of that comparison, not an assertion that alternatives were ignored entirely.

DHS may reasonably argue that a smaller program reduces oversight burdens even if the fraud rate does not fall. It should quantify or otherwise substantiate that separate claim and explain the associated loss of legitimate training. Because the receipts go to the Treasury and are not retained by ICE, they cannot be assumed to finance additional oversight under this rule.

Please withdraw the uniform charge unless its relative screening effect is adequately supported. Evaluate targeted employer verification, risk-based reviews, and other feasible controls using common outcomes: substantiated violations prevented, compliant participants excluded, remaining fraud risk, and total public and private costs.

[1] GAO-19-297, findings, recommendations, and implementation updates: https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297
comments.reason: Opposes the uniform fee as a reliable fraud prevention mechanism and criticizes the evidence used.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

While I am not an international student myself, the success of my research relies on international researchers in my lab; I do not know a single graduate worker at Yale University who would be able to say otherwise. A $70,000 fee for an F-1 student's first OPT is both prohibitive and, frankly, ridiculous. If the US continues to push international workers away from our research programs, we will lose our standing as a competitive market for biotechnology and pharmaceutical development. This will hurt all researchers looking to transition into industry science, even American citizens. I urge the DHS to withdraw this proposed rule, for the sake of your citizens and those looking to contribute to our nation's research economy.
comments.reason: Adamantly opposes the prohibitive $70,000 fee and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
For ICEB-2026-0100, I am an international graduate student who previously participated in Optional Practical Training (OPT) and am currently continuing my education with authorization for Curricular Practical Training (CPT).

I am concerned about the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. Although these fees would be paid by SEVP-certified institutions, their substantial cost could discourage schools from recommending otherwise eligible international students for OPT. Institutions may also pass these costs on to students through increased tuition or additional fees, creating further financial barriers.

My previous OPT experience provided me with valuable practical training directly related to my academic studies. It allowed me to apply classroom knowledge in a professional setting and develop skills essential to my career. I am concerned that the proposed fees could significantly limit similar opportunities for future international graduates, including those who have fully complied with existing immigration and program requirements.

While I recognize the importance of preventing fraud and maintaining program integrity, I encourage the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to consider more targeted oversight measures that do not impose disproportionate financial burdens on educational institutions and international students.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee amounts and provide transparent, evidence-based justification demonstrating how these fees correspond to the actual administrative and oversight costs of the OPT program.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to reconsider the high proposed fees due to financial barriers placed on institutions and students.

I would like to strongly oppose this new rule because of the negative impact it will have on the efficiency of university research.

This rule will dramatically decrease the number of international graduate students that are able to take postdoctoral positions at universities after graduating. University research is highly reliant on postdocs, who do not have teaching responsibilities like professors do and often bring their own funding (through grants etc) to the university. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the initiative of the government to increase the fees for the OPT. It would make it unattainable for individuals and institutions alike to maintain the successful recruitment of qualified labor. I base this position on the following arguments:
1. Weakening U.S. Competitiveness and "Brain Drain"
Global Talent Diversion: Elevated costs discourage top international graduates from staying in the U.S. Foreign talent may pivot to countries with lower costs and streamlined post-graduation work pathways, such as Canada, the UK, Australia, or Germany.
Impact on Innovation and Startups: Foreign-born STEM graduates drive a disproportionate share of U.S. patents, scientific publications, and startup creation. Substantially raising the barrier to entry for early-career researchers harms early-stage ventures that rely on specialized technical skills. This is data that is available and can be openly fact checked.
2. Financial Harm to Higher Education
Reduced International Enrollment: The post-study work experience offered by OPT is a primary factor in an international student's choice to study at U.S. universities. Significant fee increases lower international application volume, directly impacting university tuition revenues. It is a myth that at the undergraduate level there are "scholarships" available to international students that are not available to US citizens. Quite the opposite: international students do not have access to any of the support systems and Universities can increase their revenue by charging international fees to international students. This one of the main points that need to be clarified. A more important consequence of this is provided below.
Cross-Subsidization Losses: Higher non-resident and international tuition often cross-subsidizes domestic student financial aid, departmental research budgets, and academic infrastructure. A decline in foreign enrollment risks reducing funding and available seats for domestic students.
3. Economic Disincentives for Employers
Disproportionate Impact on Small Businesses & Non-Profits: While well-funded tech or finance corporations might absorb high administrative and filing costs, smaller startups, non-profits, academic research labs, and regional businesses cannot.
Labor Market Bottlenecks: Restricting the OPT pipeline shrinks the pool of high-skilled talent in key STEM industries (such as semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and biotechnology) experiencing domestic labor shortages.
4. Counterproductive Impact on Domestic Workers
Reduced Job Creation: Studies on high-skilled immigration demonstrate that complementary foreign talent often fuels business growth and company expansion, ultimately creating additional jobs for domestic workers. Curtailing this intake can lower overall firm activity. Looking into some the studies that support this could help reduce the fear that international workers reduce the possibilities of employment of US cititzens
Shifting to Alternative Visas: High OPT costs could push companies to rely more heavily on immediate H-1B filings or off-shoring technical roles to foreign subsidiaries, bypassing domestic entry-level hiring entirely. The OPT was a great mechanism to prevent early investment of H1B visas.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes increasing OPT fees, arguing it weakens U.S. competitiveness and harms higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule. Charging universities $70,000 for an international student's initial OPT authorization and another $30,000 for subsequent OPT is an outrageously disproportionate and unreasonable policy that would severely damage educational and career opportunities for international students.

As an international student pursuing a degree in Computer Engineering in the United States, I find this proposal deeply concerning. Students like myself work incredibly hard to maintain our academic standing, comply with immigration regulations, pay substantial tuition and living expenses, and compete for internship opportunities. After months of applications, technical assessments, and interviews, securing an internship is already a significant achievement.

I recently received an offer for a ten-week software engineering internship. Under this proposal, my university could face a $70,000 fee simply for recommending me for pre-completion OPT. If I later pursue post-completion OPT, another $30,000 would apply. How is a $100,000 financial burden for legitimate practical training remotely reasonable?

Even though these fees are formally imposed on universities, their consequences would fall heavily on students. Universities may stop recommending students for OPT, restrict participation, or pass financial burdens onto students. This would disproportionately hurt students from middle-income and lower-income families, making career opportunities dependent on financial privilege rather than academic merit, qualifications, or hard work.

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research, technological innovation, and the economy. We come to the United States to learn, develop valuable skills, and contribute our knowledge. Policies like this discourage talented students from pursuing opportunities in the United States and undermine the country's ability to attract global talent.

I understand the importance of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers. However, imposing enormous fees on universities for legitimate students is not a reasonable or appropriately targeted solution. Fraud prevention should focus on verification, oversight, and enforcement against actual violations, not financially penalizing students and institutions following the rules.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue fair, evidence-based alternatives that preserve legitimate educational and professional training opportunities. International students should not have their futures restricted by an arbitrary financial barrier after investing years of effort and substantial resources into their education.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule as an unreasonable financial burden that damages opportunities for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to talk about a kind of fairness this proposal ignores: a flat fee is not a fair fee. The same $70,000 means something entirely different depending on which school is asked to pay it, and the schools asked to pay the most, relative to what they have, are the ones that serve the students this country can least afford to abandon.

Consider a regional public university — the kind that anchors a small city, educates first-generation students, and runs on state funding that has not kept pace with costs. Recommending OPT for sixty graduating international students would cost $4.2 million in a single year. That is not a rounding error. It is several faculty positions, a year's worth of need-based aid, or the budget of an entire academic department. A wealthy private university with a multibillion-dollar endowment can treat the same fee as an inconvenience and carry on. The regional school cannot, and it will not try: it will cap or suspend OPT recommendations, because there is no third option.

What disappears next is not only international enrollment. At many regional and minority-serving institutions, international students paying full tuition are what keep small graduate programs, language departments, and specialized STEM tracks viable at all. Lose those students, and the programs close — for American students too. The domestic student who loses a graduate seminar, a research assistantship, or a scholarship funded by international tuition is a casualty of this rule just as surely as the international graduate who loses OPT.

DHS applied this fee uniformly, as if uniformity were neutrality. It is not. A charge that a rich school absorbs and a modest school cannot is a policy that sorts opportunity by wealth, state by state and campus by campus, until OPT survives only where it was always easiest to keep. That is not a defensible way to regulate a national program, and it is not a burden the schools doing the hardest work in American higher education should be asked to carry. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed fee increase, arguing flat fees unfairly punish regional and public universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tax Payer
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw them.

The fee harms Americans. International students contributed $42.9 billion and more than 355,000 jobs to the U.S. economy in 2024–25 [1]. New enrollments already fell 17% this fall, and NAFSA projects about 23,000 fewer jobs [2][3]. In one survey, 66% of prospective students said they would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere without post-study work [1]. A fee this large effectively ends OPT at most schools and sends that tuition, and the U.S. jobs it supports, to competing countries. International students also make up roughly 72–74% of full-time graduate students in computer science and electrical engineering [4], so the fee would weaken the programs and labs that U.S. students rely on.

OPT is not the problem. A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy study found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers [1][4]. STEM OPT already requires E-Verify employers, training plans, and wage protections.

The fee is disproportionate and doesn’t target fraud. It is roughly 40 times the current cost of OPT [5] and is charged to every school regardless of compliance record [6]. Fraud should be addressed through targeted enforcement against specific schools and employers, not a blanket fee unrelated to program costs.

Request: Withdraw the fees. At minimum, limit any fee to documented administrative cost and apply it only to institutions with compliance findings.

References
[1] NAFSA, The Benefits of F-1 Optional Practical Training (Issue Brief): https://www.nafsa.org/OPT
[2] NAFSA & JB International, Fall 2025 International Student Enrollment Snapshot & Economic Impact: https://www.nafsa.org/sites/default/files/media/document/Fall%202025%20International%20Student%20Enrollment%20Snapshot%20Economic%20Impact%20Overview%20FINAL.pdf
[3] The PIE News (via BUILA), “US talent pipeline in precarious position”: https://www.buila.ac.uk/articles/us-talent-pipeline-in-precarious-position-experts-warn
[4] Harvard Kennedy School Student Review, “Why Killing OPT Hurts American Workers More Than It Helps”: https://studentreview.hks.harvard.edu/why-killing-opt-hurts-american-workers-more-than-it-helps
[5] F1Jobs, current vs. proposed OPT costs: https://www.f1jobs.io/resources/blog/proposed-opt-fee-70000-explained-who-pays
[6] DHS/ICE, NPRM, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/pdf/2026-20660.pdf
comments.reason: Opposes the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them due to negative economic impacts on the U.S.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. DHS must nevertheless establish statutory authority for this particular assessment and reasonably explain its amounts, screening mechanism, economic assumptions, and transition provisions.

First, authority to administer OPT does not automatically resolve authority to impose this monetary assessment on educational institutions. Please explain how 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1) authorizes the proposed payer, amounts, and refund restrictions, and identify a limiting principle. Congress separately addressed student-information fees in 8 U.S.C. 1372 and adjudication-service fees in 8 U.S.C. 1356(m). Those provisions do not necessarily foreclose every additional charge, but their relationship to this assessment requires explanation. The requirement to deposit receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 does not independently authorize their collection.

Second, the proposal should distinguish reducing participation from improving compliance. A uniform charge may reduce total investigations by shrinking the program. That does not establish that payment ability identifies more honest participants or more valuable educational opportunities. A compliant student or institution may lack financing, while a well-financed violator may pay. Because schools may transfer the economic burden to students or employers, nominal school payment also does not establish the institutional financial stake on which the proposal relies. Please explain these mechanisms and why $70,000 and $30,000 reasonably address them.

State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), requires a rational connection between relevant facts and the agency's choice. This objection does not demand perfect data or a new experiment. It requests a reasoned explanation addressing specific weaknesses in the proposed mechanism.

Third, evaluate targeted controls against the same objectives. GAO-19-297 identifies risk assessment, network analysis, school oversight, and DSO training. Its July 2026 updates show that mandatory DSO and fraud-specific training recommendations remained partially addressed. Please compare completing these measures, verifying high-risk employers, targeted reviews, and lower assessments using effectiveness, implementation costs, residual risk, and exclusion of compliant participants. The proposal discusses alternatives; the issue is whether its comparison adequately supports the selected approach.

Fourth, strengthen the reliance and transition analysis. DHS has addressed reliance, but an annual participation share does not establish a graduating cohort's eventual OPT use or how OPT availability influenced enrollment decisions. Educational quality and practical training can jointly influence substantial, irreversible commitments.

DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1, 30-33 (2020), requires meaningful consideration of relevant reliance interests without guaranteeing an unchanged policy. Preserving earlier recommendations and providing 60 days may offer little practical adjustment for students already enrolled who cannot yet receive recommendations. The transition can also impose the initial $70,000 assessment on a future STEM recommendation where that assessment has not previously been paid. Please compare protection through an existing student's current degree and associated OPT/STEM sequence, phased implementation, and a longer transition.

Fifth, test the financing and opportunity-cost assumptions. Liquidity, willingness to pay, private returns, and benefits to U.S. society are different quantities. Future employers may be unidentified when payment is required. Research spillovers and benefits to other American workers or consumers may not be recoverable by the parties funding the fee. An unpaid assessment is therefore not a demonstrated ceiling on forgone value. Please evaluate alternative participation scenarios, including STEM reductions, financing constraints, pass-through, replacement workers, and uncertainty. Do not double-count fee transfers as social resource costs.

Finally, worker effects require differentiation. Demirci (2020), Canadian Journal of Economics, DOI 10.1111/caje.12478, reports adverse employment effects for recently graduated native master's recipients alongside earnings gains for experienced native master's recipients in the same field. Such evidence supports examining affected groups, rather than assuming a uniform institutional charge is appropriately targeted.

Please withdraw the assessment. If DHS proceeds, address these objections, substantiate the statutory and analytical basis, evaluate significant alternatives, provide a reasoned transition, and publish objective refund criteria, timelines, written reasons, and error-correction procedures before implementation.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed rule and requests its withdrawal due to lack of statutory authority and justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment as a U.S. citizen, engineer, and member of the public. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)) and urge DHS to withdraw them. The notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) doesn't explain its fee amounts, doesn't measure the problems it claims to address, and shifts billions in costs onto schools and students, including American students, without accounting for them.

1. DHS never explains how it arrived at $70,000.
The NPRM identifies no cost of administering OPT or investigating fraud. DHS says only that the fee is “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” and “on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur” (NPRM § IV.C), neither of which reflects any government cost. Students already pay a USCIS filing fee for adjudication (§ VII.A.2.a). Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), which DHS itself cites (§ VI), an agency must rationally connect the facts to its choice. DHS never explains why these amounts are necessary.

2. DHS identifies an enforcement resource shortage, then proposes a fee that provides no resources.
DHS states that OPT’s growth “has exponentially outpaced the number of companies that DHS is able to effectively review and investigate,” and that “agency compliance resources are not scaled to (or keeping pace with) the size of the program” (§ IV.A), with roughly 60 field representatives covering about 6,186 schools. Yet ICE cannot retain the fee revenue because “the statute does not provide legal authority” to do so (§ IV.C). The rule shrinks participation to fit DHS’s capacity rather than resourcing oversight, even though the fraud DHS cites was uncovered through site visits and investigations (§ IV.A), the very tools DHS dismissed as “reactive” (§ IV.C).

3. DHS never quantifies the fraud or the fee’s effect on it.
Despite fraud being its primary justification, DHS never estimates fraud’s prevalence or how much the fee would prevent, listing monetized benefits as “Not Estimated” (§ VII.A.1, Table 1). Its central evidence is inconsistent; the preamble cites “more than 10,000 F-1 nonimmigrant students” at “highly suspect employers” (§ IV.A), while the supporting footnote describes “10,000 highly suspected employers”. Either way, it reflects suspicion, not confirmed fraud.

4. DHS projects billions in losses but never measures the worker benefits it claims.
DHS justifies the fee as protecting U.S. workers, yet lists the rule’s “Effects on wages” and “Effects on growth” as “N/A” (§ VII.A.1, Table 1), while estimating annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion, driven largely by “opportunity costs from the lost OPT participation”. DHS asks the public to accept billions in measured losses for wage gains it never estimated.

5. DHS invites schools to pass the fee onto American students without accounting for them.
DHS twice states schools may pass the fee onto “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers,” presenting this as a way to “mitigate their budgetary impact” (§§ IV.C, VI), yet its deterrence rationale addresses only F-1 students and employers (§ IV.C). U.S. students cannot participate in OPT or commit the fraud DHS describes. Despite estimating $8.7 to $16.9 billion in annual transfers from schools, DHS never mentions tuition increases and omits domestic students from its reliance interests analysis (§ VI). A rule meant to “place the United States’ interests first” (§ IV.B) should not shift billions onto American students without justification.

6. DHS should reject charging $70,000 at each degree level.
DHS requests comment on reapplying the initial fee at each higher degree level (§ V.A). Though DHS says the rule targets “the most promising” and “high achieving” students (§§ IV.C, VI), this alternative would penalize exactly those students: a graduate earning three U.S. degrees could owe $210,000 in initial fees alone.

Requested changes
I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees in their entirety. If DHS proceeds, it should at minimum base any fee on a documented analysis of OPT’s actual administrative and oversight costs; pursue targeted enforcement, such as expanded employer site visits, instead of a blanket fee; publish estimates of fraud prevalence and the rule’s effect on U.S. wages before finalizing; prohibit schools from passing any fee onto students who do not participate in OPT; and reject the alternative of charging the initial fee at each degree level.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them as unjustified and burdensome.
