comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a university instructor, one of my biggest concerns about the proposed OPT fees is something that has received far too little attention: the potential consequences for American students.

Universities are already under considerable financial pressure. Faculty positions, academic programs, student support services, and scholarships all depend on limited institutional resources. International students are an important part of that financial picture, particularly at institutions where international enrollment contributes significant tuition revenue.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could make American universities considerably less attractive to prospective international students.

For many students, the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation is an important factor in choosing where to study. If that opportunity becomes financially uncertain, some may choose universities in other countries instead.

What concerns me is what happens afterward.

When a university loses tuition revenue, the financial consequences do not simply disappear. Administrators must find ways to balance their budgets. That may mean reducing academic offerings, limiting scholarships, postponing faculty hiring, or increasing tuition.

American students could ultimately bear part of that burden.

Smaller private universities and regional institutions may be especially vulnerable because they often lack the financial reserves available to major research universities. In communities where a university is also a significant employer, prolonged financial difficulties could affect local jobs as well.

I am not suggesting that every institution would raise tuition or that this proposal would necessarily cause university closures. However, these are foreseeable economic risks that deserve serious consideration before such substantial fees are implemented.

My objection is specifically to the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

I ask DHS to evaluate how these fees could affect international enrollment, university finances, and the cost of education for American students. Any final decision should account for those indirect consequences rather than treating OPT fees as an isolated immigration issue.

Protecting American interests should include protecting access to affordable, high-quality education for American families.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule due to negative financial consequences for universities and American students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees raise a broader question about America's long-term economic competitiveness.

The United States has spent decades building an extraordinary system of universities, research institutions, technology companies, and startup ecosystems. One of the strengths of this system is its ability to attract talented people from around the world and provide opportunities to turn academic knowledge into useful technologies.

OPT is one part of that system.

In fields such as artificial intelligence, semiconductor engineering, biotechnology, and advanced computing, professional development does not end when a student receives a diploma. Practical training allows graduates to work with complex systems, participate in research and development, and acquire experience that universities alone cannot provide.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could weaken this connection between education and industry.

The concern is not simply that fewer international students might remain in the United States. It is that talented students may increasingly decide not to study here in the first place.

Countries competing with the United States for scientific and technical talent have their own universities, research institutions, and technology industries. When qualified graduates choose to build their careers elsewhere, their future research contributions, entrepreneurial activities, and technological innovations may also occur elsewhere.

These effects are difficult to measure immediately. A lost research collaboration or a startup that is never founded may not appear in short-term employment statistics.

Yet such outcomes matter when evaluating a policy's long-term economic consequences.

DHS should therefore examine whether the proposed fees would reduce the attractiveness of American universities and limit the availability of highly trained graduates to domestic employers.

The analysis should also consider whether any anticipated employment benefits for American workers would outweigh possible losses in research productivity, innovation, and business formation.

Preventing immigration fraud is a legitimate objective. However, a broad financial requirement does not necessarily distinguish legitimate training opportunities from fraudulent arrangements.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and evaluate more targeted compliance measures.

A policy affecting the future supply of scientific and technical talent deserves an economic analysis that extends beyond immediate immigration enforcement outcomes.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the fees, stating they would weaken U.S. economic competitiveness and scientific talent attraction.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Who actually benefits if international students stop coming to American universities?

This is the question I would like DHS to answer before moving forward with the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.

International students don't just attend classes. They rent apartments, buy groceries, eat at local restaurants, use transportation, and spend money in the communities surrounding their universities.

That spending supports American businesses and American jobs.

According to NAFSA's economic analysis, international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year.

Those numbers represent real economic activity, much of it benefiting people who have nothing to do with immigration policy.

If OPT becomes too expensive or uncertain, some prospective students may decide to study in Canada, Europe, or elsewhere.

The financial consequences would not stop at university campuses.

Landlords could lose tenants. Local restaurants could lose customers. University towns could experience declining demand for services. Institutions facing enrollment losses might reduce staffing.

And many of the people affected would be American citizens.

I understand the argument that OPT should not undermine employment opportunities for American graduates. That concern deserves attention.

But shouldn't DHS also consider the American jobs that depend on international education?

Reducing one category of foreign employment authorization does not automatically produce a net increase in American employment.

I am not claiming that every international student would leave or that every community would suffer equally. I am asking DHS to measure the potential losses before implementing fees of this magnitude.

My request is straightforward: withdraw the proposed fee provisions in 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and conduct a comprehensive assessment of their potential impact on American businesses, local employment, and university communities.

If the purpose is to protect American workers, the analysis should account for all American workers who may be affected, not just those competing for OPT-eligible positions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Selena Zeng

Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 student at the University of Southern California. I will graduate in December 2026 with a B.S. in Economics and Data Science, and I plan to apply for post-completion OPT and the 24-month STEM OPT extension.

I oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later recommendation. The fee is charged to the school, but the rule itself says schools may pass the cost to students. If my school passes the cost to me, I cannot pay it, and my OPT would end before it starts. If schools pay it themselves, many schools may stop recommending OPT at all. Either way, the result is the same: students who followed every rule lose the training that is part of their degree.

OPT was a key reason I chose to study in the United States. I am now applying for entry-level roles in business operations and data analysis, all directly related to my degree. Fraud should be addressed by targeting the small number of bad actors. A $100,000 fee punishes every honest student instead.

I respectfully ask DHS not to adopt the proposed fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alexandra Tabachnikova
comments.commentText:
I am writing to urge the DHS to withdraw proposed rule No. ICEB-2026-0100. I am a PhD Candidate in the department of Immunobiology at Yale University working on Long COVID and other chronic diseases. I am scheduled to defend my thesis on January 15th of next year and am planning to pursue further postdoctoral research at another US institution after I graduate. I have a lot of flexibility in deciding on what type of research I plan to pursue, in which lab and university, and when I plan to being my postdoctoral work. This flexibility means that I can pursue the most challenging and competitive career that will help me become a professor at a leading institute myself. 

Currently, international students in the United States have the same kind of flexibility in choosing their postdoctoral careers and contributing to the growing innovation in biological sciences in the United States. A huge reason for this flexibility is due to the Optional Practical Training program and STEM OPT extension, which allows an extension on visas for up to 3 years while obtaining additional postgraduate training. However, these proposed changes would make it prohibitively expensive for international workers to pursue this option, since no student worker could possibly have access to $70,000 or an additional $30,000 for the extension. My current salary is a little over $50,00 a year, so it would take 2 full years of pay to cover this cost. 

Multiple members of my lab are on OPT or OPT STEM extension and are conducting life-changing research that will help people with debilitating illness in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic. Without these key coworkers, the chronic disease field and our understanding of Long COVID, will suffer tremendously. Additionally, we are able to recruit the most talented new postdocs to work on this unmet need with needed expertise in neuroscience, microscopy, and autoimmunity, because they have the option of easily and affordably extending their student visas.

OPT allows the US economy and leading universities and pharmaceutical companies to retain talent that has been trained in the US to continue working in the country and contributing to our nation's status as a leader in healthcare and technological innovation. As a scientist, I would like to cite some studies which have been conducted on the impact of OPT on the US economy. Kwon et al (https://bse.eu/research/working-papers/the-effect-of-retaining-high-skilled-international-graduates-evidence-from-the-stem-opt-extension) use an economic analysis method called synthetic difference-in-differences (SDID) and demonstrated that OPT stimulates the creation of new businesses and start-ups and increased demand for not only international workers, but also for native high-skilled workers with high degrees. 

Another study by Madeline Zavodny (https://nfap.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/International-Students-STEM-OPT-And-The-US-STEM-Workforce.NFAP-Policy-Brief.March-2019.pdf) at the National Foundation for American Policy analyzed data from 2008 to 2016 to ask whether OPT has an impact on competing native workers. This study found that "unemployment rates are lower in areas with larger numbers of foreign students doing OPT as a share of workers in STEM occupations," showing that the economic boost of OPT helped hire native workers and provide MORE work opportunities, not less. Thus, the assertion made in this rule change that it will protect US workers is clearly false. 

Clearly the impact of OPT is very good for the US economy, and for ALL workers, not just international workers. This proposed rule change will essentially eliminate this option for international workers due to the extreme financial burden on international workers, principle investigators, or the university. With this in mind, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule as it makes postdoctoral training prohibitively expensive.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to the Proposed $100,000 Fee

I am an international graduate student at Yale University pursuing a PhD in biology. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $100,000 fee, which I believe would have serious and long-lasting consequences for American higher education, scientific innovation, economic competitiveness, and global leadership.

For decades, the United States has been a global leader in scientific research and technological innovation, in large part because of its ability to attract talented students, researchers, and professionals from around the world. American universities have become centers of scientific excellence through the contributions of both domestic and international scholars. Imposing such a substantial financial barrier would discourage talented international students from pursuing advanced training and research careers in the United States, potentially driving them toward countries with more welcoming immigration policies.

This concern is particularly significant in STEM fields, where international graduate students and researchers make essential contributions to scientific discovery, technological development, and public health. As a PhD student working in biology, I have witnessed firsthand how international collaboration and diverse scientific perspectives accelerate research and innovation. Scientific progress depends on attracting the brightest minds, regardless of nationality. Policies that discourage talented researchers from remaining in the United States risk weakening the country's research institutions and its long-term ability to compete globally.

Furthermore, international students and highly skilled researchers should not be viewed simply as competitors for existing American jobs. They also contribute to the creation of new opportunities through scientific discoveries, entrepreneurship, technological innovation, and the development of new industries. Their contributions help expand the economy and create employment opportunities for American citizens. Restricting access to international talent may therefore undermine, rather than strengthen, the American workforce.

International students also make substantial economic contributions through tuition payments, living expenses, and participation in local economies. More importantly, those who pursue advanced research and remain in the United States contribute to the nation's long-term economic growth and technological leadership. Discouraging these individuals from building their careers in America could result in a significant loss of human capital and future innovation.

The United States has maintained its global leadership not by limiting access to talent, but by creating an environment in which talented individuals from around the world can contribute to shared progress. I fear that policies such as this one could gradually erode that advantage, with consequences extending far beyond the individuals directly affected.

I respectfully urge policymakers to reconsider this proposal and carefully evaluate its long-term effects on American universities, scientific research, job creation, and economic competitiveness. Protecting opportunities for American workers and maintaining America's ability to attract global talent are not mutually exclusive goals. In fact, they are deeply interconnected.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the fee, citing negative consequences for American higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for extensions. This cumulative $100,000 framework is an economically justified mechanism to protect qualified American workers and recent graduates during a severe tech economic contraction.
The necessity of this fee is supported by documented data and structural program exploits:
• Deviation from Statutory Intent: The F-1 visa is strictly an academic student visa, never intended to allow international students to work legally in the U.S. Permitting full-time employment decoupled from campuses for up to three years creates a massive guest-worker program under an educational guise.
• Demographic Monopolization: According to IIE data across 2023-2026, nationals from India (49%) and China (21%) consistently monopolize nearly 70% of all active OPT participants and 68% of STEM OPT extensions, operating as a localized corporate pipeline [International Students - IIE Open Doors].
• Protecting Workers Amid Tech Layoffs: The tech sector faces historic layoffs, with 245,953 workers cut in 2025 and 197,123 in 2026 to date. Massive contractions hit major entities like Oracle (21,000 jobs) and Amazon (16,000 jobs). Flooding this market with entry-level guest workers directly harms displaced citizens.
• Historical Escalation of OPT Permits: While domestic job openings plummeted, annual active OPT volume from IIE reveals an unchecked upward trajectory: 184,686 (2022); 198,793 (2023); 242,551 (2024); jumping to 294,253 (2025), with 2026 remaining at this 294,000 peak [International Students - IIE Open Doors].
• The Multi-Year Backdoor to H-1B Caps: Congress set a strict annual cap of 85,000 visas for the H-1B lottery. Because there is no restriction on the number of OPT allocations or applicants each year, corporations use it as a workaround. Combining a 12-month initial period and 24-month STEM extension gives three consecutive years of full-time work to enter the lottery repeatedly while remaining on domestic soil.
• No Minimum Wage Floor: Unlike the H-1B visa, there is no minimum prevailing salary requirement enforced for OPT applicants. Employers face no wage flooring, allowing corporations to depress entry-level technical wages by hiring foreign graduates at below-market rates.
• Corporate Tax Subsidies: Employers hiring OPT workers are exempt from FICA taxes, giving them an immediate 7.65% financial discount over identically qualified American citizens. A substantial fee balances this artificial distortion.
When extensive domestic layoffs occur, policy must prioritize the economic security of American citizens. DHS must adjust fee structures to reflect these realities. I urge the Department to finalize this rule as proposed. Putting the American people and their families first in the United States of America. Thank you, President Trump.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly supports the fees as an economically justified mechanism to protect American workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jennifer Watkins
comments.commentText:
I believe that if this is implemented it will be detrimental to US universities, as well as US culture. It will not prevent fraud
. Misalignment with Statutory Intent & Administrative Overreach
Arbitrary Financial Barrier: The $70,000/$30,000 fee structure acts as a functional ban or prohibitive penalty rather than a standard service cost-recovery fee.

General Revenue vs. Fraud Detection: DHS states the collected revenue would go into general treasury funds rather than dedicated OPT oversight resources, undermining the stated legal nexus of "anti-fraud enforcement".

2. Severe Financial & Operational Impact on Higher Education
Unfunded Institutional Mandate: Assigning fee liability directly to host colleges and universities forces impossible budgetary tradeoffs, particularly for non-profit, faith-based, and mid-sized institutions.

Disproportionate Impact on Specific Fields: Non-profit sectors, religious organizations, education, and early-stage research startups cannot afford tens of thousands of dollars to support post-graduate practical training, disproportionately penalizing non-STEM and humanitarian fields.

3. Misunderstanding of Institutional Oversight & DSU/DSO Rules
Confusing Oversight with Financial Stake: DSOs already exercise rigorous oversight via SEVIS data management, regular reporting, and employment verification. Imposing a major financial penalty does not improve compliance accuracy; it simply penalizes institutions executing standard regulatory duties.

Disruption to Educational Mission: Experiential learning and practical training are natural extensions of a university's academic mission. Decoupling degree completion from post-graduate application of learning harms educational outcomes.

4. Broad Economic and U.S. Workforce Consequences
National Talent Pipeline: Post-graduate practical training strengthens domestic research, fills critical skill gaps, and drives U.S. innovation.

Global Competitiveness: Exorbitant fee structures compromise the global competitiveness of U.S. higher education, encouraging top international talent to pursue higher education and career development in competing nations like Canada, the UK, or Australia.

comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,Hello, I am a doctoral student at University of California, Irvine, and I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Mayor Manlapidmayorm@uci.eduIrvine, California 92617
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee hikes as unreasonable, harmful to workers, and damaging to U.S. higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

My primary concern is that this proposal would significantly undermine the international competitiveness of American higher education, ultimately harming not only international students but also U.S. universities, employers, and the broader American economy.

1. Undermining the competitiveness of U.S. universities

One of the major advantages of pursuing higher education in the United States is the opportunity to combine world-class academic instruction with practical experience in American industries. OPT provides an important bridge between these two experiences.

International students make substantial financial and personal investments when choosing where to study. The availability of post-graduation practical training is an important consideration in that decision. The proposed fees could severely restrict this opportunity, making American universities substantially less attractive compared with institutions in other countries.

Although the fees would technically be paid by educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such extraordinary costs. They may instead restrict OPT recommendations, transfer some costs to students, or reconsider international enrollment strategies.

2. Negative consequences for the U.S. economy and innovation

According to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report, U.S. institutions hosted approximately 1.18 million international students during the 2024–2025 academic year. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during that academic year.

These figures demonstrate that international education provides economic benefits extending well beyond individual students. Reduced international enrollment could negatively affect university revenue, local employment, and the talent pipeline supporting American research and industry.

The United States has historically benefited from attracting talented students from around the world. Restricting access to practical training risks weakening this advantage and encouraging prospective students to pursue educational and professional opportunities elsewhere.

3. Insufficient consideration of enrollment and institutional impacts

In Section VII.A.5.b of the proposed rule, DHS acknowledges that the fees could discourage international enrollment and cause educational institutions to lose tuition revenue. However, DHS also acknowledges that it cannot precisely quantify these opportunity costs.

I believe this uncertainty deserves substantially greater consideration before imposing fees of this magnitude. In particular, the analysis should more thoroughly evaluate the effects on international enrollment, universities with limited financial resources, students from less affluent backgrounds, and U.S. economic competitiveness.

Furthermore, currently enrolled students have already committed significant resources to their education under the existing regulatory framework. A short transition period may not adequately address the disruption to their educational and professional plans.

American higher education is not only an educational resource but also a major source of economic competitiveness, innovation, and international influence. Policies affecting international students should carefully account for these broader national interests.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and pursue more proportionate, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity without substantially diminishing the attractiveness of American universities to international talent.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition due to negative impacts on higher education competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yu-Chieh Tu
comments.commentText:
I want to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (ICEB-2026-0100), which would require educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations.

As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal would create an enormous barrier to accessing professional opportunities after graduation. OPT is an essential pathway for international students to apply the knowledge and skills acquired through their education, gain practical experience in their fields of study, and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

The proposed fees could make OPT inaccessible to qualified international students, regardless of their academic achievements or professional qualifications. Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such extraordinary costs for individual students. As a result, students who have worked hard to earn their degrees and secured legitimate employment opportunities could be denied the opportunity to gain professional experience simply because their universities cannot justify the financial burden.

This proposal is particularly concerning because international students face strict immigration timelines after graduation. Unlike domestic students, we cannot freely postpone our career plans or remain in the United States indefinitely while waiting for better opportunities. Our ability to work is subject to immigration requirements, and our post-graduation plans must be made within a limited period. If our universities decline to recommend us for OPT because of the proposed fees, we may have little time to find alternatives before being forced to leave the country. Years of investment in American education could end without the opportunity to gain the professional experience we came here to pursue.

The financial burden is also disproportionate to the circumstances of recent graduates. International students have often already paid substantial tuition and living expenses throughout their education. We are at the beginning of our careers and may not have the financial resources to absorb additional costs. If universities pass these fees on to students or employers, the proposal could make it prohibitively expensive for graduates to access employment opportunities. If universities absorb the costs instead, they may reduce the number of students they recommend for OPT or restrict access to the program altogether.

I recognize the Department's stated objectives of combating fraud, strengthening the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting U.S. workers. However, imposing fees of this magnitude on educational institutions for each individual OPT recommendation may prevent legitimate students from participating in the program without necessarily distinguishing them from those who engage in fraud or abuse. Stronger oversight, verification of employment, and enforcement against fraudulent participation would be more targeted approaches that would not place such an extraordinary burden on qualified graduates.

International students contribute to American universities, research, innovation, and the economy. We invest in our education with the expectation that we will have a fair opportunity to apply what we have learned. OPT provides a structured means of obtaining practical experience directly related to our fields of study. Creating substantial financial obstacles to this opportunity risks discouraging talented students from studying in the United States and preventing graduates who have already completed their education here from contributing their skills to the American workforce.

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed fees or substantially revise the proposal to avoid imposing costs that could make OPT inaccessible to legitimate international students. If the Department determines that additional oversight is necessary, it should pursue proportionate measures that address fraud directly without undermining access to professional experience for qualified graduates.

For international students like me, the time immediately following graduation is not a period in which we have the freedom to indefinitely reconsider our plans. Our immigration status imposes real deadlines and constraints. A policy that makes OPT financially or institutionally inaccessible could fundamentally alter our career prospects with little opportunity to adapt.

Please consider the substantial consequences this proposal could have for international students, educational institutions, employers, and the long-term competitiveness of the United States.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule as it creates unreasonable barriers for international students.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I vehemently oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis. This proposal benefits no one besides the abusers of the system and aims to end a program that allows the United States to thrive as one of the global leaders in innovation. Please consider the following: 

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

Prospective students would also have reason to reconsider studying here if gaining practical experience afterward required such a large payment. [Section VII.A.5(b), Opportunity Costs]

I ask DHS to evaluate research losses beyond the immediate earnings or position of an individual OPT participant. A researcher’s contribution can include training colleagues, maintaining experimental continuity, and helping a team solve problems. Those benefits extend across projects and years. An institution’s inability to fund a large upfront fee does not demonstrate that a researcher’s work has limited value.

My own research focused on converting carbon dioxide into useful chemical feedstocks. Moving such work toward practical applications requires sustained investment in people. Restricting opportunities for graduates trained at U.S. universities risks losing the expertise that investment helped develop.

[Section IV.A, Combating Fraud and Abuse of OPT]

DHS should address documented misconduct through targeted oversight and enforcement. Ability to pay a large fee is a poor measure of whether a training opportunity is legitimate. I urge the agency to explain why existing compliance tools cannot address specific violations before imposing a financial barrier on lawful participants.

My experience organizing graduate workers also informs my opposition. I want international colleagues to have fair pay, safe working conditions, and the ability to raise concerns without jeopardizing their careers. DHS should pursue worker protections directly, including measures against employer exploitation and retaliation.

International academic workers are colleagues, mentors, and contributors to research that benefits the public. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and preserve accessible OPT and STEM OPT opportunities.
comments.reason: Commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule due to the extraordinary financial barrier it creates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fee rule and request its withdrawal.

Access to legitimate practical training should depend on academic preparation, eligibility, and compliance. A financial barrier of this magnitude risks making access depend instead on institutional wealth and a student's ability to absorb additional costs. Two equally qualified students could face entirely different opportunities simply because their schools have different financial resources.

Students make educational decisions years before graduation. They commit tuition, relocate, and choose programs partly on the basis of available opportunities to apply what they learn. Recognizing these commitments does not mean guaranteeing employment or freezing immigration policy indefinitely. It means giving serious weight to decisions that cannot easily be reversed.

The proposed transition should therefore be evaluated against the length of an educational program, not merely the time needed to announce a new payment requirement. A student approaching graduation cannot readily change institutions, recover tuition, or redesign years of academic preparation.

I ask DHS to withdraw these fees. If the agency nevertheless proceeds with changes, it should protect students already enrolled and provide a meaningful transition covering their remaining studies and associated practical training. Any revised policy should preserve access for qualified students regardless of family income or institutional resources.
comments.reason: Commenter opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests its withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jeff Ma
comments.commentText:
DHS should withdraw this proposal because its economic consequences require a more convincing assessment.

The relevant question is whether restricting practical training would produce a net benefit for American workers and communities. A reduction in OPT participation does not, by itself, demonstrate an equivalent increase in employment for U.S. workers. Employers may respond by reducing activity, postponing projects, automating tasks, or moving work elsewhere. The analysis should test these possibilities instead of assuming that each unavailable OPT participant creates a job that will be filled domestically.

The agency should also examine how graduates contribute to teams. In research, engineering, and other specialized work, employees can complement one another's skills. Losing one team member may affect the productivity and opportunities of American colleagues. These effects deserve evaluation alongside any evidence of displacement.

Requiring schools to make substantial payments also creates budget choices with consequences beyond international students. Institutions may reduce services, limit training recommendations, or seek additional revenue. DHS should examine who ultimately bears those costs, including domestic students.

Protecting American workers is a legitimate objective. It calls for evidence about wages, working conditions, and actual hiring outcomes. I urge DHS to pursue targeted labor protections and enforcement, and to reject a fee structure that could undermine productive activity without establishing corresponding benefits.
comments.reason: Commenter urges DHS to withdraw this proposal because of its negative economic consequences.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jenny Bao
comments.commentText:
I object to the proposed fee structure because willingness or ability to pay is an unreliable measure of compliance.

A legitimate student or institution may be unable to afford a large fee. A well-financed fraudulent operation may be able to pay it. Payment does not establish that an employer exists, that training relates to a student's degree, or that reported employment actually occurs. DHS should demonstrate why this financial screening mechanism would distinguish lawful participation from misconduct.

The agency should also separate two different outcomes: reducing the number of participants and reducing the rate of fraud. Fewer participants could produce fewer detected violations even if the program became no better at identifying misconduct. An effective evaluation should measure compliance outcomes and the exclusion of legitimate participants, not simply declining enrollment in OPT.

Before adopting this approach, DHS should compare its expected results with risk-based audits, verification of suspicious employment records, targeted site inspections, and sanctions against proven violations. That comparison should explain the costs, enforcement capacity, and likely effectiveness of each option.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fees. Any replacement should have measurable objectives, a transparent evidentiary basis, and a proportionate relationship to the specific conduct it seeks to address. Broadly pricing qualified participants out of a program is not sufficient evidence that the program has become more trustworthy.
comments.reason: Objects to the proposed fees and requests withdrawal of the rule.

International students invest an enormous amount of money, time, and effort to pursue higher education in the United States. Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization.

This proposal would severely undermine America’s ability to attract, educate, and retain talented researchers and engineers. It would ultimately harm the American innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in science and technology.

First, this proposal would weaken American technological competitiveness. The United States has benefited enormously from attracting talented students and researchers from around the world. International graduates contribute to scientific discoveries, develop new technologies, and support American companies. OPT provides an essential bridge between American higher education and professional experience. Imposing fees of up to $100,000 would effectively eliminate this opportunity for many qualified graduates, pushing highly trained talent toward competing countries.

Second, the proposed fees would place an unreasonable financial burden on American universities. Most universities cannot afford to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each international graduate seeking OPT. Research universities already face significant financial constraints. These fees would force institutions to restrict OPT recommendations, divert resources from education and research, or reduce opportunities for international students. Ultimately, American universities and their research missions would suffer.

Third, this proposal would discourage talented international students from choosing the United States. International students make substantial financial and personal commitments to pursue American higher education. Post-graduation practical training is an important part of that decision. If this opportunity becomes financially inaccessible, future students will increasingly choose countries with more predictable and welcoming pathways. The United States would lose talented future workers, tuition revenue, research contributions, and broader economic benefits.

Fourth, excessive fees are not an effective substitute for targeted immigration enforcement. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives. However, charging extraordinary fees to legitimate students and universities does not directly address fraudulent conduct. A more reasonable approach would strengthen oversight, verify legitimate employment, and enforce existing requirements against actual violations without penalizing students who follow the rules.

Finally, this proposal would undermine America’s long-term investment in STEM education and innovation. The United States invests substantial resources in educating and training international graduate students, particularly in critical scientific and engineering fields. Preventing these graduates from contributing their expertise to American industries would waste that investment and potentially transfer the benefits of American education to economic competitors.

America’s global leadership has been built in part on its openness to exceptional talent from around the world. Policies that make it prohibitively expensive for highly skilled graduates to participate in the American economy would weaken, rather than strengthen, the nation’s economic and technological competitiveness.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and pursue more targeted, proportionate, and evidence-based measures to maintain the integrity of the OPT program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation. These extraordinary fees are disproportionate to the stated objectives, insufficiently justified by the available evidence, and likely to impose substantial costs on legitimate students, educational institutions, employers, and the U.S. economy.

1. The evidence of fraud does not justify these specific fees.

DHS cites examples of fraud, shell companies, and questionable employment arrangements. However, evidence that fraud exists does not establish its prevalence across the overall OPT population or demonstrate that imposing enormous fees on all participants is an effective solution.

DHS should provide verified data on the percentage of OPT participants involved in confirmed fraud, distinguish proven violations from suspected cases, quantify the resulting harm, and explain how these specific fees would prevent future violations. Without this evidence, the proposed policy risks penalizing legitimate participants for misconduct they did not commit.

2. The proposed fee amounts lack adequate justification.

Why $70,000 and $30,000? DHS should provide a transparent explanation of how these amounts were calculated and how they relate to actual administrative costs, enforcement expenses, or measurable reductions in fraud.

If the primary purpose is to discourage participation, DHS should acknowledge that the policy may exclude legitimate students and explain why this outcome is necessary and proportionate. A policy should not be considered justified merely because an extraordinarily high price discourages people from participating.

3. The policy is poorly targeted at the actual problem.

The proposed fees apply regardless of whether a student, employer, or educational institution has engaged in misconduct. Legitimate students and compliant institutions could face the same financial barriers as those associated with fraudulent arrangements.

If DHS’s concerns involve shell companies, nonexistent jobs, and false employment records, targeted investigations, employer verification, compliance audits, and stronger penalties for proven violations would address these problems more directly. DHS should demonstrate why a blanket fee is more effective than these alternatives.

4. The economic analysis acknowledges significant uncertainty.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how much OPT participation would decline and the difficulty of precisely quantifying the resulting opportunity costs. Nevertheless, the proposed fees could fundamentally change hiring decisions, university recommendations, and students’ employment opportunities.

The analysis should rigorously assess the potential effects on international student enrollment, employer recruitment, small businesses, research, innovation, productivity, and U.S. competitiveness. A decline in OPT participation should not automatically be treated as a policy success if it also means lost employment opportunities, reduced economic activity, and qualified graduates taking their skills elsewhere.

Where substantial uncertainty exists, DHS should provide transparent sensitivity analyses and explain how its conclusions change under different assumptions about participation, employer demand, and cost-sharing arrangements.

5. DHS has not adequately demonstrated why less burdensome alternatives are insufficient.

The agency should compare the effectiveness and costs of the proposed fees against risk-based audits, enhanced employment verification, stronger oversight of institutions with documented compliance problems, and penalties for confirmed fraud.

Administrative convenience is not sufficient justification for imposing extraordinary financial burdens on legitimate participants. DHS must demonstrate that the proposed fees would produce meaningful improvements in program integrity that could not be achieved through more targeted enforcement measures.

6. The proposal could harm U.S. workers and the broader economy rather than benefit them.

DHS identifies protecting U.S. workers as an objective, but reducing OPT participation does not automatically create additional employment opportunities for American workers. Employers might instead reduce hiring, delay projects, abandon research, or move investment and talent elsewhere.

DHS should provide evidence of the specific labor-market harms it seeks to address and demonstrate that the proposed fees would improve employment outcomes for U.S. workers. It should also assess the consequences for universities, local economies, and the country’s ability to attract international talent.

Conclusion

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees in their current form.

Fraud prevention and protection of U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, but they do not justify a policy without a convincing evidentiary foundation.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they lack adequate justification and impose substantial costs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Feihua Fang
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

1. The fee is prohibitive and bears no relation to administrative cost. Existing OPT-related fees are modest and tied to processing. A charge of up to $100,000 per student is hundreds of times larger and cannot be justified as cost recovery. Whatever its stated purpose, its practical effect is to shut the door on the international graduates the U.S. has spent decades attracting and training.

2. It undermines America's long-term interests. OPT is the main bridge between a U.S. education and a U.S. career. International graduates, especially in STEM fields, found companies, fill critical roles and drive research. If the U.S. makes it prohibitively expensive to employ them, they will take their skills to Canada, the UK, Europe or Asia, and our competitors will gain the talent we trained.

3. It will cause direct economic harm. International students pay tuition, rent, and buy food, transportation and services throughout their studies and their time working here, and many universities rely on that revenue. Because the fee falls on schools, many institutions simply cannot absorb it. Economic Innovation Group has estimated that a $100,000 charge per OPT graduate could cut international master's enrollment by at least 35 percent. Lost enrollment means lost tuition, lost local spending and lost jobs in college towns.

4. DHS lacks the authority to impose it. The power to tax belongs to Congress. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the executive's power to regulate does not include a power to tax. Applying that reasoning, a federal court in Massachusetts struck down the $100,000 H-1B payment as an unauthorized tax, and the First Circuit declined to revive it. A fee set far above any cost of administering the program is a revenue-raising tax in substance, and Congress has not clearly delegated that power to DHS.

5. Fraud concerns call for targeted tools. If the concern is program integrity, DHS already has better options, such as employer reporting, SEVP audits and enforcement against abusive actors. A blanket six-figure fee penalizes the overwhelming majority of compliant students and schools.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the prohibitive OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees raise significant concerns regarding proportionality, regulatory effectiveness, and unintended consequences for American educational institutions and workforce development.
Preventing immigration fraud, maintaining program integrity, and protecting domestic workers are legitimate regulatory objectives. However, imposing substantial uniform fees on educational institutions may restrict legitimate practical training without meaningfully addressing the underlying causes of fraudulent employment arrangements.

1. Financial barriers should not replace effective oversight.
The proposed fees do not distinguish institutions with strong compliance records from those presenting documented regulatory risks. Financial capacity is not a reliable indicator of institutional integrity or employer legitimacy.
Universities, research hospitals, and nonprofit institutions may lack the financial resources to absorb these expenses, potentially discouraging legitimate employment and disrupting research continuity. Such consequences could undermine the return on substantial American investments in higher education, scientific research, and workforce training.

2. Adopt risk-based institutional and employer verification.
DHS should prioritize compliance resources using objectively documented risk indicators rather than imposing uniform financial barriers.
Potential measures include enhanced employer verification, targeted audits of suspicious employment arrangements, periodic confirmation of qualifying employment, and stronger enforcement against substantiated violations.
Institutional oversight should account for demonstrated compliance history, with appropriate opportunities to correct administrative errors and appeal adverse findings.
This approach would focus enforcement on identifiable misconduct while preserving legitimate training opportunities.

3. Establish proportionate, cost-based administrative fees.
If additional revenue is required, DHS should adopt fees reasonably related to documented processing, monitoring, and enforcement expenses.
A transparent cost analysis should distinguish routine administrative expenses from investigative and enforcement costs. Reduced fees or exemptions should be considered for qualifying nonprofit educational institutions, research hospitals, and federally supported research programs.
Subsequent OPT recommendations should not automatically incur substantial additional fees without evidence of corresponding administrative costs.

4. Strengthen accountability through measurable approaches.
Rather than relying primarily on financial deterrence, DHS may establish measurable compliance objectives, including verified fraud detection rates, investigation outcomes, administrative costs, and impacts on legitimate OPT participation.
Employer verification, targeted investigations, and proportionate sanctions for demonstrated misconduct would provide more direct mechanisms for improving program integrity.
DHS should publish periodic evaluations comparing the effectiveness and financial consequences of these approaches.

5. Protect reasonable reliance interests and educational continuity.
Major regulatory changes should account for individuals and institutions that made multi-year educational and financial commitments under existing rules.
Students enrolled in lengthy graduate programs may have reasonably anticipated access to practical training upon graduation. Abruptly introducing substantial institutional fees could disrupt established professional pathways and reduce the value of prior investments in education and research.
DHS should consider appropriate grandfathering protections, extended implementation timelines, and transitional exemptions for students already enrolled when the final rule is issued.

Conclusion
The proposed fee structure risks imposing significant costs on compliant institutions without demonstrating that financial deterrence is more effective than targeted oversight.
DHS should reconsider the proposed fees and conduct a comparative assessment of alternatives emphasizing risk-based verification, proportionate administrative costs, targeted enforcement, and transitional protections.
Such measures could better advance program integrity while preserving legitimate practical training and the competitiveness of American education and research.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter raises concerns that the fees restrict legitimate practical training and disrupt research continuity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Evelyne Francois
comments.commentText:
As a U.S. citizen, I recognize that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has legitimate governmental interests in deterring fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and preserving the integrity of the immigration system. However, I oppose the proposed fees because their excessive cost may undermine these objectives rather than advance them.
First, the proposed fees are not a sufficiently targeted means of combating fraud. DHS could pursue less restrictive alternatives, such as strengthening institutional oversight, conducting more rigorous background checks, and requiring institutions to verify that students and their employment opportunities satisfy established eligibility requirements. If academic achievement is relevant to the purpose of OPT, objective criteria such as GPA or class ranking could also be considered where appropriate. Imposing a prohibitive fee, however, risks penalizing genuinely qualified students rather than effectively deterring those who engage in fraud. Moreover, individuals or organizations determined to circumvent the law may not be deterred by financial penalties alone. Meanwhile, students who lack the financial resources to overcome this barrier may be discouraged from pursuing legitimate opportunities. The result could be that the proposed rule places its greatest burden on those attempting to comply with the law, while doing little to eliminate the underlying sources of fraud.
Second, the proposed fees do not adequately demonstrate how they would protect U.S. workers. If the concern is that OPT participants may displace American workers or create unfair competition, DHS should consider measures that address those concerns more directly. For example, stronger employer oversight and appropriate wage requirements could help prevent employers from using OPT participants to undercut the compensation of U.S. workers. Simply making OPT prohibitively expensive could drive international students away from the United States without addressing the incentives that may lead employers to seek cheaper labor. Furthermore, in an increasingly global economy where remote work is possible, some employers could continue hiring foreign workers abroad, potentially at lower wages and without creating employment opportunities in the United States. Consequently, the proposed fees may fail to protect U.S. workers while discouraging international students from contributing to the U.S. economy.
Finally, the proposed fees may discourage institutions from recommending students for OPT rather than incentivize them to exercise greater diligence. Requiring institutions to pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation could expose them to substantial financial liability, regardless of whether they have acted responsibly. Faced with this burden, institutions may simply stop recommending students for OPT instead of assuming the financial risk. This outcome would undermine the program without necessarily reducing fraud. It could also discourage prospective international students from studying in the United States, leading them to pursue comparable opportunities in other countries. Because the stated objective is to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers—not to discourage international students from studying in the United States—such an outcome would be counterproductive.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to consider a more narrowly tailored approach that directly addresses fraud, strengthens institutional oversight, and protects U.S. workers without imposing excessive financial barriers on legitimate OPT participants. Effective regulation should target the conduct it seeks to prevent while preserving lawful opportunities for qualified students and the institutions that serve them.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees because their excessive cost undermines DHS objectives and penalizes qualified students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

The proposed OPT fees raise serious concerns regarding their potential negative consequences for the U.S. economy, scientific research, technological innovation, and the nation's ability to attract and retain highly skilled STEM professionals.

International Ph.D. graduates and STEM researchers play a vital role in advancing scientific research at American universities. Despite receiving relatively modest compensation, these researchers perform highly specialized and demanding work, contributing significantly to federally funded research projects, scientific discoveries, and technological innovation. Their contributions are essential to maintaining the productivity, competitiveness, and global leadership of the U.S. research ecosystem.

**1. Loss of Highly Skilled STEM Talent**

International graduate students contribute significantly to research projects funded by NIH, NSF, and other federal agencies. They conduct sophisticated experiments, develop analytical methods, operate advanced instrumentation, and produce scientific publications while receiving relatively modest graduate stipends. Their contributions provide universities with highly skilled research expertise at a fraction of the cost of hiring experienced professional scientists. Substantial OPT fees could make retaining these trained researchers financially impractical, resulting in the loss of valuable scientific talent.

**2. Negative Impact on Scientific Research and Innovation**

American universities rely heavily on international graduate researchers to execute complex scientific projects. Replacing these researchers with professional scientists could substantially increase personnel expenses, reduce research productivity, and limit the number of projects supported by existing federal grants. Restricting their transition into the U.S. workforce could also disrupt ongoing research, delay scientific discoveries, and weaken innovation in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence, analytical chemistry, and other critical STEM fields.

**3. Global Competition and Loss of Talent to Other Countries**

Countries such as Canada, Germany, the United Kingdom, and Australia actively compete to attract highly educated international professionals. If the United States makes employment opportunities financially inaccessible, these countries could recruit STEM graduates already educated and trained at American universities. Instead of contributing to American industries, these scientists and engineers may develop technologies, establish businesses, create jobs, and advance scientific research in competing economies. The United States risks losing not only highly skilled professionals but also the future economic and technological benefits of their expertise.

**4. Economic Consequences and Burden on Research Institutions**

International STEM graduates contribute to the U.S. economy through employment, taxes, consumer spending, entrepreneurship, and technological advancement. Excessive OPT fees could discourage talented students from choosing American universities while placing additional financial pressure on research institutions. Universities, nonprofit laboratories, and startups operating with limited budgets may struggle to retain qualified researchers, disrupting scientific projects and reducing economic productivity.

**5. Need for a Balanced, Evidence-Based Approach**

Preventing immigration fraud and maintaining program integrity are important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective oversight, compliance monitoring, and reasonable administrative fees rather than excessive financial barriers that could undermine scientific research and economic competitiveness.

DHS should carefully evaluate the broader economic and scientific consequences of this proposal and consider less burdensome alternatives, including reasonable fees, exemptions for research institutions, and protections for students already participating in OPT.


International STEM researchers are not merely beneficiaries of the American research system; they are essential contributors to its productivity, innovation, and global leadership. Imposing substantial OPT fees risks driving highly trained talent to competing nations, increasing research costs, disrupting scientific progress, and weakening America's long-term economic and technological competitiveness. A balanced approach is essential to maintaining immigration program integrity while preserving the United States' ability to attract, develop, and retain highly skilled STEM professionals. Reconsideration of the proposed fee structure would help protect American scientific leadership, research productivity, and economic growth.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

While some proponents argue that penalizing universities with $70,000 to $100,000 fees will lower tuition or protect opportunities for U.S. students, economic data proves the exact opposite. This punitive fee is a de facto ban on experiential learning that will raise tuition for American students, devastate university budgets, and drive top innovators to global competitors.

1. International Students Subsidize Domestic Education Rather Than Draining Aid
A common misconception in comments supporting this rule is that universities divert financial aid from U.S. citizens to fund international students. In reality, international students are legally ineligible for U.S. federal aid (like Pell Grants and federal loans), and the vast majority pay full, unsubsidized tuition. At public universities in Michigan, California, and nationwide, they pay two to three times the in-state tuition rate.

National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) studies show that revenue from full-paying international students cross-subsidizes domestic students—keeping tuition lower for U.S. citizens and funding campus financial aid. DHS itself acknowledges colleges may pass this new $70,000-$100,000 fee on to the general student body. Furthermore, NAFSA data shows international students contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support 378,000+ U.S. jobs. Driving them away will force universities to hike tuition for working-class and first-generation American students.

2. OPT Creates American Jobs Rather Than Taking Them
The labor market is not a zero-sum game. Studies by the Business Roundtable and the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP) confirm there is no correlation between OPT participation and U.S. worker unemployment. High-skilled OPT participants fill acute shortages in STEM, healthcare, and manufacturing, expanding domestic operations and creating downstream jobs for Americans. Without OPT, U.S. companies will simply offshore R&D and engineering roles to Canada, Europe, or Asia.

3. What America Stands to Lose: The Track Record of F-1 and OPT Alumni
According to NFAP, nearly 25% of U.S. billion-dollar startups ("unicorns") have a founder who first came to America as an international student, creating hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs:
- Elon Musk came to UPenn as an international student before founding SpaceX and Tesla, which now employ over 100,000 Americans.
- Satya Nadella (CEO of Microsoft) and Sundar Pichai (CEO of Alphabet/Google) arrived as F-1 students, gained early experience through practical training, and now lead trillion-dollar U.S. enterprises.
- AI pioneers like Aravind Srinivas (Perplexity AI) and Ali Ghodsi (Databricks) transitioned from U.S. university research to building foundational American tech companies.
- Thousands of biomedical researchers and healthcare professionals also rely on OPT for life-saving work at U.S. hospitals and labs.

Had a $70,000-$100,000 fee existed when they graduated, no school or startup could have afforded to recommend them for OPT, and the jobs they created would belong to another country today.

4. Harm to Public Universities and Small Businesses
A $100,000 fee does not regulate billionaire endowments; only a few ultra-wealthy private colleges could ever absorb it, while regional public universities and small businesses will be completely priced out. Using a $100,000 blanket fee instead of targeted SEVIS audits is arbitrary, capricious, and exceeds reasonable regulatory fee authority.

I urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 in its entirety.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Member of the Public

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Sections IV–V — the proposed fee is not a targeted anti-fraud measure.

DHS considered extending the safeguards that already exist for STEM OPT — Form I-983 training plans, employer site visits, and enhanced reporting — to OPT generally, and rejected them because a fee "can be implemented quickly," requires no "significant additional resources" from the government, and imposes "minimal administrative burdens on the government" (91 FR 64566). That reasoning concedes the point: the fee was chosen because it is easy for DHS, not because it detects fraud. It detects nothing. It is imposed before any individualized finding of ineligibility, on every participant at every accredited school, and the refund — available only at SEVP's discretion, and only before the EAD issues — offers no meaningful process to a student wrongly priced out.

The fee also creates a conflict of interest for schools. DHS says the charge is meant to make institutions "more selective and deliberate." In practice, a school with $70,000 at stake per student will deny meritorious cases to avoid financial risk, and will favor students who can repay it. Academic eligibility decisions should be made on academic criteria, under published standards — not on a university's willingness to absorb a five-figure federal levy.

If fraud in OPT is the problem, the remedy is enforcement against the fraudulent: risk-based audits and site visits, employer verification, action against diploma mills and shell companies selling jobs, and prosecution of organizers — tools directed at the small population actually abusing the program, rather than a blanket charge on the compliant majority. DHS should withdraw the fee proposal and, if it acts further, propose measures rationally connected to identifying actual fraud.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees, arguing they are not targeted anti-fraud measures and cause harm.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Section VII (Regulatory Analyses) — I oppose the proposed fees.

DHS's own analysis is the strongest case against this rule. DHS estimates annualized costs with a primary estimate of $4.1 billion and 10-year costs of $35.1 billion (discounted at 3 percent), alongside transfers to the federal government with a primary estimate of $12.8 billion per year / $109.4 billion over 10 years. It counts 2,478 affected schools, of which roughly 56 percent are small entities, and it considered — and rejected — an exemption for small institutions. DHS should explain what public benefit justifies costs of this magnitude, because the NPRM identifies none that is quantified: the asserted benefits are qualitative, while the costs are admitted and enormous.

The predictable institutional response is rationing. Faced with $70,000 per first recommendation, schools will recommend fewer students, favor programs and students who can reimburse the fee, and in many cases exit OPT participation altogether. DHS acknowledges the cost may instead be spread to "all students" — i.e., a tuition increase for U.S. students who will never use OPT. International students pay tuition, fund research laboratories, and cross-subsidize domestic enrollment; driving down their enrollment does not protect U.S. workers, it shrinks the universities and labs that employ them.

Nor does pricing out foreign graduates create jobs for Americans. It moves the work: employers who cannot train and hire STEM graduates in the United States will expand research and engineering operations in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations.
