First, the proposed fees are disproportionate to their stated objectives. I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, ensuring regulatory compliance, and protecting American workers. However, imposing a $70,000 fee does not establish whether a student, university, or employer is complying with OPT requirements. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of program integrity. The proposed approach risks restricting legitimate participation without adequately distinguishing compliant institutions and students from those engaged in misconduct.

Second, the proposal would impose substantial financial burdens on American universities and their students. Although the rule formally places payment responsibility on educational institutions, DHS explicitly acknowledges that institutions may transfer these costs to students or employers. For public universities operating under constrained budgets, the proposed fees could make supporting OPT financially impractical. For international doctoral students, whose education often involves years of research, teaching, and scholarly contributions, such costs could effectively eliminate access to authorized practical training regardless of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance history.

Third, the proposal could undermine American research capacity and international competitiveness. U.S. universities invest substantial resources in educating and training international graduate students, many of whom contribute to federally funded research, classroom instruction, technological development, and scientific innovation. OPT provides an important opportunity to translate this specialized education into practical experience. Restricting access through exceptionally high fees could weaken universities' ability to attract international talent and reduce the return on investments already made in graduate education and research. These consequences deserve particular attention in fields where research projects, technical expertise, and institutional knowledge develop over multiple years.

Fourth, the rule raises serious concerns about equity and reliance interests. International students make substantial educational, financial, and professional commitments when entering U.S. degree programs. Students already enrolled in multiyear programs have reasonably planned their educational trajectories under an existing regulatory framework. Although DHS proposes prospective implementation, the rule would still affect currently enrolled students who have not yet received an OPT recommendation. A 60-day transition period does little to address the substantial disruption these students and their universities may experience. Moreover, the ability to participate in OPT should not depend primarily on a student's personal wealth or an institution's willingness to absorb extraordinary fees.

Fifth, DHS's own regulatory impact analysis raises questions about proportionality and alternatives. The proposed rule estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs and $12.8 billion in annualized fee transfers under its primary estimates at a 3 percent discount rate. Protecting the integrity of the immigration system and preserving America's capacity to attract, educate, and retain highly qualified international talent should be mutually reinforcing objectives, not competing priorities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Sections III–IV and proposed 8 CFR 214.13 — the proposed charge exceeds DHS's statutory authority and is arbitrary and capricious.

1. By the NPRM's own admission, this is revenue-raising, not a user fee. DHS states that the amounts collected "would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302," that "ICE would not maintain or use the funding collected," and that INA 214(a) "does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected" (91 FR 64566). A fee must bear a reasonable relationship to the cost of a service provided to the payer. Here there is no service and no cost nexus: the underlying acts — a DSO entering a recommendation in SEVIS and USCIS adjudicating Form I-765 — are already charged for, at $470 (online I-765 filing). DHS estimates annual transfers of $8.7–$16.9 billion (primary estimate $12.8 billion), orders of magnitude above any processing cost it identifies. A levy of that scale, sent to the general Treasury, is a tax, and only Congress may impose one.

2. The amount was not derived from cost at all. DHS explains that it set the initial fee to "closely align with the H-1B fees" in Presidential Proclamation 10973 in order to deter participation — that is, the number is a deterrent penalty aimed at a different visa category, not a measurement of anything OPT costs the government.

3. It fails reasoned decision-making. A flat charge cannot distinguish fraud from compliance: a fraudulent operator selling fake jobs can pass $70,000 on to its victims, while a fully compliant doctoral student at an accredited nonprofit university is priced out entirely. DHS concedes it "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation." A rule whose stated purpose is to target abuse, but whose mechanism screens solely on ability to pay, lacks a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.

DHS should withdraw the proposal. At minimum, it must identify the statutory provision that authorizes a revenue measure of this size, and reconcile the amount with the actual cost of the service.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees, arguing they exceed statutory authority and lack reasoned decision-making.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, proposed 8 CFR 214.13 — I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw them.

I am an F-1 student pursuing a graduate degree in a STEM field at a U.S. university. Like many F-1 students, I expect to seek practical training directly related to my field of study during and after my program: an internship on pre-completion OPT, a period of post-completion OPT, and, if eligible, the STEM OPT extension.

Under this proposal, my university would have to pay $70,000 before a DSO could even enter the first of those recommendations in SEVIS, then $30,000 more for the next recommendation and another $30,000 for the STEM extension — up to $130,000 for one student who has complied with every rule. No university can rationally pay that, and DHS itself acknowledges that schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers" (91 FR 64566). If the fee is passed to students, it is simply unpayable on a graduate student's stipend. If it is not, eligibility for training that is part of a degree will turn not on academic standing or compliance, but on a department's budget.

DHS defends the amount by saying it is "on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur for one or two years of education." I oppose the proposed OPT fees because their consequences could fall unevenly across American communities, placing regional universities, smaller employers, and less wealthy areas at a particular disadvantage.

A uniform fee does not create a uniform burden. The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could be more difficult for a regional institution with limited resources to absorb than for a wealthy university. If institutions pass these costs to students or seek support from employers, the financial barrier remains; it simply shifts to another participant.

This matters for communities that rely on local colleges and universities to develop their workforce. A graduate who has studied in a region has already established connections there and may be prepared to contribute to a local business. If the proposed fees prevent that graduate from accessing practical training, the surrounding community could lose an opportunity to retain someone it helped educate.

The effects could be especially significant for smaller employers. A company outside a major metropolitan area may have fewer applicants with specialized skills and fewer resources for recruiting nationally. Losing access to a qualified local graduate could delay a project, limit expansion, or increase recruitment costs. DHS should evaluate these possibilities rather than assume that another suitable worker will always be immediately available in the same location.

The proposal could also concentrate opportunities in institutions and businesses with the greatest financial resources. Wealthier organizations may be better positioned to absorb or arrange payment of the fees, while smaller institutions and firms reduce participation. That would risk making access to practical training depend more heavily on institutional wealth and geography than on the quality of the training itself.

For the United States, this is a question of balanced regional development. Communities seeking to build new industries and retain educated residents should not face unnecessary barriers to connecting local education with legitimate practical experience. A policy that concentrates talent and opportunity in a smaller number of well-resourced locations could work against those communities’ efforts.

Before proceeding, DHS should provide a geographically differentiated assessment of the proposal’s effects. National totals alone may obscure substantial local losses. The analysis should consider differences in institutional resources, employer size, local recruitment conditions, and the availability of realistic alternatives when a graduate cannot participate in OPT. comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted measures to address fraud while preserving legitimate, accessible practical training.

My concerns relate particularly to the proposal’s rationale in Section IV, its fee requirements and transition provisions, and its economic analysis. Fees of this magnitude risk making OPT financially inaccessible to many students and institutions. Although the proposal does not formally eliminate OPT, it could substantially reduce access to the program, with consequences for the American economy and the nation’s long-term talent pipeline.

First, DHS should fully account for the economic value that international students bring to American communities. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures describe international education overall, rather than the incremental contribution of OPT alone. Nevertheless, they demonstrate the scale of economic activity potentially affected if restrictions on practical training make American education less attractive. DHS should evaluate how the proposed fees could affect enrollment, tuition revenue, housing demand, local businesses, and employment connected to universities.

Second, sharply reducing OPT participation could impose immediate costs on American employers. Practical training allows graduates to apply knowledge acquired at U.S. institutions in work directly related to their studies. If otherwise qualified graduates become unavailable because their institutions cannot afford the fees, employers may face disrupted projects, additional recruitment costs, and the loss of people they have already trained. Smaller businesses, startups, and research organizations may have fewer resources to absorb these disruptions. DHS should assess these effects rather than assume that each reduction in OPT participation produces an equivalent employment opportunity for a U.S. worker.

Third, the proposal could weaken America’s long-term ability to attract and retain talent. The United States benefits when people educated in its universities can contribute their skills to American research, product development, and business formation. Making practical training prohibitively expensive could encourage talented students to choose other countries or take their U.S.-acquired skills elsewhere after graduation. The potential cost extends beyond immediate hiring: it includes future research capacity, entrepreneurial activity, professional networks, and the development of specialized expertise.

The National Science Foundation’s 2026 science and engineering indicators report that STEM employment is projected to grow faster than overall employment between 2024 and 2034. This does not establish that every STEM occupation faces a shortage, but it reinforces the need for a careful, occupation-specific assessment of future workforce needs before sharply restricting a pipeline of U.S.-educated talent.

Fourth, the proposal risks selecting participants based on financial resources rather than educational merit or compliance. A large fee does not itself establish that a training opportunity is legitimate, that a student is highly qualified, or that an employer protects American workers. Institutions with fewer financial resources could be unable to support otherwise deserving students. If costs are passed to students, access could depend primarily on personal wealth. DHS should explain why these outcomes are necessary and evaluate less restrictive alternatives.

Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. More closely targeted approaches could include verifying actual training activity, auditing high-risk employers and institutions, enforcing applicable wage and training requirements, and imposing meaningful consequences on proven violators. DHS should compare the costs and effectiveness of these alternatives against the proposed fees.

Finally, DHS should give substantial consideration to students who enrolled and invested in American education under the existing framework. A short transition period may not adequately address the reliance interests of students already pursuing multi-year degrees. At minimum, any material change should include meaningful protections for currently enrolled students and existing training arrangements.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure. Preserving accessible, well-supervised OPT would better support American businesses, local economies, higher education, and long-term competitiveness while allowing targeted enforcement against abuse.

I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01) establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students. I urge DHS to finalize the rule as proposed.Combating Fraud and Strengthening Program Integrity
OPT has become a high-volume pathway that is frequently abused. Schools, students, and employers have used the program in ways inconsistent with its original educational purpose, including as a prolonged work authorization vehicle that feeds directly into the H-1B system. Significant fees will create meaningful financial accountability, discourage low-quality or “visa mill” institutions from recommending students indiscriminately, and incentivize greater oversight by Designated School Officials before they enter OPT recommendations in SEVIS. This aligns with DHS’s stated goals of combating fraud and abuse and ensuring the program is used consistent with applicable regulatory requirements.
Addressing the Pipeline into H-1B Abuse and Nepotism
OPT serves as a primary feeder into the H-1B program. The well-documented problems of fraud, misrepresentation of job duties, wage undercutting, and nepotistic hiring practices in segments of the H-1B program are enabled in part by the large volume of OPT participants who transition into temporary worker status. By imposing substantial fees on the front end of this pipeline, the proposed rule will reduce the volume of participants who view OPT primarily as a bridge to longer-term employment authorization rather than genuine practical training related to their field of study. This is a necessary and proportionate step to protect the integrity of both programs.
Protecting American Workers
The current structure of OPT allows large numbers of foreign students to enter the U.S. labor market with employment authorization that is not subject to the same labor-market protections or numerical limits as other temporary worker categories. This depresses opportunities and wages for American workers, particularly recent graduates and mid-career professionals in STEM and other fields. Requiring schools to pay significant fees before recommending students for OPT will reduce the supply of low-cost foreign labor entering the job market through this channel and help restore a more level playing field for U.S. citizens and permanent residents.
Promoting Accountability Among Educational Institutions
Under the proposed rule, SEVP-certified schools must pay the fee before a Designated School Official can recommend a student for OPT, and USCIS will not grant employment authorization without confirmation of payment. This places the financial responsibility where the recommendation decision is made and encourages institutions to exercise greater selectivity and diligence. Schools that treat OPT as a marketing tool to attract international students, rather than a limited educational benefit, will face real costs. Collected fees deposited in the U.S. Treasury further support broader government efforts to maintain immigration system integrity.
Balancing Legitimate Use with Necessary Reform
The rule does not eliminate OPT. It simply attaches a meaningful cost to participation so that the program is no longer effectively unlimited and cost-free for the institutions that drive volume. Legitimate students and high-quality programs can still participate; the fees will primarily deter abuse and excessive reliance on foreign student labor. Efficiency and volume should not override the statutory and policy imperative to protect U.S. workers and maintain program integrity.

Conclusion
I strongly urge DHS to finalize the Optional Practical Training Fees rule as proposed, without reducing the fee amounts or creating broad exemptions that would undermine its effectiveness. Significant fees are a direct and appropriate response to documented fraud, abuse, and the role OPT plays as a pathway into problematic H-1B practices. Finalizing this rule will combat fraud, strengthen oversight, reduce the flow of cheap labor into the American job market, protect U.S. workers, and restore public confidence in the integrity of the F-1 and related nonimmigrant programs.

Dear Secretary Mullin,



I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

As an international student who completed a Ph.D. in the U.S. and is currently working as a postdoctoral researcher, I believe the proposed increase in OPT fees would place an additional financial burden on international students who have already invested significant time and resources in their education. OPT is an essential opportunity for international graduates to gain professional experience and contribute their skills to the U.S. workforce.

Higher fees, combined with the uncertainty surrounding immigration policies, would make me reconsider the long-term financial and career stability of staying in the U.S. It could also discourage talented international students from choosing the U.S. for their education and careers, ultimately reducing the country's ability to attract and retain highly skilled researchers and professionals.

International students and graduates play a critical role in advancing American science by bringing diverse perspectives, specialized expertise, and innovative ideas to research institutions. Many contribute to cutting-edge research in biomedical sciences, technology, and other fields that improve public health and strengthen the U.S. economy.

As an international researcher, I have contributed to scientific research in the U.S. throughout my Ph.D. and postdoctoral training. International researchers not only help drive scientific discoveries but also support collaboration, mentor future scientists, and strengthen the competitiveness of American research institutions. Restricting opportunities for international graduates could lead to the loss of highly trained talent and weaken America's global leadership in science and innovation.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Hyewon Han

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ariel Nievera
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) proposed rule establishing fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

This commonsense measure would require Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP)-certified schools to pay $70,000 for an F-1 student’s initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT (including STEM extensions). These fees are a necessary and overdue step to restore integrity to the student visa system, combat widespread fraud and abuse, and protect American workers.

OPT has expanded far beyond its original educational purpose into a large-scale temporary work program that often functions as a workaround to the H-1B process. The proposed fees properly align costs with the significant administrative burden and enforcement challenges the program creates. By placing the financial responsibility on the recommending institutions, the rule incentivizes schools to exercise real oversight and selectivity rather than treating OPT recommendations as routine. This will help curb “visa mill” activity and reduce the placement of students with questionable or nonexistent employers.

Protecting U.S. workers must be a priority. Allowing large numbers of foreign students to enter the labor market at relatively low cost disadvantages American graduates, especially recent college graduates competing for entry-level positions in STEM and other fields. The proposed fees help level the playing field without eliminating legitimate practical training opportunities for genuine students.
The rule is carefully structured: fees are paid before a Designated School Official can enter a recommendation in SEVIS, USCIS cannot issue employment authorization without confirmation of payment, and a refund mechanism exists if authorization is not granted. Transition provisions appropriately grandfather students already recommended or approved. Collected fees will support stronger program oversight.

I urge DHS and ICE to finalize this rule promptly and without weakening the proposed fee levels. Strong enforcement tools and proper cost recovery are essential to maintaining a lawful, secure, and fair immigration system that puts American workers first.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment in support of this important proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly supports the proposed rule and fees to combat visa abuse and protect U.S. workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this rule. That record shows a program managed for 79 years through conditions on the training, never through a price on access.

1. Training employment has been part of student status since 1947
Footnote 24 quotes the 1947 rule, 12 FR 5355, 5357: "In cases where employment for practical training is required or recommended by the school, the district director may permit the student to engage in such employment for a six-month period subject to extension for not over two additional six-month periods." The 1953 rule, 18 FR 3526, 3529, used the same terms. That allowed up to 18 months. Today's initial OPT period is 12 months.
Section VI states that "The F-1 visa was never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States." DHS's own footnotes show the opposite about training. Congress enacted the INA in 1952, five years after the 1947 rule, and footnote 23 says the Act was silent on practical training. Training employment tied to study is part of the original design.

2. Every past change used conditions, not prices
The history DHS cites runs through at least eight rules:
- 1947 and 1953: case-by-case approval by a district director, with fixed time limits.
- 1973 (38 FR 35425): a school official "must certify that the employment is recommended for that purpose and will provide the student with practical training in his field of study."
- 1991 (56 FR 55608): training must be "directly related to [the student's] major area of study."
- 1992 (57 FR 31954): OPT while school is in session, capped at 20 hours a week.
- 2008 and 2016: the STEM extension, the STEM degree list, the Form I-983 training plan with employer attestation, and site visits.
- 2024: cap-gap amendments.
Each rule met its problem with a substantive condition: a time limit, a field test, an hours cap, a training plan or an inspection. The NPRM identifies no prior rule that charged a school for recommending a student. It does not say why these tools no longer work.

3. The history points to the gap DHS should close
The 1973 rule tied the school's certification to a specific job that "will provide the student with practical training in his field of study." Current rules dropped that link for initial OPT. The NPRM notes that a student "does not have to secure a training opportunity before the DSO can recommend OPT." The fraud DHS describes in Section IV, such as shell companies and false offer letters, exploits that gap. The school vouches before anyone knows the job.
The proposed fee widens the gap. DHS states the fee "would not be tied to a specific employer." It is paid before a job exists and tells DHS nothing about the job. A job-specific relatedness check when the student reports an employer would address the cited schemes directly, with precedent dating to 1973.

4. Where this program has a fee, Congress authorized it
The 1924 Act, as the NPRM quotes it, made school responsibility a duty to "report" when a student stopped attending. IIRIRA section 641 later created the electronic monitoring program, and Congress provided for the SEVIS fee in that statute, 8 U.S.C. 1372(e). The NPRM places the OPT fee in 8 CFR 214.13, the SEVIS fee section, and renames the existing charges "SEVIS fee" so the two can be told apart (Sections IV.D and V.B). That edit marks the difference. The SEVIS fee rests on a statute and funds a program. The OPT fee rests on no fee statute. Its amount is set by comparison to "the educational costs that foreign students incur for one or two years of education."

5. A rule this far from past practice needs to explain the break
For 79 years, the school's role was academic: decide whether training is "required or recommended" and certify that it fits the field. The proposal makes the school's role financial. A DSO "may not enter the OPT recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid." The NPRM does not discuss this change or reconcile its "never intended" statement with the rules it cites.

6. Requested action
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS believes the recommendation process needs tightening, it should re-propose a rule built on its own history:
(a) restore a 1973-style certification that the student's specific job provides training in the field of study, made when the student reports an employer;
(b) keep the existing time limits, the "directly related" standard and the STEM safeguards;
(c) impose no charge on schools without express congressional authorization like 8 U.S.C. 1372(e); and
(d) correct the record on the original intent of practical training and explain, using the 1947 to 2024 history, why conditions on training are no longer adequate.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the rule, arguing the program has historically relied on conditions, not high prices.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and their potential impact on international students pursuing higher education in the United States.

I am currently an international graduate student studying Data Science and Business Analytics at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. Before moving to the United States, I worked as an auditor in New Zealand for four years. I decided to pursue graduate education in the United States to expand my technical expertise and transition into the field of data science.

This decision required a significant investment of time and financial resources, including leaving full-time employment, relocating internationally, and covering tuition and living expenses. I considered the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation an important part of my educational and professional development.

I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the OPT program, ensuring compliance with immigration regulations, and protecting the interests of U.S. workers. However, I am concerned that substantial additional OPT fees could create financial barriers for students who have already made considerable investments in their education.

In particular, fees of $70,000 for initial OPT authorization and $30,000 for subsequent authorization would be difficult for many international graduates to afford. Such costs could limit access to practical training based primarily on financial circumstances rather than academic qualifications, professional skills, or compliance with program requirements.

Practical training provides an opportunity for international graduates to apply their academic knowledge in professional settings. In fields such as data science and business analytics, this experience can be particularly valuable because it allows students to develop technical and analytical skills through real-world applications.

I am also concerned about the potential broader implications for U.S. higher education institutions. The availability of post-graduation practical training is one of several factors international students consider when deciding where to pursue their education. Significant additional costs could influence future enrollment decisions and affect the ability of U.S. universities to attract students with diverse academic and professional backgrounds.

From my perspective, the opportunity to participate in OPT was an important consideration when deciding to pursue graduate education in the United States. While employment is never guaranteed, access to practical training provides a pathway for students to gain relevant experience and contribute their knowledge and skills within the existing regulatory framework.

I respectfully encourage the Department to carefully evaluate the potential financial and educational consequences of the proposed fees, particularly for students who are already enrolled in U.S. institutions and made their educational decisions under the existing framework.

I also encourage consideration of alternative approaches that support program oversight and compliance without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on individual students. Fees that are reasonably related to administrative costs, together with targeted compliance and enforcement measures, may provide a more balanced approach.

Thank you for considering these comments and the perspectives of international students who have made substantial commitments to pursuing education in the United States.

Sincerely,

An International Graduate Student  
University of North Carolina at Charlotte
comments.reason: The commenter argues that substantial OPT fees create severe financial barriers for international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ellie Browne
comments.commentText:
I urge the withdrawal of the proposed rule Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I am a PhD teacher and researcher at Yale University. I teach chemistry to first-year undergraduate students in various majors, most of whom aspire to be medical professionals or researchers. I research the gut microbiome, aiming to elucidate its role in health and disease and using it as inspiration for therapeutic development. 

Section [IVA] provides justification for reducing the number of OPT positions, relying heavily on a single anecdote and vague data. I challenge the authors of this rule to investigate the positive outcomes of OPT positions. In my work, I have encountered many workers on OPT or who are eligible for OPT who have contributed essential findings to groundbreaking research and who have changed students’ lives through teaching. The significant achievements of workers on OPT far outweigh the minuscule instances of fraud and abuse. 

Section [IVB] posits that the proposed “fees… would ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate in OPT and the labor market is not oversaturated with low-paid foreign workers.” I’ve worked at wealthy, private institutions, like Yale and MIT, and public institutions in financial crisis, like the University of Arizona. My coworkers come from all over the world and a wide variety of economic backgrounds; many used OPT. In my eight years of experience in my field, I have learned that cutting-edge research and excellent teaching can be found at all institutions and can be carried out by people from all parts of the world and economic backgrounds. The idea that individual or institutional wealth is correlated with qualification to do a job is laughable. Placing a burden on institutions to pay an exorbitant fee widens the gaps in an already disparate opportunity landscape; this is further magnified if institutions choose to shift that burden onto individuals with far less capital. 

[IVB] also aims to address the supposed “labor market… oversaturated with low-paid foreign workers.” First, the insinuation that low pay is somehow the fault of workers is laughable. It is managers, executives, and administrators that set wages and salaries; it is these groups that decide that international workers should be paid less than their domestic counterparts, despite having comparable qualifications. Second, this proposed rule would succeed in reducing the number of workers utilizing OPT drastically: the problem is that research and teaching desperately need more workers. There are ample diseases to cure, environmental issues to address, processes to engineer, social problems to deconvolute, historical events to unravel, and texts to analyze. These mysteries lie unanswered as research is mercilessly targeted with censorious fervor; this grant proposal sounds a little too adjacent to racial justice, this one too close to renewable energy, this one uses the word “gender.” People suffer in the meantime: they die without new treatments for incurable conditions, navigate deteriorating infrastructure, and wait for policy that is conducive to their flourishing. At the same time, there are classrooms full of students excited to learn, to become the leaders and innovators of tomorrow, only to be faced by instructors who cannot teach effectively because they are overburdened. In short, there is a tremendous amount of work to be done. Even if every single American with aspirations of doing research or teaching were able to work these jobs, we would still need international workers to fulfill the tremendous demand. 

[IVB] claims to protect American workers. The truth is, attacking OPT in this way would only put increased strain on an already crumbling workforce; I say this as a domestic worker with no personal stake in this rule. Devastating harm to research and teaching is being done by cuts to NIH, NSF, and DOE funding. Graduate programs have cut their admissions drastically, putting increased demand on existing graduate students in their research and teaching duties; with this rule, the postdoctoral labor force with dwindle, too. Important research programs are already withering. Teaching is already suffering. 

Importantly, there are not good alternatives to OPT to fill the gaps left in the workforce should this rule go into effect. In the scenarios that I work in, it is common for a PhD student to transition to OPT from an F visa when they graduate. They may do this to continue their PhD research or to seek jobs at American companies. The alternative would be seeking a J visa, which has a shorter grace period in the case that someone loses their job and requires application from abroad. These are cost-prohibitive and limit the opportunities within the US that an international worker can pursue.
comments.reason: The commenter urges the withdrawal of the proposed rule, citing the vital contributions of OPT workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dawn S
comments.commentText:
I have deep concerns and encourage DHS to entirely abandon this proposed rule adding exorbitant fees to F-1 students seeking optional practical training.  I worked at several schools in New England over 30+ years. 
This is an unlawful, exorbitant tax on F-1s.  
A fee is based on the service provided and goes to the service to cover costs of processing.  A tax, by definition, goes to the US general treasury.  In this instance, there is no assurance the stated purpose of fraud detection/prevention will occur or be funded, and funds are not controlled by DHS, thus it is an enormous tax on F-1s.  
The H-1B fraud prevention fee is $500.  How does DHS justify a $70,000 fee followed by an additional $30,000 fee on OPT requests?
It is unclear how the proposed fees were determined and how DHS will guarantee the fees support the stated intent of fraud prevention/reduction.  
Designated School Officials are put into an impossible position to determine “qualified” students for OPT recommendation.
All post-secondary students are put through a strict admission process, must meet school standards for normal academic process/degree completion.  By definition, all F-1 students who meet the school’s standards are qualified.
As a job offer is not required at the time of post-completion OPT application, and 90 days of unemployment are allowed, therefore there is not a required position to be evaluated for the majority of my students at the time of the OPT application.
The idea that a DSO could compare across disciplines who is most “qualified” is preposterous.  A DSO cannot compare the options between music, engineering and history majors, or pit them against nursing or a seminary student.  Each student has gained the requisite skills in their chosen field and OPT was never designed only for high earning students.
The proposed rule is inherently inequitable.
If enacted, this rule turns OPT from an academic experience into a “pay to stay” scheme with only the most economically advantaged F-1s participating, rather than  academically qualified students.  A former university president said “The world equally distributes talent, but it does not equally distribute opportunity, and paths are not always the same.”  The proposed rule eliminates opportunities for all but the most economically advantaged and builds a systematic barrier to success.
The proposed cost of the OPT charge is stated to be transmitted by schools, who may collect it from employers or students.  The schools that I have worked for do not have the budget to pay $70-$100K per F-1 student who seeks OPT.  Many of my students struggle to pay the OPT premium processing fee, and some struggle with the base OPT fee.  At the end of studies, personal/family funds are often depleted. Many F-1 students do not have an employer lined up at the time of application, so it is highly unlikely a future employer will pay the fee.
It is inequitable that a school would grant this support to some students and not all.  It would be a taxable scholarship, which would be completely out of line with awards for domestic students.
The proposed rule, taken together with other recent changes, makes the US a less desirable study abroad destination.  This will financially impact US schools, their communities, and reduce options for domestic students.
From visa delays to increased vetting, travel bans, SEVIS and visa terminations, CPT restrictions and proposed end of D/S and restriction of academic freedoms, this proposed rule creates an extremely negative, unwelcoming environment for F-1 students.
OPT is similar to work options in multiple other countries.  Its essential elimination will encourage students to look elsewhere for their educational needs.  International education is a large export for the U.S.  If we lose our international students, we lose the dollars and talent they bring to the US.
At my current school, I see decreased international applications, fewer successful visas, reduced graduate program start terms and the elimination of in-person modality for some programs.  This also impacts our domestic students seeking those options.
A reduced number of students also decreases the number of renters, shoppers, and users of local services.  This proposed rule will result in financial hardship to our whole community.
I support appropriate review/action taken against fraud in government programs, but essentially eliminating OPT by adding excessive fees is not a fair or well thought out anti-fraud plan.
Schools provide training to F-1s who engage in OPT/STEM OPT with detailed instructions on the application, requirements and how to report OPT activity.
DSO’s support their students through the OPT/STEM OPT/Cap Gap.
USCIS may review previously reported OPT employers and the proposed STEM OPT employer at the time of STEM OPT application.  Opportunity exists for a student to respond to appropriate questions/ provide necessary evidence to establish eligibility.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Joe  Guziolek
comments.commentText:
Re: Proposed Rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
I am submitting this comment in my individual capacity as an international education professional with approximately 12 years of experience supporting international students, including my current service as a Principal Designated School Official (PDSO). The views expressed here are my own and do not represent an official position of my employer.
I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. In my work with F-1 students, I see the importance of practical training in helping students apply their education and prepare for careers in their fields. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier for students who have maintained their status and met the requirements to participate.
Affordability for Students and Employers
Allowing schools to obtain funds from students or employers does not resolve the underlying problem of affordability.
Many international students already bear substantial tuition and living expenses, including nonresident tuition charges where applicable. They and their families may spend years saving and making financial sacrifices to pursue a U.S. education. An additional $70,000 payment before a student can access practical training would place that opportunity beyond the reach of many otherwise eligible students.
The proposed fee is also disproportionate to graduates’ earnings. UToledo reports median earnings of $49,296 one year after receiving a bachelor’s degree (https://www.utoledo.edu/campus/about/student-outcomes/). The $70,000 initial fee would exceed that annual amount by more than $20,000, before taxes or living expenses. Even among UToledo engineering graduates, whose reported average starting salary in 2025 was $73,397, the fee would equal approximately 95% of an entire year’s starting salary (https://www.utoledo.edu/engineering/co-op-and-careers/). These figures are not specific to international graduates, but they show just how substantial this fee would be.
If an employer were asked to provide the funding, it could face an additional upfront cost approaching or exceeding a graduate’s annual salary, on top of wages, benefits, and other employment expenses. This would create a substantial financial disincentive to hiring an otherwise qualified graduate, particularly for smaller employers.
Educational Value and Students’ Existing Commitments
OPT allows students to apply the knowledge gained through their academic programs in employment directly related to their fields of study. In advising students, I see how this experience helps them connect their education to professional practice and develop skills for their future careers.
Pre-completion OPT presents an additional concern. It provides an option for eligible students whose training opportunities do not meet the requirements for curricular practical training. An initial $70,000 fee for pre-completion OPT, followed by another $30,000 for post-completion OPT, could make this option financially impractical, even though both periods draw from the student’s standard OPT allowance.
Administrative Burdens
The proposal would also require institutions to establish procedures for identifying funding sources, coordinating payments, verifying payment information, and addressing situations where funding is delayed or unavailable.
Program Integrity
The proposed fees would create a financial barrier for students who have followed the rules, maintained their status, and met the requirements for OPT. Those students would lose access to practical training because they cannot afford the fee, regardless of the legitimacy or educational value of their opportunity.
DHS should address fraud through targeted oversight and enforcement, clear guidance, and improvements to existing compliance processes. Students who comply with the requirements should not lose access to authorized practical training because of misconduct by others.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. Based on my professional experience, these amounts would make legitimate practical training inaccessible to almost all students and create significant obstacles for institutions and employers seeking to support them. The ability to participate in OPT should depend on meeting the program’s requirements, and an extraordinary financial barrier would prevent otherwise eligible students from doing so.
Thank you,

Joe Guziolek
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed OPT fees, citing financial barriers and urging DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
We support this proposed rule and urge DHS to finalize it.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a regulatory program that allows foreign students to work in the United States after completing their studies, with the STEM extension allowing employment for up to three years. What began as practical training connected to a course of study has grown into a major foreign-worker pipeline. In 2024, according to DHS’s SEVIS by the Numbers report, 194,554 students participated in pre- and post-completion OPT, and 165,524 participated in STEM OPT.

Unlike the H-1B program, OPT has no annual cap, generally requires neither a labor condition application nor a prevailing wage, and does not require employers to seek American workers first. A program of this size, with direct consequences for the American labor market, demands meaningful oversight, transparent reporting, and accountability—particularly for its impact on American students and recent college graduates seeking entry-level employment.

OPT also gives employers a financial incentive to hire foreign graduates over Americans. F-1 students on OPT are often exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes, depending on their tax status and circumstances. Employers hiring eligible OPT workers avoid their share of those payroll taxes, an advantage they do not receive when hiring American graduates.

OPT also serves as a pathway to the H-1B program. Foreign students can complete their degrees, work through OPT and STEM OPT for up to three years, and then seek H-1B sponsorship. Universities benefit from international enrollment and can market post-graduation employment opportunities to prospective students, while American students face increased competition for university places and American graduates face increased competition for jobs.

The training issue is equally important. When employers claim that American graduates lack the experience or specialized skills needed for available positions, the appropriate response should be to invest in training American workers—not to create incentives to recruit foreign graduates on temporary visas instead. American graduates can be told they lack the qualifications for the jobs their education was intended to prepare them for, while employers have pathways to recruit foreign workers and provide them with practical experience. If Americans need more training, public policy should expand those opportunities for Americans rather than redirect them toward temporary foreign labor.

American universities, particularly public institutions receiving federal taxpayer support, have a responsibility to serve the students and communities that fund them. They should be preparing American graduates to enter the workforce, not helping create financial incentives for employers to choose foreign workers over equally qualified Americans. American taxpayers should not be required to subsidize a system that can make American workers more expensive to employ than foreign graduates competing for the same positions.

The proposed fees place a cost on institutions that benefit from OPT and recommend students for the program. Schools that profit from international enrollment and promote post-graduation work authorization should bear a share of the program’s costs and have an incentive to recommend OPT responsibly. DHS cites fraud and worker-protection concerns in support of the rule. These concerns warrant serious attention in a program of this size.

We therefore urge DHS to:

Finalize the proposed OPT fees.
Strengthen oversight of OPT and STEM OPT employers, including site visits and enforcement of STEM OPT training plan requirements.
Publish regular data on OPT and STEM OPT employment, including employers, job titles, wages, and the share of participants who later transition to H-1B status.
Evaluate the combined effect of OPT, STEM OPT, and H-1B on entry-level employment opportunities for American graduates.
The future of the American workforce depends on developing the skills, experience, and productive capacity of Americans entering the labor market. Pushing American graduates toward unemployment or underemployment while expanding the supply of foreign workers risks undermining that goal.

A student visa should be a student visa. Post-graduation work authorization should be limited, accountable, and paid for by the institutions that benefit from it, not subsidized at the expense of American workers. The purpose of workforce policy should be to give Americans a fair opportunity to learn, work, and build careers in their own country. Immigration programs should not undermine that objective by expanding foreign labor supply without adequate safeguards, transparency, or accountability to the American public.

We urge DHS to finalize this rule.
comments.reason: Explicitly supports the proposed rule and urges DHS to finalize it to oversee the OPT program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Stella Ban
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT period.

I am a graduate student studying Environmental Engineering. International student came to the United States to receive an education, develop their professional skills, and contribute to the creative community through their field of study. They made a substantial financial investment in their American education. The proposed fees would create an additional and extraordinary barrier at exactly the point when students are trying to begin their professional careers.

A $70,000 fee is completely disproportionate to the purpose of OPT. OPT is not a shortcut to immigration or an unearned benefit. It is a structured opportunity for F-1 students to obtain practical experience directly related to the education they have pursued in the United States. Students have already complied with the requirements of their F-1 status, paid tuition, supported themselves financially, and invested years of their lives in their education.

If DHS believes that fraud or abuse exists within the OPT system, those problems should be addressed through targeted enforcement and reasonable compliance measures. A $70,000 fee imposed on every student seeking initial OPT does not distinguish between legitimate students and individuals who may abuse the program. It risks punishing students who have followed the rules.

The proposal would also create serious consequences for American colleges and universities. Even though the proposed fee would formally be paid by the educational institution, the rule could result in these costs being passed on to students or employers. This could make international students significantly less attractive to employers and could cause universities to limit access to OPT. The result would be a system in which a student’s ability to use the practical training associated with their degree depends not on their qualifications or compliance, but on whether an institution or employer can absorb an enormous additional cost.

This would be especially damaging to students in fields such as Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Environmental Engineering, where early-career employment often begins through internships, junior positions, freelance opportunities, and smaller studios that cannot reasonably absorb an additional $70,000 cost.

International students should not have to choose between abandoning the professional opportunities connected to the education they received in the United States and facing an effectively prohibitive fee.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure. 

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and ask DHS not to adopt this proposal in its current form.

Sincerely,
Stella
PhD student in Environmental Engineering 
Connecticut
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees as an extraordinary barrier that punishes legitimate students.

In fiscal year 2026, the institution where I serve processed 245 OPT recommendations and 135 STEM OPT recommendations. Applying the proposed $70,000 initial fee to those OPT recommendations and the $30,000 subsequent fee to those STEM OPT recommendations would produce a total of $21.2 million. This illustration assumes each OPT recommendation triggered the initial fee and each STEM OPT recommendation qualified for the subsequent fee because the initial $70,000 had already been paid. Costs could be higher during implementation if STEM OPT recommendations also triggered the initial fee.
An institution’s operating budget is not a pool of available funding. Those resources support personnel, academic programs, student services, facilities, and other existing obligations. In my professional judgment, expecting institutions to absorb an additional expense of this magnitude is unrealistic.
As a DSO, I take program integrity seriously and support efforts to identify and address fraud. However, imposing a substantial fee does not establish whether a student’s practical training is legitimate. A student who can secure $70,000 is not inherently more compliant than a student who cannot.
The proposed fees would create a financial barrier for students who have followed the rules, maintained their status, and met the requirements for OPT. Those students would lose access to practical training because they cannot afford the fee, regardless of the legitimacy or educational value of their opportunity.
DHS should address fraud through targeted oversight and enforcement, clear guidance, and improvements to existing compliance processes. Students who comply with the requirements should not lose access to authorized practical training because of misconduct by others.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. Based on my professional experience, these amounts would make legitimate practical training inaccessible to almost all students and create significant obstacles for institutions and employers seeking to support them. The ability to participate in OPT should depend on meeting the program’s requirements, and an extraordinary financial barrier would prevent otherwise eligible students from doing so.
Thank you for considering my comment.
Peggy Colombo
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to excessive financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to explain one piece of machinery the fee would break: for STEM graduates, OPT is not simply a year of work experience. It is the bridge that makes the rest of the immigration system workable at all.

A STEM graduate on OPT gets twelve months of initial authorization plus a twenty-four-month STEM extension, up to thirty-six months in total. That window matters because the H-1B lottery runs once a year. With the full STEM OPT period, a graduate gets up to three chances to be selected. With only the initial twelve months, a graduate gets one. A single missed lottery draw, an outcome decided by chance rather than merit, then means leaving the country and abandoning the job and the research project midstream.

The proposed fee strikes hardest at exactly this bridge. The $30,000 charge for a subsequent authorization falls on the STEM extension itself, the part of OPT that gives graduates the time the lottery system requires. A university that has already paid $70,000 for a student's initial OPT must decide whether to pay $30,000 more to keep that same graduate employed while the lottery runs. Many will not, or will ration extensions to a handful of students. The graduate who did everything the system asked, earned the degree, found the employer, and followed every rule, loses the runway through no fault of their own.

Employers cannot plan around that uncertainty. A company hiring a new graduate needs to know the person can stay long enough for the lottery to work; if the extension is rationed, the rational response is to place the role where the graduate can work without a gamble, in a lab or office abroad. University research groups face the same arithmetic: a doctoral graduate whose extension is denied mid-project takes years of specialized knowledge with them, and the grant that funded the work cannot simply hire a replacement.

DHS presents the fee as a charge on schools. In practice it is a toll on the only bridge between an American degree and an American career in STEM, and it will push the graduates this country trained into the workforces of its competitors. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: Opposes the rule because the fees break the STEM OPT bridge necessary for the H-1B lottery system.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Garfield Foster

I strongly oppose the proposed rule. I understand the government wants to stop immigration fraud, but I don't think charging universities $70k or $30k per OPT recommendation is the right solution.

If the problem is fake employers and fraudulent job offers, the government should investigate those cases directly. Making OPT extremely expensive will hurt honest students and universities without necessarily stopping fraud.

This rule could also hurt the American economy. International students pay tuition, rent apartments, buy groceries, and support local businesses. International students also contribute to medical research, science, and technology. Why would we want to push talented people away when other countries are competing to attract them?

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Laura Young
comments.commentText:
I am submitting this comment on the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees, drawing on my experience in international education and corporate immigration.

I recognize the importance of DHS's efforts to prevent fraud and strengthen the integrity of Optional Practical Training (OPT). However, I question whether the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations would effectively address these concerns. The fees would affect schools and students regardless of their compliance history, potentially restricting legitimate opportunities without improving the detection of fraudulent employment.

Rather than relying primarily on substantial fees to discourage participation, I encourage DHS to evaluate stronger employer verification and oversight. Existing programs offer useful models for employer screening, training plans, and oversight. Adapting these measures could help DHS more directly identify and address fraudulent employment arrangements.

The fees also raise concerns about cost shifting. If schools seek to recover these expenses from students or employers, the financial pressure could create incentives for improper payment arrangements or exploitative employment conditions. DHS should evaluate these potential unintended consequences.

I am particularly concerned about the impact on universities and research institutions. In my experience, OPT can support valuable scientific and academic work. The proposed fees could make these opportunities financially impractical, potentially affecting research capacity and the development of future talent.

OPT allows the United States to benefit from skills developed at its universities. International students also contribute significantly to the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, they contributed an estimated $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs during the 2024–25 academic year. Beyond these financial contributions, they strengthen research, knowledge exchange, and academic communities. Making OPT substantially less accessible could diminish these benefits, discourage future international enrollment, and weaken the country's ability to attract global talent.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure and assess whether targeted verification and enforcement would more effectively address fraudulent employment while preserving legitimate educational and employment opportunities.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: MM15 Comment Submitted by Fiona Lilly
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,To whom it may concern,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. Already, international applications are down and international students are having trouble getting their visas approved for school. Many important programs, like student affairs, will not have enough students to continue in future years without those international students. This will hurt everyone down the line, not just folks coming from overseas right now.I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. FionaFiona Lillyfiona.lilly@maine.eduBangor, Maine 04401
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee hikes as unreasonable, harmful to workers, and damaging to U.S. higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nathan Tye
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Nathan Tye, and I'm a research assistant currently on initial OPT working at the Salk Institute of Biological Studies. I recently graduated Cum Laude from the University of California, San Diego with a degree in Molecular & Cell Biology and a minor in Chemistry.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

As an international student, the proposed increased OPT fees would force me to leave the country. I wish to further pursue working and contributing to the advancement of science in the field of molecular biology, and eventually pursue a doctorate degree here in the United States. However, the proposed fees on STEM OPT extensions are something I cannot afford, and would almost certainly see my departure from the United States, stopping me from contributing to any science in the United States.

International students and scholars add to the pool of brilliant minds in the United States working to innovate and push the frontier of science. Restricting this through increasing OPT fees not only deters future scientists and scholars from adding to that pool, but strangles the already existing population of international students and graduates contributing to science in America.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Nathan Tye
comments.reason: The commenter writes to express opposition to the excessive OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Joshua Konkle
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026)

I am a U.S. worker and I support DHS's proposal to establish fees for F-1 Optional Practical Training. My reasons are program integrity and the protection of U.S. workers.

To be clear about the limits of my evidence: I do not have first-hand data about OPT itself. My experience is with a later stage of the same employment pipeline. Each week I run a labor-market test of the PERM program. I find PERM recruitment ads, apply as a qualified U.S. worker using the exact method the ad specifies, and record whether any receipt or response arrives within 24 hours. On October 14, 2026, I filed a DOL OIG Hotline complaint covering 19 roles at 16 employers. For 18 roles at 15 employers, I had received no response as of that filing: Fastly, Stanford University, Gates Foundation, Freshworks, PayPal, Cloudflare, Live Nation Worldwide, Inc. (Ticketmaster), Remitly, Xebia USA Inc., Finzly, TravelConfirm, Inc. dba Dev-Pro.net, TikTok (2 roles), TikTok (USDS), Persistent Systems, and Freeport-McMoRan Morenci Inc. (3 roles). The sixteenth, Michaels Stores, Inc., sent screening questions, received my answers, and then gave no next step. On October 27, 2026, I filed a second complaint covering 4 employers (5 roles) silent within 24 hours (Gilead Sciences (2 roles), Sigma Computing, CBRE, and D. E. Shaw), plus one stall report concerning Novelis, which engaged with me and then stalled without any written next step. Naming these employers records where my applications went unanswered or stalled; it is not an accusation of wrongdoing. I do not assert fraud. I report silence as a pattern worth attention.

The connection to OPT is this. OPT and the STEM OPT extension are a common entry point into employer-sponsored status, which can later lead to H-1B and permanent labor certification. When the safeguards for U.S. workers at the end of that pipeline do not work reliably in practice, the program that feeds the pipeline deserves closer attention. DHS has identified OPT being used to overstay or to work outside the student's field of study. A fee that funds oversight and confirms that participation is deliberate is a reasonable integrity measure.

DHS asked for comments on the burden that payment processing places on schools. Schools already maintain SEVIS records, and DSOs already confirm OPT eligibility. Recording payment confirmation in SEVIS fits within that existing role. I encourage DHS to keep the confirmation step simple and auditable so that schools carry no open-ended burden.

DHS asked about refunds. I support allowing refunds subject to ICE review, under clear published criteria and timelines, so that the process is predictable and cannot be used to get around the fee.

DHS asked about the expected decline in pre-completion OPT. I have no data on this point. As a matter of principle, a program designed to complement academic study should be used in the way that best serves that purpose, and a shift in usage patterns is not by itself a harm to U.S. workers.

On the Paperwork Reduction Act questions: the information collection is necessary, because DHS cannot verify payment without it. Its burden should be minimized by using fields in SEVIS that already exist and by allowing electronic confirmation.

The American System rests on productive sovereignty, meaning a nation that trains and employs its own workforce first. Work authorization for students should serve education and not become a low-cost channel that displaces U.S. graduates. I respectfully urge DHS to finalize this rule, and to report publicly on how the fee revenue strengthens oversight of the program.

Respectfully submitted,
Joshua Konkle, Digital Knowledge
comments.reason: The commenter supports DHS's proposal to establish OPT fees for program integrity and worker protection.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Roj G
comments.commentText:
Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 OPT fee, especially because of its potential impact on international students who are already enrolled in U.S. universities.

These students have followed all required legal processes to gain admission and pursue their education in the United States. They came with faith in America's values of inclusion, diversity, fairness, and equal opportunity. They have invested years of hard work and substantial tuition fees, while their families have sacrificed their hard-earned savings to support their dreams.

Introducing such a significant financial barrier after students have already committed to their education creates uncertainty, jeopardizes their career goals, and threatens the futures of young people who have followed the rules. Their lives and aspirations should not be put at risk by sudden policy changes.Students who enrolled and made substantial financial commitments in good faith deserve protection.

OPT is not simply an additional benefit after graduation. It is an essential bridge between classroom learning and real-world professional experience. One to three years of practical training, depending on eligibility, allows graduates to apply their academic knowledge, learn from experienced professionals, and develop industry-ready skills. In today's rapidly evolving world, this experience is vital to completing their educational journey and preparing them for successful careers.

A $70,000 fee could discourage employers from hiring qualified international graduates, prevent talented students from gaining valuable experience, and undermine America's ability to attract global talent.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reject this proposed rule. At a minimum, please protect students who were already enrolled when the proposal was announced and who made their educational and financial commitments in good faith. Any policy changes should be fair, proportionate, and implemented with consideration for the students whose futures are at stake.

I request that this public comment be carefully considered in the rulemaking process. Please preserve a fair pathway for international students to apply their education in real-world settings without placing an unreasonable financial burden on the employers and institutions that support them.

International students and their families have invested so much in the promise of American education. They deserve a fair opportunity to turn that education into practical skills, professional growth, and meaningful contributions to the U.S. economy.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee due to its negative impact on international students.
