comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. These fees would make practical training inaccessible to many international students and harm the United States.

OPT allows graduates of American universities to apply their education in fields such as science, engineering, healthcare, and business. If universities, employers, or students cannot afford these fees, American research institutions and companies may lose skilled graduates they have already invested time and resources in training. Small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and research laboratories may be especially affected.

The proposal could also discourage prospective international students from choosing U.S. universities. Fewer students would mean less tuition revenue and spending in local communities, as well as fewer graduates contributing their skills to the American economy.

DHS has identified fraud and the protection of U.S. workers as reasons for this proposal. These concerns deserve attention, but a high fee does not distinguish legitimate participants from bad actors. Targeted employer verification, investigations, and worker protections would address those concerns more directly without imposing an overwhelming burden on lawful students and institutions.

The United States benefits when people educated at American universities can contribute their knowledge and skills here. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and consider more effective, targeted alternatives.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anne Bennett
comments.commentText:
Re: Proposed Rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
I am submitting this comment in my individual capacity as an international education professional with 3 years of experience supporting international students as a DSO. The views expressed here are my own and do not represent an official position of my employer.
I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier for students who have maintained their status and met the requirements to participate.
My office assists approximately 500 students on either Post Completion OPT or STEM Extension OPT every semester. 
In fiscal year 2026, our office processed 245 OPT recommendations and 135 STEM Extension OPT recommendations. The cost for that one fiscal year would be a minimum of $21.2 million, assuming that all STEM extensions were subject to the $30,000 fee and not the initial $70,000. 
Our institution is not fiscally able to support these fees, and expecting students, who may only be working for $30,000 or less per year, is unreasonable.  We have many students who provide valuable research to our institution on OPT, and this fee would be impossible for those who are volunteer researchers.
Allowing schools to obtain funds from students or employers does not resolve the underlying problem of affordability.
An additional $70,000 payment before a student can access practical training would place that opportunity beyond the reach of many otherwise eligible students.  This fee would be required before the student graduates and without the offer of a job.  So paying it would be pure speculation about whether they are eligible to receive work authorization.  
If an employer were asked to provide the funding, it could face an additional upfront cost approaching or exceeding a graduate’s annual salary, on top of wages, benefits, and other employment expenses. This would create a substantial financial disincentive to hiring an otherwise qualified graduate, particularly for smaller employers.
Students make significant decisions about where to study, which degree to pursue, and how to finance their education. The availability of practical training can be an important consideration in those decisions. Introducing these fees could substantially disrupt the plans of students who are already enrolled and have invested years in their U.S. education.
The proposal would also require institutions to establish procedures for identifying funding sources, coordinating payments, verifying payment information, and addressing situations where funding is delayed or unavailable.
Students already must coordinate application windows, academic completion dates, and anticipated employment. Requiring a substantial payment before a DSO can enter an OPT recommendation would add another obstacle to a time-sensitive process. It would also place advisors in the difficult position of explaining that a student is eligible for practical training but cannot receive a recommendation because the required funding has not been secured.
This also creates a burden on USCIS adding another element to the adjudication process and causing even further delays in work authorization approval.  Rather than initiate an exorbitant fee, DHS should address fraud through targeted oversight and enforcement, clear guidance, and improvements to existing compliance processes. Students who comply with the requirements should not lose access to authorized practical training because of misconduct by others.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. The implementation of these fees would make practical training inaccessible to almost all students and create significant obstacles for institutions and employers seeking to support them. 
Thank you,
Anne Bennett
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT) under 8 CFR 214.13(i). As an international student at Stanford University pursuing a B.A. in Economics and an M.S. in Management Science and Engineering, I believe these additional financial burdens would undermine the educational and professional opportunities that make the United States a global leader in higher education and innovation.

OPT is not simply an employment benefit; it is an essential extension of the educational experience for international students. My studies have focused on the intersection of economics, technology, and quantitative decision-making, and practical training allows me to apply these academic foundations to real-world challenges. Through internships in investment banking and financial services, I have gained valuable experience analyzing businesses, supporting capital formation, and understanding how American financial markets facilitate innovation and economic growth. These experiences have directly complemented my education and strengthened my ability to contribute meaningfully to the U.S. economy.

The proposed additional fees would impose an unnecessary financial burden on international students who already face substantial educational and living expenses. Unlike many domestic students, international students have limited access to federal financial assistance and face significant restrictions on employment during their studies. Additional fees associated with practical training would disproportionately disadvantage students from less affluent backgrounds, making access to professional opportunities increasingly dependent on financial resources rather than academic merit or professional qualifications.

I am also concerned about the broader implications for American universities and the U.S. economy. International students contribute not only tuition revenue and local economic activity but also diverse perspectives, specialized skills, and long-term professional talent. OPT is an important reason talented students choose to study in the United States rather than in other countries competing to attract global talent. Increasing the financial barriers to practical training risks weakening the competitiveness of American higher education and discouraging talented graduates from contributing their skills to American employers.

I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the immigration system and preventing fraud. However, I believe these objectives should be pursued through targeted enforcement, improved employer verification, and stronger oversight rather than additional financial burdens imposed broadly on international students who comply with existing regulations.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and consider alternative measures that protect program integrity while preserving equitable access to practical training. The United States benefits when talented international students can translate their American education into meaningful professional contributions. Policies governing OPT should reinforce, rather than undermine, that opportunity.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees as an unnecessary financial burden.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees**

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing substantial new fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

**1. The proposed fees are excessive and disproportionate.**

Imposing fees of tens of thousands of dollars for OPT authorization would create an extraordinary financial barrier for international students and graduates. Such fees appear vastly disproportionate to the administrative costs ordinarily associated with processing employment authorization applications.

DHS should provide a transparent, evidence-based justification for the proposed amounts, including a detailed explanation of their relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs. The Department should also explain why less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient.

**2. The proposal would undermine American innovation and economic competitiveness.**

International students contribute significantly to American universities, scientific research, technological development, and the broader economy. Many pursue advanced degrees in fields where specialized expertise is essential to continued innovation.

OPT allows the United States to retain and benefit from individuals who have already received education and training at American institutions.

Excessive fees would discourage talented graduates from remaining in the United States and could redirect highly skilled workers toward competing economies. This would weaken America's ability to attract and retain international talent while reducing the economic benefits of its higher education system.

**3. The proposal would unfairly affect students already enrolled in American universities.**

International students make substantial financial, academic, and professional commitments when choosing to pursue degrees in the United States. Many have spent years working toward graduation with the reasonable expectation that they could apply for practical training under the existing regulatory framework.

Introducing extraordinary new financial requirements shortly before graduation would disrupt these expectations and impose significant burdens on individuals who cannot realistically reverse years of educational investment.

DHS should carefully consider the reliance interests of currently enrolled students and, at a minimum, evaluate appropriate transition protections for those who began their studies before any new rule takes effect.

**4. High fees do not effectively address fraud or protect American workers.**

Financial resources are not a meaningful measure of an applicant's qualifications, compliance with immigration regulations, or potential contribution to the American economy.

If DHS seeks to address fraud or misuse of the OPT program, it should pursue targeted enforcement, stronger verification procedures, and evidence-based compliance measures rather than imposing broad financial barriers on legitimate applicants.

DHS should identify the specific problems the proposed fees are intended to solve and demonstrate why more proportionate alternatives would not achieve the same objectives.

**5. DHS must adequately evaluate the economic and institutional consequences.**

The proposed fees could have substantial effects on international student enrollment, university research programs, employer recruitment, and the competitiveness of American industries.

These consequences may extend beyond individual applicants, affecting research institutions, smaller employers, startups, and regional economies.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of these potential impacts and provide a reasoned explanation of how the expected benefits of the proposal justify its economic and educational costs.

**Conclusion**

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue a more proportionate, evidence-based approach to OPT oversight.

The United States benefits from attracting talented students, educating them, and allowing qualified graduates to contribute to its workforce and research ecosystem. Imposing extraordinary financial barriers would undermine these benefits without necessarily improving program integrity or protecting American workers.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee requirements because they would impose substantial economic costs on American educational institutions while offering insufficient evidence that these charges would effectively prevent immigration fraud. According to DHS's own regulatory analysis, the proposal could generate approximately $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers under its primary estimate. The analysis further projects that, even after the transition period, 98 small affected educational institutions could face fee obligations exceeding 20 percent of their estimated annual revenue. These figures raise serious concerns about the financial sustainability of the proposal, particularly for smaller universities, research institutions, and employers with limited resources. OPT provides a valuable mechanism for translating education into practical experience, supporting university research, technological innovation, and the development of a highly skilled workforce. Making such opportunities prohibitively expensive could discourage talented international graduates from contributing to the American economy and weaken the competitiveness of U.S. higher education. Furthermore, DHS acknowledges that the proposed fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than directly allocated to OPT compliance monitoring or fraud investigations. The ability to pay an extraordinary fee is not a reliable measure of whether a student or employer is acting lawfully. More proportionate alternatives, including risk-based audits, improved employment verification, targeted institutional oversight, and stronger penalties for documented fraud, would address program integrity more directly. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and conduct a more rigorous evaluation of its economic consequences and the effectiveness of less burdensome alternatives before considering further regulatory action.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee requirements due to economic costs.

I am a professor of environmental science at a university in Boston, Massachusetts. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

My primary concern is the impact these fees would have on environmental research and the development of skilled professionals in fields that directly serve American communities.

Environmental science is not a discipline that can be fully taught in a classroom. Students may spend years studying water quality, air pollution, climate modeling, and environmental risk assessment, but applying that knowledge requires practical experience. Graduates need opportunities to work with monitoring equipment, interpret real environmental data, conduct field investigations, and understand how scientific findings inform regulatory and public health decisions.

OPT provides an important bridge between academic training and professional practice. For example, a graduate who has studied water contamination may use OPT to gain experience with an environmental consulting firm, testing laboratory, or research organization. That experience develops skills that cannot be acquired through coursework alone.

The proposed fees threaten to interrupt this educational process.

Environmental research programs often operate under restricted budgets, including grants designated for specific research activities. These funds cannot simply be redirected to cover unrelated administrative expenses. A $70,000 fee for a single initial OPT recommendation could exceed what some programs can reasonably accommodate. Even when a university is formally responsible for payment, individual departments and students would ultimately face the consequences if institutional support becomes financially unsustainable.

I am particularly concerned about the effect on smaller environmental organizations and research institutions. These employers contribute to water quality monitoring, pollution assessment, environmental remediation, and other work that benefits American communities. Many operate with limited financial resources and depend on access to appropriately trained graduates.

Restricting that talent pipeline would not necessarily create additional opportunities for American workers. It could instead leave specialized positions vacant, delay environmental projects, and reduce the capacity of organizations performing essential scientific work.

I recognize DHS's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud. However, the proposed fee structure does not appear to distinguish between legitimate, well-documented practical training and arrangements that present actual compliance risks. The ability of a university to pay a substantial fee is not a reliable indicator of whether an OPT placement is genuine.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2). A more reasonable approach would strengthen employer verification and conduct targeted compliance reviews where evidence suggests potential violations, without imposing extraordinary financial barriers on legitimate educational training.

Environmental challenges do not become easier to address when qualified graduates are prevented from applying their education. The United States should maintain strong immigration oversight while preserving practical training opportunities that support scientific research, environmental protection, and the public interest.
comments.reason: The professor expresses strong opposition to the high OPT fees, citing negative impacts on environmental research.

I am a software engineering lead at a large technology company in California. I was also an international student in the United States earlier in my career, so I understand the OPT program from both sides: as someone who benefited from practical training and as someone who now helps develop engineering talent.

One thing I have learned over the years is that graduating with a computer science degree and becoming an effective software engineer are two very different things.

Universities teach algorithms, operating systems, databases, and software architecture. But building production systems used by millions of people requires another level of experience. Engineers must learn to debug complex failures, review code written by others, maintain legacy systems, respond to security incidents, and make technical decisions that affect entire teams.

These are not skills that can be fully developed through classroom assignments.

OPT helps bridge that gap. It allows graduates to apply their education in professional environments while developing the judgment and practical skills necessary for long-term careers.

When I first entered the industry, I still had a great deal to learn despite my academic preparation. Working alongside experienced engineers helped me understand how software development actually functions at scale. Today, as an engineering lead, I see that same learning process in junior engineers. Their growth depends on mentorship, meaningful responsibilities, and exposure to real technical challenges.

This is why I am concerned about the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and the $30,000 subsequent fee under § 214.13(i)(2).

These fees could fundamentally change which international graduates have access to practical training. Even though the payment obligation would fall on educational institutions, universities have limited budgets and competing priorities. Some may reduce their support for OPT applications, particularly when faced with substantial costs for individual students.

My second concern is the long-term effect on America's technology workforce.

At a large technology company, hiring is not simply about filling today's vacancies. We invest significant time in mentoring junior engineers because they become the senior developers, technical leads, and architects who build future products.

International graduates are part of that talent development process. Some eventually build their careers in the United States, contribute to American companies, mentor other engineers, and help create products and services used around the world.

Making OPT financially inaccessible could interrupt that pipeline before these graduates have an opportunity to demonstrate their abilities.

I understand the need to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers. Those are legitimate responsibilities of DHS. However, I would like to see a clearer explanation of how fees of this magnitude would address fraudulent employment arrangements or improve compliance.

A university's ability to pay $70,000 does not establish whether a student's training opportunity is legitimate.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider and withdraw the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and instead evaluate targeted employer verification, stronger compliance monitoring, and enforcement measures directed at documented abuses.

The United States has benefited from combining world-class education with opportunities to apply that education in practice. As someone who has experienced that transition and now mentors the next generation of engineers, I believe preserving a meaningful connection between education and practical training is important to the country's continued technological development.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. I have five concerns.

1. The fee is not tied to the fraud it targets (Section IV.A, IV.C). The fraud DHS documents involves shell employers, “phantom” worksites, and job-letter sellers. Its own evidence points to roughly 10,000 students tied to highly suspect employers, against 194,554 OPT participants in 2024. The fee would fall on every legitimate student at every legitimate school. Fraudulent operators already charge students for fake job letters, and DHS acknowledges (Section IV.C) that schools may pass the cost to students or employers. The likely result is a $70,000 charge on honest participants and a pricing adjustment for bad actors.

2. DHS has not shown the benefits. Table 1 lists monetized benefits as “Not Estimated” and effects on wages as “N/A.” Yet DHS projects $4.1 billion in annualized costs (up to $8.2 billion) and about $109 billion in 10-year transfers (Tables 1, 4, 10). The labor-market rationale in Section IV.B cites unemployment statistics and a 2017 study, but the rule never estimates how many U.S. jobs or what wage effects it would produce. A rule of this size needs a quantified case for its benefits.

3. The enforcement-resources rationale does not hold (Section IV.C). DHS justifies the fee partly by the strain on its investigative capacity, but it states that the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and that ICE “would not maintain or use” them. The fee therefore adds no enforcement capacity. It is also unrelated to the cost of any service DHS provides. DHS should explain how a charge of this size, untethered from cost and from any program funding, falls within its authority to set “time and conditions” of admission under INA 214(a), and it should address the serious legal questions this raises.

4. The burden on small institutions is severe and the rule rejects relief (Section VII.B). DHS estimates that 1,389 of the 2,478 affected schools are small entities. By its own analysis, 841 of them (60.5 percent) face costs above 1 percent of revenue in the transition year, and 116 face costs above 20 percent (Tables 15 and 17). DHS rejected a small-school exemption because most schools are small, which is a reason the rule is poorly designed rather than a reason to apply it uniformly. The rule also penalizes non-STEM programs. DHS’s low scenario assumes schools stop recommending non-STEM students altogether (Section VII.A.3), which cuts against its stated aim of supporting training “directly related” to a student’s major.

5. The process and reliance analysis are inadequate (Section VI). A rule projected to move over $12 billion a year deserves more than a 30-day comment period, especially when the information-collection comment period is 60 days. DHS’s reliance analysis dismisses the interests of students who enrolled expecting OPT access and of schools that budgeted accordingly. Applying the fee to any recommendation dated after the effective date, including for students already mid-program, does not address those interests. DHS also says that without the fee it “may shut down the program entirely,” which is an unexplained threat to end a program the agency itself created by regulation.

6. This will ultimately lead to a catastrophic loss in international talent that the U.S has leveraged over the past century to get to where it is today. Losing this talent will mean slower growth and a threat of losing global dominance. 

Alternatives. DHS dismissed targeted measures in Section IV.C without quantifying them. Options include employer-side verification for initial OPT, stronger SEVP recertification penalties for schools tied to fraud, enhanced site visits funded from existing SEVIS fees, and consequences for shell employers. These address the documented misconduct directly.

Request. I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If it proceeds, I ask DHS to (a) extend the comment period to at least 60 days and publish the underlying OPT data, (b) grandfather all students enrolled before publication, (c) exempt small and nonprofit institutions or scale the fee to demonstrated cost, and (d) publish a quantified analysis of the claimed labor-market benefits before finalizing.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Luma
comments.commentText:
As a business owner in the United States, I have had the privilege of working with incredibly talented people from all over the world. Many of my best employees are immigrants or foreign nationals, and I can confidently say that they have played an essential role in helping my company grow and succeed.

These are hardworking, highly skilled, dedicated individuals who bring not only their professional expertise but also different perspectives, fresh ideas, and a remarkable work ethic to our team. Some have helped us solve complex problems that we struggled with for months. Others have introduced innovative approaches, improved our products and services, and helped us reach new customers. They contribute to our success every single day, and I am genuinely grateful to have them.

At the same time, I have witnessed something heartbreaking. I have interviewed outstanding candidates who had exactly the skills, experience, and passion we were looking for, only to see their excitement turn into anxiety when the conversation shifted to immigration status and visa sponsorship. Some were worried about whether they could remain in the country after graduation. Others faced uncertainty about their work authorization, despite having spent years studying, working hard, paying taxes, and building their lives here. In some cases, we simply couldn’t move forward with hiring people we genuinely wanted on our team because of immigration complications.

It is painful to watch talented, ambitious people lose opportunities because of circumstances that have nothing to do with their abilities or potential. It is also frustrating as an employer because businesses lose access to exceptional talent that could help them grow, innovate, create jobs, and contribute to the American economy.

I understand that immigration requires thoughtful policies, clear rules, and responsible enforcement. But I also believe we need to recognize the enormous value that immigrants bring to this country.

America is a nation built by generations of immigrants. People came here from different backgrounds, cultures, and countries, bringing their dreams, determination, knowledge, and willingness to work hard. Together, they helped build the businesses, universities, scientific institutions, and communities that make this country what it is today.

We should not view talented people from other countries as threats or outsiders simply because they were born somewhere else. We should recognize them as colleagues, neighbors, entrepreneurs, researchers, and potential contributors to our shared future.

I want to live in an America where hard work, talent, integrity, and contribution matter more than someone’s birthplace. An America where businesses can hire the people they need, where international graduates have a fair opportunity to apply their education, and where people who want to contribute are given a reasonable path to do so.

America’s strength has never come from everyone having the same background. It comes from people with different backgrounds working together toward something greater.

As an American business owner, I don’t want to see talented people pushed away when they have so much to offer. I want us to build a country where opportunity, innovation, and shared prosperity continue to thrive.

We don’t make America stronger by shutting out everyone who comes from somewhere else. We make it stronger by recognizing what each person can contribute and by building a future together.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kyle Hofer-Mora
comments.commentText:
RE: Comments on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN: 1653-AB01 | Document Citation: 91 FR 64566
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees." Levying an unprecedented $70,000 fee on higher education institutions for each F-1 student recommended for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT)—and $30,000 for extensions—is legally improper, economically counterproductive, and highly damaging to American higher education and innovation. DHS should withdraw this proposed rule entirely.
1. The Assessment Is an Unauthorized Tax, Not a Legitimate User Fee
Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701) and established administrative law, a regulatory "fee" must be a nominal sum tied directly to an agency's operational costs for processing or enforcement. A $70,000 charge per student bears no rational connection to the actual administrative cost of processing an OPT recommendation or maintaining SEVP database records. Furthermore, because revenue goes to the U.S. Treasury rather than funding agency operations, this payment functions as a revenue-raising levy. Under Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution, taxing power rests exclusively with Congress. Attempting to impose a punitive tax under the guise of an administrative fee exceeds DHS's authority under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and is illegal without congressional action.
2. The Fee Negates Higher Education Affordability Initiatives
A $70,000–$100,000 assessment per student far exceeds the entire tuition cost at most public institutions. College budgets cannot absorb these fees, effectively forcing institutions to abandon OPT participation altogether. This contradicts broad federal efforts aimed at lowering education costs, revising student loan programs, and easing institutional burdens. Forcing universities to either absorb astronomical costs or pass them to students through tuition directly negates affordability goals, systematically dismantling international practical training in the U.S.
3. Misalignment with Labor Markets and Superior Regulatory Alternatives
STEM OPT was established because domestic graduates do not fulfill critical national needs in technology, engineering, and science. F-1 graduates on OPT drive innovation, complement native-born workers, and generate secondary jobs. While DHS cites localized labor gluts (such as computer science graduates) to justify restrictions, a blunt $70,000 fee across all academic fields is a disproportionate remedy. If specific gluts exist, a reasoned regulatory solution would be to refine program eligibility based on labor market data, rather than penalizing all disciplines uniformly.
4. Economic Harm and Loss of Global Competitiveness
Experiential learning through OPT is a primary reason international students choose U.S. universities over peer nations like Canada, the UK, or Australia. Making OPT non-viable will sharply reduce international enrollment, depriving U.S. universities of revenue that subsidizes domestic programs, research, and operations. U.S. employers will lose access to top global talent, ceding competitive advantages to foreign rivals. U.S. universities use international student revenue to subsidize programs for domestic students, this rule would eliminate that revenue and disadvantage the future “American workers” it purports to want to help. 
5. Unconsidered Interagency Impacts and Statutory Mandates
DHS's regulatory impact analysis is legally deficient because it completely ignores severe adverse impacts on sibling agencies, specifically the U.S. Department of State. Under the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (Fulbright-Hays Act, 22 U.S.C. § 2451 et seq.), Congress mandated the promotion of U.S. higher education abroad and the recruitment of global talent. Programs like EducationUSA invest substantial federal resources marketing U.S. post-graduation opportunities.
Destroying OPT directly undermines the State Department's diplomatic mission and wastes federal recruitment investments. By ignoring these interagency costs and conflicting statutory objectives, DHS produced an arbitrary and capricious economic analysis under the APA.
Conclusion
Because the proposed fee operates as an unconstitutional tax, undermines higher education affordability, and fails to consider interagency impacts or tailored economic remedies, DHS must immediately withdraw this proposed rule.
Respectfully submitted,

K.J. Hofer
San Diego, CA
Note: Views expressed are my own and do not represent my employer or any other entity.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the unauthorized tax and damaging fee structure, urging withdrawal.

Students like me are working hard to build a future despite financial challenges. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

The rule would require an SEVP-certified school to pay $70,000 before a DSO may recommend an F-1 student for OPT the first time, and $30,000 before any later recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. Proposed 8 C.F.R. §§ 214.2(f)(11), 214.13(i). DHS states that ICE cannot keep the money. It would be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt under 31 U.S.C. § 3302. 91 Fed. Reg. at 64,576.

That charge is a tax. Congress has not authorized it. Congress has authorized a student-program fee, and it designed that fee differently: the SEVIS fee must be based on the cost of the program and deposited in the Immigration Examinations Fee Account for SEVP’s expenses. 8 U.S.C. § 1372(e), (g). The current I-901 fee is $350. A $70,000 exaction, untied to cost and unavailable for enforcement, does not fit that statute or INA § 214(a)’s authority to set the time and conditions of admission. A federal court has already vacated the $100,000 H-1B payment this rule uses as its benchmark, holding that the payment was a tax Congress never delegated. California v. Mullin, No. 25-cv-13829 (D. Mass. June 8, 2026). The First Circuit declined to stay that vacatur.

The rule also fails as policy. It is paid before many students have an employer, it is not tied to an employer, and DHS says schools may pass it on to students or employers. It therefore does not screen the shell companies described in the preamble. It exempts curricular practical training, which DHS says presents the same fraud risk and which already covered 130,586 students in 2024. It misreads DHS’s own SEVIS statistics, comparing a 24-month participant stock to a 2016 forecast of annual participants. And it treats a payroll-tax difference of roughly $6,700 a year as a reason to charge $70,000.

The labor-market, innovation, and enrollment evidence cuts the other way. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024–25. Peer-reviewed and working-paper research finds that OPT expansions raised the number and the measured quality of international STEM students, and that restrictions on high-skilled visas push research jobs offshore. DHS leaves those effects unquantified, then reports a primary annualized transfer of $12.8 billion and a primary annualized cost of $4.1 billion.

I also oppose the alternative, raised in Section V.A, of charging another $70,000 at each higher degree level.

The full comment, with citations and section-by-section responses, is in the attached file.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule, arguing the fee is an unauthorized tax and fails as policy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
8 CFR Part 214
[DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100] 
RIN 1653-AB01
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees -- Comment Opposing Proposed Rule and Requesting Its Withdrawal 

To the Department of Homeland Security:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01) and respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.
The proposed fees -- $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation -- are legally unauthorized, procedurally defective under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and fundamentally misallocated.
DHS should withdraw the rule based on the following six legal and administrative defects:

1. Lack of Statutory Authority: Under INA § 286(m) (8 U.S.C. § 1356(m)) and the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701), administrative user fees must be strictly tied to direct cost recovery for services rendered. DHS cannot use fee-setting mechanisms as punitive deterrents. Assessing non-cost-based deterrent fees converts an administrative charge into an unauthorized tax, violating the Appropriations Clause.
2. Arbitrary and Capricious Fee Amounts: Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, an agency must articulate a rational connection between facts and choices made. DHS has provided no transparent cost-accounting data justifying why processing an OPT recommendation costs $70,000 or $30,000. DHS's attempt to benchmark these amounts against high H-1B visa costs to deter program switching is legally ungrounded: F-1 academic training and H-1B commercial employment operate under fundamentally distinct statutory frameworks, and using an unreasoned H-1B cost baseline to justify an OPT charge renders the selection arbitrary and capricious (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)).
3. Lack of Evidentiary Support: While DHS asserts concerns regarding fraud and worker displacement, it presents no empirical record evidence establishing that issuing initial OPT or STEM OPT recommendations causes U.S. workers to lose jobs or lowers domestic wages. Imposing a massive, universal financial barrier without demonstrating a factual, data-driven link between OPT participation and actual adverse labor-market impacts on U.S. workers violates the fundamental APA requirement for reasoned decision-making (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)).
4. Improper Vicarious Financial Liability: An institution's administrative role in managing SEVIS records does not make it financially liable for downstream employment practices. Charging educational institutions tens of thousands of dollars for actions taken by independent third-party employers is legally unreasoned and financially unviable.
5. Failure to Consider Mandatory Factors & Alternatives:
1) Reliance Interests: DHS failed to evaluate the reliance interests of current F-1 students and universities who structured multi-year plans under existing rules (DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal.).
2) Regulatory Alternatives: DHS failed to consider less restrictive enforcement measures, such as targeted SEVP audits or individual enforcement.
3) Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. § 601 et seq.): DHS failed to analyze the severe economic disruption to small, non-profit institutions with modest endowments.
4) Brain Drain & Loss of Global Talent: DHS failed to evaluate the severe risk that constructing prohibitive financial barriers will cause top foreign talent, researchers, and highly skilled STEM graduates to seek opportunities in competitor nations, directly undermining U.S. innovation and global competitiveness.
6. Structural Defects Cannot Be Cured by Revisions: Shifting the fee to employers/students or slightly lowering the amounts does not cure the core defect: assessing deterrent penalties under user-fee authority without statutory authorization or cost justification.

Conclusion:
DHS must withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01). Any future integrity measures must be grounded in explicit statutory authority, supported by transparent cost accounting, and directly targeted at non-compliant parties rather than blanket penalties on educational institutions and students.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and requests that DHS withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT. Protecting American workers and stopping fraud are essential. But making lawful participation expensive is not the same as making America stronger. The proposal could weaken American businesses, universities, and economic competitiveness without adequately addressing the underlying misconduct.

**1. Keep American-trained expertise and economic activity in the United States.**

American universities are global leaders in science and technology. According to the National Science Board's *The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026*, temporary visa holders earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2024, including 61% in computer and information sciences, 54% in engineering, and 52% in mathematics and statistics.

This illustrates the importance of international talent to U.S. research, not a right to work. If lawful practical training becomes unaffordable, highly trained graduates may pursue opportunities abroad, and American businesses may lose research, innovation, and future employment to competing economies. An America First strategy should keep these benefits in America.

**2. Fight fraud directly instead of imposing indiscriminate costs.**

DHS identifies real concerns involving fictitious employment, shell companies, and potential harm to American workers. These abuses warrant enforcement. But paying $70,000 does not verify jobs, employers, or wages. A financially strong bad actor could still pay; a compliant institution could be priced out.

If the objective is to protect U.S. workers, DHS should prioritize targeted employer verification, worksite inspections, wage protections, and serious penalties for fraudulent activity. Those steps address the problem directly. A blanket fee instead distinguishes between those who can afford it and those who cannot, not between legitimate and fraudulent employment.

**3. Do not shift costs onto American students or weaken local economies.**

Although institutions would formally pay the fees, DHS acknowledges they may pass costs to "all students" or employers. American families and businesses could therefore bear costs. In its own post-transition, historical-participation modeling, DHS estimates that 98 small affected institutions could face fee exposure exceeding 20% of estimated annual revenue.

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in 2024–25. This is not a forecast of the rule's impact, but illustrates international education's economic value. Lower enrollment could affect American jobs in education, housing, retail, and other local industries.

**4. Do not put American startups and smaller employers at a competitive disadvantage.**

Large corporations may be better positioned to accommodate a massive fee than smaller American companies, research teams, and startups. Losing lawful access to specialized expertise could delay domestic projects or encourage research and hiring overseas. Protecting workers should not make it harder for American companies to innovate and create jobs.

**5. Require evidence that the claimed benefits justify the costs.**

DHS projects approximately $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary scenario at a 3% discount rate, plus approximately $12.8 billion in annualized fee transfers to the federal government. These transfers should not be mistaken for net economic benefits. DHS also acknowledges uncertainty about future OPT participation and the costs of lost opportunities for U.S. institutions and employers.

Importantly, DHS explains in Section IV.C that these fees would go to the U.S. Treasury and would not be earmarked for ICE, SEVP, or immigration enforcement. DHS should show why these fees would outperform targeted oversight and examine their effects on American jobs and innovation.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and reject the alternative of charging another $70,000 following advancement to a higher degree. A narrower approach should focus on actual misconduct: verify employers, enforce wage and training requirements, investigate suspicious arrangements, and penalize fraud.

**Putting America first means protecting domestic workers while keeping research, businesses, investment, and good jobs on American soil.** The proposed fees risk undermining those national interests without demonstrating corresponding benefits. Please do not finalize this rule.

Sources: DHS, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), Sections IV.C and VII.A; National Science Board, *The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026*; NAFSA, 2024–25 international-student economic contribution estimates.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees, citing negative economic impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shrikanth  Hegde
comments.commentText:
I am writing to formally express my strong opposition to the proposed fee increase for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. This drastic increase introduces significant financial barriers that will ultimately harm the United States' standing as the premier destination for global talent.
I urge the agency to consider the following critical impacts:
1) Erosion of US Higher Education Competitiveness: The United States operates in a highly competitive global market for international education. Competing nations—such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia—offer robust post-graduation work pathways without imposing prohibitive, repetitive financial burdens on students. This fee increase will cause prospective students to view US universities less favorably, redirecting top-tier global talent to competing markets.
2) Severe Financial Strain on Loan-Dependent Students: The vast majority of international students self-fund or rely heavily on educational loans to afford the substantial cost of a US degree. Adding a massive financial hurdle on top of existing tuition and cost-of-living investments will price out qualified candidates. Students will actively seek alternate, more affordable educational options globally.

Without access to OPT due to cost barriers, students will return to their home countries or enter the global market without the practical exposure required to be competitive. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zhengqing Wan
comments.commentText:
I am a PhD student in finance at a U.S. research university, and I will soon begin full-time work at a U.S. economic consulting firm. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

1. The fee is not a cost-based user fee. Federal user fees are meant to recover the government’s cost of providing a service. Entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS and processing the related application costs a tiny fraction of $70,000. DHS’s own estimate that the rule would collect about $12.4 billion a year shows that the fee is a revenue measure and a deterrent, not cost recovery. DHS should explain the legal authority for a fee set this far above its costs, or set the fee at cost.

2. A blanket fee is the wrong response to fraud. Where OPT fraud exists, DHS already has targeted tools: employer site visits, Form I-983 training plan requirements, SEVIS reporting, and enforcement against bad actors. Charging $70,000 for every student punishes the large majority of compliant students, schools and employers for the misconduct of a few. More enforcement capacity, stronger employer attestations and targeted audits would address fraud without dismantling a lawful program.

3. In practice, the rule would end OPT for most students. Because schools may pass the full cost to students, the fee works as a $70,000 to $100,000 surcharge on an international degree. Few students can absorb that, and many schools, especially smaller and public institutions, are likely to stop recommending OPT altogether. Congress and decades of regulation have made practical training a recognized part of F-1 study. A rule that ends it through pricing should be openly considered as a policy change, not presented as a fee.

4. The comparison to H-1B is flawed. OPT is temporary, degree-related practical training that completes a student’s education. H-1B is an employer-sponsored work visa. Charging schools an H-1B-level fee to train their own students treats education as employment and puts the cost on the wrong party.

5. U.S. competitiveness and research would suffer. Practical training is one of the main reasons talented students choose the United States over the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and others. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars a year to the U.S. economy, support university finances that also benefit domestic students, and are heavily represented in STEM and doctoral research. Pricing OPT out of reach would push top talent to competitor countries, reduce enrollment, and hurt U.S. labs, startups and employers, including professional services firms that rely on graduates with specialized quantitative training.

6. Charging again for a higher degree would penalize advanced study. DHS asks whether to charge the full $70,000 again when a student begins OPT after a higher degree. This would discourage students from pursuing master’s and doctoral degrees in the United States, which is exactly the advanced training that drives U.S. innovation. I strongly oppose this option.

7. The economic analysis should account for the costs. The analysis should fully weigh lost tuition and spending, reduced university research capacity, harm to U.S. employers, and the likely drop in enrollment, not just the revenue moved from schools to the government.

Requested action: Withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should (a) limit any fee to the actual administrative cost, (b) prohibit passing the cost to students, (c) not charge again for higher degrees, and (d) address fraud through targeted enforcement instead of a blanket fee.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, arguing the fees are excessive and function as a deterrent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michelle DuBarry
comments.commentText:
The OPT Tax Would Hurt U.S. Higher Education, the STEM Workforce, and the U.S. Economy

Because the U.S. offers very few immigration pathways for workers with advanced education and specialized skills, OPT is one of the few options for international students to remain and work in the U.S. after graduation. A prohibitively expensive tax on that pathway would deny many qualified students the chance to make the transition, because their school, employer, or the student could not afford or justify the cost. This proposed tax, along with the recently proposed $103,265 H-1B tax, would make the U.S. by far the most expensive place in the world to retain global talent, adding more than $200,000 to the cost of hiring a single U.S. educated STEM graduate.

While DHS argues that reduced OPT participation would boost U.S.-born employment, research shows that OPT participation benefits U.S.-born workers, and that the more likely outcome of this tax is that jobs would either remain unfilled or move overseas.

There is substantial evidence that the proposed tax would discourage many prospective students from coming to the U.S. in the first place. Labor economist Michael Clemens modeled the impact of the proposed tax and found that OPT applications would fall by more than 78% for universities recommending students, and would result in up to $4.2 billion in lost revenue for universities as students would ultimately decide to not enroll.

International students contribute to the U.S. by growing the economy and creating jobs. They also make up an important share of the STEM workforce that powers critical and emerging industries like AI, semiconductor manufacturing, quantum computing, and biotechnology. Further declines in international student enrollment would mean a shrinking STEM workforce for the U.S. while competitors claim more of the talent of the future.

Facing these costs and lower enrollment, schools could pass the price on to domestic and international students through higher tuition and fees, or cut programs that benefit all students.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT tax would hurt U.S. higher education, the STEM workforce, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this rule because it uses an administered price to raise federal revenue from American institutions and to ration a lawful program. That approach runs against the principles of limited government and deregulation that this Administration has adopted.

1. The E.O. 14192 carve-out does not fit the rule's real burden
DHS says the rule is not an E.O. 14192 regulatory action because it concerns an immigration-related function. The order directs agencies to "significantly reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal regulations." The parties who pay this fee are not aliens. They are 2,478 U.S. schools: 1,044 public, 1,294 private nonprofit and 140 for-profit. DHS's primary estimate is $12.4 billion in fees per year. Its 10-year cost estimate reaches $69.9 billion at 3 percent. A rule that sends this burden to domestic institutions deserves the scrutiny the order intends, whatever its formal label. DHS should explain why it chose the exemption and identify offsets anyway.

2. This is a revenue measure
DHS's footnote 130 says the fee "would shift resources between private entities and the government." The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. It funds no adjudication, no SEVP oversight and no fraud unit. A new revenue stream of this size is a decision for Congress, which holds the taxing power under Article I. Other comments address the legal fee-versus-tax question. My point is about the proper role of an agency. It should not raise billions by rule because it lacks other tools.

3. The price was set by fiat
The $70,000 figure does not come from the cost of any service, from market data or from fraud data. DHS chose it as "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" and "on par with the educational costs" of one or two years of study. An administered price set this way has no link to the value of any training placement. The parties who know that value are the employer and the student. DHS instead asks schools to weigh "the value each F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT participation brings to the institution." That places the decision with the party that has the least information and the smallest stake in the job.

4. A toll on a lawful activity is not a free choice
In its UMRA section, DHS says state and private entities "make the cost-benefit decisions of whether to expend finances to engage" with OPT. A $70,000 charge per person, imposed by the regulator on a program authorized by its own rules, is a toll. DHS also says that absent the fees it "may shut down the program entirely." Using a lawful program as leverage to collect revenue is the kind of government action a deregulatory agenda should avoid.

5. The rule steers which degrees earn work experience
DHS's low scenario assumes schools will fund OPT only for students eligible for the STEM extension. Students in business, economics, finance and other non-STEM fields would lose access. That outcome would come from a price DHS set. Government should not pick which fields of study get practical training through a fee schedule.

6. It charges the many for the acts of a few
DHS's evidence describes specific bad actors, many of them employers. The current rules already require STEM OPT employers to use E-Verify and to report material changes (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)). The rule of law assigns liability to those who break the rules. A flat charge on every recommendation reverses that.

7. It grows bureaucracy on both sides
DHS expects schools to build new budgeting, accounting and audit processes for these payments. DHS must build payment verification and a refund process. None of this adds a fraud investigation. It adds paperwork and administrative staff at schools and at the agency.

8. Requests
DHS should withdraw the rule. If DHS believes OPT oversight needs more money, it should:
(a) publish a cost study and propose only a cost-based fee tied to actual OPT oversight costs;
(b) ask Congress for any authority to retain and spend such a fee;
(c) apply the E.O. 14192 offset approach on a voluntary basis to any final rule;
(d) direct enforcement at the employers and schools its own evidence identifies; and
(e) include a sunset date and a retrospective review in any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule, arguing it acts as an unauthorized revenue measure and imposes huge burdens.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am [a current/former F-1 student and I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I understand and support DHS's goal of preventing fraud, but I believe this fee structure would do far more harm to the U.S. economy and its universities than it would prevent fraud.

1. The cost burden changes decisions before students ever arrive.
The proposed fee is assessed on schools, but the rule allows schools to pass it on to students or employers. Most schools cannot absorb tens of thousands of dollars per student. A student deciding from outside the U.S. already weighs tuition, living costs, loans, and visa risk. Adding a possible $70,000 charge, with a further $30,000 for STEM OPT, makes the total cost of a U.S. education unpredictable and, for most families, unaffordable. Prospective students will simply choose Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, or other countries that offer clearer post-study work options. OPT is often the reason they choose the U.S. in the first place.

2. Not every OPT job is a high-paying one, and the economy is uncertain.
Much of the public discussion assumes international graduates land high-paying jobs. In reality, many OPT positions are entry-level roles at small companies, nonprofits, research labs, and startups, and pay far less than the highest-paying technology and finance roles. In a slowing economy with cautious hiring, employers are less willing to take on a new graduate who carries a five-figure fee, and students may struggle to repay education loans while also absorbing a charge that can approach or exceed a year of pay. [Add your own situation or numbers here.]

3. International students build companies, create jobs, and strengthen the economy.
According to the National Foundation for American Policy (June 2026), immigrants founded or cofounded 59% (455 of 775) of current U.S. billion-dollar startups, and about 24% were founded by someone who first came to the U.S. as an international student. These companies have created an average of more than 1,100 jobs each. Many of these founders spent their OPT years learning the American market, building networks, and refining the business ideas that later became companies. A fee that discourages students from coming, or from using OPT to gain U.S. work experience, will reduce the number of future founders, employers, and taxpayers.

Requests
- Withdraw the proposed fee structure, or substantially reduce it so that it does not function as a barrier to study in the U.S.
- Address fraud through targeted enforcement against fraudulent schools and employers rather than a blanket fee on every student.
- Extend the comment period so that students, universities, and employers have adequate time to respond to a rule of this size.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

These fees would create extraordinary financial barriers for international students, educational institutions, and employers while doing little to address the fraud concerns identified by DHS. Rather than strengthening program integrity, the proposal would reduce participation in lawful practical training, discourage international enrollment, undermine research and innovation, and weaken the competitiveness of U.S. higher education.
International students represent a significant share of graduate STEM enrollment and contribute substantially to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and workforce development. OPT serves as a critical bridge between U.S. education and practical professional experience. Imposing fees of this magnitude would make participation unrealistic for many students and employers, encouraging talented graduates educated in the United States to pursue opportunities elsewhere.

The proposal functions as a wealth test rather than an integrity measure. DHS suggests that institutions would recommend only the most promising students, but a $70,000 fee screens based on financial resources rather than academic merit, compliance, or potential. Students from modest backgrounds, smaller institutions, nonprofit colleges, and startup employers would be disproportionately affected.
The economic analysis also appears to underestimate the impact of these fees. It assumes enrollment and participation will remain relatively stable despite unprecedented costs. In reality, such fees would likely reduce OPT participation, international enrollment, tuition revenue, research activity, local economic spending, and tax contributions. The resulting losses could far outweigh any projected fee collections.

The proposal would also harm American research and innovation. International graduate students contribute to federally funded research, scientific advancement, and emerging technologies. For many doctoral graduates and postdoctoral researchers, fees of this magnitude could effectively eliminate opportunities to continue their work in the United States.

In addition, DHS does not adequately address research showing that international graduates often complement rather than displace U.S. workers. A policy with such significant economic consequences should fully examine the available evidence regarding labor market impacts.
The burden on educational institutions would be substantial, particularly for smaller colleges and universities. A single $70,000 OPT recommendation could exceed the annual salary of a Designated School Official at some institutions. Schools would face significant administrative and financial challenges that are not fully accounted for in the proposal.

Most importantly, the proposed fees target the wrong actors. The fraud concerns cited by DHS primarily involve fraudulent employers and employment schemes, not universities or compliant students. Charging institutions tens of thousands of dollars per OPT recommendation will not prevent fraudulent employers from operating. More effective alternatives include enhanced employer verification, targeted audits, site visits, and stronger enforcement against bad actors.
Finally, the proposed fees appear unrelated to the actual cost of administering OPT and would be deposited into the Treasury rather than dedicated to oversight or fraud prevention. DHS has not demonstrated how fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are reasonably connected to the cost of providing services or ensuring compliance.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that address fraud directly without imposing disproportionate costs on students, educational institutions, employers, and the U.S. economy.

Thank you for your consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter respectfully opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they create extraordinary financial barriers and reduce participation.
