comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Lydia Watt
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This will directly impact the employability chances of graduating international students. Following attempts to change CPT, the Duration of Status of F1 visas, and a fee for H1B visas, the DHS is now attempting to reduce the viability of beginning employment in the US via OPT, a common route for all international students regardless of their subject. This is a transparent attempt to drive international researchers and professionals - researchers and professionals who could serve the American people and boost the American economy - out of the US. Additionally, DHS's reasoning rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis. 

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. The proposal would harm American research, American employers, and the return on investments American taxpayers have already made.

I am a PhD candidate at a U.S. university, and my research is funded by a NASA fellowship. Federal agencies have invested in training me as a scientist. Like many international PhD students, I plan to begin my career at a U.S. employer through OPT after graduation. Under this proposal, that investment would be far more likely to benefit another country.

1. It wastes federal investment. NASA, NSF, NIH, DOE, and other agencies fund research that trains large numbers of international graduate students. OPT is a main way that training turns into work done in the United States. Pricing students out of OPT means American taxpayers pay to train scientists and engineers, who then take those skills to compete against American firms.

2. It hands talent to competitors. Canada, the UK, Australia, and other countries actively recruit graduates of U.S. universities and offer post-study work pathways at a small fraction of this cost. Prospective students compare these options before they apply. A $70,000 fee tells them the U.S. no longer wants them, and the strongest applicants will go elsewhere.

3. It hurts American employers and universities. U.S. companies, startups, and research labs rely on OPT to hire graduates in fields with persistent shortages. American universities, especially public ones, depend on international enrollment to sustain programs that also serve domestic students. Neither can absorb a fee of this size.

4. It does not match its stated purpose. DHS cites fraud prevention, but a flat charge applies equally to every compliant student and does nothing to identify actual fraud. Targeted measures such as employer site visits, stronger SEVIS verification, and enforcement against specific bad actors would protect program integrity without driving away legitimate students. Existing STEM OPT rules already require training plans and pay comparable to similarly situated U.S. workers; enforcing those requirements protects American workers more directly than a fee does. DHS also estimates $8.4-16.5 billion in annual collections, far beyond any plausible cost of administering OPT, and should explain how the amount was set.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. If it proceeds, DHS should at minimum exempt students enrolled before the final rule's effective date, since they made multi-year commitments based on existing rules, and clarify that students whose initial OPT predates the rule are not charged for a STEM OPT extension.
comments.reason: The commenter writes to oppose the proposed OPT fees, stating the proposal would harm American research and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Consider a student who has spent the past two years completing a master's program in engineering. They have paid substantial tuition, worked on academic projects, and developed technical skills through university research. Their goal is to apply what they learned in a real engineering environment after graduation.

That is what makes OPT so valuable. Classroom learning and professional experience are not interchangeable. An engineering student can understand the theory behind a system without having experience working with real equipment, production deadlines, or industry safety requirements. OPT helps bridge that gap.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1).

For many students, this amount is simply beyond reach. Even if the payment is formally required from the university, the practical consequences would likely fall on students. Schools could limit OPT recommendations, increase fees, or stop supporting certain applications.

I am especially concerned about the proposed 60-day transition period under § 214.13(i)(3).

Students make decisions about studying in the United States years in advance. They choose universities, arrange financing, and commit to degree programs partly because of the educational opportunities available after graduation.

A student who is only months away from completing a degree cannot realistically change those decisions within 60 days.

This proposal could leave students with American degrees but without a realistic opportunity to gain the practical training that complements their education.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. If the Department proceeds with any changes, it should provide meaningful protections for students already enrolled before the final rule takes effect.

Immigration enforcement is important, but students who have followed the rules should not face sudden financial barriers unrelated to their academic qualifications or compliance.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and raises concerns about the transition period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
A graduate student spends two years learning specialized equipment, collecting experimental data, and developing methods that are not easily transferred to another researcher overnight.

When that student graduates, OPT provides an opportunity to apply those skills in industry or continue developing practical expertise related to their degree. The STEM OPT extension can be particularly valuable for projects that require sustained technical work and professional development.

This is why I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

Universities do not have unlimited financial resources. A department supporting dozens of international graduates could face extraordinary costs. Even well-funded institutions would have to make difficult decisions about which students to support.

Smaller universities and less-funded academic programs could be affected even more severely.

If prospective students believe that completing a degree in the United States may leave them without a realistic path to practical training, some will choose universities in other countries.

Over time, this could weaken American research programs and reduce the talent available to American companies.

I understand the importance of preventing immigration fraud. However, a large fee imposed broadly on educational institutions does not directly identify fraudulent employers, falsified employment records, or violations of OPT requirements.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As the director of a small financial services firm, I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. I believe this proposal overlooks how small businesses actually operate and could create unintended consequences for American employers and workers.

Our firm operates with a limited budget and a small team. Unlike large financial institutions, we cannot afford extensive recruitment programs or months of unfilled positions. Every employee plays an important role, whether in financial analysis, accounting, compliance, or client services.

Finding qualified candidates is not always easy. In financial services, we need people who understand accounting principles, financial regulations, data analysis, and professional responsibilities. International graduates from American universities can bring valuable skills to these positions, and OPT allows them to apply what they learned in school under real workplace conditions.

OPT also has genuine educational value. There is a significant difference between studying financial reporting in a classroom and preparing reports under actual deadlines, working with accounting systems, or learning how regulatory compliance functions in a business. These experiences are an important continuation of a student's education.

My primary objection is to the proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2). Although the fees would be paid by educational institutions, their consequences would extend to employers. Universities facing such substantial costs may restrict OPT recommendations, leaving otherwise qualified graduates unable to participate.

From a financial management standpoint, I also question the economic justification for these amounts. What evidence demonstrates that charging $70,000 per initial OPT recommendation would reduce fraud or improve employment opportunities for American citizens?

If our firm cannot hire a qualified candidate, that does not mean we automatically hire someone else. We may have to redistribute responsibilities among existing employees, delay projects, or turn down additional clients. None of those outcomes strengthens the American economy.

I also oppose the related payment requirements under § 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and (iii). Financial capacity should not be treated as evidence of immigration compliance. A university's ability to pay an enormous fee tells DHS nothing about whether a student has a legitimate training opportunity or whether an employer follows the law.

I fully support efforts to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers. However, those objectives would be better served through employer verification, targeted audits, and stronger enforcement against actual violations.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee provisions and conduct a more thorough economic impact analysis, particularly concerning small businesses, university budgets, and the availability of qualified workers.

A sound regulatory policy should address misconduct without creating unnecessary financial barriers for legitimate participants or imposing indirect costs on American businesses.
comments.reason: As a small business director, the commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and their consequences for employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose DHS’s proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for a student’s initial Optional Practical Training recommendation and an additional $30,000 fee for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

I am an F-1 doctoral candidate who has passed my qualifying examinations and is currently seeking employment. This proposal would create an extraordinary financial and administrative barrier at the moment when international doctoral graduates are beginning their professional careers. Graduate students already face sharply rising rent, health insurance premiums, tuition, transportation, and other living costs. At the same time, layoffs, reduced entry-level hiring, inflation, and restructuring in technical industries have made the job market exceptionally difficult.

Although the proposed rule would formally require SEVP-certified schools to pay the fee, DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students, employers, or other students. This uncertainty could discourage universities from recommending qualified students and could cause employers to avoid candidates whose OPT eligibility depends on a fee of this magnitude. A student who receives post-completion OPT and then qualifies for the 24-month STEM OPT extension could generate $100,000 in fees.

This concern is not hypothetical. A recent Eaton Electrical Engineer, Custom Order Engineering posting stated that Eaton would not provide employment immigration sponsorship or support for CPT, OPT, or STEM OPT plans, F-1 to H-1B transitions, or H-1B cap registration. Such postings demonstrate how immigration-related restrictions can exclude qualified international graduates before they have an opportunity to compete. A $70,000 school-level fee would intensify this existing barrier.

The proposal would also harm the U.S. economy and weaken American technological competitiveness. The United States depends on attracting talented students, researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs from around the world. International students contribute billions of dollars to the U.S. economy, support hundreds of thousands of jobs, strengthen university research, and help sustain laboratories, startups, and high-technology industries. OPT and STEM OPT connect American educational investment to the U.S. workforce.

A fee of up to $100,000 would signal to prospective students and employers that the United States no longer offers a realistic pathway from education to professional experience. International students may instead choose countries with clearer and more affordable post-study work opportunities. If education, research, and entrepreneurial activity move elsewhere, the United States could lose tuition revenue, scientific talent, patent activity, startup formation, and future workers in strategically important fields. The proposal could therefore make it more difficult for U.S. companies to compete with countries that actively recruit global talent.

The labor-market context makes this proposal particularly unreasonable. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reports that unemployment among recent college graduates was approximately 5.6 percent in the second quarter of 2026, while underemployment reached approximately 42 percent. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that average unemployment duration was 24.8 weeks in September 2026 and that 27.1 percent of unemployed workers had been unemployed for at least 27 weeks. International graduates, who face strict OPT deadlines and limited unemployment allowances, cannot reasonably be expected to overcome a potential $70,000 barrier.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve OPT and STEM OPT as essential components of the U.S. talent and innovation pipeline. This proposal would weaken the United States’ ability to attract and retain global talent, undermine higher education and research, and reduce American economic and technological competitiveness.

Sources

Federal Reserve Bank of New York. (2026). The labor market for recent college graduates. https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/college-labor-market
NAFSA. (2025, November 17). International students contributed $43 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024-2025. https://www.nafsa.org/about/about-nafsa/international-students-contributed-43-billion-us-economy-2024-2025-fall-2025
Eaton. (n.d.). Electrical engineer, Custom Order Engineering [Job posting]. https://career.eoss.asu.edu/jobs/eaton-electrical-engineer-custom-order-engineering/

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ruben Saavedra II
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rule making published on October 8, 2026, which proposes a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) applications and an additional $30,000 fee for STEM-OPT extensions.

Imposing a total fee burden of up to $100,000 on international graduates drastically exceeds reasonable cost-recovery mechanisms and functionally destroys a vital workforce pipeline. I urge DHS to withdraw this rule based on the following critical points:

Devastating Impact on the U.S. Economy and Competitiveness: International students contribute nearly $43 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support over 355,000 domestic jobs. As America’s 7th largest service export, international higher education directly subsidizes domestic student tuition and funds university research infrastructure. Pricing students out of OPT will severely harm U.S. global economic standing, with economic research estimating annual U.S. GDP losses between $240 billion and $481 billion due to lost innovation and high-skilled labor.

Severe Crippling of Key STEM Pipelines: International students represent over 50% of U.S. graduate students in critical fields like computer science and electrical engineering. Currently, 30% of U.S. STEM workers and nearly half of all U.S. STEM PhD holders are foreign-born—the vast majority of whom launched their careers through OPT. Because over half of all H-1B holders transition directly from OPT, this rule creates an insurmountable barrier at the entry level, starving U.S. companies of the talent required to lead in fields like AI, semiconductor manufacturing, and biomedical research.

Unreasonable Financial Burden and Arbitrary Fee Setting: A $70,000 to $100,000 fee is entirely disproportionate to the actual administrative cost of processing Form I-765 for OPT. By making the program economically inaccessible for up to 80% of eligible graduates, this proposed rule functions as a de facto termination of a program authorized by Congress, bypassing standard legislative processes.

For these reasons, DHS should immediately rescind the proposed fee structure and maintain an accessible, cost-effective OPT pathway that supports U.S. economic prosperity and national security.

Best,
Ruben
comments.reason: The commenter writes to express strong opposition to the DHS Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding OPT fees.

The analysis also understates reliance and distributional harms. DHS calls reliance speculative because only about 20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is roughly 280,000 people who chose programs and took on debt expecting it. Using both pre- and post-completion OPT would cost $100,000, against $70,000 for post-completion alone, penalizing integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed. In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 above 20%, yet DHS declines relief. The UMRA discussion says both that the rule falls below the threshold and that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and finds no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

V. Procedure
DHS allows 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a paperwork burden estimated at five minutes. Its baseline and vetting assumptions rely on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) without acknowledging that rule's postponement. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw the proposal and direct its resources to targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw its proposal to charge high fees for OPT authorizations, citing unsupported fraud justifications.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Betsy Schein
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express opposition to the proposed changes to the OPT fee structure for international students. The proposed changes to OPT to incorporate substantial new taxes are poorly designed and not feasible for many SEVP approved institutions and F-1 students. The proposed changes could harm US workers and reduce American global competitiveness, especially in STEM fields and technological innovation. 

The proposed rule is stated to be an effort to combat fraud. However, the proposal does not provide evidence of widespread fraud or abuses that would justify these measures. Additionally, the funds from the tax are not designated to help address fraud investigation or strengthen systems. Additionally, the proposed rule states that it is an effort to protect US workers. There is no evidence that OPT negatively impacts conditions or opportunities for US workers. In fact, OPT can lead to increased wages for domestic workers and does not reduce the number of opportunities available to domestic workers according to 2019 and 2023 research (NFAP, Niskanen Center).  

There are a few practical issues regarding the design of the proposal. The new tax is attached to schools and not students. Schools are expected to pass this fee on to employers and/or students. What happens if a student’s status changes or if they transfer? The proposed tax cannot legally be referred to as a fee because it does not go towards administering the program but rather directly to the treasury. The funds will not be used to strengthen OPT or combat fraud.  

Most institutions and employers do not have the financial capability to pay this tax for any students. The financial burden of this makes OPT impossible for students at most institutions. Many of the students who engage in practical training opportunities do so with healthcare providers and critical STEM companies who will lose many qualified workers if OPT is restricted.  

Restricting OPT can lead to expected negative consequences for American workers and employers. OPT is one of the largest sources of high skilled workforce in the US (Pew Research, 2017). Losing this pool of skilled workers will reduce innovation and harm the ability of the US to be competitive in areas such as technology and engineering because talented individuals will be driven to other countries (Forbes). International students value practical training in their education, and the US will not be able to attract students globally if this is not an offering.  

Universities, employers, and local economies rely on enrollment from international students, who contribute billions of dollars through tuition, housing, transportation, and consumer spending. A policy that discourages international enrollment would negatively affect educational institutions, local communities, employers, and US workers. I urge DHS and USCIS to review this proposal and only implement changes that are evidence-based, detailed, and narrow in focus. I also urge DHS and USCIS to consider the wellbeing of US workers, educational institutions, and employers in these decisions.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses opposition to the proposed OPT fee structure, arguing it harms US workers and competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose DHS's proposal to charge $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one.

I have spent four years as a PhD student at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. My early years went mostly to coursework and to learning the methods of my field. That investment is now paying off: my work is producing results faster than ever, and new research ideas keep coming out of it. After I graduate, I hope to continue this research as a postdoctoral researcher in my advisor's lab.

My situation is very common. Every year, many international PhD graduates hope to stay at U.S. universities and research institutes to continue the work they started here, and OPT is one of the main ways they begin those positions. Postdoctoral salaries are paid from research grants, and a $70,000 fee is about a full year of postdoctoral salary. Few labs can cover that from a grant, and few new graduates can pay it themselves. Faced with that cost, many of us would have to take research positions abroad, where we would be welcomed.

This would harm the United States in several ways:

1. The U.S. pays for the training and loses the return. A PhD works like most investments: the costs come first and the returns come later. Federal grants and U.S. universities pay for years of this training. The fee would push researchers out at exactly the point when their work starts producing papers, patents, and new technology for the country that funded it.

2. Federally funded projects lose continuity. When a researcher who knows a project leaves, the lab has to recruit and train a replacement, and taxpayer-funded work slows down or stalls. Keeping trained researchers on the projects they built is the most efficient use of federal research dollars.

3. American students lose mentors. Senior PhD students and postdocs train the next generation in the lab, including American students. Losing them weakens the training of domestic researchers as well.

4. Academic research is the wrong target. Postdoctoral positions are research training roles in university labs, largely funded by federal grants, and their results are openly published. A fee meant to fight fraud or protect American workers should not fall on this kind of work.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. If it proceeds, DHS should at minimum exempt OPT employment at universities and nonprofit research institutions, consistent with how these employers are treated under the H-1B cap, and exempt students who were already enrolled before the final rule takes effect.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees, citing negative impacts on PhD researchers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a software engineer working in the US tech industry. I support DHS taking action against fraud and abuse in the OPT and H-1B programs.

In parts of the IT staffing and consulting industry, abuse is widespread: resumes fabricated with years of fake experience, proxy interviews where a different person takes the interview than the one who does the job, workers kept “on the bench” unpaid or charged fees by their own employers, and shell companies that exist mainly to keep someone’s OPT or STEM OPT status active.

This fraud hurts genuine students and workers the most. It lowers trust in all international candidates, makes employers suspicious of honest applicants, and lets people with fake credentials take jobs from people who actually earned them.

I urge DHS to target this abuse directly: verify OPT/STEM OPT employers are real and actually supervising the work, audit staffing companies with patterns of bench placement, require identity verification at interviews and onboarding, and penalize employers who fabricate experience or underpay visa workers.

A blanket fee alone will not stop the bad actors, who can absorb or pass on costs, and it will push out talented, honest students. I ask DHS to pair any changes with real enforcement against fraud, so the system rewards genuine skill instead of manipulation.
comments.reason: While supporting fraud reduction, the commenter opposes a blanket fee because it pushes out honest students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on the people for whom this is not a future policy debate but a commitment already made: the students holding job offers, and the graduates already partway through OPT.

The recruiting calendar does not wait for rulemaking. Employers made offers this fall to students graduating in 2027 — offers accepted, start dates set, relocation plans begun — on the understanding that post-completion OPT would be available on the same terms it has always had. An internship that was supposed to convert to a full-time role now depends on a university being willing, and able, to pay $70,000 to enter a recommendation in SEVIS. If the school declines, the offer collapses through no fault of the student or the employer, and the student is left with a degree, a broken plan, and no time to rebuild one.

The students already on OPT are in a worse position still. A graduate partway through a 24-month STEM extension has built a life around that authorization — a lease, a team, a research project with a deadline. The proposal would attach a fresh $30,000 charge to the next recommendation, and its refund provisions offer no real protection: a refund is available only before the employment authorization document issues, decided case by case, with no right of appeal. Once the document exists, the money is gone, whatever happens next.

DHS also floats an alternative that would charge the $70,000 fee again each time a student moves to a higher degree level — so a student who earns a bachelor's degree and then a master's degree in the United States could trigger the fee twice for what is, in substance, one continuous course of study. That is not a transition policy. It is a decision to punish the students who invested most deeply in American education.

A rule that breaks offers already accepted, strands graduates mid-extension, and offers no grandfathering for anyone already enrolled is not a prospective reform. It is a retroactive change of terms, and I urge DHS to withdraw it.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule, highlighting how it disrupts existing job offers, commitments, and current students.

I am writing in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing a $100,000 fee structure on F-1 Optional Practical Training. This astronomical cost acts as a constructive ban on post-graduation practical training rather than a legitimate administrative cost-recovery mechanism. By pricing out international scholars, the rule will directly destabilize the U.S. higher education system. American universities rely on international enrollment to subsidize critical research infrastructure, faculty positions, and domestic student financial aid, all of which will suffer immediate harm as enrollment plummets.

Furthermore, access to post-graduation work experience is a decisive factor for top scholars choosing where to pursue higher education. Imposing a six-figure barrier will instantly divert the world's brightest minds to competing nations like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, which offer streamlined post-study work pathways. The United States will effectively educate world-class researchers only to force them abroad, accelerating American brain drain. Depriving domestic technology, engineering, and artificial intelligence sectors of top U.S.-trained STEM graduates will stunt domestic innovation and permanently compromise America's position as the global technology leader.

The proposed fee rule is economically destructive, counterproductive to national strategic interests, and unjustified by administrative oversight needs. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule entirely.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the six-figure fee structure, calling it a constructive ban that damages higher education.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: MM17 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I, an American citizen and graduate student, strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations in document ICEB-2026-0100. I urge DHS to remove this fee structure and preserve access to integral, legitimate, degree-related practical training for students on F-1 visas.

The proposed rule claims to “deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its students” in Section IV.C. It is incredibly unclear how a $70,000-100,000+ financial barrier per individual promotes hiring legitimacy and prevents the OPT-related fraud it claims to address. Instead, the proposed fee clearly serves as a de facto ban on most, if not all, OPT and legitimate degree-related practice under the shallow guise of ‘protecting United States workers.’ 

I have deep concerns with the impact of the proposed fee structure on the ability of students on F-1 visas to study and engage in fully legitimate degree-training in the United States. The document is primarily concerned with mitigating ‘false employers,’ fraud, and ‘shell companies’ related to temporary employment through OPT (Section IV.A). An excessive, pre-application demonstration of wealth borne by academic institutions fundamentally does not contribute or aid in the purported goal of increased oversight and assessment of the legitimacy of potential employers.

The document claims that the “fees which would ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate in OPT.” First, an OPT recommendation from an SEVP certified school has nothing to do with qualification. Job-seeking students, in addition to overcoming paperwork, recommendation, and field-of-study hurdles, must still go through the application process post-recommendation. Further, the ability to bear a $70,000+ fee before acquiring a job has no logical or practical connectivity to the legitimacy of the job opportunity, the employer, the role the job plays in the student’s degree-related training, or the student’s aptitude for a certain job. All it demonstrates is the ability of the school, student, or potential employer to bear a massive financial burden.

Given the inability of many institutions and individual students to meet such an excessive demand, particularly with no continued job guarantee after, what the proposed rule instead serves as is a functional ban on most OPT pursuits, regardless of ‘legitimacy.’ This functional ban threatens the opportunity for international students who are studying and training in the United States to gain important degree-related practice, apply their academic training into valuable work within the United States, and even to pursue higher education post-baccalaureate. No person should have to pay $70,000+ to apply for a summer internship. Once again, given the jarring impact of its implementation on F-1 students, their academic institutions, and its inability to achieve the goals it claims to advance, I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure in document ICEB-2026-0100 (Federal Register No. 2026-20660) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the OPT fee, calling it a de facto ban on legitimate practical training.

comments.title: MM18 Comment Submitted by Maia Feigon
comments.commentText: As a practicing clinical neuropsychologist, I request that the proposed fees for initial and subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) be reconsidered and eliminated because they would be harmful to the profession and to the many individuals we serve. Clinical neuropsychologists are required to complete two-year fellowships following doctoral education to prepare for competent practice.  OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships.  The proposed fees would impose financial burdens on institutions employing international trainees, restricting their access to required training. The likely outcome would be the loss of talented international trainees who could be serving many unmet health needs in our communities. International professionals contribute to the United States through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning that improves the health of American children and adults. For the benefit of all Americans, DHS needs to maintain the status quo by not imposing any  OPT fees on international students.  Fees would create barriers to professional development that would be counterproductive for our economy and harmful to preserving and treating the health of our families and friends.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am deeply concerned about the negative financial consequences this proposed rule could have for American universities, American students, and taxpayers.
International students often pay substantially higher tuition than in-state students, providing an important source of revenue for American universities. At a time when many universities are already facing funding shortages and budget cuts, this tuition revenue helps support faculty, research, academic programs, and campus facilities that benefit American students as well.

The opportunity to gain professional experience through OPT is a major reason talented international students choose to study in the United States. If the proposed fees make OPT financially inaccessible, many prospective students may choose universities in other countries instead. Declining international enrollment would mean significant losses in tuition revenue, potentially forcing American universities to cut programs, reduce educational opportunities, or increase tuition for domestic students.
According to NAFSA, international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2024–2025 academic year. Losing these students would affect not only universities but also the local businesses and communities that depend on their spending.
While protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud are legitimate priorities, the government must also consider the broader economic consequences of discouraging international enrollment. Policies intended to protect American interests should not unintentionally weaken our universities, reduce educational opportunities for American students, or undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.
I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed OPT fee structure and carefully evaluate its potential impact on university finances, international student enrollment, and the American economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mona Dolton
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal.

As a community college student services leader with more than 25 years of experience in higher education, I believe students should have meaningful opportunities to apply their education and prepare for their careers. I am submitting this comment in my individual capacity.

OPT provides an important connection between academic learning and professional practice. It allows eligible international students to apply what they have studied, develop skills in their field, and gain experience that complements their education. Making this opportunity financially inaccessible would undermine that educational purpose.

According to information shared by Portland Community College, PCC currently serves 270 F-1 international students and would be unable to cover the proposed fee. For perspective, supporting just 10 students at $70,000 each would cost $700,000. For a community college balancing limited resources and substantial student needs, this would create an extraordinary barrier. Otherwise eligible students could lose access to practical training because their institution cannot afford the fee.

I am also concerned that this proposal would make access to OPT depend on institutional wealth. Students attending community colleges deserve opportunities to put their learning into practice, just as students at better-resourced institutions do. Federal policy should support that access.

International students bring perspectives, experiences, and talents that enrich education and community life. Restricting their access to practical training could also discourage prospective students from choosing U.S. colleges and reduce opportunities for local employers to benefit from their skills.

Program integrity and accountability are appropriate goals. DHS should pursue targeted, proportionate measures that address documented concerns while preserving access for eligible students and participating institutions. A fee that colleges cannot afford would place a sweeping financial barrier in the way of an established educational opportunity.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve affordable access to OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the initial OPT fee and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to institutional barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent periods. This unprecedented financial barrier will devastate the U.S. innovation economy by forcing highly skilled international graduates to abandon their careers in the U.S.. The rule's justification does not support a measure of this size. As explained below, it rests on (1) selective anecdotes rather than systematic evidence of fraud, (2) untested assumptions about how schools, students and employers will respond, (3) inconsistent data, and (4) a cost-benefit analysis that leaves the largest costs to students and the U.S. economy unquantified.

1. Selective anecdotes (Sec. IV.A). DHS calls fraud "rampant" but never estimates its prevalence. It cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news report, 2025 site visits in Northern Virginia, and 10,000 students at "highly suspect employers." That last figure reflects suspicion, not findings, and is under 3% of the roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants DHS reports for 2024. Several cases were prosecuted under existing authority. The fee amount was set to match H-1B fees, not derived from fraud data, and DHS concedes the revenue goes to the general Treasury, not to oversight.

2. Untested assumptions (Sec. VII.A.3). DHS admits it "cannot confidently predict" participation changes, yet assumes schools will keep paying $100,000 for every STEM-eligible student. No scenario models any fee-driven drop in STEM participation. The evidence points the other way. Economist Michael Clemens estimates universities net about $13,700 a year per international master's student, far below the fee, and projects OPT starts falling by a third or more in every scenario (IZA DP 18933). After the 2025 $100,000 H-1B proclamation, initial consular H-1B petitions fell 91%. DHS also assumes costs can be passed to students or employers and that enrollment will not fall, without analysis.

3. Inconsistent data. Sec. IV.B reports 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024; the impact analysis uses 95,384 for the same year, unreconciled. The low and high scenarios use different baseline years, so neither isolates the fee's effect. The claim that only 20% of F-1 students use OPT divides by all F-1 students, most not yet eligible; about 54% of F-1 graduates use OPT. The fee "aligns" with an H-1B fee covering up to six years, while OPT lasts at most three. And DHS's July 2026 duration-of-status rule acknowledged that reduced enrollment harms the economy, a point this rule treats as speculative.

4. Incomplete cost-benefit analysis. DHS estimates costs up to $8.2 billion a year and transfers of $8.7 to $16.9 billion, yet monetizes no benefits and omits the largest costs:
• Students lose field-related training and the bridge to an H-1B.
• Universities lose international tuition that helps fund seats for U.S. students; one estimate finds about 45,000 fewer Americans enrolling each year (Institute for Progress).
• The economy loses STEM talent, innovation, firm creation and tax revenue, none of which DHS estimates.
• Research on the 2016 STEM OPT extension found it increased demand for U.S. workers with similar skills, undercutting the worker-protection rationale.

DHS also dismissed targeted alternatives, such as extending STEM OPT safeguards to all OPT, cost-based SEVP fees, or barring the employer patterns its own investigation found, each of which would address fraud without charging up to $100,000 for every student who follows the rules.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they impose financial barriers and lack proper justification.

comments.commentText:
This is unconstitutional. Under constitutional law, international students are a class which is evaluated under rational basis review. While I understand ICE's goal to protect American jobs, this rule is counterproductive to the goal of "Combating Fraud and Abuse of OPT" and "Protecting American jobs". 

First, this rule does nothing to combat the issue of for profit/degree mill schools issuing OPT under the nose of the government who are permitting international students to take jobs unrelated to their field of study. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am interested in this legislation as a fellow graduate student among many people seeking to enter the OPT program. As an American citizen with international students alongside me, I see the hard work that all of us have put in leading up to graduation. As a result, I have become more aware of laws and regulations in this area and taken it upon myself to find out more for myself and for my peers. 
The part of the regulation I am commenting on is the fee price. The goal of the regulation is to strengthen the immigration system, but a large fee paid to universities is ultimately another burden for students wanting to contribute to the US, not wanting to take from it. There are reasons to believe that fraudulent employers are an issue, but not significant enough to punish universities for this behavior. Only less than 3% of students currently on OPT are suspected of having fake or fraudulent employers. A 70,000$ fee is not justifiable with this small of an issue. The fee will ultimately be passed to international students or even the entire university student body instead of being paid by universities that already have tight budgets. 
300,000 students on OPT have come to the US legally to learn and eventually contribute to the American economy. This is the basis of the American Dream and takes away the ability of highly educated students from contributing to the country they were educated in only contributes to brain drain. As an American, I have already in school with International students to get into undergraduate school and then graduate school, and these students work just as hard as myself and my peers if not harder. Realistically, accepting or hiring an international student is much harder than an American student so this group is already the best of the best. There is no reason to push them out of a country they have worked so hard to get to. OPT is one of the only options international students have to get to sponsorship and ultimately to an H1B visa. Immigration is one of the hallmarks of the American dream, and it should be protected.
Instead of creating a hefty fee that will ultimately be passed on to students rather than the employers the regulation claims to protect Americans from, the regulation should focus on payroll taxes that allow OPT to become a way for employers to get cheap labor. Increase oversight on fraudulent employers and bring them further into the process. The burden of this should not fall on universities or compliant students but on the very small proportion of people doing the wrong thing. This program is incredibly expensive for the DHS, all while costing too much for students and universities to pay back the costs associated with the program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under Section V.A and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i). I urge DHS to withdraw these fees.

I am a doctoral researcher at a U.S. public research university. My work involves computational imaging, microscopy, and machine-learning approaches to scientific problems, including protein structure determination. I have spent years developing skills that connect engineering, computation, and biomedical research, and I am exploring both academic and industry research paths where I could apply this training.

For researchers in my position, degree-related practical training can help translate doctoral education into useful scientific work. These fees would create a serious barrier at that transition. Requiring schools to pay does not eliminate the burden: institutions may pass the cost to students or employers, or decline to recommend students for OPT. Access to training could then depend on available funding rather than educational value or research ability.

University laboratories, smaller biotechnology companies, and emerging research ventures may have limited budgets. Losing access to a trained researcher can interrupt projects and collaborations and diminish the value of resources already invested in doctoral education. DHS should evaluate these consequences explicitly.

I also object to the treatment of current students in Sections V.C and VI. Students pursuing multi-year degrees have already made substantial educational and personal commitments. A transition based on future OPT recommendation dates does not adequately protect those commitments.

DHS should address documented abuse through targeted compliance checks and enforcement while preserving legitimate practical training and protecting U.S. workers. If DHS proceeds with new fees, it should provide a transparent justification, thoroughly assess research and educational impacts, and exempt currently enrolled students and their associated STEM OPT extensions.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them because they create serious barriers for researchers.

Imposing high fines is not an effective way to prevent fraud, as the fines will simply keep hard-working, well-deserving students from being able to remain in the U.S. and work in their field. This will hurt our economy. If universities pay these fines, it will waste valuable resources that should be used for educating Americans. If they do not pay the fines, we lose educated workers to other countries, as highly qualified and skilled individuals are forced to leave the country. 

I have already been told by international PhD students that they are seeking employment elsewhere, as the unwelcoming environment this rule produces makes it not worthwhile to make their contributions to science here. This is a trajedy that will affect our country for years to come if it is allowed to continue.

Please withdraw this rule, or at the very least extend the period of public comment so that data on its potential impact can be gathered.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Relly Zhang
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee structure of $70,000 for initial participation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

International students make substantial financial and personal investments to pursue higher education in the United States. OPT is a critical opportunity for graduates to gain practical work experience directly related to their degrees and transition from academic study to professional employment. Imposing fees of this magnitude could effectively undermine access to this opportunity, even if the fees are formally paid by educational institutions rather than students.

A $70,000 initial fee and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation could place an unreasonable financial burden on universities and colleges. Many institutions, particularly smaller schools with limited budgets, may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to OPT opportunities not because they lack academic qualifications or professional skills, but because their schools cannot afford to support them.

This proposal could also create serious consequences for STEM graduates, who often rely on the STEM OPT extension to gain additional professional experience. Employers may become less willing to recruit international graduates if their hiring depends on schools paying substantial fees. Students who have already invested years of study and significant tuition costs could face reduced employment opportunities and greater uncertainty about their futures.

Furthermore, the proposed fee structure raises concerns about proportionality and fairness. If the goal is to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers, the government should consider targeted enforcement, stronger verification procedures, and penalties for demonstrated violations rather than imposing extraordinary fees that could restrict access for legitimate students. The proposal should also be supported by clear evidence that these fees are necessary and that less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient.

International students contribute to U.S. universities, businesses, research, innovation, and local economies. Policies that make it substantially more difficult for qualified graduates to gain practical experience could discourage talented students from choosing American universities and encourage them to pursue educational and career opportunities in other countries.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed fee structure or substantially revise it. At a minimum, the Department should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the economic impact on educational institutions, international students, employers, and the U.S. workforce; consider less restrictive alternatives to address fraud; and provide appropriate protections for students who have already made significant educational and career commitments in reliance on the existing OPT framework.

**The integrity of the OPT program is important, but it should not be protected through a fee structure that could make legitimate participation financially impractical.** I urge the Department to adopt a more balanced, evidence-based approach that protects U.S. workers while preserving fair opportunities for qualified international graduates.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee structure, citing unreasonable financial burdens on schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

International students contribute to colleges and universities, and many hope to use their education to build careers in the United States. If the costs of participating in Optional Practical Training become too high, schools may be less willing to support these students, which could limit their career opportunities. This could also discourage future international students from choosing American universities, potentially affecting schools and businesses that benefit from their skills and contributions.

I understand that the government needs funding to process applications, enforce immigration laws, and prevent misuse of the program. The government should consider setting fees based on actual administrative costs and offering more affordable options for students and educational institutions. I encourage ICE to reconsider the proposed fees and find a reasonable balance between protecting the integrity of the program and allowing international students to gain valuable work experience after completing their education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nigel Goldenfeld
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Nigel Goldenfeld, a professor of physics at the University of California San Diego, writing in my personal capacity.  I have supervised about 60 early-career physicists during my 40 year career.  Many of these were international students or postdocs, and of these the majority remained in the US after working with me.  As such, they found jobs in industry and academia, and contributed extensively to the Nation's economic well-being and scientific success.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

The proposed increased OPT fees would act as a serious deterrent for early-career scientists to remain in the US and thus would be detrimental to the scientific and economic well-being of the country.

These international students make a major impact to American science and economic prosperity.  The graduates from my group alone have contributed to science as well as industrial sectors ranging from quantitative finance to genomics, biotechnology and medicine.  The US cannot afford to lose these individuals if it wants to create a high standard of living in the future and be competitive economically.  In summary I oppose the proposed increases in OPT fees.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Dr. Nigel Goldenfeld
comments.reason: The commenter expresses opposition to the excessive OPT fees and cites harm to the STEM pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gabriella Comer
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on Optional Practical Training.

I am a U.S. university student, and my partner is an international student from the United Kingdom who has worked toward studying and building a career in the United States for years. comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees for F-1 Optional Practical Training. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 extension fee. These excessive charges would undermine America's long-term economic competitiveness without meaningfully improving employment opportunities for American workers.

The United States has historically benefited from attracting talented students, researchers, and entrepreneurs from around the world. Many contribute to scientific discoveries, technological innovation, business formation, and job creation. Making practical training prohibitively expensive would discourage future talent from choosing American universities and encourage graduates to pursue opportunities in competing economies.

The damage would extend beyond international students. Universities could face declining enrollment and tuition revenue, threatening research programs, faculty positions, and local businesses that depend on student spending. American companies, particularly startups and smaller employers, would face greater difficulty recruiting specialized talent.

Most importantly, restricting access to skilled graduates does not automatically create jobs for American citizens. Businesses may instead move research, engineering, and other operations overseas, taking associated American jobs and future investment with them.

Rather than protecting American workers, this proposal risks weakening the very institutions and industries that create American employment opportunities.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue evidence-based policies that protect program integrity while strengthening American universities, innovation, domestic investment, and job creation.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the excessive charges and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gil M
comments.commentText:
I am a research mathematician working at a university in the United States. My research involves working with graduate students and postdoctoral visiting faculty members. Our department has four post-doctoral visiting faculty positions that are filled on a fixed term of three years each. We typically hire early-career mathematicians who have recently earned a PhD. These scholars spend their three years in our department building their research portfolios before moving on to other positions in academia or industry. They teach classes and breathe vital energy into the research life of our department. It is not uncommon for us to hire foreign nationals who switch to the OPT portion of their F-1 visa when they begin. The new proposed fees for OPT extensions are exorbitant, roughly equivalent to the entire salary of that faculty member. Our university does not have the resources and would not allow us to hire any individual needing the OPT recommendation; as aresult we could not recruit the best and brightest mathematicians to conduct research in our department and provide instruction to our undergraduate and graduate students. Not only would the applicant pool for such positions contract dramatically, but it would also decimate doctoral programs in the US because foreign students would not longer be interested in doing a PhD in the United States if the postdoctoral job market is not open to them. This would significantly damage the graduate mathematics education and research endeavors of the United States by cutting off an essential source of mathematical talent in our system (i.e. foreign-born mathematicians). The United States would fall behind in mathematics research and miss out on the unforeseeable technological advancements that would have resulted from applying unrealized mathematical theories. The effects of having fewer talented research mathematicians in our workforce would trickle down to cause lower-quality undergraduate and high school education, and a less well-equipped STEM workforce. I do not believe the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Bureau has properly estimated the impacts on the mathematics and science research endeavor and the costs to society that will result from this. The recent study from the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation in 2025 (https://itif.org/publications/2025/09/15/how-reducing-federal-rd-reduces-gdp-growth/) estimated that the cost to the US economy resulting from a loss of federal support for STEM research would quickly mount into the billions and trillions of dollars from a contraction of just a few percentage points in federal spending. The effects of this regulation would be analogous since contracting the labor market and supply of high-quality students and researchers would have the same effect as removing federal monetary support for research. This would not serve the purpose of "protecting US workers" because there simply would not be enough applicants to fill all the graduate programs in the US.

I strongly recommend not implementing these exorbitant fees, which would effectively be excluding foreign nationals from graduate-level STEM research in the United States and destroy US competitiveness in STEM research.
comments.reason: The commenter highlights how the exorbitant fees would harm university research and recruitment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mackenze Jones, Psy.D.
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees

As a postdoctoral fellow in clinical neuropsychology, I request that the proposed fees for initial and subsequent OPT be reconsidered and eliminated due to the  potential harm to the profession and individuals that we serve. 

The ethnically and linguistically diverse population in the U.S. continues to expand, requiring a culturally competent neuropsychology workforce. International graduate trainees bring valuable cultural and linguistic assets to the field of clinical neuropsychology but face significant structural barriers, even without the proposed $70,000 fee that will be imposed on fellowship institutions (e.g., Nayar et al., 2025). This proposal would increase the already present obstacles for international students to not only receive appropriate and equitable training, but increase obstacles for diverse patient populations to receive appropriate care. 

As a white, U.S.-born individual I have never felt my job or training was at risk due to the involvement of trainees from other countries, nor have I felt that they should be prevented from training at the same capacity as myself or others born here. My job, and the jobs of many clinicians, are not at jeopardy because of international students/practitioners. If anything, the field of clinical psychology/neuropsychology is in a precarious spot due to long waitlists, lack of access to patient resources, and lack of appropriate payment for services from insurance companies. These are structural issues embedded in the U.S. healthcare system (by design) that have little to do with clinicians/trainees regardless of background. Adding an additional $70,000 financial barrier for already underfunded institutions who provide vital services is disheartening. This amount is more than most of us even hope to make during our postdoctoral fellowships, and institutions would by no means be able to undertake this exorbitant amount.

Moreover, it is already incredibly difficult to access the tools required in healthcare (e.g., interpreters) to provide equitable services for non-U.S. born patients, and this proposal is a disturbing evolution to the already growing problem clinicians face. Neuropsychologists in the U.S. are largely White, monolingual English speakers, and the field's lack of diversity is a great disservice to the many people we are expected to evaluate. 

I have felt honored to work with trainees from diverse backgrounds. They have taught me valuable tools to improve my own clinical work, they have provided mentorship and friendship. There is simply no justifiable reason for this proposal to exacerbate existing barriers to training, which eventually affects patients we must care for. I encourage the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Bureau to consider the downstream effects of this proposal. If you will not consider the proposal's clear disadvantage to international (and national) students, please consider the patients we pledge to do no harm against (APA Ethics Code). These patients are your friends and your family members.
comments.reason: The postdoctoral fellow requests that the proposed OPT fees be eliminated due to potential harm to the profession.

Hello! I am an affected F-1 student pursuing my PhD in Chemical Engineering at Northeastern University. At our College of Engineering, over 70% of the graduate student body is international. For people like me, that means losing the opportunity of contributing to science and technology development to advance a country I have grown to really admire. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Heather Miller
comments.commentText:
I am writing as an educator and concerned citizen to share my perspective on the proposed rule regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.

Optional Practical Training is a critical element of higher education in the United States. International students bring immense value to our classrooms, research projects, and campuses. Beyond the academic contributions, the presence of global scholars exposes American students to diverse cultures, perspectives, and problem-solving approaches. Learning alongside peers from around the world helps prepare domestic students to navigate and lead in an increasingly interconnected global economy.

At the same time, OPT acts as a powerful tool for global diplomacy and soft power. When international students study and work in the U.S., they experience American democratic values, civic institutions, and workplace ethics firsthand. When they return to their home countries or lead global organizations, they carry those experiences with them, fostering long-term international goodwill and cultural understanding.

Imposing steep fees or restrictive burdens on OPT threatens to turn talented international students toward higher education institutions in other countries. In doing so, we risk depriving domestic students of key peer-to-peer learning opportunities and weakening the cultural exchange that keeps American higher education a globally recognized standard.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposed rule and preserve the strengths of the OPT program for the benefit of both international and domestic students.

Thank you for considering this comment.
