comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nadia Kellam
comments.commentText:
I am a Professor of Engineering and the Engineering Undergraduate Program Chair at The Polytechnic School, Ira A. Fulton Schools of Engineering, Arizona State University. I strongly oppose this proposed rule. A $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee would not meaningfully reduce fraud. They would damage engineering education and weaken the U.S. technical workforce that universities like mine exist to build.

1. The rule would push talent we educate to our competitors. U.S. universities invest years of faculty mentorship, research funding, and lab infrastructure in international engineering students. International students make up a large share of U.S. STEM graduate enrollment, 54% of master’s and 44% of doctoral enrollments, and OPT is the primary pathway that keeps these graduates working in U.S. industry and research. Peer nations offer post-study work rights without six-figure barriers. Pricing OPT this way means the United States pays to train engineers and then exports them. 
icef

2. The fee is a wealth test, not an integrity test (Sections IV.C and V.A). DHS says the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students.” In practice, it selects students by whether an institution, employer, or family can pay $70,000. DHS itself acknowledges that costs may be passed on to students (Section IV.C). That fee exceeds a year of tuition at many institutions. Talented students from modest backgrounds, and the institutions that serve them, would be shut out first.

3. It effectively eliminates pre-completion OPT, which is core to engineering education (Section VII.A.5.d(3)). DHS anticipates that institutions will steer students away from pre-completion OPT to avoid paying $100,000 instead of $70,000. Internships and co-ops during the degree are central to how engineering programs develop professional competencies, especially at polytechnic, hands-on programs like ours. The rule treats this educational loss as a side effect rather than a cost.

4. The fee targets the wrong actors. The fraud cases DHS cites in Section IV.A involve shell employers, staged worksites, and sold offer letters. These are employer-side abuses. A fee charged to universities does nothing to stop a fraudulent employer. DHS also rejected targeted enforcement, such as expanded site visits and employer verification, mainly because a fee is quicker (Section IV.C). Speed is not a justification for a policy aimed at the wrong party.

5. The fees would not fund oversight. Section IV.C states that the fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to SEVP. The rule therefore does nothing to address the resource gap that DHS identifies as the core problem.

6. DHS’s own analysis does not support the rule (Section VII.A, Table 1). DHS lists monetized benefits as “Not Estimated.” Meanwhile, it estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion and transfers of up to $16.9 billion. It also finds that 841 of 1,389 small institutions, about 60%, would bear impacts above 1% of revenue in the transition year (Table 17). A rule with unquantified benefits and multibillion-dollar costs should not proceed.

7. Public universities and states were not considered (Sections VII.B.3 and VII.D.5). DHS excludes all 1,044 public institutions from its small-entity analysis. It also states that it did not consult state governments, even though state universities would bear these costs. This omission is significant for states like Arizona that depend on engineering talent for semiconductor and advanced manufacturing growth.

8. Reliance interests are dismissed (Section VI). Current students chose U.S. programs, and often took on debt, with a reasonable expectation that OPT would be available. DHS calls that expectation “speculative.” A comment period of roughly 30 days is also inadequate for a rule of this economic significance.

I also oppose the alternative of re-imposing the $70,000 fee at each degree level (Section V.A). It would further discourage students from pursuing the graduate study that our research enterprise relies on.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted, employer-focused enforcement instead.

I submit this comment in my individual capacity; my title and affiliation are provided for identification only, and these views do not necessarily represent those of Arizona State University.

Respectfully,
Dr. Nadia Kellam, Professor of Engineering; Engineering Undergraduate Program Chair, Associate Director for Strategic Initiatives, The Polytechnic School, Arizona State University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by EnglishUSA
comments.commentText:
RE: Comments on Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. 2026-20660)

To the Department of Homeland Security:

On behalf of EnglishUSA, the national association representing post-secondary English language programs in the United States, I am submitting these comments expressing our opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urging the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed rule.

EnglishUSA represents a diverse community of university-governed and independent English language programs that prepare international students for academic, professional, and personal success. Our member programs play an important role in the U.S. international education ecosystem, serving students who come to the United States specifically to study English, as well as those who begin their educational journeys in English language programs before progressing to undergraduate or graduate degree study.

While OPT is not directly applicable to students enrolled solely in English language training, its availability is an important consideration for many international students planning a longer educational pathway in the United States. Students and families evaluate the full range of educational opportunities when choosing where to invest their time and resources, including the ability to gain practical experience related to their degree studies.

The proposed fees, including an initial $70,000 institutional payment and potentially additional payments, would create substantial financial barriers to practical training opportunities. These barriers could discourage prospective international students from choosing the United States, affecting not only colleges and universities but also the English language programs that frequently serve as their first point of entry into U.S. higher education.

At a time when the United States faces significant competition from other study destinations, policies that diminish the accessibility and attractiveness of the U.S. educational experience risk weakening the broader international education ecosystem. English language programs contribute to that ecosystem by helping students develop the skills necessary for academic success, supporting international student mobility, and building lasting connections between the United States and communities around the world.

EnglishUSA supports appropriate oversight and the integrity of international student programs. However, imposing substantial financial barriers on institutions and otherwise eligible students is not an effective substitute for targeted oversight and compliance measures.

We urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue approaches that protect program integrity while preserving the accessibility, educational value, and global competitiveness of U.S. international education.

Sincerely,

Cheryl Delk-Le Good
Executive Director
EnglishUSA
comments.reason: Submits comments expressing opposition and urging the withdrawal of the proposed OPT fees.

Fees of this magnitude could make OPT inaccessible to many qualified individuals, regardless of their academic achievements or professional potential. It could also discourage international students from choosing U.S. universities in the first place, thus weakening the ability of American institutions to recruit talented researchers and compete internationally.These consequences would extend beyond international students themselves; scientific research depends on collaboration among researchers with diverse backgrounds and expertise. Reducing opportunities for international graduates to participate in the US Workforce could disrupt research teams and ongoing projects and limit the knowledge exchange that supports scientific innovation. In fields such as wildlife conservation and environmental science, where research often requires specialized expertise in long-term collaboration, losing talented early-career researchers could undermine important research and conservation efforts. Any changes to OPT policies should preserve access to professional opportunities for qualified international graduates, support the competitiveness of U.S. universities and research institutions, and advance worker protections without imposing prohibitive costs on students and researchers. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are excessive, poorly justified, and likely to cause substantial harm to American higher education and the economy.

First, DHS has not provided convincing evidence that fees of this magnitude are necessary to prevent fraud. The proposal identifies problems such as fraudulent employers, fabricated job offers, and shell companies. However, charging universities enormous fees does not verify whether an employer is legitimate or whether a student is complying with immigration regulations. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of compliance. A university unable to afford the fee may be entirely legitimate, while fraudulent organizations with sufficient resources may continue their activities. DHS should focus on investigating actual misconduct rather than imposing financial barriers on legitimate participants.

Second, the proposed rule could seriously weaken American universities. International students contribute substantial tuition revenue that supports faculty positions, academic programs, research, and campus operations. Making OPT financially inaccessible would discourage prospective students from choosing American institutions, reducing enrollment and university revenue. Meanwhile, universities attempting to preserve OPT opportunities would face significant additional expenses. These financial pressures could force institutions to reduce scholarships, cut academic programs, or increase tuition. American students and families could ultimately bear some of these costs.

The damage would extend beyond university campuses. In many rural communities and smaller cities, universities are major employers and important drivers of economic activity. International students rent apartments, purchase groceries, use transportation, and support local restaurants and businesses. Fewer international students would mean less revenue for landlords, retailers, and service providers, potentially harming American jobs and local economies. These consequences deserve serious consideration.

The proposal also threatens America's scientific and technological competitiveness. International students contribute to medical research, engineering, technology, and other fields critical to economic growth. OPT allows graduates educated in the United States to apply their skills and contribute to American innovation. If these opportunities become prohibitively expensive, talented individuals may choose to study and work in competing countries. The United States risks losing valuable researchers, entrepreneurs, and future technological advances.

DHS's economic analysis raises further concerns. The agency estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario, yet does not estimate annualized monetized benefits. Without demonstrating that the proposed fees would meaningfully reduce fraud, it is difficult to justify imposing such substantial costs on universities, students, and employers. Reducing OPT participation should not automatically be treated as evidence of successful fraud prevention.

A more reasonable approach would strengthen employer verification, expand targeted investigations, conduct risk-based inspections, and impose meaningful penalties on fraudulent organizations. These measures would address misconduct directly without undermining legitimate educational and employment opportunities.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Protecting immigration integrity should not come at the expense of American universities, educational affordability, local economic stability, scientific innovation, and the nation's long-term competitiveness.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the rule as excessive, poorly justified, and harmful to higher education and universities.

This new rule and fee would be a huge deterrent to international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong concerns regarding the current structure of the STEM Optional Practical Training (OPT) program and its impact on domestic graduates entering the technology workforce.
My son recently graduated with a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science  (CS) from a top-tier research university in Colorado. Despite his strong academic credentials, he faced an incredibly brutal job market, ultimately searching for nine months before only being able to secure a temporary internship rather than a permanent role. New American graduates are currently facing a dual crisis: the rapid integration of artificial intelligence, which is reducing entry-level positions, and a regulatory framework that creates hiring incentives for foreign students over domestic citizens.
While I support legal immigration, the current implementation of the 3-year STEM OPT extension creates an uneven playing field. Unlike the H-1B visa program, the OPT program lacks a prevailing wage or minimum salary requirement. This regulatory gap allows corporations to hire OPT participants at lower wages, inadvertently disincentivizing the hiring of U.S. citizens and suppressing fair market wages for all entry-level engineers.
To argue that foreign graduates possess superior qualifications that justify this displacement is disingenuous. When a domestic student and an international student graduate from the same university, with the same degree, having mastered the exact same curriculum and achieved similar academic marks, their baseline qualifications are identical. The defining difference becomes the regulatory and financial framework surrounding their employment. Under the current system, corporations are financially incentivized to favor international applicants due to the lack of wage floors and the FICA tax exemptions associated with student visas.
Higher education institutions and federal regulations should prioritize ensuring that domestic graduates—who have invested heavily in their education—have a fair and competitive path to entry-level employment. I urge the agency to implement the proposed fee structure as a necessary mechanism to adjust hiring economics, offset administrative burdens, and help level the playing field for domestic workers.
Sincerely,
A concerned parent

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 financial requirement associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT), as it would undermine American economic competitiveness, weaken the domestic talent pipeline, and ultimately harm U.S. businesses, universities, and taxpayers.

The United States has long maintained a competitive advantage by attracting talented individuals from around the world to its universities and research institutions. American higher education does more than provide academic credentials; it develops specialized expertise, supports scientific innovation, and creates a pipeline of skilled professionals who contribute to American industries. Imposing an excessive financial barrier between education and employment would weaken this system by encouraging highly trained graduates to pursue careers in competing economies instead.

This proposal would also impose significant costs on American employers, particularly those operating in highly specialized industries. Businesses in fields such as financial risk management, engineering, healthcare, and advanced technology benefit from access to graduates with rigorous quantitative and technical training. Employers should be able to select candidates based on business needs, professional qualifications, and potential contributions. An excessive financial requirement would distort hiring decisions, reduce access to specialized talent, and make American businesses less competitive internationally.

Furthermore, the economic consequences extend beyond individual employment decisions. International students contribute to local economies through tuition, housing, consumption, and other expenditures. When these students subsequently enter the American workforce, they can contribute additional economic activity, tax revenue, innovation, and productivity. Policies that discourage graduates from remaining in the United States risk transferring these potential benefits to other countries.

The proposal could also undermine the international reputation and competitiveness of American universities. Students considering higher education increasingly evaluate not only academic quality but also opportunities to apply their education after graduation. If the United States establishes disproportionately expensive barriers to practical training, talented prospective students may increasingly choose universities in countries offering more predictable employment pathways. Over time, this could reduce tuition revenue, weaken university research ecosystems, and diminish America's ability to attract global talent.

Importantly, supporting American workers and maintaining access to highly skilled international graduates are not inherently conflicting objectives. A strong labor market requires investment in domestic education, fair employment practices, and the ability of businesses to recruit individuals with specialized skills. Rather than strengthening American workers, a blanket financial barrier risks encouraging companies to move certain activities overseas, where qualified talent may be more accessible.

The United States should pursue immigration and employment policies that strengthen domestic productivity, encourage innovation, and preserve its position as a global leader in education, research, and business. A disproportionately costly OPT requirement would work against these objectives.

I respectfully urge the government to reject this proposal and adopt policies that protect American workers while allowing U.S. employers and educational institutions to retain the economic benefits of internationally trained talent.

As an international PhD student at a U.S. university, I am deeply concerned about the consequences of this proposal for international students, American universities, scientific research, and the long-term competitiveness of the United States.
The proposed fees create an unreasonable financial barrier to educational and professional opportunities. Although the fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, universities may have little choice but to pass these costs on to students or employers or stop recommending students for OPT altogether. A $70,000 fee is beyond the financial reach of most students and many academic employers. Access to practical training should depend on academic qualifications and legitimate training opportunities, not financial resources.

International graduate students contribute substantially to research at U.S. universities, including federally funded projects addressing critical public health challenges such as cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment. OPT provides an important opportunity for these highly trained individuals to apply their expertise and continue contributing to American research institutions. International students are not merely beneficiaries of the American education system; they are also contributors to its scientific advancement, academic excellence, and economic vitality. The United States should foster an environment where talented graduates can contribute to research and innovation rather than creating financial barriers that drive them away.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i). DHS should withdraw these fees and address fraud through targeted, risk-based enforcement.
Fraud should be investigated and punished. But a flat fee of this size does not distinguish a legitimate graduate, employer, or university from a fraudulent one. It distinguishes only who has access to money. Because the fee must be paid before a school can recommend a student, it will exclude capable graduates from less wealthy institutions, startups, smaller employers, and regions outside the largest technology hubs. That is a wealth test, not a fraud test.
The rule would sharply reduce the United States’ capacity to innovate, commercialize discoveries, and develop new technologies. OPT lets U.S.-educated graduates apply specialized knowledge in American laboratories, startups, manufacturers, hospitals, and technology companies. Destroying that bridge after the United States has trained these graduates hands their skills—and the inventions, companies, and jobs they may create—to competing countries.
The National Science Board reports that foreign-born workers account for 46 percent of U.S. science and engineering workers with doctorates, including 57 percent of doctoral-level computer and mathematical scientists and 58 percent of doctoral-level engineers. Temporary visa holders earned 38 percent of U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2024 and 61 percent of doctorates in computer and information sciences. These are precisely the fields in which the United States faces intense global competition.
Research published by the American Economic Association finds that immigrants are 16 percent of U.S. inventors but author 23 percent of patents and, including spillovers to U.S.-born collaborators, account for an estimated 32 percent of aggregate U.S. innovation. Research specifically on OPT finds that expansions increased STEM degree completions by 14–15 percent, including increases among domestic students rather than displacement. A 2026 STEM OPT study also finds large increases in first-time immigrant inventors near research universities, with no evidence of displacement of first-time native inventors.
The proposal’s own analysis confirms the danger. DHS estimates annualized costs as high as $8.2 billion. Its low-participation scenario assumes schools would stop recommending non-STEM graduates for OPT, and it estimates approximately $8.07 billion in annual opportunity costs after transition. DHS acknowledges that these losses include foregone output, contributions to the U.S. economy, employer productivity, and educational benefits. Its proxy still cannot capture lost patents, startups, research spillovers, future tax revenue, reduced enrollment, or long-run damage to America’s ability to attract talent.
The fee is poorly matched to its stated purpose. DHS acknowledges that the revenue would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and would not fund ICE, SEVP, investigations, or site visits. The proposal offers no evidence that a legitimate school paying $70,000 makes employment more genuine. A uniform financial barrier will deter legitimate participation at enormous scale while leaving the underlying verification problem unresolved.
DHS should instead use measures tied directly to risk: data matching across SEVIS, payroll, tax, corporate-registration, and worksite records; targeted and randomized site visits; employer attestations and training plans; rapid investigation of shared addresses, shell companies, phantom employees, and pay-to-stay arrangements; and meaningful sanctions against actors that knowingly facilitate fraud. Congress should provide resources for these activities. Any administrative fee should reflect actual processing costs, be proportionate, and protect small institutions and legitimate students.
DHS should withdraw the proposed fees. At minimum, it should conduct a credible innovation, competition, startup, small-entity, geographic, and international-enrollment analysis before proceeding. Protecting program integrity and American workers is compatible with preserving the talent pipeline that makes U.S. workers and firms more productive. This proposal instead taxes away a major source of American scientific, technological, and economic strength.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Margaret Kurdziolek
comments.commentText:
SUBMITTED VIA REGULATIONS.GOV

Department of Homeland Security
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01
Re: Comments on Proposed Rule: "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566)

Dear Docket Manager,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, 91 FR 64566). 

As an alumna of Virginia Tech with an advanced background in computing and human-centered technology, and as a practitioner working in the American technology sector, I have witnessed firsthand how essential Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the 24-month STEM OPT extension are to maintaining America's technological leadership, supporting world-class university research, and driving industry innovation. 

Imposing a $70,000 fee on institutions for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation (an aggregate of $100,000 per STEM graduate) is arbitrary, economically destructive, and exceeds statutory authority. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety for the following reasons:

1. Unprecedented Financial Burden on Public Land-Grant Institutions Like Virginia Tech
Under the proposed rule, the legal obligation to pay these exorbitant fees falls squarely on SEVP-certified institutions prior to entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. Public institutions like Virginia Tech cannot absorb these costs within state-allocated budgets and research funding. 

In premier computing and engineering programs, international graduate students play an indispensable role: they conduct groundbreaking research in artificial intelligence, robotics, and cybersecurity; staff labs; and serve as graduate teaching assistants. Forcing institutions to either absorb millions of dollars or pass these prohibitive fees onto students will decimate international student recruitment. Prospective students will simply choose peer institutions in the UK, Canada, Australia, or Germany, severing the academic talent pipeline that underpins American engineering excellence.

2. Severe Harm to U.S. Industry and Innovation Leadership
In the technology industry, OPT is not a loophole; it is the primary bridge allowing top U.S.-educated graduates to immediately apply their specialized technical skills in domestic industry. 

The proposed fees—representing a more than 150-fold increase over existing filing costs—will severely bottleneck early-career hiring in high-demand, cutting-edge technical sectors. Leading American companies, from innovative AI and robotics ventures to foundational tech leaders like Google, rely on access to top-tier technical minds educated at U.S. universities. Forcing these graduates out of the domestic labor market will not increase domestic employment; rather, it will handicap American research and development velocity and incentivize companies to expand their engineering and R&D operations abroad.

3. Violation of Administrative Principles and Arbitrary Justification
Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency rulemaking must be reasoned and supported by evidence. DHS justifies these astronomical fees as a means to "combat fraud and abuse." However, levying a blanket $70,000 to $100,000 fee on universities bears no rational connection to the administrative cost of processing SEVIS recommendations or conducting program oversight. 

Setting fees intentionally designed to induce an estimated 80% contraction in program participation represents a de facto administrative dismantling of a program authorized under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Using disproportionate financial penalties to suppress legitimate program usage constitutes arbitrary and capricious agency action.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fee rule will irrevocably harm American higher education, cripple institutional research programs at universities like Virginia Tech, and compromise the competitive advantage of the United States tech sector. 

I strongly urge DHS to rescind this proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,

Meg Kurdziolek
Alumna, Virginia Tech
Technology & User Experience Professional

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees (FR Doc. 2026-20660). The rule moves the real OPT decision from federal eligibility rules to a school's budget choice, and it gives that choice no standards, no reasons, no review and no protection against discrimination.

1. A recommendation becomes a purchase
Today a DSO "must ensure that the F-1 nonimmigrant student is eligible for the type and period of OPT." Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), no DSO may enter a recommendation until the school pays $70,000, or $30,000 for a later OPT period. Eligibility is no longer enough. DHS says schools "would need to consider both the costs of OPT participation and the value each F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT participation brings to the institution," and that a DSO "can elect not to pay the fee for a particular F-1 nonimmigrant who is not a strong candidate." The rule never defines "strong candidate." DHS also declines to define "genuine educational value," saying schools are "in a better position" to judge it.

2. The test DHS sets is the school's interest
Value "to the institution" is not program integrity. A school may weigh rankings, employer partnerships, donor ties or whether a student can repay the fee. None of these measures fraud risk. The fraud DHS describes is employer fraud: shell companies, staged worksites, "phantom employees." For initial OPT the student need not have an employer when the DSO recommends. The school is asked to screen for a risk it cannot see.

3. DHS hands a bigger job to staff it calls overwhelmed
The NPRM says DSOs are "often overwhelmed by the program responsibilities and not fully trained." The rule adds a discretionary $70,000 decision per student. It offers no training, criteria or model policy for making them.

4. Discrimination risk with no guidance
With no neutral criteria required, schools may reach for proxies. DHS's lead fraud example involved false documents sold primarily to Chinese students. A school that rations recommendations by country, or by a student's ability to reimburse, invites claims under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. 2000d, which bars national-origin discrimination by recipients of federal financial assistance. DHS does not discuss this risk or tell schools how to avoid it. Schools will face legal exposure whether they ration or pay.

5. Students get no process at all
A student who meets every regulatory requirement can be refused because the school chose not to pay. The rule requires no written reasons, no internal review and no appeal. USCIS never sees the case, because no recommendation is entered. Timing makes this worse. Post-completion OPT must be requested within a set window after the program ends. A late or silent refusal can end the option for good. A separate comment addresses review of SEVP refund decisions. This gap comes earlier and falls on the student.

6. Equal cases, unequal results
Two graduates with the same degree, field and record will get different answers based on their schools' budgets and internal politics. Nothing in the rule promotes consistent treatment across 6,186 certified schools. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), a rule is arbitrary if the agency failed to consider an important aspect of the problem. Here DHS did not consider how private, conflicted, standardless decisions will be made, or by whom.

7. Requests
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any role for schools beyond today's eligibility check, it should:
(a) require a school to enter a recommendation for any student who meets the regulatory criteria, with no added payment condition;
(b) if any discretion remains, require each school to publish neutral written criteria tied to defined integrity factors;
(c) require written reasons for any refusal, a prompt internal review, and a toll of the OPT filing window while review is pending;
(d) issue civil rights guidance with the Department of Education and the Department of Justice before any rule takes effect; and
(e) place integrity checks at the employer stage, where DHS's own evidence locates the fraud.

comments.commentText:
I want to focus on who will actually decide the fate of American international enrollment if this rule takes effect — and it will not be DHS. It will be the education agents, counselors, and families in sending countries who steer students toward one destination or another, and they will not need a legal opinion to read a $70,000 fee on each OPT recommendation. They will read it as a closed door.

The scale of what is at stake is easy to miss. Roughly 294,000 international students used OPT in the 2024-25 academic year — more than double the number a decade earlier. That growth did not happen by accident. It happened because American universities could credibly promise something no tuition brochure can fake: a lawful bridge from graduation to employment. OPT is the product feature that lets a recruiter in Hyderabad or Lagos say, honestly, that an American degree leads somewhere. Attach a $70,000 charge to that bridge, and the honest pitch changes overnight.

Competitors are already positioned to catch the diverted demand. Canada offers post-graduation work permits of up to three years with no fee on schools. The United Kingdom's Graduate route gives two years of unrestricted work, three for PhD graduates. Australia's post-study work stream runs up to four years. None of these countries charges the student's university six figures for the privilege. Their recruiters do not need to exaggerate; they only need to quote the American rule.

And the loss, once it happens, is not deferred — it is permanent. A student who chooses Toronto over Texas in fall 2027 does not transfer to an American campus in 2028. That cohort's tuition, rent, research assistance, and eventual startups are gone for the full length of a degree and beyond. Universities that lose a recruiting cycle do not recover it with a press release; they recover it, if at all, over years of rebuilt trust.

DHS may believe it is regulating a domestic program. In reality it is setting the price at which the world's most mobile, most sought-after students stop choosing America. Our competitors will not have to outbid us. This rule outbids us on their behalf. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mira Jasmin
comments.commentText:
I oppose the new proposed rule for optional practical training fees. I am a private individual and U.S. citizen who has recently received my undergraduate degree from a public University and had the privilege to know and work alongside several international students. The proposed $70,000 and subsequent $30,000 fees would have a significant negative impact on these students and their abilities to work and live in the United States. I urge the DHS to withdraw the proposed rule or at minimum significantly reduce fees. 

Under section IV A the document authors cite “combating fraud and abuse” as part of their reasoning for increasing OPT fees. Examples cited include reports of students using OPT for employment unrelated to their field of study and examples of “pay-to-stay” fraudulent employers. While DHS has the authority and obligation to prevent these types of fraud, the document does not provide satisfactory evidence to explain how the increased fees would adequately address the issue of fraud. Under section IV C the document authors purport that fees “would deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its students.” However, because the extraordinarily high fees will certainly decrease participation in OPT on their own, schools may not be motivated to increase levels of scrutiny when endorsing applicants from a severely limited pool. A survey of 734 current and formal international students conducted by the Institute of Progress found that 80% fewer students would attempt to stay in the country and pursue OPT with the proposed changes. [International Student Survey on OPT and Experiential Learning (Institute for Progress, October 2026)]. The document does not clearly explain how this decreased participation due to fees would impact the anticipated increased selectivity of schools in endorsing applicants. Additionally, because the fees could be payable by the school, student, or employer, fraudulent employers or students with the financial means to pay the fee outright may not be subject to increased scrutiny because they are not costing schools any additional financial resources. Overall, the document does not provide strong enough evidence that the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees would effectively reduce fraud. 

I am also opposed to the new proposed rule for OPT fees because I believe it would unfairly punish honest, hardworking and talented students by limiting participation in OPT. In section IV C the document authors state the following; “DHS acknowledges that the schools may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.” Therefore, the proposed rule provides no protections against students having to bear the financial burden of increased fees. During my time as an undergraduate student at a public University I have had the privilege of knowing an international undergraduate student pursuing their degree in industrial design. This individual is an exemplary student; has excelled in their classes and held several on-campus jobs related to their field of study. Currently, they are employed at a medical lab at the University conducting research on how to design vital medical devices such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines for children and face masks that increase protection from respiratory illness. This student has already faced difficulties in obtaining Curricular Practical Training (CPT) employment due to their status as an international student. If the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees were to fall to this student after they graduate, they would be unable to pay the fee, and thus would be unable to remain in the country and continue to contribute their talents, knowledge and skills to their medical design work which directly benefits the health and wellness of U.S. residents. It is my firm belief that international students such as themselves–who do not fall into the pool of applicants considered “fraudulent”–would be unfairly punished by the establishment of blanket fees.

In conclusion, I oppose the new proposed rule for optional practical training fees and urge the DHS to withdraw the rule or significantly reduce fees. The document outlining the proposed rule does not provide satisfactory evidence that such fees would adequately reduce fraudulent activities. Additionally, the proposed rule does not provide enough financial protections to prevent students from bearing the cost of fees, and as such has the potential for unfairly punishing honest and hardworking students pursuing employment related to their field of study.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alik Widge
comments.commentText:
I am a biomedical research scientist at a university, performing work at the intersection of biology and engineering. I oppose the proposed rule, as it would harm both my own work (much of which is done on behalf of the Federal government) and American competitiveness more broadly. It should be withdrawn.

DHS did not provide clear evidence that OPT students displace American workers or depress their wages. From personal experience, I employ researchers and engineers who need to have specific technical skills and a deep interest in learning more about a focused area on the technical frontier. At any given time, there are perhaps five such people on the job market, only one of whom is willing to relocate to my city. Further, when I make a hire, I am required to pay them within a salary band set by the university, regardless of their visa status. In other words, DHS' stated rationale is factually incorrect and there is no analysis presented to consider whether hiring policies invalidate the argument.

DHS did not establish that the problem of fraud and abuse is sufficiently widespread to justify the burden of a new rule and fee. "Reports" are cited, of a few egregious cases. However, even the report of 10,000 students does not establish that a substantial proportion of OPT/STEM OPT recipients are engaged in fraud. It is not known if all of the students claimed in those reports are engaged in fraud, and even then, that would be less than 5% of OPT recipients by DHS' own numbers.
This particularly invalidates DHS' claim that "To the extent that an institution may have to alter its budget that was prepared without consideration of being required to pay the proposed fee, DHS has weighed those interests with those explained in this rule and determined that the purpose of and urgent need to address fraud through this proposed rule far outweigh such interests. "
There is no urgent need, and there is a substantial burden on entities that have relied on the existing system. As such, reliance interests were not considered.

DHS does not actually propose a correction to the problem. As is clearly stated in the proposal, fees would be general US government revenue. They would not go to DHS, would not be used for visa oversight/surveillance/enforcement, and would in no way actually offset the costs of any actual enforcement. Thus the rule fails to achieve its stated purpose and cannot be legitimately proposed.

In fact, DHS acknowledges that the proposed fee would not help oversight at all, "This approach does not require DHS to deploy significant additional resources for enforcement or oversight. " As such, the point of the fee is solely to burden international students, which does not align with legislative principles or American values.

DHS did not present an analysis of alternate, less burdensome approaches, e.g. requiring additional reporting from OPT participants and/or their employers, which in an age of artificial/superintelligence, could easily be used to identify fraud without substantial cost. It did not balance those questions against reliance interests.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the rule runs counter to the Administration's larger priority: insuring American predominance in the global economy and on the global battlefield, particularly against the growing threat posed by China and its allies. The fact is this: when we educate an international student, we can either send them back to their home country and let that country reap the benefit of their new knowledge, or we can keep them, turn them into an American, and make their talent ours. That latter has been our economic engine for over a half-century. It is not coincidence that so many people founding and working in our technological companies are foreign-born or the children of immigrants. It is a direct consequence of America's "brain drain" strategy. If we truly want to Make America Great Again, we do it by taking away what other nations need most -- their human capital. 

The rule is flawed, it has no legitimate purpose and does not support the interests of the American people, and it must be withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed rule, arguing it harms research and American competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01

I oppose this proposed rule. I hold an MS in Mechanical Engineering from a U.S. university and work on post-completion OPT. 

1. The rule penalizes students already on OPT. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3), the $30,000 fee applies only if the $70,000 fee was previously paid, so students whose initial OPT predates the rule would owe $70,000 for a STEM extension. The regulatory analysis confirms all Year 1 participants, "including those in STEM OPT," pay $70,000. DHS admits current students are differently situated (fn. 124) but gives them no protection. At minimum, exempt STEM extensions for students whose initial OPT began before the effective date.

2. The fee funds no enforcement. The NPRM states fees go to the Treasury general fund (31 U.S.C. 3302) and ICE cannot retain them. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service operates as a tax, which DHS has not shown INA 214(a) authorizes.

3. It is not targeted at fraud. DHS cites about 10,000 students linked to suspect employers, versus 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, under 3 percent. Yet the fee hits every participant, including employers already subject to E-Verify, I-983 attestations, and site visits. DHS rejected targeted alternatives such as expanded site visits because a fee is faster, not because they are less effective. Refunds are discretionary and unappealable, so even a legitimate student whose job falls through has no assured remedy.

4. There is no evidence of harm to American workers. The OMB A-4 statement lists benefits as "Not Estimated." DHS relies on unemployment rates for computer science majors and offers no data on engineering fields like mine. Research points the other way: Gong et al. (2019) found the 2008 STEM OPT extension raised domestic STEM employment 4.4-5.8% and wages 2.4-3.3%; a study reviewed by DOL's CLEAR database (Mukherjee, 2019) found no link to domestic STEM salaries or labor force participation; NFAP (2019) found more OPT approvals relative to U.S. workers associated with lower U.S. unemployment. STEM OPT employers already attest that trainees will not replace U.S. workers and will be paid commensurately (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)).

5. The FICA rationale does not fit the remedy. DHS argues the payroll tax exemption makes OPT workers cheaper. That saving is 7.65% of salary, and DHS concedes (fn. 108) many STEM OPT workers already pay FICA after five calendar years. A $70,000-$100,000 fee per student is grossly disproportionate to that saving, and if FICA is the concern, Congress can address it directly.

6. DHS understates reliance. It says only about 20% of 1.4 million F-1 students used OPT in 2024, but that compares OPT users with all enrolled students, many of whom are still studying and not yet eligible. The relevant group is graduates, for whom OPT is a central reason to study in the U.S. Students like me enrolled, paid tuition, and accepted job offers under the current rules.

7. Costs far exceed any demonstrated benefit. DHS estimates $8.7-16.9 billion in annual transfers and up to $8.2 billion in annualized opportunity costs. In the transition year, 841 of 1,389 small institutions face impacts above 1% of revenue, and 116 above 20%. The fee is calibrated to the $100,000 H-1B fee, which a federal court vacated on September 30, 2026.

8. The fee distorts training choices. DHS admits it would push students away from pre-completion OPT because combining pre- and post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for the same 12 months. A rule that discourages legitimate, school-supervised training does nothing to stop fraud.

9. It harms U.S. employers and their U.S. workers. STEM OPT requires employers to commit to a formal I-983 training plan. Employers invest months training these engineers, and project teams that include U.S. workers rely on them. Pricing trainees out mid-project disrupts that work. DHS dismisses employer reliance by saying employers can simply hire others, without any data showing qualified replacements exist.

10. The data are inconsistent. Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, but Table 2 uses 95,384. DHS should explain which figure drives its estimates.

11. Thirty days is inadequate for an economically significant rule. Executive Order 12866 recommends at least 60.

I ask DHS to withdraw the rule, or at minimum exempt STEM extensions for current OPT participants, exempt employers in good standing with E-Verify, or adopt targeted enforcement against the employers it has already identified.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and request withdrawal of the rule. This comment addresses an issue distinct from whether DHS may regulate OPT: how the agency accounts for people and institutions that have made substantial commitments in reliance on the existing framework. A change can be prospective in form yet impose severe consequences on decisions that cannot realistically be undone.

Students choose U.S. degree programs years before graduation. Their decisions may involve tuition payments, loans, relocation, and declining opportunities elsewhere. Universities likewise make admissions, staffing, and program commitments on multi-year timelines. Employers plan recruitment and training around expected graduation dates. Although no student is guaranteed OPT approval or an unchanged regulatory environment, these decisions create reliance interests that deserve explicit consideration when the government proposes an abrupt and extraordinary new financial condition.

The Supreme Court's decision in Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), illustrates the importance of considering serious reliance interests when changing an established policy. FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502 (2009), likewise recognizes that a change in policy may require a more detailed explanation when prior policy has engendered reliance. Neither decision freezes OPT rules or guarantees any particular transition period. Both underscore the need for reasoned decision-making rather than treating existing commitments as irrelevant.

DHS should therefore identify which cohorts would face the proposed charges and when. Would the fees affect students who enrolled before publication, students already pursuing degrees, those who have received job offers, or those approaching an OPT application window? What notice would these groups have, and what realistic options would remain? An announcement shortly before graduation cannot restore years of tuition or permit a student to select a different country or degree program retroactively.

The agency should also evaluate whether universities could make sudden funding commitments without disrupting existing obligations. A requirement directed at institutions does not eliminate the reliance of students whose practical training depends on institutional recommendations. DHS should examine whether schools would withdraw support for particular cohorts, limit recommendations, or apply inconsistent internal selection criteria when budgets cannot absorb the charges.

Reasonable transitional alternatives merit separate analysis. These include exempting students already enrolled by a defined date, protecting recommendations already in process, delaying implementation for at least a complete academic planning cycle, and phasing in any new requirement. DHS should explain the integrity benefits lost under each option and why those losses would outweigh the disruption avoided. It should also consider whether narrowly targeted enforcement could address immediate misconduct during a transition.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposal. At minimum, before adopting any replacement, DHS should publish a cohort-by-cohort reliance analysis, specify the effective-date consequences for pending and planned recommendations, and give a reasoned explanation for accepting or rejecting meaningful grandfathering and phased implementation. A fair and defensible rulemaking must account not only for future incentives but also for commitments made under the government's existing framework.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees and requests withdrawal of the rule due to severe reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
OPT and STEM-OPT directly contribute to learning for fields such as engineering. An engineering student must get hands-on experience in order to understand the applicability of those concepts learned in school. For instance, observing different mechanisms, using industry standards, witnessing validation tests, learning current state of technology, collaborating with multiple sub teams within an engineering project, so imposing such a high fee seems to be restricting that experiential learning by making it harder to access it. Especially, students who never had that hands-on experience before and are not eligible for CPT but are here to genuinely study and learn more about their respective fields.

Although the intentions of this proposal are reasonable and valid, which is for the safety of the public and opportunities for the citizens, the proposed policy or even any policy can be shaped to be fair to the ones who are here with genuine reasons while also making it harder for people committing fraud. As an example, it could be adding metrics such as GPA requirement (although GPA isn't inherently the best metric to measure one's talents) to be eligible to apply for OPT and STEM-OPT, a letter of recommendation from one of the faculty, a resume or statement (depending how accessible it is to conduct projects while studying) that showcases one’s curiosity, etc. Hopefully, this adds a different perspective to the making of this policy that is fairer.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the high fee restricts experiential learning and suggests fairer alternative policies.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kathryn Williamson
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to OPPOSE the proposed requirement that colleges and universities pay $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations (including STEM OPT extensions).

As an anthropologist researching and teaching at an R2 research university, my deepest concern is the disproportionate institutional burden this rule would impose.

R2 institutions serve substantial international student populations while operating with far more constrained budgets than wealthy private universities. We cannot absorb these costs without passing them directly to students. For many departments -- including anthropology, where graduate fellowships are already stretched thin -- this fee structure would force us to stop recommending international scholars for practical training altogether.

This rule creates a two-tier system where OPT access depends not on academic merit or field alignment, but on institutional wealth. Smaller public research universities like mine become second-tier players in international education overnight, undermining our ability to compete for global talent and weakening the pipeline of researchers entering our fields.

The financial reality is simple: we cannot pay $70,000 per recommendation. Without withdrawal or substantial revision of this proposal, international graduate students at R2 institutions will lose access to post-completion work opportunities essential to their careers and to our research missions.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this rule pending consultation with affected higher education institutions.

Thank you for your consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed fee requirement due to institutional budget constraints.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an American college student studying computer science and business, and I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security's proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I urge DHS to finalize the strictest available version of the rule without reduced fees, broad exemptions, or unnecessary implementation delays.

I fully support the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions. American students invest substantial time and money in earning degrees and preparing for internships and entry-level employment, especially in technology. Federal policy should prioritize opportunities for American workers and graduates rather than maintain additional pathways for employers to hire temporary foreign labor.

I oppose the continued use and expansion of OPT. The program provides employment authorization outside the traditional H-1B process, and I am concerned that it enables employers to rely on foreign graduates rather than recruit qualified American applicants. I favor substantially restricting OPT and ultimately ending the program through appropriate legal action. Until then, I support the highest fees and strictest oversight DHS can lawfully impose.

I strongly support the alternative in Section V.A requiring a new $70,000 initial fee when a student qualifies for another initial OPT period after completing a higher degree. When someone uses OPT after a bachelor's degree and later earns a master's degree, a new $70,000 initial fee should apply to that OPT recommendation, with the same rule at subsequent qualifying degree levels. Treating these new periods as merely subsequent recommendations subject to the lower $30,000 fee would weaken the proposal and encourage repeated use of academic enrollment to obtain work authorization. DHS should select the stricter alternative.

I oppose exemptions for small schools, financial hardship, or other institutional circumstances. All SEVP-certified institutions should face the same fees. Allowing exceptions would weaken enforcement and create ways to avoid the intended requirements. I support payment in full before a designated school official enters an OPT recommendation into SEVIS, and no USCIS employment authorization unless the required fee has been paid. I also support the proposed limits on refunds. DHS should not create routine waivers, reduced-fee pathways, or loopholes that undermine these provisions.

I support more extensive eligibility screening, school compliance reviews, employment verification, and fraud investigations before OPT approval. Thorough review matters more than fast adjudication. If legitimate compliance checks increase individual application processing times, I support that outcome. Expedited procedures should never bypass required checks. At the same time, DHS should implement the new fee rule as quickly as legally permissible; delaying its effective date would postpone the restrictions I support.

I also urge DHS to pursue stricter restrictions on Curricular Practical Training (CPT) through separate action. Schools and employers should face rigorous scrutiny over whether claimed training is academically necessary and properly authorized. Arrangements that primarily use enrollment to facilitate employment should be investigated and prohibited when inconsistent with program requirements.

I likewise favor tougher H-1B restrictions through separate rulemaking and legislation, including higher financial requirements, stricter employer standards, extensive verification, and stronger penalties for violations. These pathways should not give employers an incentive to bypass qualified American workers.

The United States should reduce its reliance on temporary foreign employment programs and prioritize domestic workers, particularly students and recent graduates seeking their first professional opportunities. I oppose expansion of OPT, CPT, and H-1B and favor further lawful restrictions on each.

Please finalize the full $70,000 initial OPT fee, the $30,000 subsequent fee, and the stricter higher-degree alternative. Reject reductions, broad exemptions, waivers, and implementation delays. Apply strict payment controls and comprehensive verification, even when individual applications take longer to process. I urge DHS to adopt the strongest available measures and continue pursuing further restrictions on temporary foreign employment pathways.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly supports the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to finalize the strictest version.

comments.title: MM14 Comment Submitted by S. R.
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees


The Asian Neuropsychological Association (ANA) OPT Ad Hoc Committee respectfully opposes the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.


Clinical neuropsychology requires extensive specialized training, including two-year postdoctoral fellowships following doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled, competitive neuropsychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates.


These consequences extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning and linguistic/cultural considerations that strengthen neuropsychological assessment, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and limit the availability of clinical-researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S.'s diverse population.


We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.


Thank you for considering our comments.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed OPT fees and highlights negative impacts on specialized medical training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fees (Docket ICEB-2026-0100).

I came to the United States on an F-1 visa. I earned my bachelor's degree at a public university. My family and I paid for both in full. As an undergraduate, I paid out-of-state tuition several times the in-state rate. I received no federal aid, because F-1 students are not eligible for it.

I used OPT for an entry-level software engineering job directly related to my degree. That training made me a productive professional, and it is how my employer came to sponsor me for an H-1B. Today I pay well over $35,000 a year in taxes.
My story is not unusual. Most international students are primarily funded by personal and family sources. At public universities, out-of-state tuition averages about $31,880 a year, against $11,950 for in-state students. That premium does not push Americans out. Research on graduate programs found that every 10 additional international students were associated with about 8 additional domestic students, because international tuition helps pay for those seats.

I chose the United States for the quality of its universities and for its openness to people who work hard and contribute. OPT was part of that promise. It has existed for decades, and a federal appeals court upheld it. Students deciding where to enroll today, and students already enrolled, rely on it.

A $70,000 fee would end that promise for almost everyone in my position. For a one- or two-year master's student, the fee could rival the cost of the degree itself. DHS says schools may pass the fee on to students or employers, but it does not show that either can absorb it. In practice, students like me would go elsewhere, taking their tuition, their skills and, eventually, their taxes with them.

DHS has a legitimate interest in stopping fraud by shell employers, and I support that. But a flat fee on every student cannot tell a legitimate, degree-related job from a fake company. The proposal also dismisses students like me by saying the F-1 visa "was never intended to provide a pathway to employment." For decades, the government's own regulations said otherwise, and people made life decisions based on them.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers instead.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees and shares their personal background as an F-1 visa holder.
