comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

I am writing to urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations, which together total $100,000 for a typical STEM graduate. This rule would not protect American workers. It would effectively end the OPT program without DHS saying so, and it would push American jobs, investment, and innovation to other countries.

We have already seen what happens when the U.S. restricts skilled foreign talent. When DHS previously made it more difficult for companies to hire workers on H-1B status, companies based in the United States responded by offshoring more of their operations abroad. That allowed countries like China, India, and Canada to gain new jobs and inventions that would otherwise have been created on American soil. The jobs did not go to American workers. They left the country, along with the supporting positions, tax revenue, and patents that came with them.

The OPT fee would repeat that mistake earlier in the pipeline. OPT is how many of the most talented graduates of American universities gain their first professional experience in the United States. These students were trained here, often with the help of American research funding. If OPT becomes unaffordable, employers who depend on these graduates will not stop needing their skills. They will hire them in Toronto, Bangalore, or Shanghai instead, and build their teams and research centers there. Other countries are actively recruiting these same graduates with fast, low-cost work pathways.

Schools will not absorb this cost, so students will pay it or lose access. Although the fee is formally charged to universities, few if any institutions can afford to pay $70,000 to $100,000 per student. Schools will either pass the cost on to students or stop recommending students for OPT. Either way, the result for students is the same: the program is closed to them. Smaller and regional institutions, which have the fewest resources, will be hit hardest. The Economic Innovation Group estimates that a $100,000 per-graduate charge could reduce international master’s enrollment by at least 35 percent, which would harm university budgets, graduate programs that American students also rely on, and the local economies around these schools.

In practice, this fee ends the OPT program without DHS saying so. For most international students, a $100,000 charge is no different from a $1,000,000 one: either way, the program is out of reach. The proposal itself acknowledges that DHS is considering shutting down OPT entirely. If DHS’s real goal is to end OPT, it should propose that directly, explain its reasoning, and account for the students, universities, and employers who have built their plans around the program. Setting a fee so high that almost no one can pay it is not a fee for a service. It is the elimination of the program presented as something else. That approach denies the public an honest debate about the program’s future and avoids the analysis the law requires.

The fee is also disproportionate to the stated concern about fraud. If DHS has identified fraudulent employers, the appropriate response is targeted enforcement against those employers, such as site visits, employer verification, and penalties. A flat fee of this size punishes every student and school, including the overwhelming majority who follow the rules. It does little to stop bad actors who already operate outside the law.

What this looks like up close. My spouse works with international students in higher education. In that work, he has seen no fraud. What he has seen are talented students who have worked incredibly hard for years, often far from their families and at great expense, to earn their degrees and the chance to put their training to use. This rule would pull that pathway out from under them, in many cases after they have already committed years and their families’ savings based on the program as it exists today. I am submitting this comment anonymously because people who work with these students are concerned about the consequences of speaking publicly. DHS should consider that many of the people with the most direct knowledge of OPT may not feel free to put their names on their comments.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. At minimum, DHS should not adopt the alternative under consideration that would charge the $70,000 fee again at each higher degree level. Keeping talented graduates working in the United States is how we keep the jobs and inventions they create here as well.

Respectfully submitted.
comments.reason: Commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule imposing high OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dennis Ma
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. The proposal exceeds DHS's statutory authority and is arbitrary and capricious under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) and (C).

First, this is a tax, not a fee — and only Congress may impose taxes. DHS invokes general authority under INA § 214(a) to set conditions of admission, not the user-fee framework, under which a fee must be reasonably related to the cost of the service provided. The $70,000 charge bears no stated connection to any processing cost — roughly 200 times the $350 SEVIS fee — and the proceeds would go to the general Treasury rather than fund SEVP. The same hallmarks led federal courts to enjoin the $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee as an unlawful tax, and the Supreme Court's 2026 tariffs decision confirms that general regulatory authority is not authority to collect money as the price of an activity.

Second, the fee is charged to the wrong party: schools, for a benefit the student receives — and DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students.

Third, the fee is a lever to end OPT, not cost recovery. DHS states that without these fees it "may shut down the program entirely." An agency may not use fee-setting authority to nullify a program the D.C. Circuit upheld in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022). DHS has published no cost study tying $70,000 or $30,000 to any actual expense, and its own estimate — $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year across 2,478 schools — confirms this is a revenue measure.

Finally, the proposal states it does not address Curricular Practical Training. I urge DHS to preserve CPT as a distinct curricular program and not to use OPT fees as a basis for restricting it.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

Respectfully submitted,
Dennis Ma
comments.reason: Commenter respectfully opposes the proposed OPT fees, calling them an unlawful tax.

comments.title: MM1 Comment Submitted by Mark Willis
comments.commentText: Optional Practical Training (OPT) was created out of thin air and needs to be eliminated. However, until the program is terminated, I support the proposed fees. DHS is right that the F-1 visa “was never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States.” A student visa is for study, and it should end with the degree. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking)

October 26, 2026,

Dear Government Official,

I am writing to object to the proposed rule imposing new fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). The rule would add a $70,000 charge before a school may first recommend a student for OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. This is not a modest adjustment. It is a steep penalty on a benefit that has long been part of the F-1 academic student status, and I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The charge is a tax, which only Congress may impose. A fee is a compulsory payment that offsets an agency’s cost of providing a specific service. A tax is a compulsory payment that funds public goods generally. A charge of $70,000 bears no plausible relationship to the cost of processing an OPT recommendation. The proceeds would go to the Department of the Treasury rather than being tied to the cost of the service, which further indicates that this is revenue-raising. Congress has not authorized DHS or ICE to levy taxes, and an agency cannot do so by regulation. The rule exceeds the agency’s statutory authority and is unlawful on that basis.

2. OPT is a longstanding benefit, and the rule would effectively destroy it. OPT lets international students gain practical work experience in their field of study, and it has been a defining feature of the F-1 status for decades. Because the fee is levied on each school’s recommendation, institutions would be forced either to absorb a cost most cannot bear or to pass it on to students and employers, or to stop recommending students for OPT at all. Whichever path they take, the rule would sharply reduce access to OPT.

3. The rule would reduce international enrollment and harm U.S. universities. The opportunity to work in the United States after graduating is a major reason students choose American institutions over competitors in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere. Removing or devaluing OPT will likely cut the number of international students who come to the United States. Colleges and universities, and the communities and local economies around them, depend on these students.

4. The rule would damage the U.S. economy and American innovation. International students contribute substantially to the U.S. economy through tuition, living expenses, and the skills and research they bring to American employers. OPT is the main pipeline through which this academic talent enters the U.S. workforce, and for many it is the first step toward employment-based immigration categories such as EB-1, EB-2, and EB-3. Cutting off this pipeline limits innovation and the opportunities that this talent creates for American workers, who often work alongside these graduates in growing companies and research teams.

5. Retaining talent serves American interests. Public officials, including President Trump, have spoken in favor of allowing foreign graduates of American universities to stay and obtain green cards. A fee that shuts down the main pathway by which such graduates gain experience and employer sponsorship is inconsistent with that goal.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, protect OPT, and preserve the international talent pipeline that sustains American excellence and competitiveness.

Respectfully submitted,

Concerned U.S. citizen
comments.reason: Commenter objects to the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
My daughter is currently on a dependent visa. She completed her high school education in the United States and is now pursuing an undergraduate degree in a STEM program. The Optional Practical Training (OPT) program provides students with a valuable opportunity to gain practical, hands-on experience in their field of study and apply the knowledge they have acquired through their academic programs.

As nonimmigrant parents, we already pay taxes in the United States and bear the substantial cost of our daughter's college education. In addition to these existing financial commitments, how can families reasonably afford an additional $70,000 in OPT-related fees?

Such a fee may be more understandable for students who completed their prior education outside the United States and subsequently chose to pursue undergraduate or postgraduate studies here. However, the circumstances of dependent visa holders like my daughter are fundamentally different. Due to our immigration status, she has pursued both her high school and undergraduate education in the United States, incurring significant educational expenses along the way.

Introducing such a substantial OPT fee, particularly without adequate advance notice or consideration for students already enrolled in U.S. institutions, would place an enormous and unexpected financial burden on families like ours. These students have followed the educational path available to them under their family's immigration circumstances and should not be unfairly disadvantaged as a result.

I respectfully urge the relevant authorities to reconsider this proposed fee and take into account the unique circumstances of dependent visa holders and their families. At a minimum, appropriate exemptions or transitional provisions should be considered for students who have already completed their high school education in the United States or are currently pursuing undergraduate or postgraduate degrees at U.S. institutions.

Students who have invested years in their education in the United States should have a fair opportunity to gain practical experience in their chosen STEM fields without facing an unreasonable and potentially prohibitive financial barrier.
comments.reason: Commenter argues the steep OPT fee places an unfair and unexpected financial burden on families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Carleton College
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule requiring $70,000 fees for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extension recommendations.

OPT is an essential extension of higher education that allows international students to apply classroom learning to real-world career paths. Imposing an unprecedented $70,000 to $100,000 fee on universities for each participating student will inevitably price out academic institutions or force those costs onto students. This policy effectively destroys experiential learning opportunities for international scholars who contribute immensely to local economies, academic research, and campus communities across the United States.

I see firsthand how international peers enrich our academic discussions and campus life. Threatening their access to post-graduation practical training disincentivizes global talent from choosing U.S. higher education. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted.
comments.reason: Commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed fee structure and urges withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing as a New Jersey resident and U.S. citizen to express my opposition to the proposed OPT fees of $70,000, followed by an additional $30,000. My greatest concern is the inequity this would create among international students who have worked hard to earn their degrees at American colleges and universities. Students attending wealthy institutions that can afford these fees may continue to have access to practical training, while equally qualified students at smaller universities with limited financial resources would lose that opportunity entirely. Many colleges simply do not have the funds to pay even one $70,000 fee, much less cover the costs for multiple graduates. It seems fundamentally unfair that a student's opportunity to gain practical experience related to their education would depend on the financial resources of their university rather than their academic achievements or eligibility. I find this especially troubling because equal opportunity, fairness, and rewarding hard work are values that Americans have long taken pride in.

I am also concerned about the broader economic impact, particularly here in New Jersey. According to NAFSA, international students contributed approximately $950 million to New Jersey's economy and supported more than 8,200 jobs during the 2024–25 academic year. Nationally, their contribution was $42.9 billion, supporting more than 355,000 American jobs. Beyond these immediate economic benefits, we should also recognize the long-term value of educating international students in the United States. Many return to their home countries after completing their studies and practical training, eventually becoming leaders in business, government, education, and other fields. They take with them an understanding of American society, institutions, and values, along with personal and professional relationships that often last a lifetime. These connections are enormously valuable to the United States, supporting diplomacy, international trade, business development, and cooperation across borders. I also question the assumption that international graduates participating in OPT are taking jobs away from American workers. OPT is temporary, directly related to a student's education, and many participants ultimately take their skills and experience back to their home countries. We should recognize the benefits of these exchanges rather than view international graduates primarily as competitors for American jobs.

I understand and support the need to prevent fraud and ensure that OPT operates as intended. However, I question whether these fees would actually accomplish that goal. The proposed rule identifies concerns about fraud, but it also acknowledges that the fees collected would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than directly supporting fraud prevention or program oversight. I would much rather see resources directed toward identifying employers or individuals who misuse the program and enforcing the rules already in place. Imposing such substantial fees on universities and students who follow the rules seems unlikely to address the underlying problem. I hope DHS will reconsider this proposal and pursue a more targeted approach that protects the integrity of OPT without creating such significant financial barriers or limiting opportunities based on institutional wealth.
comments.reason: Commenter expresses opposition to the proposed OPT fees due to inequity and economic impact.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Douglass Endrizzi
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Doug Endrizzi. I did my PhD and PostDoc at the University of Wisconsin-Madision, and have been a fellow there since.  The average time to completion in experimental plasma physics is above 6 years, and so these OPT fees become inevitable. There are multiple graduate students in our lab who would be crippled by these fees, and all of the labs I know who be unable to cover these fees. 

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

The entire field of plasma physics recruits the most capable and idealistic students from abroad. The field benefits from their work as graduate students, and from when they stay in the US after and continue working. 

Our recruitment of the best students from abroad has been to our tremendous advantage, both for the labs doing the work and for us when those people decide to stay and make their careers in the US. 

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Douglass Endrizzi
comments.reason: Commenter expresses opposition to the excessive OPT fees and asks to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Irina Levin
comments.commentText: My name is Irina Levin and I am a lecturer at Princeton University. As a PhD student at NYU and then a faculty member and administrator at a wide range of higher ed institutions--Delgado Community College in New Orleans, Queens College- and Brooklyn College-CUNY, Arizona State University, and now Princeton--I have gotten to know and work with many international students, both undergraduate and graduate, across a wide range of fields. From undergraduate engineering and neuroscience students to PhD students in computer science and anthropology, I have learned so much from these folks, including how to appreciate the opportunities that American higher ed offers and where improvements are needed. OPT gives these highly talented and ambitious people the opportunity to gain work experience while continuing to make important contributions in their fields and to US society and our economy. There is plenty of research, including by the federal government, that demonstrates the mutual benefits. On the other hand, there is no compelling reason to think that restricting access to OPT by imposing burdensome fees will help anyone. Curtailing OPT opportunities by imposing the proposed fees, whatever the supposed short-term gains, would ultimately be a huge loss for the American people. I urge you to reconsider the proposed rule and, more fundamentally, the negative understanding of international students that it seems to be based on. They are our friends, neighbors, colleagues, mentors, doctors, etc. If they can appreciate how fortunate they are to learn, work, and live here--and I know that they do--we should be able to appreciate how fortunate we are to have them.
comments.reason: Argues that imposing burdensome OPT fees is a huge loss and urges reconsideration of the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate policy objectives, the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are disproportionate, insufficiently justified, and likely to cause significant economic harm.

The proposal fails to establish a convincing relationship between the proposed fees and effective fraud prevention. DHS identifies fraudulent employers, fabricated employment records, and shell companies as major concerns. However, imposing substantial financial obligations on educational institutions does not directly address these violations. A university's ability to pay does not establish that an employment opportunity is legitimate, nor does financial inability indicate misconduct. DHS should demonstrate why these specific amounts are necessary and why targeted enforcement measures would be insufficient.

The economic justification is equally concerning. DHS estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario, while annualized monetized benefits remain unestimated. This raises serious questions about whether the rule's anticipated benefits justify its financial consequences. A reduction in OPT participation alone cannot be considered evidence of successful fraud prevention.

The proposed fees would also impose considerable pressure on American universities. International students contribute tuition revenue that supports academic programs, faculty employment, research facilities, and university operations. Making OPT financially inaccessible could discourage international enrollment, particularly at smaller and regional universities. Institutions facing declining revenue and additional financial obligations may be forced to reduce educational services, limit scholarships, or increase tuition. American students and families could ultimately bear part of these costs.

The broader economic consequences should not be overlooked. Universities are major economic contributors in many American communities, particularly rural areas and smaller cities. International students support local housing markets, retail businesses, restaurants, and transportation services. Declining enrollment could weaken these local economies and reduce employment opportunities for American workers.

Furthermore, the proposal threatens America's long-term scientific and technological competitiveness. International students and graduates contribute to medical research, engineering, scientific discovery, and technological innovation. OPT enables these individuals to apply their education within the American economy. Creating excessive financial barriers would encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities abroad, potentially benefiting competing economies at the expense of American research institutions and businesses.

DHS should instead prioritize employer verification, targeted compliance inspections, stronger reporting requirements, and meaningful penalties for fraudulent activities. Such measures would address identified misconduct without imposing extraordinary costs on legitimate students and institutions.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Immigration enforcement should be effective, proportionate, and supported by evidence. It should not undermine American higher education, increase financial burdens on domestic students, or weaken the nation's economic and technological leadership.
comments.reason: Submits comment in opposition to the proposed OPT fees, citing disproportionate and harmful economic impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gabrielle Brihn
comments.commentText:
I, Gabrielle Brihn, strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional
Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations in
document ICEB-2026-0100. I urge DHS to remove this fee structure and preserve access to
integral, legitimate, degree-related practical training for students on F-1 visas.
The proposed rule claims to “deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the level of
oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its students” in Section IV.C. It is
incredibly unclear how a $70,000-100,000+ financial barrier per individual promotes hiring
legitimacy and prevents the OPT-related fraud it claims to address. Instead, the proposed fee
clearly serves as a de facto ban on most, if not all, OPT and legitimate degree-related
practice under the shallow guise of ‘protecting United States workers.’
I have deep concerns with the impact of the proposed fee structure on the ability of students on
F-1 visas to study and engage in fully legitimate degree-training in the United States. The
document is primarily concerned with mitigating ‘false employers,’ fraud, and ‘shell companies’
related to temporary employment through OPT (Section IV.A). An excessive, pre-application
demonstration of wealth borne by academic institutions fundamentally does not contribute or aid
in the purported goal of increased oversight and assessment of the legitimacy of potential
employers.
The document claims that the “fees which would ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1
students participate in OPT.” First, an OPT recommendation from an SEVP certified school has
nothing to do with qualification. Job-seeking students, in addition to overcoming paperwork,
recommendation, and field-of-study hurdles, must still go through the application process
post-recommendation. Further, the ability to bear a $70,000+ fee before acquiring a job has
no logical or practical connectivity to the legitimacy of the job opportunity, the employer,
the role the job plays in the student’s degree-related training, or the student’s aptitude for a
certain job. All it demonstrates is the ability of the school, student, or potential employer to bear
a massive financial burden.
Given the inability of many institutions and individual students to meet such an excessive
demand, particularly with no continued job guarantee after, what the proposed rule instead
serves as is a functional ban on most OPT pursuits, regardless of ‘legitimacy.’ This
functional ban threatens the opportunity for international students who are studying and training
in the United States to gain important degree-related practice, apply their academic training into
valuable work within the United States, and even to pursue higher education post-baccalaureate.
No person should have to pay $70,000+ to apply for a job. Once again, given the jarring
impact of its implementation on F-1 students, their academic institutions, and its inability
to achieve the goals it claims to advance, I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure in
document ICEB-2026-0100 (Federal Register No. 2026-20660) and urge DHS to withdraw
the rule.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee structure and urges DHS to remove it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jonathon Henderson
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise its proposed OPT fee rule. The proposed fee structure would impose extraordinary financial burdens on universities, employers, and international students while failing to demonstrate that the benefits justify the costs.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies must provide a rational explanation of a rule's costs and benefits, consider significant reliance interests, evaluate risks, and meaningfully assess less burdensome alternatives. The proposed rule does not appear to satisfy these requirements.

First, DHS substantially understates the degree to which students, universities, employers, and local economies rely on Optional Practical Training (OPT). OPT has served as a bridge between U.S. higher education and the workforce for decades. Many international students choose to study in the United States in part because of the opportunity to gain practical training after graduation. Evidence submitted by researchers and higher education organizations suggests that fees of the magnitude proposed would dramatically reduce participation in OPT and STEM OPT, leading many students to pursue education in competing countries rather than in the United States.

DHS also fails to adequately account for the broader economic consequences of reducing OPT participation. International students contribute billions of dollars annually in tuition, housing, consumer spending, and research activity. Their participation supports jobs, strengthens university budgets, and helps meet workforce needs in critical sectors such as engineering, computer science, health care, and research. The NPRM does not sufficiently evaluate the impact that reduced OPT participation would have on universities, local businesses, research programs, startups, and regional economies.

In addition, DHS does not adequately consider OPT's role as a pathway to longer-term lawful employment. Many graduates use OPT to transition to H-1B status or other employment-based immigration pathways. Without OPT, many highly skilled graduates would have no practical means of remaining in the United States long enough to access those opportunities. The NPRM does not fully analyze the resulting loss of talent to competing nations.

The proposed fee structure also creates significant practical and compliance challenges. Universities would be expected to administer extraordinarily large payments and related processes despite lacking clear guidance on funding, approvals, accounting, refunds, and compliance controls. DHS does not adequately quantify these administrative burdens.

Most importantly, DHS has not demonstrated that it seriously considered less burdensome alternatives. If the agency's objectives are preventing fraud and protecting American workers, there are numerous targeted approaches that could achieve those goals without imposing blanket fees of $70,000 for OPT and $30,000 for STEM OPT extensions. Examples include expanded employer eligibility requirements, broader use of E-Verify, targeted enforcement against high-risk employers, increased reporting requirements, risk-based oversight of institutions, enhanced site visits, and other compliance measures already used in the STEM OPT program. The NPRM does not sufficiently explain why these alternatives were rejected.

The rule may also create unintended consequences that DHS did not fully evaluate. It could reduce access based on wealth rather than merit, disadvantage small businesses and startups relative to large corporations, concentrate talent among a limited number of employers, and potentially increase incentives for unauthorized employment among graduates who can no longer access practical training opportunities.

For these reasons, DHS should reconsider the proposal, conduct a more thorough analysis of its costs and economic impacts, meaningfully evaluate less burdensome alternatives, and provide a more complete explanation of how the proposed fees would achieve the agency's stated objectives.

Thank you for considering these comments.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed OPT fee rule.

The OPT work authorization program has been particularly vital in STEM area -- fields in which the US does not produce enough domestic graduates qualified for the growing range of professional roles needed (e.g., in computer science, AI development, data analytics, scientific research, etc.) -- and so raising these OPT fees will only harm our own economy and our wider society. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure. My concern is that it would weaken the U.S. economy by discouraging legitimate practical training and driving U.S.-educated talent and economic activity elsewhere.

Under section V.A, schools would have to pay before recommending eligible students for OPT. Section IV.C acknowledges that schools may pass the burden to students or employers. Changing who submits the payment does not remove its economic cost. Institutions could stop recommending qualified graduates, while students and employers with fewer resources could lose access to otherwise lawful training. Ability to pay is not a reliable measure of educational value, professional merit, or compliance.

The economic effects extend beyond the parties paying the fee. Discouraging international students from choosing U.S. universities could reduce tuition revenue and spending in local communities. Preventing U.S.-trained graduates from applying their skills here could also reduce research capacity, business formation, and future tax revenue. Some graduates and the work they perform could move abroad rather than create opportunities for American workers. These are risks DHS should evaluate, not assume away.

The American Physical Society's October 19, 2026 comment warns that the proposal would damage the scientific talent pipeline and U.S. competitiveness. Its concerns about retaining U.S.-trained researchers deserve a substantive response. See https://www.aps.org/about/news/2026/10/comment-proposed-changes-optional-practical-training .

In section VII.A, DHS uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity cost of lost participation and assumes parties could collectively share costs when OPT's value exceeds the fee. That assumption is inadequate. Benefits such as innovation, local spending, and future tax revenue can accrue to people who cannot coordinate to finance an individual student's fee. A school's inability to pay does not establish that the training lacks value to the United States. DHS should assess these wider effects and explain the evidence supporting its assumptions before proceeding.

Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are legitimate goals. But a large blanket fee also burdens compliant schools, students, and employers. DHS should compare targeted employer verification, compliance reviews, and enforcement against demonstrated misconduct with this approach, including their effects on legitimate training and U.S. workers. Lower participation alone should not be treated as proof that fraud has fallen.

Section V.C proposes implementation 60 days after a final rule is published. Students and institutions may have made long-term educational and financial decisions under the existing framework. Calling the rule prospective does not eliminate those reliance concerns.

Please withdraw the proposed fees. Any alternative should address documented misconduct without pricing legitimate practical training out of reach, and should include a transparent economic analysis and meaningful protection for existing educational commitments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Brescia University
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
Optional Practical Training Fees

These comments are on behalf of Brescia University and its Board of Trustees in Owensboro, Kentucky.

The proposed $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training would dramatically reduce participation in the program and reduce the number of qualified international students from attending our University.  Although DHS characterizes the proposal as a fee, the reality is that, for our international students, it functions as a prohibition.  Few students can afford such a fee after already investing tens of thousands of dollars in a U.S. education, and few employers will be willing to absorb it for them.  The result is predictable.  Students who would otherwise choose to study in the United States will choose another country.  During a time when demographic challenges are already causing enrollment issues for American colleges and universities, this regulation would compound the problem.

The Department's proposal is built around two main arguments: combating fraud and protecting American workers.  Both are legitimate policy goals.  The problem is that the proposed fee does not appear reasonably connected to either objective, and seems to be, on its face, arbitrary as a result.
The proposed rule identifies several instances of fraud and abuse of the OPT system.  The concerns of DHS are real.  If stopping fraud is the goal, then fraud, and fraud alone, should be the target.  Strict employer verifications, additional reporting, increased site visits, and laser-focused enforcement actions all directly combat fraud.  A $70,000 fee does not.

Instead, the fee applies equally to the student working for a legitimate employer and the student participating in a fraudulent arrangement.  It imposes the same burden on institutions that diligently comply with federal requirements as it does on institutions that do not.  Simply put, this regulation does not distinguish between bad actors and the overwhelming majority of students and universities who follow the rules.

At Brescia University, we see firsthand the value international students bring to our campus community.  They enrich classroom discussion, broaden perspectives, and contribute to the educational experience of domestic and international students alike.  They also make substantial financial investments in an American education, and without burdening our federal financial aid system.  For many students, the opportunity to gain practical experience through OPT is not a secondary benefit-- it is part of the reason they choose the United States in the first place.

The practical consequences of this regulation are clear.  A substantial reduction in international enrollment would affect colleges and universities across the country, particularly smaller private institutions like Brescia.  It would also affect communities that benefit economically from international students as they spend their money locally.  Most importantly, it would make the United States less competitive in attracting talented students from around the world.

The answer to fraud cannot be a fee so high that it effectively eliminates participation by legitimate students.  If DHS believes additional resources are necessary to strengthen oversight of OPT, then the Department should pursue solutions that are targeted toward bad actors and proportionate to the risks identified.

For these reasons, Brescia University respectfully urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and consider alternative approaches that strengthen program integrity without undermining the ability of international students to participate in practical training opportunities.

Sincerely,

Madison C. Silvert,
President
comments.reason: Argues the proposed OPT fee functions as a prohibition and will dramatically reduce participation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I want to examine where the money from this proposal would actually go, because the answer exposes what the fee really is. Under the proposed rule, universities would pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one — and the proceeds would be deposited into the general Treasury, not into the accounts that fund the Student and Exchange Visitor Program or the adjudication of employment authorization applications. A fee that does not fund the service it is attached to is not a user fee. It is a revenue measure.

That matters because of the authority DHS claims. The Immigration and Nationality Act lets the executive set fees tied to the cost of providing immigration benefits — the reason the Form I-765 fee sits around $470 to $520, and the reason the I-901 SEVIS fee exists to fund SEVP operations. What the statute does not grant is a general power to raise revenue by charging regulated parties whatever the market will bear. DHS's own framing concedes the point: the agency says the fee will deter schools from recommending OPT and acknowledges some will stop altogether. A charge whose stated purpose is to suppress participation, priced at roughly 140 times the cost of adjudicating the underlying application, cannot be described as cost recovery with a straight face.

The recent history of the $100,000 H-1B fee shows where this argument leads. Federal courts blocked that fee — in California, for bypassing required rulemaking and acting without statutory authority; in Massachusetts, for usurping Congress's power to tax. This proposal repeats the same error in a new form: a levy on universities, calibrated to destroy a program Congress created, justified by an authority Congress never granted, with the proceeds flowing to the general Treasury rather than to any program the fee supposedly supports.

If Congress wants to tax universities, tax international education, or end OPT, it can do so through legislation, in the open, with a vote. What the executive cannot do is use fee-setting authority as a substitute for that vote. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: Challenges the legality and justification of the proposed OPT fees as a revenue measure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed additional fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider their potential consequences for American higher education, economic competitiveness, and international educational exchange.

Having worked in American higher education for over 25 years, particularly in arts and design education, I have witnessed the extraordinary contributions international students make to our institutions, communities, and economy. Policies that make the United States a less attractive destination for talented students risk undermining benefits that extend far beyond individual colleges and universities.

International students are a significant economic asset to the United States. According to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the American economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–25 academic year. These benefits extend well beyond tuition revenue, supporting housing, transportation, restaurants, retail, and other businesses in communities nationwide.

International graduates also contribute to American innovation and economic growth. In creative disciplines, graduates bring specialized skills to industries including advertising, animation, film, digital media, architecture, design, and technology. OPT provides a critical bridge between academic study and professional experience, allowing graduates to apply their education while contributing to American employers and creative industries.

The value of international students cannot be measured solely in dollars. Their presence fundamentally enriches the education of American students.

In arts and design education, international students introduce different visual traditions, cultural histories, artistic practices, and approaches to problem-solving. An American student collaborating with peers from South Korea, India, Brazil, or China encounters perspectives that may challenge assumptions about communication, identity, aesthetics, and the social responsibilities of creative work.

These exchanges occur daily in classrooms, studios, critiques, collaborative projects, and informal conversations. They help American students develop cultural literacy, empathy, adaptability, and the ability to work across differences. Such skills are increasingly essential in a global economy.

International students also help American institutions prepare graduates to work with diverse communities and international partners. These educational benefits extend to domestic students who may never have the opportunity to study abroad.

OPT is an important component of the value proposition of American higher education. Students choosing where to pursue an education consider not only academic quality but also whether they will have meaningful opportunities to apply their knowledge professionally.

The Institute of International Education reported that nearly 1.18 million international students studied or participated in OPT in the United States during 2024–25, including approximately 294,000 on OPT. These students represent an extraordinary pool of global talent that American institutions and employers have helped educate and develop.

Additional fees imposed on OPT participation could discourage talented students from choosing American institutions, particularly those from less affluent backgrounds. They may also disproportionately affect graduates entering creative fields, nonprofit organizations, and smaller businesses, where early-career compensation is often modest.

It is especially important to consider the cumulative financial burden of tuition, living expenses, visa costs, existing application fees, and other requirements. An additional fee may seem manageable on its own, but it becomes a meaningful barrier when added to these existing expenses.

I recognize the Department's responsibility to administer immigration programs effectively and ensure appropriate oversight. However, additional financial barriers should be supported by a clear demonstration of necessity, proportionality, and expected benefits.

I urge DHS to withdraw or substantially reconsider the proposed OPT fees, assess their cumulative financial impact, consider alternatives that do not discourage international enrollment, and preserve accessible opportunities for graduates to gain practical professional experience.

The United States benefits when talented students from around the world choose to study here, collaborate with American classmates, contribute to our communities, and participate in our economy. Maintaining that advantage is in the national interest.

Sources: NAFSA, International Student Economic Value, 2024–25 (nafsa.org/economicvalue); Institute of International Education, Open Doors 2025 (opendoorsdata.org).
comments.reason: Respectfully opposes the proposed additional OPT fees and urges DHS to reconsider.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations in document ICEB-2026-0100. I urge DHS to remove this fee structure and preserve access to integral, legitimate, degree-related practical training for students on F-1 visas.

The proposed rule claims to “deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its students” in Section IV.C. It is incredibly unclear how a $70,000-100,000+ financial barrier per individual promotes hiring legitimacy and prevents the OPT-related fraud it claims to address. Instead, the proposed fee clearly serves as a de facto ban on most, if not all, OPT and legitimate degree-related practice under the shallow guise of ‘protecting United States workers.’ 

I have deep concerns with the impact of the proposed fee structure on the ability of students on F-1 visas to study and engage in fully legitimate degree-training in the United States. The document is primarily concerned with mitigating ‘false employers,’ fraud, and ‘shell companies’ related to temporary employment through OPT (Section IV.A). An excessive, pre-application demonstration of wealth borne by academic institutions fundamentally does not contribute or aid in the purported goal of increased oversight and assessment of the legitimacy of potential employers.

The document claims that the “fees [which] would ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate in OPT.” First, an OPT recommendation from an SEVP certified school has nothing to do with qualification. Job-seeking students, in addition to overcoming paperwork, recommendation, and field-of-study hurdles, must still go through the application process post-recommendation. Further, the ability to bear a $70,000+ fee before acquiring a job has no logical or practical connectivity to the legitimacy of the job opportunity, the employer, the role the job plays in the student’s degree-related training, or the student’s aptitude for a certain job. All it demonstrates is the ability of the school, student, or potential employer to bear a massive financial burden.

Given the inability of many institutions and individual students to meet such an excessive demand, particularly with no continued job guarantee after, what the proposed rule instead serves as is a functional ban on most OPT pursuits, regardless of ‘legitimacy.’ This functional ban threatens the opportunity for international students who are studying and training in the United States to gain important degree-related practice, apply their academic training into valuable work within the United States, and even to pursue higher education post-baccalaureate. No person should have to pay $70,000+ to apply for a job. Once again, given the jarring impact of its implementation on F-1 students, their academic institutions, and its inability to achieve the goals it claims to advance, I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure in document ICEB-2026-0100 (Federal Register No. 2026-20660) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider applying the proposed $70,000 OPT fee uniformly to international students. I understand the goal of preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the OPT program, but a fee of this size could also prevent many legitimate and highly trained students from using OPT, particularly PhD graduates who have spent many years studying and conducting research in the United States.

PhD students are in a different situation from students completing shorter academic programs. A PhD commonly requires five or six years of research and training. During that time, doctoral students may publish research papers, develop new technologies, contribute to patents, work on federally or industry-funded projects, and build expertise in areas that are important to the U.S. economy and technological competitiveness. When these students graduate, they are finally at the point where they can take the knowledge and skills developed at U.S. universities and apply them in U.S. industry, research laboratories, and academia.

The proposed fee could interrupt that transition. Although the rule requires the university to pay the $70,000 fee, such a large cost must ultimately be funded somehow. Some universities may not have the resources to pay $70,000 for each graduating international student, particularly public universities and institutions with large international graduate populations. DHS itself recognizes in the proposed rule that institutions may obtain funding from students, employers, or other entities, and that some institutions may be unable or may choose not to pay the fee.

For a graduating PhD student, this could mean that access to OPT depends not on the student's qualifications, research record, or legitimate employment opportunity, but on whether the university, student, or prospective employer can provide tens of thousands of dollars simply for the OPT recommendation. This would place a particularly heavy burden on graduates entering universities, research laboratories, startups, and other organizations that may not have the resources to absorb such a cost.

There is also a broader question of whether this outcome serves the long-term interests of the United States. By the time an international PhD student graduates, the student may have spent five or six years being trained at a U.S. university and contributing to research conducted in the United States. If OPT becomes financially inaccessible, some of these graduates may instead continue their careers in other countries. In that case, the United States would educate and train researchers for many years but lose some of the benefit of their expertise just when they are ready to enter the workforce.

Long-term international students can also contribute to the U.S. tax base. Under IRS rules, F-1 students are generally treated as nonresident aliens for purposes of the substantial presence test during their first five calendar years. After that period, many become resident aliens for tax purposes if they meet the substantial presence test and generally become subject to Social Security and Medicare taxes on their employment, subject to applicable exemptions. This is especially relevant to PhD students because their programs often extend beyond five years.

I encourage DHS to distinguish between fraudulent or abusive use of OPT and legitimate graduates who have completed substantial academic and research programs in the United States. If additional oversight of OPT is necessary, it should target the sources of fraud rather than create a financial barrier so large that legitimate students and universities may be unable to participate.

At a minimum, I ask DHS to consider alternatives to a uniform $70,000 fee, including substantially lower fees, exemptions or reduced fees for graduates of advanced-degree programs, and approaches that focus additional costs and scrutiny on cases presenting identifiable indicators of fraud or abuse.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to reconsider the fee, arguing it would prevent legitimate students from using OPT.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international Ph.D. student in Chemical and Petroleum Engineering at the University of Kansas, a public research university. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and the $30,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation. While I recognize the Department of Homeland Security’s responsibility to prevent fraud, ensure program integrity, and protect American workers, I believe these proposed fees are disproportionately high and could undermine the educational, scientific, and economic benefits that international students contribute to the United States.

As a doctoral researcher, I work on developing technologies for converting carbon dioxide into valuable chemicals, including methanol. This research supports efforts toward sustainable chemical production, energy innovation, and environmental protection. My Ph.D. training combines advanced coursework with laboratory research, experimental design, data analysis, and the development of specialized engineering skills relevant to scientific research and industry.

OPT provides an essential bridge between academic education and professional practice. It allows international graduates to apply their knowledge in real-world settings, gain industry experience, contribute to research and development, and collaborate with professionals addressing important scientific and engineering challenges. For students in specialized STEM fields, this opportunity can be critical to translating years of rigorous academic preparation into practical contributions.

The proposed fees could create substantial financial barriers to these opportunities. Although schools would be required to pay the fees before recommending OPT and could collect the funds from employers, students, or other sources, the financial burden would remain. Employers may be unwilling or unable to absorb such extraordinary costs, particularly small businesses, startups, and research organizations with limited budgets. As a result, qualified international graduates could face fewer employment opportunities, regardless of their skills, qualifications, or potential contributions.

As an F-1 student, I have invested significant time, effort, and resources in pursuing advanced education in the United States. A fee of this magnitude could jeopardize my ability to access practical training opportunities after graduation, even after years of academic and research preparation. It could also discourage talented international students from pursuing advanced degrees at American universities, potentially weakening the pipeline of highly trained scientists and engineers who contribute to U.S. innovation and competitiveness.

I question whether fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are a proportionate or necessary means of addressing fraud and protecting American workers. These are legitimate objectives, but the Department should provide clear evidence explaining how the proposed amounts were determined and how they would effectively address the identified problems. More targeted fraud detection, stronger compliance measures, and enforcement against demonstrated violations could protect program integrity without imposing excessive financial barriers on legitimate students, universities, and employers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees or substantially revise the rule to establish a reasonable, evidence-based fee structure. Any final rule should consider its potential effects on international students, public universities, employers, STEM workforce development, and scientific research. The Department should also evaluate whether these fees could discourage employers from hiring qualified graduates and reduce the United States’ ability to attract talented researchers and engineers.

International students who pursue advanced degrees in the United States contribute to university research, technological development, and the preparation of a skilled workforce. OPT helps connect this educational investment to practical experience that can benefit American employers, research institutions, and the broader economy. Excessive fees could prevent these benefits from being realized.

I support a fair, secure, and accountable immigration system. However, I believe the proposed OPT fees risk imposing costs that are disproportionate to their intended purpose and could undermine research, innovation, and workforce development. I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and adopt a balanced approach that protects program integrity while preserving reasonable opportunities for F-1 students to apply their education and contribute to the United States.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter respectfully opposes the proposed fees, believing they are disproportionately high.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nathan Hawkins
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

As the Principal Designated School Official (PDSO) of Indiana Wesleyan University (IWU), I respectfully submit this public comment regarding DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100-0001. I am writing in opposition to the fees for Optional Practical Training as outlined in the proposed Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule.

I have the honor of serving more than 7,000 individuals actively connected to IWU through student visas or post-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT). These students are essential not only to IWU’s mission and global impact but also to Indiana’s economic vitality and American national competitiveness.

According to DHS’ own financial analysis in Tables 15 & 17, institutions would be forced to pass these proposed fees on to students or refuse OPT participation. If IWU were to pass on the proposed $70,000 fee to students, the cost increase would be 38% of the stated cost of a 4-year undergraduate degree and between 250% and 350% of the cost for common majors among our existing international students. The 4-year undergraduate degree increase does not reflect any typical academic or financial need support that is regularly granted to all students.
 
The proposed rule contends this fee would combat fraudulent use of the existing OPT work authorization benefit. Instead of combatting fraud, the exorbitant cost of this fee would essentially close the door to most qualified and law-abiding prospective students seeking admission to institutions in the United States. The proposed rule would favor only those with significant financial means or those connected with fraudulent employers willing to cover the costs of maintaining operations.

United States agencies have consistently held that it is not the DSO’s role to investigate or be responsible for vetting employers. The proposal now places the DSO in the position to collect and/or pay a significant fee to recommend a student for any practical training opportunity. This raises new concerns regarding the DSO’s role and liability regarding these recommendations. Similarly, in our institutional role as a DSO, we aim to serve all international students by providing clear guidance on US compliance expectations. The expectation in the proposal to recommend only “the most promising students” also falls outside the traditional scope of a DSO and would, in practice, likely be based solely on students' ability to cover the fee.


As a PDSO, I would support measures and tools to oversee OPT students, ensuring that employment complies with existing regulations and that known fraudulent activity is identified and eliminated. However, the proposal provides no calculation of the costs associated with existing or planned OPT investigations to justify the exorbitant proposed fee. No clear agency cost or service has been cited in the justification. In fact, the proposal notes on page 33 that the fee would not even be retained by ICE but deposited into the Treasury of the United States, where it would provide no direct benefit to OPT oversight or enforcement.

I support updates to the management of OPT through improved interagency cooperation and DHS cooperation with institutional sponsors of international students. However, this proposed rule does not address DHS’ stated concerns with the OPT program. Rather, the proposal decreases higher education enrollment and affordability, thereby reducing US economic productivity. I ask that DHS please withdraw this proposal and engage in meaningful discussions to properly regulate OPT moving forward.

Nathan Hawkins
comments.reason: As a PDSO, the commenter writes in direct opposition to the proposed OPT fees.

Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. I see the importance of practical training in helping students apply their education and prepare for careers in their fields. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier for students who have maintained their status and met the requirements to participate. Allowing schools to obtain funds from students or employers does not resolve the underlying problem of affordability. Many international students already bear substantial tuition and living expenses, including nonresident tuition charges where applicable. They and their families may spend years saving and making financial sacrifices to pursue a U.S. education. An additional $70,000 payment before a student can access practical training would place that opportunity beyond the reach of many otherwise eligible students. The proposed fee is also disproportionate to graduates’ earnings. The $70,000 initial fee would exceed that annual amount by more than $20,000, before taxes or living expenses. If an employer were asked to provide the funding, it could face an additional upfront cost approaching or exceeding a graduate’s annual salary, on top of wages, benefits, and other employment expenses. This would create a substantial financial disincentive to hiring an otherwise qualified graduate, particularly for smaller employers. A student could meet every eligibility requirement and have a legitimate training opportunity directly related to their degree yet still be unable to participate because neither the student, the institution, nor the employer could realistically fund the fee. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. Based on my professional experience, these amounts would make legitimate practical training inaccessible to almost all students and create significant obstacles for institutions and employers seeking to support them. The ability to participate in OPT should depend on meeting the program’s requirements, and an extraordinary financial barrier would prevent otherwise eligible students from doing so. Thank you for considering my comment.

This rule, its proposed method of implementation and its supposed intention are all simply preposterous. It is clear this is simply another attack on higher education, hitting institutions where it hurts - their income streams. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael Mwirichia
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international graduate of the University of Kansas, where I earned my Master of Science in Business Analytics in 2025, and I am currently participating in the 24-month STEM Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee because they would create significant financial barriers for international graduates, American employers, and institutions of higher education.

I recognize and respect DHS’s responsibility to protect American workers, prevent fraud, and maintain the integrity of immigration programs. However, I believe these proposed fees would disproportionately affect law-abiding students and employers without directly addressing the underlying causes of program abuse.

My Contributions to American Businesses

I came to the United States to obtain a world-class education, develop specialized analytical skills, and contribute meaningfully to the American economy.

Since completing my graduate studies, I have applied my education in manufacturing, business development, sales operations, and organizational performance. My responsibilities have included improving business processes, developing analytical reporting systems, supporting operational decision-making, and helping American organizations become more efficient.

During my experience in manufacturing, I developed a training and performance measurement model that contributed to a 15% improvement in safety and operational efficiency within approximately three months. The model continued to be used after my internship ended. This demonstrates how international graduates can translate American education into measurable benefits for American businesses and workers.

Beyond my professional contributions, I participate in the American economy through employment, taxes, housing, and everyday spending.

The Financial Consequences of the Proposed Fees

A $70,000 fee represents an extraordinary financial burden for recent graduates who have already invested substantial resources in American higher education. For many, this amount could exceed their annual earnings.

Although the proposal allows schools to recover fees from students or employers, this does not eliminate the financial burden. Smaller businesses may be unable to absorb these costs, potentially limiting employment opportunities for qualified graduates.

The result could be a system in which access to practical training depends more on financial resources than academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration requirements.

Had these fees existed when I was considering graduate education, they would have significantly influenced my decision to study in the United 
My master’s degree provided a strong foundation in analytics, data-driven decision-making, and business strategy. However, OPT has allowed me to apply these skills to real business challenges, collaborate with American professionals, and contribute to organizational improvement.

Practical training is an essential complement to classroom education. Without it, international graduates may struggle to fully realize the professional value of their American degrees.

Restricting this opportunity through exceptionally high fees could also discourage talented international students from choosing American universities, affecting institutions, local economies, and employers.

Protecting American Workers Through Targeted Enforcement

I support measures that prevent fraud, protect American workers, and ensure that OPT participants comply with immigration regulations.

However, I respectfully encourage DHS to consider more targeted alternatives, including stronger employer verification, improved compliance monitoring, enhanced institutional oversight, and enforcement against documented violations.

These measures could protect program integrity without imposing substantial financial barriers on legitimate students and employers.

In conclusion

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee structure and evaluate alternatives that protect American workers while preserving access to legitimate practical training.

My experience demonstrates how international education and practical training can produce measurable benefits for American businesses. I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute my skills to the United States, and I believe future international graduates should have a reasonable opportunity to do the same.

Protecting American workers, preventing immigration fraud, and maintaining access to practical training should not be mutually exclusive goals.

Thank you for considering my comment.
Respectfully,

Michael 
University of Kansas, MS Business Analytics, Class of 2025
Current STEM OPT Participant
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees because they create significant financial barriers for graduates and employers.

I am writing to express my strong OPPOSITION to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule that seeks to impose exorbitant fees on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.

This proposed fee structure represents an unprecedented financial barrier that would effectively dismantle the OPT program and severely damage the United States' standing as a global hub for education and innovation.
First, this proposal places an intolerable and unrealistic financial burden on international students and their families. International students already pay substantial out-of-state tuition and contribute billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and local communities. Forcing students or their potential employers to pay tens of thousands of dollars just for the opportunity to gain short-term, entry-level work experience is both unjust and economically non-viable.

Second, the policy will trigger a severe "brain drain" and harm American businesses. OPT is a crucial mechanism that allows U.S. employers, especially in critical STEM fields, to recruit and retain high-skilled global talent. By effectively blocking international graduates from entering the U.S. workforce, this rule will lead to immediate labor shortages in innovation-driven industries, hindering American competitiveness and economic growth.

Third, this rule will devastate the U.S. higher education sector. The ability to gain practical experience through OPT is one of the primary reasons top-tier international students choose to study in the United States. If implemented, this extreme cost will drive talented individuals to pursue their education and careers in countries with more welcoming policies, such as Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia. U.S. universities will face declining enrollments, resulting in severe financial strain and diminished academic resources for all students.

The implementation of these fees is short-sighted and self-defeating. Instead of strengthening the U.S. economy, it penalizes legitimate students who have respected immigration laws and chosen to invest in America. I urgently request that DHS withdraw this harmful proposal and maintain accessible, reasonable fee structures for the OPT program.

Sincerely,

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2)

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

The stated goal is to protect American workers, but I don't see how making it harder for international graduates to work legally automatically creates more jobs for Americans.

From a small business perspective, hiring is not a simple matter of replacing one candidate with another. Employers need specific skills, and sometimes a position stays open because the right candidate is difficult to find.

If these fees discourage universities from supporting OPT, businesses could lose access to qualified graduates who have already studied and trained in the United States. Some employers may delay projects or leave positions unfilled. That doesn't necessarily help American workers either.

I also question why the same enormous fees would apply regardless of the student's field, the employer's history, or the actual risk of fraud.

If DHS believes OPT is being abused, it should investigate abusive employers and fraudulent arrangements. Charging legitimate participants tens of thousands of dollars does not directly address those problems.

Before adopting these provisions, DHS should provide credible evidence that the proposed fees will improve employment opportunities for American workers rather than simply reduce participation in OPT.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee provisions in 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they make it harder to work legally without addressing fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(3) — 60-Day Transition Period

I want to raise a concern about something that seems to be overlooked in this proposal: students who are already halfway through their education.

Imagine spending three or four years working toward a degree in the United States, paying tuition and living expenses, only to find out shortly before graduation that the practical training opportunity you planned around may now depend on your university paying $70,000.

How is a 60-day transition period supposed to help someone in that situation?

Students cannot simply undo years of financial commitments. They cannot easily transfer to another country, change their degree, or recover the money they have already spent.

I understand that immigration policies can change. But there is a difference between changing the rules for future applicants and imposing a massive financial obstacle on people who made decisions under the existing system.

My objection is specifically to the transition provision in proposed 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(3), together with the initial fee under § 214.13(i)(1).

At a minimum, DHS should exempt students who were already enrolled in eligible programs before the final rule takes effect. A 60-day window is not meaningful protection for a decision that takes years to complete.

Fair policy should recognize reasonable reliance on existing rules.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the fee provisions and the transition period, arguing they impose massive obstacles on current students.

comments.commentText:

I am submitting this comment as an F-1 international student pursuing higher education in the United States, with concerns about how the proposed OPT rule could affect international students, the U.S. economy, and the skilled workforce.

I respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security consider the following potential consequences:

Negative impact on international students: International students invest significant time, money, and effort in U.S. education. Restricting OPT could prevent graduates from gaining practical experience and create financial and career difficulties.

Civil engineering workforce shortages:
 
Civil engineering is essential for maintaining bridges, roads, transportation systems, water infrastructure, and buildings. Restricting OPT could reduce the pool of qualified graduates available to support these critical projects.

Reduced productivity for U.S. employers:

Economic losses for the United States: International students contribute through tuition, living expenses, employment, taxes, and innovation. Losing skilled graduates could reduce these economic benefits.

Classroom education provides theoretical knowledge, while OPT helps eligible graduates apply that knowledge in real-world settings. Without practical training, students may miss essential professional experience.

I encourage the Department to preserve reasonable OPT opportunities for eligible international graduates so they can apply their education, develop professional skills, and contribute to the United States.

Thank you for considering my comments.
