comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on ICEB-2026-0100 — 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii) and § 214.13(i)(1)–(2)

I have a basic question about this proposal: What exactly does a $70,000 payment prove?

It doesn't prove that a student has a legitimate job. It doesn't prove that an employer follows the law. And it certainly doesn't prove that someone won't commit fraud.

Yet under the proposed changes to 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and (iii), payment becomes a condition for moving forward with OPT recommendations and employment authorization.

That seems like the wrong approach.

If the problem is fake employment, investigate the employers. If the problem is students working outside their authorized field, improve compliance checks. If certain schools repeatedly violate reporting requirements, audit those schools.

But why should a university supporting a legitimate engineering graduate face the same enormous fee as an institution associated with questionable employment arrangements?

The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) don't appear to distinguish between low-risk and high-risk cases.

I am also concerned that these fees could discourage universities from recommending perfectly qualified students while doing little to stop well-funded bad actors.

I support immigration enforcement. I support protecting American jobs. But enforcement should focus on evidence of wrongdoing, not the ability to pay.

I ask DHS to withdraw these provisions and explain why more targeted compliance measures would not achieve the same objectives at a substantially lower cost.

Making something expensive is not the same as making it secure.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the fee provisions, arguing enforcement should focus on wrongdoing rather than ability to pay.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an administrator at a US university in the southeast US, which has had over 100 students on OPT annually, for the past 5 years.
The purpose of the proposed rule is stated as combating fraud, strengthening the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting U.S. workers.
The true purpose seems to be to discourage international students from attending US universities, making it prohibitively expensive for all but the wealthiest students to participate in OPT, and obtain practical training experience related to their degree. 
In August 2026, SEVP released broadcast messages to schools hosting international students in F-1 status, stipulating that Curricular Practical Training (CPT) was limited to academic programs where the practical training “is required for all students participating in that curriculum, regardless of citizenship.” This interpretation marked a departure from the common practice, not previously challenged by government guidance, that many schools had of permitting students to do CPT if enrolled in a related course. Because most US universities do not require practical training or internships for most of their academic programs and degrees, the result has been a chilling effect of CPT around the country, where practical training and internship options for currently enrolled international students have been drastically reduced.
With the reduction of CPT availability, OPT is the primary alternative for students and recent graduates to gain practical experience in the US related to their degree. OPT differs from CPT, and many employer sponsored work authorizations such as H-1B and TN, in that it does not tie students to a specific employer, but instead allows them to dabble, participating in start-ups, switching seamlessly from employer to employer, and even being self-employed, provided they do practical training related to their degree. OPT works for students from a broad range of fields, from those with a music degree, who might be employed by numerous gigs, to those from business fields, who might be employed through a more traditional employer, to those in computer science, who might create and participate in start-ups. It allows students to develop practical skills that they cannot obtain in an academic setting. 
The proposed $70000 fee is set to apply to a student’s first OPT application with a school, with an additional $30000 charged for subsequent OPT applications. For students not eligible for CPT, the primary way to gain practical experience in the US is to apply for pre-completion or post-completion OPT. This fee will make OPT impossible for most students; common expected funding sources are the personal funds of a student and their family, their employer, or the school itself.
US News and World Report reports that average college tuition and fees for ranked colleges in 2026-2027 was $46973 for private institutions, and $26034 for public out of state schools. Universities do not have the funding to pay this fee; in many cases, such as 1 year graduate degrees, or 4 year undergraduate degrees at public institutions, the fee exceeds the tuition charged to students, other university costs notwithstanding.  
This fee is a monumental amount for an employer to cover. There may be a few lucky students who employers recruit and cover this fee, but most companies will not want to pay this for an intern or a new, untested, college graduate, particularly one who has been prohibited from developing practical skills through internships previously, due to these regulatory limitations.
In July 2022, the National Foundation for American Policy released a policy brief stated that immigrants have started more than half (55%) of US start up companies valued at $1 billion or more. The brief also stated that “one-quarter (143 of 582, or 25%) of billion-dollar startup companies in the U.S. have a founder who first came to America as an international student.”
The Center for Security and Emerging Technology released an October 2020 Data Brief that estimated that in 2019, in Forbes’s list of the “most promising” U.S.-based AI startups, an estimated 66% had one or more immigrant founder, and of these, an estimated 72% first came to the US using a student visa.
Programs like OPT give international students flexibility and options to gain practical experience in the US, and exercise creativity, like founding companies, or participating in start-ups, which often would not have enough funding to pay this fee.
Rather than preserve immigration integrity, and protecting US workers, this fee seems designed to stifle US innovation, preventing talented international graduates from joining the US workforce, particularly not in unstable, creative companies like start-ups. A logical outcome of this fee may be that talented recent international graduates go to other countries to create successful, innovative companies. It is unclear how this reduction of talent and innovation will benefit the US.
comments.reason: The commenter criticizes the true purpose of the rule as making OPT prohibitively expensive and discouraging students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing this comment as a Professor of Chemistry at a major R1 university in the midwest to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for initial F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT) applications and $30,000 for subsequent applications.

As structured, these unprecedented fees will create an insurmountable financial barrier for American universities, scientific research institutions, and recent international graduates. Imposing a $70,000 fee per applicant will severely disrupt the U.S. higher education system, stifle academic research, and systematically filter out world-class talent trained at American institutions.

Here is a summary of my key concerns regarding the proposed rule: 

1. Prohibitive financial burden on higher education institutions
A $70,000 upfront fee per OPT candidate is financially non-viable for colleges and universities seeking to hire recent graduates. Academic departments, university research labs, and grant-funded projects operate on constrained, non-commercial budgets. University employers cannot absorb tens of thousands of dollars in administrative fees per entry-level scholar, nor can academic departments reallocate restricted federal research grants or tuition revenue to cover these costs. Expecting institutions to finance these fees creates an immediate freeze on hiring qualified foreign graduates.

2. Critical necessity of postdoctoral positions for academic careers
Postdoctoral fellowships are an essential, non-negotiable prerequisite for launching a career in academia and advanced scientific research. Postdoc appointments provide specialized, practical training under mentor faculty, serving as the bridge between doctoral completion and tenured faculty or senior research roles. Because postdoctoral positions are temporary, training-focused positions funded through modest stipends, neither the postdoctoral researcher nor the host academic institution can sustain a $70,000 fee burden. Penalizing these positions threatens the core training model of U.S. higher education.

3. Loss of top national talent and U.S. competitiveness
By effectively pricing international graduates out of post-graduation practical training, this rule will filter out some of our nation's top scientific, technical, and academic talent. U.S. universities invest years educating and mentoring extraordinary global scholars. Denying them the ability to complete post-doctoral training in the United States drives world-class researchers to institutions in Canada, Europe, and Asia, inflicting long-term damage on American technological leadership, scientific innovation, and economic competitiveness.

4. Unrealistic burden on recent international students
If institutions pass these fees on to students, the rule creates an extreme equity issue. Recent graduates—having already invested significantly in their U.S. degree programs—cannot afford an additional $70,000 entry fee to work in their fields. This renders the OPT pathway accessible only to the ultra-wealthy, rather than the most academically and professionally qualified candidates.

5. Other types of visas are not a substitute
J-1 visas are not a viable substitute because these visas can trigger a mandatory two-year home-countery residency requirement (INA § 212(e)) that forces postdocs to leave the U.S. before they can move into tenure-track faculty roles or apply for permanent residency. Additionally, changing status to a J-1 can take many months, during which the student may lack work authorization, forcing labs to pause their employment and defer critical research projects. 

In sum, the proposed fee structure is detrimental to the mission of American higher education and national research leadership. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and maintain reasonable, accessible fee structures that enable U.S. institutions to retain exceptional global talent.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: The professor expresses strong opposition to the OPT fees, citing insurmountable financial burdens on universities and research.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but these charges lack a demonstrated statutory basis or reasonable connection to the identified misconduct.

1. The Proposed Fees Exceed DHS's Demonstrated Statutory Authority.

Congress holds the taxing power. Agencies may impose authorized fees, but general regulatory authority does not itself authorize extraordinary charges designed to deter participation.

DHS invokes INA §§ 103(a) and 214(a), 8 U.S.C. §§ 1103(a), 1184(a), to administer immigration law and prescribe nonimmigrant conditions. Neither provision clearly authorizes a $70,000 or $30,000 exaction disconnected from adjudication costs. DHS acknowledges that these receipts will go to the Treasury under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, without being earmarked for OPT enforcement, and that ICE lacks authority to retain them. Section 3302 governs disposition of receipts; it is not an independent fee-setting statute.

The charges therefore resemble deterrent exactions, potentially taxes in substance, rather than ordinary regulatory fees. The district court's decision invalidating implementation of the $100,000 H-1B payment in California v. Mullin (D. Mass. June 8, 2026), though arising under different statutes and subject to appellate proceedings, reinforces the need for clear authority. DHS's decision to use that contested H-1B payment as a benchmark for the $70,000 OPT fee warrants particular scrutiny.

2. DHS Has Not Established That High Fees Will Prevent Fraud.

The rule identifies sham employers and fictitious employment. Yet ability to pay does not establish compliance. A legitimate student or school may be priced out, while a well-funded bad actor may simply pay. Fewer OPT participants do not necessarily mean fewer fraudulent participants, much less a lower fraud rate.

Nor does the fee verify employer operations, actual work, or a connection to the student's field of study. The problem is especially pronounced for initial post-completion OPT, for which a job offer is not generally required when the DSO recommends the student. DHS's own estimate of only 0.5 additional DSO hours per recommendation, including payment-related SEVIS updates, does not demonstrate meaningful additional screening. DHS must substantiate how the proposed amounts prevent fraud.

3. DHS Has Not Adequately Considered Direct Enforcement Alternatives.

DHS dismisses expanded site visits, employer verification, training plans, and reporting as administratively burdensome and incapable of eliminating all fraud. But no measure, including a fee, eliminates all fraud. These alternatives directly target sham employment and inaccurate records; an indiscriminate financial barrier does not. DHS should assess risk-based inspections and existing safeguards rather than treating administrative convenience as proof of effectiveness.

4. The Suggestion That DHS Must Either Impose Extraordinary Fees or Discontinue OPT Presents an Unjustified False Choice.

DHS repeatedly suggests that without these fees it may be unable to operate OPT consistently with its priorities and may shut down the program entirely. That is not a demonstrated necessity; it is an unsupported choice between two extremes.

DHS already has authority to investigate fraud, enforce reporting obligations, conduct authorized site visits, and pursue rulemaking to strengthen oversight. Resource constraints may justify seeking appropriations or targeted enforcement measures. They do not establish that DHS is incapable of operating OPT without imposing $70,000 and $30,000 charges.

The proposed fees would not even provide ICE with dedicated enforcement funding. If insufficient investigative capacity is the concern, how does depositing billions in the Treasury, rather than directing funds to enforcement, solve it? DHS's proposal is not a fraud-detection measure; it is a financial barrier. Charging $70,000 and $30,000 will not expose sham employment, verify actual training, or strengthen ICE's investigative capacity. DHS cannot justify these charges by warning that it may otherwise end OPT program entirely while failing to explain why it cannot enforce the rules already on the books.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express concerns about the proposed DHS rule which would require schools to pay $70,000 for nonimmigrant students to participate in OPT. I have three connected concerns: the cost to colleges, the dissuasion of foreign students, and the long-term impact on science in the United States.  First, I am concerned about the high cost, which will essentially eliminate nonimmigrant international students ability to seek OPT. Colleges and Universities cannot afford to pay the cost, and employers are not able to pay the cost either. The rate is similar to the $100,000 cost for H1b visas, which even hospitals are unwilling to pay for physician recruitment (64% anticipate pausing recruitment in this survey: https://www.aha.org/2026-04-01-fact-sheet-impact-h-1b-filing-fee-health-care-workforce). Second, I am concerned that the lack of ability to work briefly outside of college as students seek full-time employment will harm the ability of colleges and universities to attract international students. Attraction of international students is important for College and University budgets, as these students pay full tuition and thus subsidize the education of US citizen education at these institutions. Third, I am concerned about the impact to science and technology long term to the United States. OPT provides a bridge between college and full-long term employment and permanent residence for foreign students. Without OPT the students who do come to the United States for education must quickly leave the United States (within 60 days), taking their knowledge back with them to their country, or to another country who will grant them a visa. The United States has succeeded in drawing the smartest individuals across the world through our student visa process, which then keeps our country a top innovator in science and technology. 
The DHS expressed concerns about abuse of OPT as the reason for adding the fee. If OPT is a concern for DHS, there are alternatives that could be considered. One option is allowing students to stay on their student visa for a longer period of time after graduate (90 or 120 days) as the student seeks full-time employment within the United States with a new employer sponsored visa. The student visa would prohibit employment, as it already does, but grant the student the ability to seek work and an employer-sponsored visa.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses deep concern regarding the high cost of the proposed OPT fees and their negative impacts.

comments.title: MM15 Comment Submitted by Francesco Cantatore
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Francesco  Cantatorefrancesco.cantatore@mssm.eduNew York, New York 10029

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment opposing proposed OPT fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. My comments address the proposed fees and Section IV's justifications concerning fraud and protection of American workers.

Hiring an international graduate should not automatically be treated as evidence that an employer is harming American workers. Employers may select an international candidate because that person's education, skills, experience, or knowledge of international markets fits the position. Citizenship alone does not tell us which applicant is best qualified. American and international graduates should have an opportunity to demonstrate their abilities, and employers should be able to evaluate them on merit within the law.

I am not claiming that every international hire is more qualified than every American applicant, or that abuse never occurs. Rather, DHS should distinguish legitimate recruitment and practical training from actual misconduct. If employers exploit workers, misrepresent jobs, or violate program requirements, enforcement should target those violations. A large fee imposed across the program does not establish that a particular student or employer has done anything wrong.

International students also contribute to the economy while studying. NAFSA estimates that international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. This is an estimate of the broader economic contribution of international students, not proof that every OPT placement creates a job. However, it shows why DHS should consider potential losses to universities and local businesses if these fees discourage students from choosing the United States.

Source: NAFSA International Student Economic Value Tool, https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2

Practical training allows graduates to apply classroom knowledge to real assignments, learn from experienced professionals, and develop skills that coursework alone cannot fully provide. Making this opportunity depend on access to $70,000 risks selecting participants by wealth or access to a wealthy employer rather than educational merit or the quality of the training.

Requiring schools to pay the fee does not remove this burden if the cost is passed to students or employers. Smaller employers may be unable to fund it, even when a graduate is an excellent fit. Students who have already committed years and substantial resources to an American education would also face a major change in the practical training opportunities available to them.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw these proposed fees and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures against fraud and worker exploitation. Any necessary administrative fee should be supported by a transparent explanation of actual costs. DHS should assess the effects on educational access, small employers, university enrollment, and local economies, and protect currently enrolled students from abrupt changes. Protecting American workers and allowing qualified international graduates to receive legitimate practical training can be compatible goals.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees and addresses justifications regarding fraud and workers.

comments.title: MM5 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorization and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT periods. These fees are unprecedented in size and would effectively eliminate access to OPT for many international students attending U.S. colleges and universities.

OPT serves as a critical bridge between academic study and practical workforce experience. It allows international students educated in the United States to apply the skills they have gained in American classrooms while contributing to U.S. employers, research institutions, and the broader economy. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier that many educational institutions would be unable or unwilling to absorb.

The proposal would disproportionately harm students in STEM fields, where OPT and STEM OPT are often essential pathways for gaining practical experience and contributing to innovation. At a time when the United States competes globally for highly skilled talent, imposing fees of this magnitude would encourage students to pursue education and employment opportunities in other countries rather than in the United States.

The economic impact would extend beyond students. Universities rely on enrollment from international students, who contribute billions of dollars annually to local economies through tuition, housing, transportation, and consumer spending. A policy that discourages international enrollment would negatively affect educational institutions, local communities, and employers seeking qualified talent. The proposal estimates annual fees in the billions of dollars across affected institutions, creating a significant burden on schools.

Additionally, the stated purpose of combating fraud and protecting U.S. workers does not justify fees at the proposed levels. Less burdensome measures exist to address compliance concerns without effectively dismantling the OPT program. Any regulatory action should be narrowly tailored, evidence-based, and proportionate to the problem it seeks to address.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. At a minimum, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive analysis of the economic, educational, and workforce consequences before proceeding with any fee increases.
comments.reason: Commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule, stating the fees are unprecedented and would eliminate access to OPT.

As a training director of graduate students in neuropsychology, I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.

OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees. I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.
Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Cesia Espinal Moncada
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Proposed OPT Fees for F-1 Students

I am an international graduate student on an F-1 visa, and I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees for Optional Practical Training. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal or, at minimum, to substantially reduce the fees and create exemptions for students in academic and public-interest fields.

The fee is out of reach for the people who would be asked to bear it. The proposal states that schools may pass the cost on to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers. Whichever route is chosen, the amounts are very large relative to graduate-student finances. My annual assistantship stipend is $23,000, or about $19,000 after taxes. A $70,000 fee is more than three years of my gross stipend and nearly four years of my take-home pay, before housing, food, or transportation. As a nonresident alien, my access to credit is very limited, so borrowing is not a realistic option.

Employers in academia will be discouraged from hiring OPT participants. Universities and research units that rely on international graduates for research, teaching, and administrative work operate on tight budgets. If the cost of recommending OPT is passed to employers, many will simply stop hiring OPT participants. If it is passed to students, only those with substantial personal wealth will be able to use the program. In both cases, the result is a narrower and less diverse academic workforce.

Timing matters. Finding a professional position often takes months, and OPT is a time-limited authorization. Any additional barrier to obtaining the school’s recommendation can delay the start of employment and put a graduate’s status at risk.

OPT participants contribute to US academic and civic life. As a graduate student, I have led a graduate symposium that became an international event, bringing together keynote speakers and scholars. The following year we organized a film festival that sparked discussion about film, society, and relationships across US and Latin American cultures. I hope to continue this kind of work after graduation. Policies that price out students like me would remove precisely the people who build these intellectual communities.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

Respectfully,
An F-1 graduate student
comments.reason: An international student opposing the proposed OPT fees and urging DHS to withdraw or reduce them.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis. Practically, I do not see how this rule will prevent future fraud; it only limits the US's ability to draw international talents into its workforce and contributes to the brain drain that the nation is facing. 

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Devan MassinDMASSIN@UCI.EDUIrvine, California 92617
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee hikes as unreasonable, harmful to workers, and damaging to U.S. higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)

I am a graduate student in a STEM field at a U.S. university, and I write in opposition to proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and 214.13(i)(2).

The proposed fees bear no reasonable relationship to the cost of the activity being charged for. The action that triggers the $70,000 fee is a designated school official entering a recommendation in SEVIS — an administrative database entry that takes minutes and costs the government a negligible amount to process. DHS does not claim the fee recovers the cost of adjudicating or overseeing OPT, and the rule directs the proceeds to the general Treasury rather than to program administration. A charge set at this level, untethered from any cost of service and deposited as general revenue, functions as a tax rather than a fee. DHS cites INA 214(a) as its authority, but that provision concerns conditions of admission, not revenue generation, and Congress has not authorized a charge of this kind.

The fee structure also does not match the rationale DHS offers for it. The rule is justified by fraud identified through SEVP, including problematic worksites and pay-to-stay schemes, yet the proposed fee would apply uniformly to every OPT recommendation at every one of the 2,478 SEVP-certified institutions, regardless of compliance history. It would impose identical costs on an institution with documented violations and one with none. A fee that cannot distinguish between the conduct it targets and the conduct it does not is not a fraud-reduction measure. If the concern is specific bad actors, targeted enforcement against those institutions and employers would address it directly, where a universal charge would not.

The practical effect of the rule would be to end OPT rather than reform it. DHS estimates $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual fees and acknowledges that institutions may pass the cost to students. No university can absorb $70,000 per student and no student can pay it, so the predictable result is that schools simply stop issuing recommendations. DHS should address directly, in the final rule, whether the elimination of OPT in practice is the intended outcome, and if so, explain why that outcome was not proposed openly and analyzed as such.

The burden on STEM students in particular is understated. A student eligible for the 24-month STEM extension would trigger $70,000 for post-completion OPT and a further $30,000 for the extension — $100,000 attached to a single student over the course of one degree. Many students in this position have already received full-time offers from U.S. employers, offers that exist because OPT made an earlier internship possible. The rule would foreclose that path for every student who follows the same route.

Finally, the comment period is inadequate for a rule of this magnitude. A regulation carrying an estimated $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual costs across nearly 2,500 institutions warrants more than 30 days of public comment. Affected universities cannot model budgetary impact, consult governing boards, and submit substantive analysis in that window, and I urge DHS to extend the period.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter writes in opposition to the proposed OPT fees, calling them unreasonable.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees — Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. As a graduate student in statistics and data science, I am concerned that these fees would make legitimate practical training inaccessible and undermine the educational value of graduate study. My comments address Sections V.A, V.C, and VI.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier. An initial OPT recommendation followed by a STEM OPT extension would require $100,000 in new fees. Requiring universities to pay does not eliminate this burden. If institutions absorb the costs, fewer resources may remain for education and research. If they pass the costs to students or employers, access to training would depend heavily on financial resources. A student's ability to obtain relevant practical training should not depend on whether someone can afford a six-figure payment.

In statistics and data science, practical experience helps students learn how to apply methods to real problems, evaluate their limitations, and work with interdisciplinary teams. Restricting these opportunities could disrupt research projects and make it harder for universities, nonprofit organizations, and smaller employers to benefit from graduates they have helped train. DHS should evaluate these consequences rather than assume that reducing OPT participation necessarily benefits American workers.

I support effective enforcement against fraud and worker exploitation. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate. Conversely, an inability to pay does not indicate misconduct. DHS should explain why these particular amounts would improve compliance and evaluate more targeted alternatives, including employer verification, compliance audits, and enforcement against documented violations.

The proposed transition also fails to adequately protect students already enrolled in degree programs. Students make educational and financial commitments over several years. A 60-day transition cannot reasonably accommodate those commitments. Applying fees only to future recommendations still affects students who began their studies under the existing framework.

DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and preserve affordable access to OPT and STEM OPT. If it proceeds with changes, it should protect currently enrolled students and provide a transparent, evidence-based justification for any fee, including its amount and its effects on legitimate training.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Supplemental Opposition — Economic Analysis and Opportunity Costs
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and request its withdrawal. I previously submitted an opposing comment under tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl. This supplemental comment addresses a separate concern: the opportunity-cost analysis in Section VII.A.5.b, particularly its use of unpaid proposed fees to estimate the losses from reduced OPT participation.

A fee chosen by the agency is not an independent measurement of the value of an opportunity that the fee would eliminate. Changing the proposed fee would change this proxy even if the educational and research value of the affected training remained the same. DHS should therefore explain and empirically validate the relationship between the fee and the losses being estimated, rather than treating the fee itself as sufficient evidence of those losses.

The analysis also assumes that affected parties could share the cost when the benefits exceed the fee. That assumption needs support. Students, universities, and employers have different budgets, incentives, and time horizons. A valuable research placement may generate benefits over many years, while the required payment is immediate. Benefits to future patients, scientific knowledge, or the wider community may accrue to people who cannot participate in a funding agreement. An inability to assemble the payment would not establish that the training has low social value.

For the same reason, a university's financial capacity should not be treated as a reliable test of the quality of its students or training opportunities. DHS should examine how the rule would affect institutions with limited unrestricted funds, nonprofit research employers, and students without substantial savings. Aggregate estimates can conceal a concentrated loss of access among these groups.

Before proceeding, DHS should publish sensitivity analyses that vary participation responses, financing constraints, and the availability of substitute workers. The agency should separately explain expected effects on educational outcomes, research continuity, and U.S. workers, and compare those effects with the likely results of targeted compliance enforcement. A reduction in total OPT participation alone would not demonstrate a reduction in fraudulent participation.

The uncertainty in the current analysis is a reason to gather better evidence before imposing such a large barrier. It is not a persuasive basis for adopting the proposed amounts. I urge DHS to withdraw the rule and preserve affordable OPT and STEM OPT while developing proportionate measures supported by evidence.

Reference: Notice of proposed rulemaking, Section VII.A.5.b, 91 FR 64588-64589 (October 8, 2026).
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests its withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Supplemental Opposition — Training Timing, Repeated Fees, and Refunds
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and request its withdrawal. I previously submitted an opposing comment under tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl. This supplemental comment addresses the fee structure in Section V.A, the effect on pre-completion training discussed in Section VII.A.5.d(3), and the refund provisions in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i).

The proposal penalizes when a student receives training, even where the total authorized OPT period is unchanged. DHS describes a $100,000 total charge when the available 12 months are divided between pre-completion and post-completion OPT, compared with $70,000 when all of that training occurs after graduation. The additional $30,000 would therefore arise without an increase in the total training period. DHS should explain why that difference is justified by program integrity or oversight needs.

Training before graduation can help students test ideas, identify gaps in their skills, and bring practical lessons back to their remaining coursework and research. Deferring an opportunity until after graduation may eliminate those benefits, and the same placement may no longer be available. A fee structure that pressures students to postpone legitimate training undermines an educational purpose of OPT. The agency should assess these losses directly rather than treating a shift toward post-completion OPT as an adequate solution.

The initial flat fee also creates a disproportionate burden for shorter training opportunities. DHS should explain why the same initial charge is appropriate across different durations and how students and institutions could realistically fund it. For example, a short research placement may be educationally valuable even when its immediate financial return cannot support a very large upfront charge.

The refund restrictions add further risk. Section V.A bars refunds after the relevant employment authorization document is issued. Authorization does not ensure that a planned placement will actually occur or continue. An employer might cancel a project, funding might end, or illness might prevent participation. These examples do not imply misconduct. Nevertheless, an absolute cutoff could leave an institution bearing the entire fee for training that produces little or no benefit, encouraging it to reject otherwise sound recommendations in advance.

DHS should withdraw the proposed fees. If the agency continues to consider a fee system, it should evaluate eliminating additional charges for splitting an existing OPT allowance, substantially lower charges supported by documented needs, and clear, reviewable refund protections when training cannot proceed. My primary recommendation remains withdrawal: legitimate educational opportunities should not be priced out by this fee structure.

References: Sections V.A and VII.A.5.d(3), 91 FR 64577 and 64590-64591; proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i).
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests its withdrawal.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Freya White
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 | Document ICEB-2026-0100-0001

Please see the attached document for my full comment. A summary follows.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) would require schools to pay new fees before recommending students for Optional Practical Training (OPT): $70,000 initially per student and $30,000 for later recommendations. OPT provides qualifying international students with employment authorization for training related to their studies. DHS already describes ongoing evaluation of the fee's impact and effectiveness to inform future policy decisions. Please spell out what information and comparisons that evaluation will use and when DHS will first assess and publicly report the results. Please also identify where it will explain whether the fees achieve its goals and what the findings support: retaining the fees, changing their amounts or scope, or using other measures.

I submit this comment as a member of the public in my personal capacity. This comment takes no position on any substantive choice in the proposed rule. These requests do not address DHS's legal authority to impose the fees.

This comment was prepared after reviewing the proposed rule, its SEVIS supporting statement and the public comments cited below.

1. Explain what information will help DHS judge whether the fees achieve its goals.

Please identify the available information and comparisons DHS will use to assess program integrity, protection of U.S. workers and oversight burdens. Identify the baseline conditions before implementation that will provide the comparison, using available records and explaining their limits. Submission 0196 requests a pre-implementation baseline (attachment 1, section 2, p. 2).

Recommendations, payments, authorizations and actual training describe different stages. A school's remittance alone does not show who ultimately bore the cost. DHS already discusses schools' financial records and disclosures as possible sources for tracing funds (91 FR 64575). Please explain what the available information can show about the institutional response DHS expects. Recommendation records alone do not identify requests abandoned because of the cost.

Fewer recorded violations could reflect a smaller program, improved compliance or changes in detection. The assessment needs context about what was checked. For worker protection, please explain what information can help distinguish increased domestic hiring from other employer responses, including work moving elsewhere. DHS may identify more useful evidence or explain what available information cannot establish.

2. State when the first assessment and public account will occur.

Please identify in the final rule the responsible office and the first date or interval from implementation for assessing results and publishing the account. An applicable existing review can serve. If different effects need different observation periods, explain what the first account will cover and when the remaining questions will be considered.

3. Publish the judgment and explain what it means for the next decision.

At the stated occasion, please publish a brief account of what the results show, their limits and what they support: retaining the fees, changing their amounts or scope, improving administration or using other measures. Identify in the final rule where the account will appear. A public report, rulemaking notice or another suitable public channel could serve.

DHS calls the fee “a crucial first step” in “a graduated strategy” and says it seeks flexibility for additional regulatory measures (91 FR 64576). Please use the public judgment to explain whether another step is warranted and, if so, what it should be.

DHS states its priorities and weighs reliance interests in section VI. Please explain how the observed consequences bear on those priorities and tradeoffs. Reduced participation alone would not settle that judgment. If experience is inconclusive, explain what can and cannot be concluded.

Please state the disposition of each numbered request in the final rule and explain the reasons for any request not adopted.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Tables and supporting sources are in the attachment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Wojciech Skulski
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Wojciech Skulski. I am a Chief Technology Officer of the high-tech company SkuTek Instrumentation, serving Nuclear Physics and High Energy Physics communities.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

According to my own experience with international students and graduates, they are extremely well educated and highly motivated. Their contribution to American science and technology is outstanding. Excessive fees levied upon the OPT program will adversely affect American science.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Wojciech Skulski

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule under Docket ICEB-2026-0100, which would introduce fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization.

As an international graduate of a U.S. university and a technology professional working in the United States, I believe this proposal would create unreasonable financial barriers, discourage international talent, and negatively affect American universities, businesses, and economic competitiveness.

1. Unreasonable Financial Burden

International students already invest significant resources in American education. Many pay high tuition fees, living expenses, health insurance, and immigration-related costs without access to federal financial assistance.

After completing their degrees, students deserve a reasonable opportunity to gain practical experience related to their education. Although the proposed fees would be imposed on educational institutions, universities may ultimately pass these costs to students or stop supporting OPT applications.

Requiring such excessive payments would make practical training inaccessible to many qualified graduates, regardless of their academic achievements or professional capabilities.

2. Negative Impact on the U.S. Economy and Innovation

International graduates contribute directly to American businesses through technological innovation, research, cybersecurity, software development, and engineering.

In my professional experience, I have contributed to modernizing enterprise systems, improving application security, resolving critical technical issues, and supporting services used by American customers.

These contributions help businesses operate efficiently and remain competitive. Creating extraordinary financial barriers to practical training could prevent American employers from benefiting from qualified graduates who have already received their education in the United States.

3. Damage to American Higher Education

The United States attracts international students because of its world-class universities, research opportunities, and ability to connect classroom education with practical experience.

If OPT becomes financially inaccessible, prospective students may choose countries with more affordable and predictable post-graduation opportunities.

This could reduce international enrollment, university revenue, research contributions, and America’s ability to attract global talent. The long-term economic consequences could extend well beyond individual students.

4. Fraud Prevention Requires Targeted Enforcement

I fully support DHS’s responsibility to prevent immigration fraud, ensure compliance, and protect American workers.

However, imposing excessive fees on legitimate students and universities is not an effective substitute for investigating actual violations.

DHS should strengthen employer verification, monitor institutions and training arrangements, investigate fraudulent employment practices, and enforce penalties against organizations that violate immigration regulations.

These targeted measures would address misconduct without penalizing students who follow the rules.

5. Lack of Proportionality and Economic Justification

I respectfully ask DHS to explain how the proposed fee amounts were determined and provide evidence demonstrating that these specific fees are necessary and proportionate to the stated objectives.

DHS should carefully evaluate the financial impact on universities, students, employers, international enrollment, and U.S. economic competitiveness. Less restrictive alternatives should be considered before implementing such substantial financial requirements.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements.

International students make substantial investments in American education and contribute valuable knowledge and skills to the U.S. economy. Those who comply with immigration laws should not face unreasonable financial barriers to obtaining practical training.

Protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud are important goals, but these objectives should be achieved through targeted enforcement and evidence-based policies rather than excessive financial restrictions.

The United States should continue to attract talented individuals who study, innovate, and contribute to its economic growth.
comments.reason: The commenter writes to strongly oppose the proposed rule introducing OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule under Docket ICEB-2026-0100. The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee raise serious legal concerns regarding statutory authority, administrative law, proportionality, and procedural fairness.

1. Questionable Statutory Authority

DHS relies on 8 U.S.C. §§ 1103 and 1184 to justify this proposal. While these provisions authorize DHS to administer immigration laws and establish nonimmigrant conditions, regulatory authority does not automatically grant unlimited authority to impose extraordinary financial charges.

Congress has established specific provisions governing immigration-related fees. DHS must identify the precise statutory authorization permitting these charges and explain whether they constitute legitimate regulatory fees rather than financial penalties or revenue-generating measures.

Without clear congressional authorization, this proposal raises significant concerns about agency overreach.

2. Administrative Procedure Act Violations

Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), courts may set aside agency actions that are arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise contrary to law.

DHS must provide a reasoned explanation supported by evidence demonstrating why fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary.

The proposal seeks to prevent fraud and protect American workers. However, DHS must establish a rational connection between these specific fee amounts and those objectives.

DHS should explain why less burdensome alternatives, including employer verification, compliance audits, targeted investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent institutions, would not achieve comparable results.

3. Failure to Consider Reliance Interests

In Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the Supreme Court emphasized the importance of considering serious reliance interests when changing established immigration policies.

International students invest substantial financial resources in U.S. education with the reasonable expectation that existing practical training opportunities will remain accessible.

Students already enrolled cannot easily recover tuition payments, relocate, or restructure their education.

Applying extraordinary fees to currently enrolled students could severely disrupt these expectations.

DHS should assess these reliance interests and consider transitional protections for students who began their education under existing regulations.

4. Regulatory Flexibility Act Concerns

The Regulatory Flexibility Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 601–612, requires agencies to assess certain economic impacts on small entities and consider appropriate regulatory alternatives.

Smaller universities and nonprofit educational institutions may lack the resources to pay these fees.

This could prevent institutions from recommending qualified students for OPT, creating unequal access based on institutional financial capacity.

DHS must carefully examine these consequences and evaluate less burdensome approaches.

5. Disproportionate Financial Barriers

OPT is an established component of the F-1 student regulatory framework.

Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 or $30,000 before recommending eligible students could effectively restrict practical training to institutions with substantial financial resources.

Placing the formal payment obligation on universities does not eliminate the financial consequences for students.

DHS must demonstrate that these extraordinary financial conditions are reasonably connected to legitimate regulatory objectives and supported by lawful authority.

6. Request for Legal Justification

Before adopting this rule, I respectfully request that DHS:

* Identify the specific congressional authorization supporting these fees.
* Explain the calculation and justification for the proposed amounts.
* Provide evidence connecting these fees to meaningful fraud prevention.
* Evaluate impacts on currently enrolled students and institutional reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees under Docket ICEB-2026-0100.

My primary concern is that this proposal would fundamentally change how students access practical training by introducing additional administrative barriers, institutional discretion, uncertainty, and potentially irreversible consequences for students who have complied with all immigration requirements.

1. Universities Should Not Become Financial Gatekeepers of Employment Authorization

Under the proposal, educational institutions must pay the required fee before a Designated School Official (DSO) can enter an OPT recommendation into SEVIS.

This creates a serious problem. A student’s ability to pursue practical training would depend not only on eligibility under immigration regulations but also on whether their university agrees and is financially able to make the payment.

Two students with identical qualifications, immigration histories, and employment opportunities could receive entirely different outcomes simply because they attend different universities.

2. Risk of Missing Strict Immigration Deadlines

OPT applications already operate under strict filing deadlines. Students must coordinate graduation dates, DSO recommendations, Form I-20 issuance, USCIS applications, and employment authorization.

Requiring universities to arrange payment before entering an OPT recommendation introduces another administrative dependency.

What happens if a university experiences payment processing delays, internal approval problems, or administrative errors?

A student could miss an application deadline despite completing every requirement within their control.

DHS should not introduce a process where institutional delays can permanently affect an otherwise eligible student’s immigration opportunities.

3. Unfair and Inadequate Refund Protections

The proposal raises serious concerns about the treatment of payments when circumstances change.

Students may experience unexpected delays, withdrawn employment offers, academic schedule changes, or other events beyond their control.

If an employment authorization document has already been issued, the proposed refund provisions appear to provide limited protection even when the student cannot ultimately benefit from the authorized training period.

This creates an unreasonable allocation of financial risk.

Any payment system should include transparent refund procedures, clear eligibility criteria, meaningful administrative review, and protections against losses caused by circumstances outside the applicant’s control.

4. Uncertainty for Students Already Participating in OPT

The proposal creates particular uncertainty for students who began OPT before the rule takes effect but later apply for a STEM OPT extension.

Under the proposed language, the lower subsequent fee appears to depend on the initial $70,000 fee having previously been paid.

This raises an important question: Would a student who completed initial OPT before implementation face the full $70,000 charge when applying for a STEM extension?

DHS should explicitly address this situation rather than leaving students and universities to interpret conflicting or unclear requirements.

A student already participating in authorized training should not face unexpected consequences because of ambiguity in a newly introduced payment structure.

5. Unintended Consequences for Internships and Early Career Training

The proposal also applies to pre-completion OPT.

Students frequently pursue practical experience during their academic programs to understand industry expectations, explore career interests, and connect classroom knowledge with professional responsibilities.

Charging the initial fee for pre-completion OPT could discourage universities from recommending students for internships and other legitimate training opportunities.

Furthermore, students who pursue additional practical training after graduation could face another substantial fee.

This structure creates an unnecessary distinction between students based on when they choose to gain professional experience.

The regulatory system should encourage responsible educational planning rather than discourage practical experience during academic programs.

Conclusion

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

The consequences extend beyond the stated fee amounts. The rule could create inconsistent access to practical training, additional administrative delays, uncertainty for current students, inadequate refund protections, and avoidable risks to immigration compliance.

Students who follow established immigration procedures should not lose opportunities because of institutional payment decisions, administrative processing failures, or unclear regulatory language.

Federal immigration policies should provide consistency, predictability, and fair procedures for everyone subject to them.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the OPT fees, citing institutional financial gatekeeping and missed immigration deadlines.

comments.title: MM17 Comment Submitted by Kathleen Till
comments.commentText:
I, Kathleen Till, strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations in document ICEB-2026-0100. I urge DHS to remove this fee structure and preserve access to integral, legitimate, degree-related practical training for students on F-1 visas.

The proposed rule claims to “deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its students” in Section IV.C. It is incredibly unclear how a $70,000-100,000+ financial barrier per individual promotes hiring legitimacy and prevents the OPT-related fraud it claims to address. Instead, the proposed fee clearly serves as a de facto ban on most, if not all, OPT and legitimate degree-related practice under the shallow guise of ‘protecting United States workers.’ 

I have deep concerns with the impact of the proposed fee structure on the ability of students on F-1 visas to study and engage in fully legitimate degree-training in the United States. The document is primarily concerned with mitigating ‘false employers,’ fraud, and ‘shell companies’ related to temporary employment through OPT (Section IV.A). An excessive, pre-application demonstration of wealth borne by academic institutions fundamentally does not contribute or aid in the purported goal of increased oversight and assessment of the legitimacy of potential employers.

The document claims that the “fees which would ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate in OPT.” First, an OPT recommendation from an SEVP certified school has nothing to do with qualification. Job-seeking students, in addition to overcoming paperwork, recommendation, and field-of-study hurdles, must still go through the application process post-recommendation. Further, the ability to bear a $70,000+ fee before acquiring a job has no logical or practical connectivity to the legitimacy of the job opportunity, the employer, the role the job plays in the student’s degree-related training, or the student’s aptitude for a certain job. All it demonstrates is the ability of the school, student, or potential employer to bear a massive financial burden.

Given the inability of many institutions and individual students to meet such an excessive demand, particularly with no continued job guarantee after, what the proposed rule instead serves as is a functional ban on most OPT pursuits, regardless of ‘legitimacy.’ This functional ban threatens the opportunity for international students who are studying and training in the United States to gain important degree-related practice, apply their academic training into valuable work within the United States, and even to pursue higher education post-baccalaureate. No person should have to pay $70,000+ to apply for a job. Once again, given the jarring impact of its implementation on F-1 students, their academic institutions, and its inability to achieve the goals it claims to advance, I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure in document ICEB-2026-0100 (Federal Register No. 2026-20660) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.
