comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers, I believe this proposal would create severe unintended consequences for the U.S. economy, higher education system, and long-term global competitiveness.

1. Undermining America’s Ability to Attract and Retain Global Talent

The United States has long benefited from attracting talented international students who contribute to scientific research, technological innovation, and economic growth.

OPT provides an important bridge between American education and practical professional experience. Imposing fees of up to $100,000 for initial OPT and a subsequent extension would make this pathway financially inaccessible for many qualified graduates, regardless of their academic achievements, professional abilities, or potential economic contributions.

As a result, talented individuals may increasingly choose to study and work in countries offering more accessible opportunities. The United States risks educating future innovators only to lose their contributions to competing economies.

2. Damaging American Universities and Research Institutions

International students contribute substantial tuition revenue, research capacity, and intellectual diversity to American universities.

The availability of post-graduation practical training is an important consideration when students choose where to pursue higher education. Making OPT prohibitively expensive could significantly reduce the attractiveness of American universities, particularly for students pursuing advanced degrees in STEM fields.

Declining international enrollment could reduce university revenue, weaken research programs, and ultimately affect educational opportunities and research infrastructure that benefit both American and international students.

Notably, DHS acknowledges in its own regulatory analysis that institutions may experience declining enrollment and reduced revenue, while also recognizing uncertainty about the extent of these impacts.

3. Weakening American Innovation and Economic Competitiveness

American technological leadership depends on a dynamic ecosystem of universities, research institutions, startups, and established businesses.

International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to this ecosystem. Restricting their access to practical training could reduce the availability of highly trained workers, slow research commercialization, and discourage entrepreneurship.

Furthermore, employers and universities may increasingly move research activities, investment, and employment opportunities overseas if retaining internationally educated talent becomes economically impractical.

These consequences could ultimately weaken American competitiveness rather than strengthen it.

4. Questionable Economic Trade-Offs and Insufficient Impact Assessment

DHS acknowledges that it cannot confidently predict how significantly OPT participation would decline under the proposed fee structure.

This uncertainty is particularly concerning given the extraordinary magnitude of the proposed fees.

The regulatory analysis should more thoroughly evaluate the potential long-term economic losses associated with reduced international enrollment, diminished research productivity, lost entrepreneurship, decreased consumer spending, and the relocation of skilled talent and business activities abroad.

Any projected benefits from increased fee revenue or potential labor-market adjustments should be weighed against these broader economic consequences.

5. More Targeted Alternatives Are Available

Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate policy objectives. However, imposing exceptionally high fees on educational institutions is not necessarily an effective or proportionate way to achieve them.

DHS should instead consider targeted compliance audits, improved employment verification, stronger enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employers, and risk-based oversight.

These approaches would address actual misconduct without indiscriminately restricting legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Conclusion

The United States should not undermine one of its greatest competitive advantages: its ability to attract, educate, and retain talented individuals from around the world.

A policy intended to protect American economic interests should not inadvertently weaken American universities, discourage innovation, and transfer valuable human capital to competing nations.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees and pursue more targeted, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity without sacrificing America’s long-term economic strength and global competitiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fees, arguing they undermine global talent retention and damage universities.

I came across this proposed rule and it immediately held my attention. I am submitting this public comment in my professional capacity as an Assistant Registrar at a four-year institution of higher education. My responsibilities include maintaining student academic records and supporting the accurate administration of academic programs and student enrollment. Through this work, I have a firsthand understanding of how academic policies, degree requirements, and administrative decisions can affect students’ ability to make progress toward graduation.

Recently, I participated in a meeting with the Office of International Studies at my university to discuss issues affecting our international student population, including students studying in the United States under F-1 status. Although I work at a reginal campus and it does not have a particularly large number of international students, but we still have them, and they have chosen this school to pursue their educational goals. The size of this population should not diminish the importance of protecting their access to a fair, supportive, and attainable educational experience.

One of the concerns discussed during our meeting was the difficulty international students may encounter when they need or wish to change their major or course of study. For example, an incoming international student or a student who would be classified as an F-1 student initially admitted to a biochemistry program may later determine that a nursing program is a more appropriate academic and professional path. This student will need to wait 1 year or equivalent of sophomore standing based on sufficient credits before pursuing the change. Graduate students and post-baccalaureate students may face even more restrictive circumstances when attempting to change their program or plan of study.

These examples illustrate a broader concern: international students must navigate the academic requirements of their institutions while also maintaining compliance with federal immigration requirements. A decision that might be a relatively routine academic adjustment for another student can have substantially greater consequences for an F-1 student, potentially affecting the student’s program timeline, immigration documentation, and ability to complete a degree. Under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) final rule, F-1 visa students are no longer admitted for an open-ended "duration of status." Instead, they are granted a fixed period of admission tied to the length of their program of study, not to exceed four years. Reference back to that hypothetical example I provided, that the bio-chemistry student who now wants to change their major to nursing, the system has already set them up for failure because they might not be able to graduate in time within that four year period if they had the option to change their major within the first year. 

I recognize the Department of Homeland Security’s responsibility to administer immigration laws and establish appropriate oversight to track students. In my role we track a variety different of students based on demographics, program of study, number of years it takes a student to complete a program or athlete. Tracking international students is just another statistic. However, I respectfully urge DHS to consider the practical consequences of its policies for students and the universities. Policies should be designed with an understanding of how higher education operates in practice, including the realities of degree progression, changes in academic direction, and the differing financial resources of institutions. I recommend that the Department of Homeland Security reconsider the proposed OPT fee structure and adopt a more reasonable, equitable, and transparent approach. They need to come to an understanding on how to evaluate these proposed fees. Having the college or university pay a flat rate of $70k per student is outrageous and not feasible. The government states it wants to prevent fraud of students to by-pass work visa requirements and proposing this seems a bit unconventional. I feel that this will draw the tuition rates for  every student, not only international students, if the school has to pay for this fee. 
 
My proposal is that maybe have an additional section on the application process when the student goes through admissions to submit their application on their intention of education. Though this may seem invasive, my institution has an application to receive in-state tuition benefits based on residency. Or have a tiered fee structure based on if the university is a public or private institution. 

I urge DHS to reconsider the OPT fee structure since it only hinders the affordability of higher education especially institutions with limited resources.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed rule raises serious questions about its economic assumptions, proportionality, and unintended consequences.

1. Would restricting OPT actually create jobs for American workers?

In Section VII.A.6, DHS suggests that reduced OPT participation could transfer employment opportunities to U.S. workers. However, this assumes employers would maintain those positions domestically and hire American replacements.

Companies may instead outsource work, relocate research operations, delay projects, or reduce hiring. Labor demand is also influenced by broader economic conditions, automation, and artificial intelligence.

Has DHS evaluated these alternative employer responses and estimated the net effect on American employment? Restricting access to international graduates does not automatically create domestic jobs.

2. Does DHS underestimate the economic value of international talent?

In Section VII.A.5.b, DHS uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity costs of reduced participation. Yet the economic value of a skilled graduate cannot necessarily be measured by an institution's ability to pay $70,000 upfront.

Research by Hunt and Gauthier-Loiselle (2010), published in the *American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics*, found that a one-percentage-point increase in the population share of immigrant college graduates was associated with a 9–18% increase in patents per capita. Although this study does not specifically estimate OPT's effects, it demonstrates why the innovation contributions of skilled immigrants deserve consideration.

Has DHS adequately accounted for potential losses in innovation, productivity, and future job creation? Why should the proposed fee amounts serve as proxies for economic contributions that may extend far beyond the initial employment period?

3. Could the proposed fees drive talent and investment overseas?

Post-graduation employment opportunities influence where international students choose to study and work. Substantial fees may discourage enrollment at American universities and encourage graduates to pursue careers in competing economies.

DHS acknowledges potential enrollment declines and employer productivity losses but also assumes that parties receiving sufficient benefits from OPT could share the fees.

This overlooks financing constraints. Even economically valuable employment may not generate enough immediate funding to cover these charges, particularly when a graduate has not yet secured an employer.

Has DHS adequately evaluated the effects on university enrollment, research capacity, and companies' decisions to expand operations overseas? Could the policy ultimately reduce investment and employment within the United States?

4. What evidence justifies these specific fee amounts?

DHS argues that high fees would encourage institutions to scrutinize OPT recommendations more carefully. However, what evidence establishes that $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary or proportionate to this objective?

How would expected fraud reduction differ under substantially lower fees? Has DHS demonstrated that broad financial barriers would be more effective than targeted audits, employer verification, and enforcement against fraudulent arrangements?

Financial capacity is not evidence of compliance. A legitimate graduate may be excluded because of funding constraints, while fraudulent practices may remain unaddressed.

In conclusion, the proposed rule risks discouraging international talent, reducing innovation, and shifting economic activity overseas without establishing that American workers would receive corresponding benefits.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure, reassess its economic assumptions, and evaluate more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing fraud.

Protecting American workers should involve encouraging investment and job creation in the United States, not assuming that excluding international graduates will produce those outcomes.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the OPT fees, questioning their economic assumptions and potential negative unintended consequences.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I’m an international student studying Electrical Engineering at Purdue University, and I’m expecting to graduate in May 2027. I’m writing because I’m really worried about how the proposed OPT fees could affect my future.

Coming to the United States to study has meant a lot to me and my family. We have invested so much in my education, and I’ve worked hard to learn as much as I can and build a career in engineering.

I recently received a full-time engineering job offer from a semiconductor company in Arizona. When I got the offer, I was excited because I could finally see a path from everything I’ve been learning in school to a job where I could use those skills. I’ve been looking forward to joining the team, learning from other engineers, and contributing to the work they do.

After hearing about the proposed $70,000 OPT fee, I started worrying about whether I would still be able to take that opportunity. I spoke with my university’s international student office, and they told me that the proposal is not final and that the university would not cover the fee if it were implemented. I don’t yet know whether my future employer would be able to help. The possibility of facing a cost this large is frightening, especially when I’m so close to graduating.

I know the proposed fee would be charged to schools, but students could still be affected if the cost is passed on to us or if schools are unable to pay it. For me, $70,000 is far more than I could reasonably afford as a new graduate. It’s difficult to think that after years of studying and preparing, I might not be able to start the job I’ve worked so hard for because of a fee.

I hope there can be a way to address those concerns without making practical training financially impossible for students who have followed the rules and planned their education around this opportunity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Vas Tsolak
comments.commentText:
OPT is a valuable opportunity for international students in the United States to gain professional experience in the American workforce. Students who study in the U.S. and gain work experience often return to their home countries with valuable skills and experience that can help them stand out professionally. They also share their experiences and contribute to America's reputation as a place where young people can study, develop their careers, and build their futures.

However, working legally in the United States as an international student is not easy. Optional Practical Training (OPT) provides an authorized pathway for eligible international students to gain work experience related to their field of study. If additional taxes or financial burdens are imposed specifically on this pathway, it could discourage students from pursuing professional opportunities in the U.S. and make America less attractive to international talent.

# **The key distinction is that OPT is a legal work authorization pathway, not a pathway used by people who work illegally.** An international student who qualifies for OPT applies for authorization and must follow the applicable rules. Someone who works without the required authorization is operating outside that legal pathway, regardless of whether there are 500 or 70,000 such individuals.

Therefore, imposing additional costs on OPT could disproportionately affect people who are trying to follow the legal process, while not necessarily addressing unauthorized employment. If the goal is to encourage legal compliance, policymakers should consider whether such measures would discourage authorized work without effectively addressing unauthorized work.

The United States benefits when international students can gain experience legally, contribute to the economy, and become ambassadors for American education and professional opportunities around the world.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that imposing additional financial burdens on OPT could discourage international talent from the U.S.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Andrea Erdas

Dr. Andrea Erdas

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Audrey Fong

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Veronica Shangguan
comments.commentText:
I think one of the biggest problems with this proposed OPT policy is how unfairly it could affect international students who are already studying in the U.S., simply because of when they graduate.

For example, two students could attend the same university, study the same major, and start their degrees in the same year. They could spend four years paying tuition, working hard, and preparing for their careers. But if one student graduates and receives their OPT recommendation just before the new rule takes effect, while the other receives theirs 60 or 90 days later, they could face completely different situations. One could go through the existing OPT process, while the other's university would face a $70,000 fee before making the OPT recommendation.

How is that a reasonable outcome when both students have made essentially the same commitments and met the same academic requirements?

Graduation timing is not always something students can control. Sometimes a required class is only offered in a certain quarter, or a university has different academic schedules. A student shouldn't face such a significant difference in their opportunities just because their graduation date happens to fall a few months later.

I understand that new regulations need an effective date, and there will always be people on either side of that date. But when the financial consequences are this significant, a 60-day transition period doesn't seem sufficient, especially for students who have already spent years working toward their degrees.

Many international students made the decision to study in the U.S. years before this proposal existed. They've already invested substantial time, money, and effort based on the rules that were in place when they enrolled. It's not realistic to expect them to completely rethink their education and career plans within just 60 days.

I think DHS should seriously consider protecting students who are already enrolled, rather than applying such a major change to them based on a cutoff date they have very little control over. At the very least, students who started their degrees before this rule was introduced should be allowed to complete their studies and pursue OPT under the previous fee framework.

I'm not saying regulations can never change. I'm saying that students who made the same long-term commitments shouldn't face dramatically different consequences just because one graduates a couple of months later than another. That's exactly why a more reasonable transition policy is needed.
comments.reason: The commenter highlights unfair timing effects and negative financial consequences of the proposed policy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment on Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

Dear U.S. Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my serious concerns regarding the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

My educational journey reflects years of hard work, dedication, and a commitment to academic excellence. I completed my education from elementary school through high school in the Lake Washington School District in Washington State, consistently earning top grades. Through years of effort and determination, I earned admission to the University of Washington's prestigious Computer Science program.

I have worked hard to develop the knowledge and technical skills necessary to contribute meaningfully to the technology industry. Like many other students, I pursued my education with the goal of applying what I learned to solve real-world problems, build innovative products, and contribute to the American economy.

However, this proposed rule puts that future at risk.

A $70,000 fee associated with recommending a graduate for initial OPT could create an enormous financial barrier for employers and educational institutions. For a fresh graduate entering the workforce, this is an especially serious concern. Employers hiring recent graduates typically evaluate candidates based on their skills, potential, experience, and the value they can bring to a team. Adding such a substantial fee to the process could discourage companies from considering otherwise qualified graduates, particularly those seeking their first professional opportunity.

Even if I have the talent, education, and technical skills to succeed, I am concerned that this fee could make it significantly more difficult to secure an opportunity to use them. Many employers may simply choose candidates who do not involve this additional expense. Universities and other educational institutions may also be unable or unwilling to absorb such a high cost.

The consequences extend beyond an individual student's career. When students invest years in their education, develop specialized technical skills, and graduate from American universities, they should have a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate their abilities in the workforce. A fee of this magnitude risks making that opportunity depend less on merit and more on whether an employer can justify an extraordinary additional expense.

I understand that the Department seeks to prevent fraud, maintain the integrity of the immigration system, and protect American workers. These are important considerations. However, I respectfully ask the Department to consider whether imposing such substantial fees on legitimate students is a proportionate and effective way to achieve those objectives.

Measures designed to prevent fraud should distinguish between fraudulent activity and students who have followed the rules, worked hard academically, and genuinely intend to contribute their skills to the economy. A blanket fee of $70,000 could impose severe consequences on legitimate graduates without necessarily ensuring that the underlying problems are addressed more effectively.

I respectfully urge the Department to reconsider the proposed fee structure and evaluate less burdensome alternatives, such as targeted fraud-prevention measures, individualized enforcement against abuse, and fees proportionate to the actual costs of administering the program. If additional fees are deemed necessary, they should not be set at levels that effectively prevent qualified graduates from accessing legitimate employment opportunities.

My concern is deeply personal. I have spent years working toward an education and a future in computer science. I studied hard, earned strong grades, and gained admission to a respected university because I wanted to develop my abilities and put them to productive use. It is disheartening to think that, despite these efforts, an extraordinary financial barrier could prevent me from obtaining the professional experience necessary to begin my career.

I ask the Department to consider the real people behind this proposed rule: students who have invested their time, effort, and resources in their education and who want a fair opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Please ensure that efforts to protect the integrity of the immigration system do not inadvertently shut qualified graduates out of the workforce.

Thank you for considering my comments and for giving the public an opportunity to provide input on this proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,

A concerned student and future computer science professional
comments.reason: The commenter expresses serious concerns, stating the fee creates an enormous financial barrier.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Linh Zhang

I am an international graduate student currently studying at Columbia University, and I expect to graduate in 2027. I am particularly concerned about how this proposal would affect students who began their studies before these fees were announced.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by nomoreh1bs.com
comments.commentText:
We support this proposed rule and urge DHS to finalize it.
 
Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a regulatory program that allows foreign students to work in the United States after completing their studies, with the STEM extension allowing employment for up to three years. What began as practical training connected to a course of study has grown into a major foreign-worker pipeline. In 2024, according to DHS’s SEVIS by the Numbers report, 194,554 students participated in pre- and post-completion OPT, and 165,524 participated in STEM OPT.
 
Unlike the H-1B program, OPT has no annual cap, generally requires neither a labor condition application nor a prevailing wage, and does not require employers to seek American workers first. A program of this size, with direct consequences for the American labor market, demands meaningful oversight, transparent reporting, and accountability—particularly for its impact on American students and recent college graduates seeking entry-level employment.
 
OPT also gives employers a financial incentive to hire foreign graduates over Americans. F-1 students on OPT are often exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes, depending on their tax status and circumstances. Employers hiring eligible OPT workers avoid their share of those payroll taxes, an advantage they do not receive when hiring American graduates.
 
OPT also serves as a pathway to the H-1B program. Foreign students can complete their degrees, work through OPT and STEM OPT for up to three years, and then seek H-1B sponsorship. Universities benefit from international enrollment and can market post-graduation employment opportunities to prospective students, while American students face increased competition for university places and American graduates face increased competition for jobs.
 
The training issue is equally important. When employers claim that American graduates lack the experience or specialized skills needed for available positions, the appropriate response should be to invest in training American workers—not to create incentives to recruit foreign graduates on temporary visas instead. American graduates can be told they lack the qualifications for the jobs their education was intended to prepare them for, while employers have pathways to recruit foreign workers and provide them with practical experience. If Americans need more training, public policy should expand those opportunities for Americans rather than redirect them toward temporary foreign labor.
 
American universities, particularly public institutions receiving federal taxpayer support, have a responsibility to serve the students and communities that fund them. They should be preparing American graduates to enter the workforce, not helping create financial incentives for employers to choose foreign workers over equally qualified Americans. American taxpayers should not be required to subsidize a system that can make American workers more expensive to employ than foreign graduates competing for the same positions.
 
The proposed fees place a cost on institutions that benefit from OPT and recommend students for the program. Schools that profit from international enrollment and promote post-graduation work authorization should bear a share of the program’s costs and have an incentive to recommend OPT responsibly. DHS cites fraud and worker-protection concerns in support of the rule. These concerns warrant serious attention in a program of this size.
 
We therefore urge DHS to:
 
1. Finalize the proposed OPT fees.
2. Strengthen oversight of OPT and STEM OPT employers, including site visits and enforcement of STEM OPT training plan requirements.
3. Publish regular data on OPT and STEM OPT employment, including employers, job titles, wages, and the share of participants who later transition to H-1B status.
4. Evaluate the combined effect of OPT, STEM OPT, and H-1B on entry-level employment opportunities for American graduates.
 
The future of the American workforce depends on developing the skills, experience, and productive capacity of Americans entering the labor market. Pushing American graduates toward unemployment or underemployment while expanding the supply of foreign workers risks undermining that goal.
 
A student visa should be a student visa. Post-graduation work authorization should be limited, accountable, and paid for by the institutions that benefit from it, not subsidized at the expense of American workers. The purpose of workforce policy should be to give Americans a fair opportunity to learn, work, and build careers in their own country. Immigration programs should not undermine that objective by expanding foreign labor supply without adequate safeguards, transparency, or accountability to the American public.
 
We urge DHS to finalize this rule.
 
nomoreh1bs.com
comments.reason: The organization explicitly supports the proposed rule and urges DHS to finalize it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by K Brymer
comments.commentText:
Optional Practical Training is a central part of the U.S. value proposition for international students. The proposed increased OPT-related fee would create additional cost pressure, weaken student demand, and undermine the ability of U.S. institutions and employers to attract global talent.  This would undermine U.S. innovation and the strength of the U.S. economy.
OPT is essential to maintaining America’s standing as the leading destination for global talent. Evidence consistently shows that post-study work opportunity is a primary factor in where international students choose to study.
•	International students pay substantially higher average tuition than many domestic students and contribute meaningfully to local economies through housing, transportation, food, retail, and other spending.  Data source: https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an alum of a Washington, D.C. university, I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to levy a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorizations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent authorizations, such as STEM OPT extensions. While intending to protect American labor, this rule introduces severe unintended consequences that disrupt higher education, exclude brilliant minds based on wealth, and choke off a proven pipeline of economic growth. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal based on the following concerns:

1.	Prohibitive Costs Passed to Students
While universities must pay the fee upfront to complete the SEVIS recommendation, the framework allows institutions to pass this cost directly to students. A $70,000 or $30,000 fee is prohibitive for recent graduates navigating entry-level salaries or educational debt. Shifting this burden turns post-graduate training into an exclusive luxury for the ultra-wealthy, filtering talent by bank account size rather than merit.

2.	Failure to Recognize Contributions of Former F-1 Visa Holders
Foreign student work programs drive American business history. Research by Stuart Anderson (National Foundation for American Policy, June 2026) shows that roughly 25% of U.S. billion-dollar "unicorn" startups were founded by individuals who first arrived on F-1 visas. Anderson's research highlights no empirical evidence of economic harm to U.S. workers justifying such a barrier. When the U.S. allows talented international students to stay and work, they generate immense wealth. For example:
•	Elon Musk (SpaceX, Tesla): Arrived as an undergraduate transfer student, building enterprises employing tens of thousands of Americans.
•	Sergey Brin (Google): Co-founded Google as a Stanford graduate researcher, creating a backbone of global commerce.
•	Michelle Zatlyn (Cloudflare): Attributes Cloudflare's success to the 12 months of post-graduation OPT that allowed her to build its business plan.

3.	Lack of Justification and Faulty Accounting Mechanics
This astronomical fee increase is not logically tied to operational costs. While DHS claims the fee will enhance compliance and target fraud, the collected funds will not be retained by DHS to fund internal F-1 administration. Instead, they will be deposited directly into the general U.S. Treasury, bypassing agency operational budgets completely.

4.	Executive Overreach and Unlawful Taxation
Because the proposed fee routes revenue straight to the Treasury general fund rather than functioning as a cost-recovery mechanism, analyses—including research by economist Michael A. Clemens (IZA, September 2026)—characterize this fee as an outright tax on high-skilled immigration. Under the Constitution, the executive branch lacks authority to levy taxes; that power is reserved for Congress. This makes the rule highly vulnerable to immediate court challenges.

5.	Severe Demand Shock to the STEM Talent Pipeline
Econometric modeling by Michael A. Clemens projects that this penalty will trigger an immediate 33% to 80% collapse in OPT participation, threatening technological leadership. According to a September 2026 report by the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), immigrants make up nearly half of all U.S. recipients of prestigious STEM awards, and most first arrived as international students. Choking this pipeline starves domestic businesses of talent and damages U.S. GDP.

6.	Persistent Backlogs and Deficient USCIS Adjudication
The current immigration infrastructure is deeply backlogged, causing career delays and hiring disruptions. Historically, past fee increases have yielded no noticeable decrease in adjudication times. Charging an unprecedented premium for a delayed process is unjustifiable when the agency shows no correlation between higher fees and reduced backlogs.

7.	Unfair Transfer of Administrative Burdens to Universities
The rule forces higher education institutions to take on substantial administrative overhead to process and track these massive payments before a Designated School Official (DSO) can make a recommendation. This forces university staff to act as a clerical extension of federal agencies, draining operating budgets away from financial aid, research, and campus infrastructure.

8.	Degradation of the Core Academic Environment
A Washington, D.C. university education is uniquely enhanced by its focus on international relations and global business, which depends entirely on classrooms shaped by diverse geopolitical perspectives. Prohibitive fees will cause international enrollment to plummet, diluting the educational experience for domestic students and diminishing our nation's soft power.

Conclusion
This rule does not protect American workers; instead, it penalizes universities, starves businesses of talent, and degrades a major driver of the US economy.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the DHS proposed rule due to prohibitive costs and unintended consequences.

Divine Word College

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jacqueline  Griswold
comments.commentText: This comment is in relation to ICEB-2026-0100. I will comment on section V. A. where the amount of $70,000 is to be required for first-time applicants to OPT or $30,000 to returning applicants. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on the Proposed OPT Fees
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am writing as an international PhD student in German Studies to express my concern about the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations.

I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of immigration programs and protecting U.S. workers. However, I am concerned that fees of this magnitude could create significant barriers to the employment of qualified international graduates and impose substantial financial burdens on the educational institutions that support them.

Under the proposal, the educational institution recommending a student for OPT would be responsible for paying the fee. Nevertheless, these costs could influence institutional decisions about whether to recommend students for OPT and whether to support the associated expenses. Universities and other employers, particularly those with limited budgets, may find it financially difficult to hire qualified international graduates if doing so entails such substantial additional costs.

These concerns are especially relevant to humanities disciplines such as German Studies. German Studies encompasses language, literature, philosophy, history, translation, and cultural analysis. Scholars in this field contribute to foreign-language instruction, historical and literary research, cross-cultural understanding, and international academic collaboration. Their work helps American students develop language skills, engage with different intellectual traditions, and understand the historical and cultural contexts that shape our world.

International doctoral students contribute to these educational and research activities through teaching, scholarship, mentoring, and academic service. After graduation, their expertise can benefit universities, language programs, libraries, archives, museums, publishers, and cultural institutions. The proposed subsequent fee of $30,000 could create further difficulties for later OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions where applicable.

Consequently, the proposed fees could make it financially impractical for institutions to support qualified graduates, even when those graduates possess skills relevant to their educational and professional missions. Such an outcome could limit employment opportunities, reduce institutional hiring flexibility, and diminish the benefits of the investment that students and American universities have made in advanced education.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fees and provide a clear, evidence-based explanation of how the amounts relate to the rule’s stated objectives. The Department should evaluate the potential effects on university budgets, academic hiring, and employment opportunities across disciplines, and consider less burdensome alternatives that address program-integrity concerns without creating disproportionate barriers to legitimate practical training.

As an international PhD student in German Studies, I believe that the value of advanced education extends beyond immediate financial returns. Humanities scholarship contributes to language education, cultural understanding, historical knowledge, and the intellectual development of American students. Immigration policy should account for these contributions when assessing the consequences of proposed regulations.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed fees after carefully considering their potential effects on students, universities, employers, and the broader American higher-education system.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by David Slichter
comments.commentText:
I am an associate professor of economics at Binghamton University in Binghamton, NY. In that capacity, I advise a number of PhD students and undergraduates, many of whom have used their OPT after completing their studies. In my experience, OPT has provided great benefits to the students, and their employers have benefited from having highly capable workers.

At least in economics, US dominance in academia and in business activities requiring PhD economists seems heavily driven by the fact that the talent pool is better in the US. Making it more difficult for highly skilled workers to remain in the US straightforwardly damages the quality of American universities by constraining them to hire from a smaller pool (mathematically, the optimum in a larger set is better than or equal to the optimum in a subset), thereby harming American students. See Barbara Biasa and Song Ma's paper "Frontier Knowledge in Higher Education" for evidence that students benefit from the hiring of faculty with frontier disciplinary knowledge; Warnick, Light, and Kim's "Instructor Value-Added in Post-secondary Education" for evidence that faculty quality affects students' long-run outcomes; and references therein for additional evidence that students benefit from stronger faculty.

The justification for the rule claims that the fee would help to dissuade fraudulent OPT applications. But basic economic reasoning suggests a tax/fee should be placed on an undesired behavior, not on desired ones. The rational policy to achieve the stated goal is to impose fines on fraudulent applications but not on legitimate ones. While the government may not necessarily know which applications are fraudulent, it could surely devise a scheme in which greater fees are imposed when there is a greater risk of fraudulent applications. I struggle to envision a scenario in which this is the optimal policy unless the goal, contrary to the stated rationale, is simply to deter non-fraudulent applications.

David Slichter
Vestal, NY

Through internships at U.S. technology companies, I built models that improved a large production system and helped launch a new AI-powered product feature, work that directly benefited American businesses and their customers.
This is exactly the kind of talent pipeline OPT was designed to support. The United States has invested in my training through university fellowships and research funding. As a PhD student, I live on a modest stipend, and a $100,000 OPT fee would equal several years of my total income. For nearly every doctoral student, this fee would make OPT impossible, regardless of merit or the value of their work.
Other countries, including Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia, are actively recruiting researchers in artificial intelligence. If this fee had existed when I applied, I would have seriously considered pursuing my PhD elsewhere, and I believe many top international students will now make that choice. The result would be fewer skilled researchers in American labs, fewer publications and patents from American institutions, and less AI talent for American companies at a moment when leadership in this field matters enormously.
I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud and abuse in the OPT program. However, a flat fee of this size does not distinguish between fraud and legitimate contribution. It applies equally to everyone, including students whose work is clearly valuable to this country. Targeted employer verification, reporting requirements, and enforcement would protect program integrity without closing the door on qualified graduates.
I chose the United States, and I have worked hard to earn my place here. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

By attaching a prohibitive $70,000 price tag to this authorization—a cost that will inevitably burden already financially strained students, host institutions, or prospective employers—the rule effectively eliminates access to hands-on experience for all but the most affluent. Consequently, foreign graduates are stripped of the critical stepping stone needed to establish their careers in an increasingly competitive global job market. Furthermore, because the prospective return on investment for studying in the United States relies heavily on post-study work authorization, restricting OPT severely diminishes the appeal of American universities. Prospective international students will increasingly choose competing host countries like Canada, the UK, or Australia, which offer far more accessible pathways to early-career work experience. Ultimately, this excessive fee not only stifles individual career prospects but also deprives the U.S. economy and innovation sector of the top global talent trained right within its own universities.

Having an international student serves as a chance for American students to learn from them and collaborate whilst utilising each others differences to create startups, projects and even tackle global change.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Sarah Fernandes

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". Jaida Dones

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of San Diego
comments.commentText: I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish an initial fee of $70,000 and subsequent fees of $30,000 for F-1 nonimmigrant students engaging in Optional Practical Training (OPT). This proposal is unconscionable, disproportionate, and clearly designed not to regulate the program, but to intentionally price international students out of gaining practical experience in the United States. OPT is designed as a short-term, supplemental extension of an international student's academic degree, allowing them to gain temporary hands-on experience in their field of study. For most students, it lasts 6 to 12 months. Charging tens of thousands of dollars for a brief educational training period bears no logical relationship to the program's nature or scale. F-1 students and participating institutions already support the operational oversight of the immigration system through mandatory SEVIS fees and USCIS application processing fees (such as Form I-765 for Employment Authorization Documents). Adding a $70,000 burden on top of existing tuition and processing costs is an arbitrary penalty, transforming a temporary educational benefit into an insurmountable financial barrier for most students who are here to gain education and experience. Practical training offers invaluable global learning opportunities. Students bring innovative ideas to U.S. institutions and employers during their stay, and many take the high-level technical skills and knowledge gained back to their home countries, strengthening global economic and educational ties. By targeting OPT with exorbitant fees, the Department is actively diminishing the attractiveness of the U.S. higher education system and discouraging world-class talent from coming to American universities. Public agencies like DHS and ICE should be funded through congressional appropriations, not through exorbitant user fees extracted from students or educational institutions. Using international students as a revenue mechanism to fund broader departmental initiatives or offset enforcement budgets is inappropriate and misuses the administrative rulemaking process. This proposed rule is a targeted attempt to restrict international student participation under the guise of program integrity. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety and preserve OPT as an accessible, valuable educational training program.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees, calling them an insurmountable financial barrier.

Increasing this fee will make this opportunity beyond the reach of majority of students, because many universities like ours will never be able to afford to pay the proposed fee. Gaining practical experience is an essential part of any career training/education process. Not being able to get that experience will divert international students from applying to educational institutions in the US. Having international students is not just a matter of attracting a diverse student body to our programs, but for smaller tuition-driven institutions, it is also a matter of receiving tuition at higher rate that can offset our expenses for providing high-quality education to everybody, including domestic students. Our industries will also benefit from attracting international talent. And these are the best of the students who would eventually participate in the OPT training program. Low performing students will not be able to compete to find a job placement in highly competitive job environment.

International students and graduates are important to the American science, because they come from the backgrounds that offered a different approach to education. Their background knowledge and education that sometimes substantially differs from what they learn in American educational institutions then combines with American education that allows them to approach scientific tasks from a non-traditional standpoint. That alternative way of thinking is extremely important when addressing challenging scientific problems. We need to attract more students who a capable to think outside of the box. International students are very often the best examples of these thinkers. 

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Dr. Tikhon Bykov

Dear Secretary Mullin,

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Over the course of my career as a professor of chemical engineering, I have trained more than 30 PhD students, many of whom came to the United States as international students. Today, these highly trained scientists and engineers are contributing to the American economy at major companies such as Dow, Shell, Intel, and Merck, helping drive innovation, develop new technologies, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness.

These students came to the United States because of the exceptional educational and research opportunities our universities provide. We invest years in their education and training, only to now propose extraordinary financial barriers that could prevent them from applying their expertise here.

It is difficult to understand how this policy serves our national interests. At a time when the United States should be competing to attract and retain the world's best scientific and engineering talent, we are instead sending a message that their contributions are not welcome.

OPT is not simply a benefit to international students. It is an investment in America's scientific leadership, technological innovation, and economic future. These graduates create value for American companies, contribute to research and development, and help maintain our competitiveness in critical industries.

We should be doing everything possible to retain the talent we have spent years training, not creating financial barriers that encourage them to take their expertise, ideas, and innovations elsewhere. This proposal is shortsighted, counterproductive, and deeply frustrating to those of us who have dedicated our careers to educating the next generation of scientists and engineers. 

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Lisa Biswal
